News.title: Two rushed to hospital after being crushed by falling scaffolding that collapsed during Storm Boelo
News.content:
WIND CHAOS Two rushed to hospital after being crushed by falling scaffolding that collapsed during Storm Boelo







Next

TWO people have been hospitalised after being crushed by scaffolding swept over by Storm Boelo.

The pedestrians became trapped after winds knocked the structure down at around 1.30pm today.



The pedestrians were walking in Streatham High Road, south west London, when the incident unfolded.

People passing the scene managed to pull the pair out of the wreckage.



Pictures show firefighters at the scene of a crumbled metal and wooden structure along the high street.

The area was taped off as emergency services attended the incident and took the two away in ambulances.

It is understood their injuries are not serious.

A London Fire Brigade spokesperson said: “Firefighters are responding to an incident involving collapsed scaffolding on High Road, Streatham.



“Two people were trapped under the scaffolding and rescued before the Brigade arrived. Both people were taken to hospital by London Ambulance Service.

“The Brigade’s Control Officers received the first of five calls at 1331 and have mobilised crews from Tooting, Lewisham, West Norwood and surrounding fire stations to the scene.”

A London Ambulance Service spokesperson said: “We sent resources to the scene including ambulance crews, an incident response officer and paramedics from our hazardous area response team (HART) to the scene.

“We treated two patients at the scene and took both of them to a hospital.”

This comes as the country faces nation-wide chaos from Storm Boelo, leaving tens of thousands without power and flooding towns.



A 60-year-old man was tragically killed by a falling tree in Dumfries, Scotland, earlier this morning.

Met Office warnings are in place across the UK for high winds – with gusts of up to 84mph in parts of the country.

An amber alert for wind is in place until 9pm tonight.

Brits have been warned not to travel if possible, as severe disruption hits all modes of transport.

Trees have blocked roads and smashed into cars and homes from the gusts of up to 84mph today.



Tens of thousands have been left without power, with the Energy Networks Association reporting that 83,000 homes have been cut off.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It said: “The networks have been focussed on reconnecting customers this morning, though the continuing severe weather in some regions is limiting network engineers’ opportunities to safely start the work of restoring customers’ power today and access to certain areas remains difficult.”

The Met Office added: “Injuries and danger to life are likely from large waves and beach material being thrown onto coastal roads, sea fronts and properties.”

News.title: At least 41 injured with 20 in serious condition after bus crashes into car and plunges 65ft down slope in Barcelona
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

CRASH HORROR At least 41 injured with 20 in serious condition after bus crashes into car and plunges 65ft down slope in Barcelona







Next

AT least 41 people have been injured with 20 in a serious condition after a bus crashed into a car in Barcelona.

The passenger bus veered off the road after the collision and plunged 65ft down a steep slope sparking an emergency rescue operation.

The terrifying ordeal unfolded on the BV-5144 road in Fogars de Montclús in the Barcelona province.

Authorities say 20 of the 41 wounded passengers are in serious condition.





A major emergency response team including firefighters, 15 ambulances and two helicopters rushed to the scene to help injured passengers.

Reports say some of the wounded people were able to walk back up to the road without support.

Local authorities said the bus plunged 65ft down a slope moments after the initial impact.

The President of the Generalitat of Catalonia, Salvador Illa, said he was monitoring the situation “with great concern”.



He said he remains in contact with local authorities to stay informed of the case.

Illa said: “All my support to the people affected and my gratitude to the emergency services for their work.”

Authorities were first alerted to the crash at 4.23pm local time.

The road has been closed in both directions as the recovery operation continues.



It is currently unclear what caused the two vehicles to crash into each other.

It comes after nearly 50 people were injured in a horror bus crash in Spain this summer.

A coach carrying 55 passengers smashed into a council office on Rambla Ferran in Lleida.

The city’s mayor Fèlix Larrosa said: “This is the most serious accident that has occurred in the city of Lleida”.

The bus was travelling through the city centre from Lleida to the historic village of la Granja d’Escarp when it suddenly veered off course.

News.title: ‘Experienced’ zookeeper in coma with head & neck injuries after being mauled by leopard as park reveals predator’s fate
News.content:
Next

AN experienced zookeeper remains in a coma with a “very slim” chance of recovery after a leopard attack left her with critical head and neck injuries.

The worker, a woman in her 50s, underwent a successful operation after the attack but is still fighting for her life and being kept sedated.



She was working in the enclosure of two male Persian leopards when she was mauled at Safaripark Beekse Bergen in Hilvarenbeek, The Netherlands on Saturday morning.

The zookeeper, who has worked at the park since she was 17, was found inside the big cat enclosure with severe head wounds.



Horrified colleagues said they heard her crying for help over a walkie-talkie.

The leopard who launched itself at the zookeeper will not be put down, park staff said.



Head of Animal Care at the zoo Martin van Hees revealed: “We are not going to do anything with the leopard.

“It just sat in its enclosure and did what it did. The animal cannot help it.”

A spokesperson told ANP that the animal had behaved naturally, saying leopards “are and remain predators”.



Despite sustaining serious injuries after the mauling, the woman was still conscious as she was helicoptered to hospital.

She was immediately operated on, with a park spokesperson saying the procedure went well, but that her condition remained “concerning”.

The woman survived the night, but her chances of recovery are very slim, according to the park’s statement.

It continued: “We are naturally deeply saddened by this news and are doing everything we can to support her family, colleagues, and other loved ones as much as possible and to provide additional guidance where necessary.”



The woman was described as “a very experienced caretaker” by park officials, who said she had worked at the zoo for 25 years.

A spokesperson said that she had worked in the predator section of the zoo for the last eight years.

The zoo said work is organised so that keepers are never penned into the same enclosure as the leopards.

Zoologist Van Hees said: “In principle, the enclosures are separated for humans and animals.

“In this case, however, something went differently than it should have.



“She entered the enclosure while the leopards could also get there, and as a result, she was caught.

“Her immediate colleague heard the cry for help and rushed to her aid.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A park spokesperson added: “Something went wrong there, but we don’t know what yet. There are no cameras in the enclosure and she was working alone.”

A probe has been launched to investigate the full circumstances of the attack.

News.title: Power cut at major UK airport sees hundreds of passengers stuck in ‘two-hour security queues’ & baggage systems affected
News.content:
Next

A POWER cut at a major UK airport has seen hundreds of passengers stranded and left queuing for hours.

Travellers are facing chaos at Stansted Airport after a power surge wreaked havoc on the travel hub’s security and baggage systems.



Furious passengers took to social media with images showing hundreds of people stranded in departures and queuing on escalators at passport control.

One posted there had been a “total systemic collapse”, reporting problems with luggage belts and getting through security.



“No guarantee I will see my luggage again today or even make my flight (in two hours). Staff explaining nothing at all,” they said.

Another user posted a video showing a sea of frustrated travellers queuing at security with the airport’s alarms blaring in the background.



A third reported Stansted was “rammed” saying they heard it was “taking two hours to get through security”.

Others blasted the situation as a “mess” and an “absolute shambles”.

A spokesperson for Stansted Airport said: “Due to an earlier power surge that has affected the airport and local area, a number of airport systems were temporarily impacted.

“All systems are now back in service with operational teams working hard to provide support to passengers on their journeys through the airport.



“We thank passengers for their patience and apologise for any disruption and inconvenience they may have experienced while services were being restored.”

It comes after Storm Boelo caused chaos on Britain’s railway lines this weekend, including cancellations to dozens of Stansted Express services.

London Stansted handles around 85,000 passengers a day and nearly 30million passengers annually.

News.title: Man ‘stabbed in face and back’ during horror broad daylight attack at Tube station – as cops arrest suspect in his 40s
News.content:
TUBE HORROR Man ‘stabbed in face and back’ during horror broad daylight attack at Tube station – as cops arrest suspect in his 40s







Next

A MAN has been stabbed in a horror broad daylight attack at a tube station – as cops arrest a suspect in his 40s.

Cops were scrambled to Brixton Underground station in South London at 3.49pm on Saturday to reports of a stabbing.

There, officers from British Transport Police and the Metropolitan Police found a man suffering injuries, including to his face and back.

He was raced to hospital but his injuries are not thought to be life-threatening or life-changing.





A man in his 40s has now been arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm with intent.

British Transport Police said they are not looking for anyone else in connection to the shocking incident.

Anyone with information has been urged to get in touch with the force quoting reference 499 of October 24.

News.title: Nepo babies really ARE taking over our screens…the shock stats laid bare – is it the end of the working class hero?
News.content:
FAMILY AFFAIR Nepo babies really ARE taking over our screens…the shock stats laid bare – is it the end of the working class hero?







Next

IT’S like celebrity deja vu as the kids of famous actors take over Hollywood.

No, you’re not imagining that so-called ‘nepo babies’ are taking over our screens as figures reveal a quarter of top movies feature at least one actor with family in showbiz.



But does the success of actors like Lily-Rose Depp, Lily Sheen, Dakota Johnson and Mia Threapleton, daughter of Kate Winslet, come at the expense of working-class kids who already face an uphill battle to make it big?

Statistics also show that 32 percent of high-profile actors enjoyed a private education while the same number attended special arts schools which cost as much as £18,000 a year.



The latest nepo baby to join the ranks is Aran Murphy, the 19-year-old son of Oscar-winning Peaky Blinders and Oppenheimer star Cillian Murphy.

Aran is making his face known as the son of a battling couple in the Sky Atlantic divorce drama War, was picked by Sharon Horgan to star in her comedy-drama Youth and is about to appear in the movie adaptation of Klara And The Sun, which hits cinemas on Friday.

It was revealed this week that Scots actor Ewan McGregor’s daughter Esther has also hit the big time after being cast in the lead role in Rebecca Yarros’ bestselling fantasy romance, Fourth Wing, on Prime Video.

While it looks like Aran and Esther, 24, inherited their parents’ acting chops, there’s no doubt that having a famous parent gets you noticed.

“It’s as much who you know as what you know,” British actor Dickon Thompson told The Sun “Unless you win the lottery and can afford acting lessons or are picked from obscurity, success comes hard in this industry. It’s very, very tough.”

Dickon runs the Anna Scher Theatre in Islington, London, one of the first drama schools geared towards working-class and disadvantaged kids.



It counts Kathy Burke, Pauline Quirke and Patsy Palmer among its alumni but statistics show that BAFTA-nominated actors are five times more likely to have attended a private school.

According to social mobility charity, The Sutton Trust, 32percent of leading actors went to an independent school and almost one in three attended an arts school.

Just under 70 percent went to university while one-in-three went to a school for the arts, which can cost up to £18,000 a year. Nine percent attended Oxbridge.



Many argue nepo babies are simply following in their family footsteps getting into acting.

But industry analyses show that around one in four young actors come from entertainment families. That compares with seven percent of British kids who end up in the same (usually normal) job as their parents, shows research by Ancestry.co.uk.

British film industry analyst Stephen Follows found that 70 percent of the highest-grossing movies between 2020 and 2025 featured actors, writers and directors with family links to the industry.

Dickon said: “If you want to become an actor you need time and you need a financial safety net and no working class family can keep that up for very long.

“We run sessions for just £9 but it’s still a challenge for some people. With the cost-of-living squeeze on finances, drama classes are the first thing to go.



“Acting seemed to really open up to working class people in the 1970s and 80s but before that it was very much a middle class profession and it’s gone back to being that again.

“As a career, everything is stacked against the poorer echelons of society.”

Some of the most well-known faces in Hollywood are kids whose parents have already had their time in the limelight.

Lily-Rose Depp, daughter of Johnny Depp and Vanessa Paradis, got her break with a minor role in comedy-horror movie Tusk in 2014 while modelling and was a leading lady just two years later playing Isadora Duncan in The Dancer,



Dakota Johnson, 37, whose parents are Don Johnson and Melanie Griffiths, has enjoyed huge success thanks to the Fifty Shades film trilogy while British-born Lily Sheen, daughter of Kate Beckinsale and Michael Sheen, won recognition with her role as Addy Cage in 2022 film, The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent.

Mia Threapleton, 26, took the name of her film director dad Jim in the hope of building a career away from famous mum Kate Winslet but the pair starred alongside each other in Channel 4 drama, I Am Ruth.



Titanic star Kate has previously said she finds the term nepo baby “silly” and insisted her kids are building their own future without a “leg up” from her, yet she made her directorial debut with the movie, Goodbye June – written by her 21-year-old son Joe.

Joe also starred opposite his mum in the 2023 film Lee, about photographer Lee Miller and appeared in the World War I film 1917, directed by his father and Winslet’s ex Sam Mendes.

Other lucky offspring include Maya Hawke, daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman, who played Robin Buckley in Stranger Things, Jack Quaid, son of Dennis Quaid and Meg Ryan, known for The Boys and Oppenheimer, and Euphoria actress Maude Apatow, whose parents are actress Leslie Mann and filmmaker Judd Apatow.

Out of the main cast of 12 comedians on the new SNL UK show, seven were privately educated.

While only a handful of actors only make it to the very top of their game, and even fewer to Los Angeles, Alison Rashley, who runs Nottingham’s acclaimed Television Workshop project, says working class and northern kids might never even get a shot.



The workshop, which has produced the likes of world-class actress Samantha Morton, Line of Duty star Vickly McClure and Game of Thrones’ Bella Ramsey, gives ordinary kids an opportunity of stardom.

Alison says while the arts has made headway in representing black, LGBTQ and ethnic minorities, lower income children are still left behind.

She said: “We know we have to do so much better in other aspects, but somehow it’s okay to overlook the working class?

“The industry has never levelled up the playing field. These figures have been like this for years.

“I look to cast kids every day in my job and the words I hate most in the English language are ‘must be London-based’.



“Parents don’t happen to have a little pierre de terre tucked away in the capital. While that phrase is in use, we are shutting the door to these children.

“I think production company budgets should allow kids to travel and stay in London and drama schools need to be far more affordable. There’s a lot of money in the industry and we should be using it to help this talent.

“I’m fine with nepo babies if they are talented enough. We’d all want to help our kids if we can, but let’s make room for everybody and have the same rules for everyone.



“If you’re not prevented from becoming an actor because you have a famous mum or dad, then it shouldn’t stop you because you don’t have funds for an audition or to become a member of Spotlight (the casting platform).”

Mega-star Owen Cooper became a household name after playing Jamie Miller in last year’s Netflix psychological drama, Adolescence.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Show creator Stephen Graham wanted to hand the role to an ordinary kid and found the 16-year-old taking classes at his local drama school.

Owen, of Warrington, Cheshire, whose mum Noreen works as a carer and dad Andy is an IT support analyst, went on to win an Emmy, Bafta and Golden Globe – proof that working class kids have what it takes.

News.title: We live in UK’s shoplifting capital where ‘desperate’ drug addicts raid shelves & bike thugs run riot – cops don’t care
News.content:
Next

THE BRAZEN shoplifter opens up her Lidl bag for life and frantically swipes bottles of fabric conditioner and detergent from the shelves of her local convenience store.

Looking at the CCTV footage, you could be forgiven for thinking this woman is in an episode of ITV’s Supermarket Sweep.



But sadly, this thief is just one of hundreds in Hartlepool contributing to a crime epidemic which has resulted in the town being crowned among the worst in the country for shoplifting.

Locals in the area, 18 miles from Durham city, say “desperate” drug addicts and mothers hit hard by the cost of living crisis resort to stealing to feed their children, their habit or to merely survive.



Meanwhile, shopkeepers have to pay the price of having their stock swiped on a daily basis.

Shan Sharma, who runs the King Oswy Drive Post Office in the town, has shared videos with the Sun Online of thieves stealing products from his shelves.



The woman who takes the fabric conditioner is rumbled and has to empty her bag for life before she is allowed to leave the shop.

But too many thieves escape with products Shan never sees again.



However, the 41-year-old does have a clever ploy to deter shoplifters from his post office and convenience store.

Claiming he can’t rely on the police to stop the criminality, he posts pictures and videos on Facebook of thieves swiping goods and only takes them down once the culprit has apologised and paid him what’s owed.

Shan said: “It’s a really bad situation.

“I have had this shop for five years, and worked in the retail industry for 15.

“I can tell when someone is about to steal, just by looking at them, but sometimes it’s hard to stop.



“When they come in groups, it’s difficult.

“The shoplifting happens three or four times a week.

“If I am here, it’s controlled, but I can’t be here all the time.

“I know from a person’s face, whether or not they are going to steal.

“I’ll approach them and say, ‘Can I help you?’ I get them out of the shop.



“If they’ve stolen before, I tell them to leave straight away.

“There’s a local Facebook group I post on. If someone steals, I will upload their image and a video.

“If they see it, they will come in.



“They say sorry, and pay for what they have taken.

“I’ll remove the pictures if they do that.”

He added: “Alcohol is the most popular thing to steal, or crates of soft drinks like Coca Cola.

“If there’s a big shoplifting incident I will report it to the police, but it works quite well posting the images on Facebook.

“We lose a lot of money.



“On one occasion a man came in and stole four bottles of vodka, worth £30 each.

“I reported that, but the police did not do anything.

“They don’t care.

“That’s why this is happening.

“We lose hundreds of pounds a month to shoplifting.



“I’m used to it now.”

Shan points to a picture he’s stuck on the wall behind his counter of a shoplifter who he says has been stealing for ten years.

He added: “The poster is there to remind people what she looks like, so they can tell her to leave if she comes in.



“She actually wants to go to prison as she has nowhere to live.

“Once these people get out of prison, they don’t know what to do.

“Prison isn’t the answer.

“Shoplifters need to be forced to pay for what they have stolen, through fines, or cuts to their benefits.

“The supermarkets are better able to absorb the cost of shoplifting, but for small businesses like ours, it’s very tough.”



According to Police Data statistics which have been analysed by the BBC, Hartlepool is the second worst area in the whole of England, Wales and Northern Ireland for shoplifting.

For every 1000 residents of the town, there are 25 shoplifting offences, compared to the average of eight.

The town is the worst in the North for the crime, and is only surpassed by Westminster, in London, where there are 40 incidents per 1000 people.

And the problem is getting worse, not better.

Cleveland Police say 9,568 shoplifting offences were reported to them across their force area from 2025 to 2026 – a 15 percent increase when compared to the previous year.



In the streets surrounding Shan’s shop to the north of the town youths tear around on e-bikes wearing full face coverings and at times, the smell of cannabis is overwhelming.

Hartlepool began to boom in the Victorian era, when coal from the pits in County Durham was exported from its docks in huge quantities.

At the same time, timber was imported, with much of it travelling to the coalfields for use in maintenance.

This led to the development of shipbuilding, marine engineering and employment on the railways, which transported coal from the pits to the docks.

It was a time of prosperity for the town, but when the interconnected industries began to decline in the 20th century, the economy was never able to recover.



The residents of Hartlepool now struggle with unemployment, poor health and high rates of obesity and smoking.

Healthy life expectancy in the town is just 52-years-old for men, compared with an average of 61 across England.

Meanwhile, women can expect to live a healthy life until they are only 51 – ten years younger than the rest of the country.



Saqib Khan, 28, runs Tech & Games in the town centre, which is awash with charity shops and bargain stores.

He said: “Shoplifters will walk in and ask to see a phone, then grab it off you and run away.

“Or, they will go and take things from the display, like laptops.

“We are losing a lot of money to shoplifting.

“We call the police, and they say, we can’t do anything, but they give us a reference number.



“Nothing ever comes of it.

“The police should be doing more but I think it’s difficult for them to prioritise shoplifting.

“Hartlepool is a good town, but every town has bad people and good people.

“Shoplifting is bad in a lot of towns.

“I think the reason Hartlepool has a problem is due to a lack of education and also drugs.



“People are stealing out of desperation, they don’t have any money to buy what they need.”

Brothers Adam and Keenan Day both have jobs in shops in Hartlepool.

Keenan, 23, who works in Morrisons, said: “I witness shoplifting every single shift.

“Sometimes multiple times per shift.



“You’d expect people to steal things like alcohol, but they actually take chicken, and items that can be resold.

“When I see it I don’t do anything.

“I don’t put a hand on them.

“We’re told to do nothing.



“The security guards will do their job.

“With teenagers, they just tell them to get out.

“If it’s an adult the police will be called.

“I’m not shocked that Hartlepool is the worst.

“It’s only to be expected.



“People know they can get away with it.

“It’s easy to do.

“One person will do it, they tell other people how easy it is, and it spreads.

“All ages do it.

“There was a 60-year-old last week.



“He dressed as a DPD delivery driver as a disguise and he filled his delivery bag.

“I don’t think there’s much the police can do.”

Adam, who works in a shop selling hardware which can’t be stolen, added: “You see kids putting packets of sweets into their pockets.

“The other week, I was in a Sainsbury’s Local, I saw someone just pick up what they wanted and walk away.

“There’s not much you can do about it.



“I think it’s worse now than it was years ago, and part of it is the cost of living.

“There’s a lack of respect.

“I don’t think the police are at fault.

“I am not sure how many officers they have.

“I heard that they had to go and help in Middlesbrough, after the A66 crash, so they will be even more thin on the ground than they usually are.”



Claire Gill, a 42-year-old pharmaceutical worker, said: “It’s really sad.

“People are poverty stricken, people haven’t got enough money.

“They do what they can, to get what they can, and that means resorting to crime.

“I don’t advocate for it, but thieves see themselves stealing form corporations as opposed to individuals so there’s no personal aspect to it.

“But people round here will take what they can, from where they can get it.



“I think the authorities should be doing more to protect the shop workers.

“The shop workers feel like they have a need to intervene and that can result in violence.

“If people are desperate they will do what they can to get food to eat, or money for drugs.”

One young man, who didn’t want to be named, told us: “It doesn’t surprise me because the council tax rates are so high.

“People are struggling.



“You see it every day.

“What do we pay council tax for?

“We’ve got potholes everywhere, the cost of water is high. It’s ridiculous.

“I can understand why people are shoplifting.

“What’s the point in going to work?



“You can just steal and you’re not going to get arrested.

“Crime is never a good option, but sometimes it’s the only option round here.

“I’m more privileged than most, and I have never had to resort to crime for an income but I have loads of friends who do it.

“I have family who do it.

“Sometimes, they are stealing food so they can eat.



“I have seen first hand women stealing formula for their kids.

“They are not just stealing things to sell, like they would have ten years ago.

“People are stealing to survive.

“But are they just lazy, and don’t want to get a job? I don’t know.

“I am from round here. I work, I don’t steal.”



A worker at a mobility scooter shop, who didn’t want to named, told us thieves even attempt to steal the mobility scooters parked outside.

She said: “Shoplifting is absolutely rife here.

“People try and steal the mobility scooters we have chained up outside. It’s disgusting.

“A lot of it is drugs.

“Recently, a guy was so drugged up he walked straight into our window and smacked his head on the glass.”



A shopkeeper at another convenience store on the high street, who also didn’t want to be named, added: “Shoplifting happens every day.

“They steal anything they can get their hands on.

“We’re losing a lot of money because of it.

“Kids, older people, it’s everybody.

“The police don’t do anything.



“The shoplifters are getting away with it.

“The police should be doing more to help.”

Acting Superintendent Jamie Bell, who is the lead for retail crime at Cleveland Police, said: “Cleveland Police is committed to tackling retail crime as we recognise the significant impact on local businesses.

“We are aware of the challenges around retail crime, which are also being reflected nationally, and we’re working hard, alongside retailers, to tackle these issues.

“Despite the challenges, in Cleveland our solved rate for shoplifting remains with 31.2% over the last 12 months which is higher than national average.



“We are able to charge individuals without interview where there is overwhelming evidence which helps streamline the process and delivers effective justice.

“We continue to use all the tools at our disposal and, where possible, we ask the court to impose Criminal Behaviour Orders (CBOs) on offenders which can ban them from entering stores or locations as well as other stringent conditions.

“If a CBO is breached, then the offender can receive a custodial sentence.

“As well as continuing to take action against offenders, we have a number of problem-solving plans where we work with retailers and other community safety partners to address concerns around specific stores or locations where there are high reports of shoplifting.

“This allows us to take a collaborative, preventative approach to tackle the issue and deter further criminality.



“We have recently implemented a new process that allows retailers to use technology to report crime and provide evidence to us online.

“This provides a more efficient service to retailers and allows us to more effectively gather evidence so that our Neighbourhood Policing Team can focus on arresting shoplifting suspects who are causing the most harm in our communities.

“We regularly engage with our retailers and communities to ensure we listen to their concerns and have dedicated PCSOs in each district to help build a wider picture of what is happening in our communities.

“We would always encourage people to come forward and report incidents to us so we can take action.”

A Hartlepool Borough Council spokesperson added: “Shoplifting is a challenge to many retail environments across the country.



“It is a criminal matter and therefore a matter for the Police.

“We are committed to supporting, and working in partnership with, the Police and Tees Valley Combined Authority, in their efforts to improve safety, including tackling shoplifting.

“Hartlepool is expected to secure £1.3m through the Tees Valley Investment Zone, subject to final approval, to deliver a dedicated Town Centre Crime and Safety Project from October 2026 to March 2029, developed in partnership with businesses, community organisations and the Police.

“The project will include four dedicated enforcement officers, additional CCTV monitoring and an expanded Apex Radio Scheme – which will link shop managers via radio to the town’s CCTV monitoring centre and the Police – to help tackle crime and anti-social behaviour and improve safety for businesses, residents and visitors with activity focused on the town centre in Hartlepool.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“A dedicated role of Town Centre Manager will be created, to develop a Town Centre Business Network to strengthen support for retailers and businesses, helping to improve confidence and create a safer, more vibrant town centre in Hartlepool.



“Alongside enforcement, the programme will invest in prevention, youth outreach, community initiatives and environmental improvements, with the aim of reducing crime and anti-social behaviour while improving public perceptions of safety within Hartlepool.”

News.title: Inside the lives of Dubai’s fraudsters and money launderers as two Brit crooks get travel ban over-turned and vanish
News.content:
MONEY TALKS Inside the lives of Dubai’s fraudsters and money launderers as two Brit crooks get travel ban over-turned and vanish







Next

IT’S the go-to destination for influencers and wannabe reality stars flaunting their gym honed bodies.

But amid the glitz and glamour of the buzzing holiday destination, criminal kingpins from across the globe are blending in while hiding their ill-gained cash.



Experts reckon that Dubai is still one of the easiest places in the world to spend questionablly acquiredmoney by buying property or changing it into gold that can legitimately be taken back home.

And The Sun can reveal that the UAE state will allow two multi-million pound fraudsters with links to Russia to vanish – despite a UK high court order being backed up by a lifelong travel ban from the state to force them to pay back their victims.



Father-son duo Muhammad Tahir Lakhani and Muhammad Ali Lakhani owe $45million to British companies after failing to repay loans for their ship recycling company.

The pair jetted out of the UK following the ruling in 2024, and have holed up in the glamorous Arab state ever since.

UAE authorities then banned them leaving the country while they paid off the money owed back in the UK, but more than two years on the Brit companies have not seen a penny.

Astoundingly the family have used local courts to overturn the travel ban claiming they can’t pay their debts while stuck in the state, and have a chance to flee to another country that won’t force them to pay.



Speaking exclusively to The Sun a source close to the case said the Lakahnis’ claim that they couldn’t manage their debts while subject to a travel ban was “nonsense”.

He said the father and son had settled a previous debt imposed by the High Court in 2020, while in Dubai and subject to the ban.

He said: “It’s just hoodwinking people, this is an example of fraudsters using local courts to play this game and if this is happening in the UAE it could happen anywhere.

“When the travel ban was in place it didn’t prevent them from agreeing a settlement on the first judgement. The fear is they can now escape the UAE, and where they go next, who knows.”

Court documents published in Arabic and seen by The Sun show the two men applied to the Dubai Court of First Instance so they could leave the country and the ban was eventually lifted by a judge on August 26.



In 2020 during an earlier court case Tahir, his son Ali and his other son Hassan were found to owe YieldStreet a whopping $76.7m. The High Court judgement also saw a global order to freeze all their assets extended.

Yieldstreet accused the family of selling 13 ships for scrap in Pakistan and Bangladesh without notifying the lender or properly applying the proceeds to the mortgages, effectively concealing the sales and pocketing the cash.

The High Court ruled for Yieldstreet and while in Dubai over the last few years the Lakhanis settled the case by agreeing to pay back just $5m of the $76.6m.

Tahir Lakhani, 64, who states on his Linkedin page that he is the MD and Chairman of Dubai Trading Agency, as well as being a tennis player who once competed in the Davis Cup and at junior Wimbledon, described the misery settlement as “amicable”.

The source added: “We need Gulf money in the UK, it’s probably a good thing that we trade more with the UAE but what about the risk that comes with it. People in the UAE can use their local courts and if the UAE let the Lakhanis leave, it can happen again. The UAE authorities need to co-operate with the UK.”



The Sun has tried to contact Muhammad Tahir Lakhani and Muhammad Ali Lakhani for comment.

In September 2022, the UAE government circulated a memo to Dubai Courts stating that UK judgments may be enforced.

This followed the UK Court’s enforcement of a Dubai judgment in the £48m Lenkov Energy v Puri case.

Professor Michael Levi, a criminologist at Cardiff University said: “People will always try to find a place where they can live off the proceeds of crime.

“Living in Dubai is expensive, but you can live there in comfort and continue doing your deals.



“For the UAE, it might place less pressure on them to let this pair go, or it could be that the father and son didn’t find the country as relaxed as they thought it would be so they wanted to move on.

“The big question here is, that while they might be free to go, is their money. It’s subject to a worldwide freeze order, which means the financial institution that has it shouldn’t let it leave the country too.



“It could be that their cash is sitting in nice air-conditioning in Dubai while they’re away somewhere else. But we don’t know where the money is.”

The duo are far from the only crooks heading out to Dubai in a bid to get away with their crimes.

And it’s become a popular hotpost for money launders, despite more being caught out than before.

Branislav Hock, Professor of Economic Criminology at the University of Portsmouth, said: “Dubai is one of the biggest trading hubs in the world, for goods, for gold and for property, and when that much money moves through one place, some of it is going to be dirty.



“One of the oldest tricks is laundering through trade. You ship goods, put a false value on the invoice, and the difference is dirty money crossing borders as if it were normal business. Property is the other big one. If you buy an expensive flat through a company, it can be very hard to see who really owns it.

“As for why criminals look abroad, I think it is a mix of things. The money is welcomed with fewer questions, the lifestyle is good, and for a long time Dubai felt like a place where you would not be sent back to face trial.

“But to be fair, a lot of this is not only a Dubai problem. Free zones carry similar risks wherever they are, and that includes the freeports in the UK. And plenty of dirty money still goes through London property and UK companies.”

A free zone is a territory where goods can be stored, manufactured, handled and re-exported with eliminated or reduced customs duties as well as simplified administrative procedures and less tax.

Earlier this month the National Crime Agency saw guilty verdicts for a gang that is understood to have smuggled £30million in cash to the Arab state to be laundered.



The gang would pack thousands of pounds into their clothes and suitcases to smuggle to Dubai without declaring it as they’re legally meant to.

They flew from Manchester, Birmingham and Brussels airports on Dubai-bound Emirates flights between December 2017 and November 2019.

They were snared when officials seized £788,455 in cash at UK airports and the investigation began. The ringleader is currently unnamed and is awaiting extradition to the UK.



He used a WhatsApp group to instruct his mules when to bring the cash through.

Mum Heather Jeffrey, 58, and her children Sheldan Noel, 30, and Laura Noel, 34, all from Bradford, smuggled out £12.9million between them over ten trips each.

NCA branch commander Jon Hughes said: “This crime group smuggled enormous quantities of cash, to remove it from the attention of law enforcement.

“Illicit cash is the lifeblood of organised crime groups, fuelling violence and insecurity around the world.

“This is why disrupting its supply is a priority for the NCA and our partners, hitting crime groups in the pocket where it hurts the most.”



Less savvy crooks have been caught traipsing through airports with bags stuffed full of gold bars.

In February, GMP seized five gold bars worth £1.8million from a man attempting to take them to the Middle East from Manchester Airport.

The mule had 15kg of the metal in his hand luggage – raising suspicions and leading to him being stopped.



Legitimate bullion being moved in and out of the UK, documents verifying acquisition and legitimacy of the gold are presented, and anything over £10,000 has to be declared to customs with the appropriate certifications.

The man smuggling the gold didn’t have any documents to confirm the gold was legal and legitimate, leading a judge to rule the haul was likely proceeds of crime and that police could seize it.

Detective Inspector Sarah Langley, from the Economic Crime Unit, said: “This case reflects our unwavering commitment to tackling all forms of money laundering — whether it involves cash, gold, or any other high value assets used to hide criminal profits.

“Criminals continuously adapt their methods, and so must we. By targeting the movement of illicit wealth at every stage, we are dismantling the financial networks that allow organised crime to thrive.”

More and more crooks are turning to putting their ill-gotten profits into gold.



In November last year the force seized seven gold bars from a car leaving Manchester Airport – with an estimated total value of £700,000.

Across the country in West Yorkshire, a gang of four was sentenced for one of the biggest

A high ranking police source told The Sun: “It’s pretty unusual and idiocy for criminals to take gold bars to Dubai to be melted down as they’re highly likely to get caught. It’s not something that can be easily hidden in a suitcase



“We are aware that UK criminals living in Dubai are using gold as currency and for laundering purposes.

“It’s easy to buy gold out there and bring it back to the UK in your case.”

Those lucky enough to get the bars out of the UK without being caught by police or border force won’t struggle to off-load it once in the Middle East.

In Dubai’s gold souk, known for having more rules around buying, selling and trading the precious metal, vendors have admitted to not doing checks.

The industry is made up of a complex web of physical gold traders, who operate from a number of hubs throughout the city, gold refineries where the precious metal can be melted down and moulded, vaults where gold bullion is stored and online trading platforms, where gold worth billions changes hands at the press of a button.



But Dubai is becoming more perilous for high profile crooks to launder their money after they were put on the Financial Action Task Force grey list.

The list places countries believed to have poor money laundering practices under increased scrutiny.

Professor Hock, author of Trade-Based Money Laundering: Compliance and the Law, said: “Dubai has changed. The UAE came off the international grey list in 2024, it sends back more wanted people than it used to, and the authorities in Dubai have recently broken up some big laundering networks, including one running between the UK and Dubai.

“What I would watch now is whether they go after the professionals who make it all possible, like lawyers, estate agents and the firms that set up companies, and not only the smaller players.”

An HMRC spokesperson said: “We play a critical role in the UK’s response to money laundering. We work with partners in the UK and overseas to identify, investigate and disrupt criminal activity and convict those who profit from money laundering and other organised crime.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“This is an international threat and we work closely with international partners, including the UAE, to share intelligence and target those seeking to move and conceal the proceeds of crime.”

A government spokesperson told The Sun they don’t comment on individual cases.

News.title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
News.content:
The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.

Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said a new relationship with Brussels could include full EU membership or joining the single market, requiring free movement.

Asked about Burnham's remarks, Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg "you can't take anything off the table", adding the prime minister was saying "we've got to be pragmatic to get the best deal for Britain and he wants to have the conversation."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch responded that the prime minister "hasn't thought this through", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick dismissed the idea as "mad".

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

He has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, would is due by 2029.

"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the Sunday Times, external, adding he believed the type of migration had changed from revolving door movement of young people.

"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said. "The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

But he stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.

His remarks were made ahead of an EU summit on 20 November in Brussels, where the prime minister is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.

On Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Rayner said she wanted to see the best possible deal with the European Union, which may well involve concessions.

"What the prime minister is saying now, and what I want, is that we have an honest conversation about the facts of what the trade-offs are to get the best deal for Britain going forward," she said.

"The frustration for me in the previous debate we had when we had the referendum is that a lot of those facts didn't get the airtime... So I would like us to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be and then put that to the people at a general election."

Writing on X, Badenoch dismissed it as "yet another example of Burnham's foot in mouth syndrome".

She added: "Most people who voted for Brexit did so because they didn't want free movement. Too many politicians have failed to understand the significance and impact of immigration on communities."

Conservative MP and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, who backed Remain, warned the Brexit debate was "incredibly divisive" and insisted the current Brexit deal can still be made to work.

"I was at the top of a government that was paralysed for several years while we were trying to wrestle with the implications of that vote and I think, having made the decision, we should stick with it and make the most of it - I think we can make it a success," he told Kuenssberg.

Pointing to the one million young people not in work or training, he added: "Surely our priority in that situation is to get those jobs filled by the young people we have here instead of parking them on welfare.

"Which is why I think it's astonishing to lead on the issue of free movement... Something that is actually going to stop young people here getting jobs."

But Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper told Kuenssberg she believed allowing freedom of movement would be "a really good thing for growth" and pushed for the UK to rejoin the single market, the customs union, and also be involved in the bloc's defence pact.

The UK currently has "the worst of both worlds" on immigration, she said, as it was excluded from the EU's "new asylum pact with biometric data" that could be used to "tackle the small boats crisis".

Reform UK's economy spokesperson Robert Jenrick told Kuenssberg he had never believed freedom of movement "was a good thing", despite supporting the Remain position before the 2016 referendum when he was a Conservative MP.

"I think it's completely mad, the idea that this country needs more immigration," he said, claiming data shows mass migration "has been a disaster for working people, for Brits".

"The last thing they want is their wages being undercut by a load of low wage, low-skilled migrants from overseas," he added.

News.title: Couple were celebrating anniversary before Bahamas tragedy
News.content:
He said both boys had been so excited and had been snorkelling in shallow water as they sorted out their towels and bags on the beach when the boys got into difficulties.

Both parents went into the sea and tried to save them as they were swept out by the current, he added, and the whole ordeal happened in less than 10 minutes.

Nathan said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable", but she was a "hero... in life and in death" as she helped to rescue the two boys.

"I've known her since infant school," he told the BBC. " We first got together when we were 14... so 22 years."

"There are no words I can use to describe Leanne, same as anyone she has ever known.

"She was the purest of people, the most generous kind and beautiful person who ever walked the earth.

"Our relationship was perfect. She was the perfect mother, the perfect wife the foundation of our entire family."

Nathan said: "Royal Caribbean and Virgin Airlines were absolutely incredible to us and made an impossible journey home so much easier.

Now, as he "keeps strong for his boys", a gofundme has generated nearly Â£9,000 in donations to support them.

News.title: Carrick future under major threat - can he survive?
News.content:
Michael Carrick's future as Manchester United manager is under major threat following the home loss to Bournemouth on Sunday.

The Red Devils lost 3-0 as their poor start to the season continued - they have won just one of their eight Premier League matches so far and sit 16th - 14 points off the top.

Carrick, 45, took interim charge in January following Ruben Amorim's departure and he was rewarded with the permanent job in May after securing Champions League qualification with an impressive run that resulted in them finishing third.

But United have not won in the top flight since 30 August, when they defeated newly promoted Ipswich 5-2.

"See what happens," Carrick told BBC Sport when asked if he was expecting any conversations on his future.

"I'm not expecting anything. It's just digesting today - we knew it was an important day to try and get us moving forward and we haven't done that.

"For me it's just digesting that and the emotions at the end of the game is something I've not really had before."

Carrick made a big call on Sunday by dropping his captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench.

That decision came after the Portugal midfielder questioned Carrick's tactics in Wednesday's 4-1 loss at Como in the Champions League.

The comments from Fernandes came in the wake of defender Lisandro Martinez issuing an apology following his controversial remarks criticising the club's hierarchy.

Martinez said he had expected more investment in the Manchester United squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]".

News.title: Board of Deputies of British Jews declares Greens to be racist party
News.content:
The Green Party of England and Wales has been declared a racist organisation by the Board of Deputies of British Jews.

The Jewish body, which is the largest in the UK, was responding to the "Zionism is racism" policy motion passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.

Board of Deputies president Phil Rosenberg said a vote passed by 118 votes to one to declare that the Greens had, "by adopting an antisemitic platform, become a racist party".

A spokesman for the Greens insisted the party does not discriminate against people who hold Zionist views and said it rejected the Board of Deputies' "characterisation of this motion and our party".

They added the decision "will not stop us from speaking out against the genocide in Gaza and pushing for stronger sanctions against the Israeli government and its leaders". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

The motion passed by the Board of Deputies, external urged other parties not to do deals with the Greens unless they rejected the policy.

Forming coalition deals with Greens at local or national level would be "failing to take antisemitism with the requisite seriousness", it said, unless the party's local leadership have rejected the policy and committed to overturn it.

Labour has already issued an ultimatum to local Green groups it is currently in coalition with, telling them to disown the motion or lose the party's support.

Rosenberg said: "By adopting an antisemitic platform, the Green Party of England and Wales has become a racist party. We will treat it accordingly.

"No political party has the right to tell Jews that a central part of our identity, rooted in thousands of years of history, faith and peoplehood, is racist.

"The Green Party's policy brands much of our community, including our synagogues and communal organisations, with that slur. It gives prejudice against Jews a political licence.

"The Green Party's leadership must now take responsibility for reversing this policy and confronting the antisemitism it has legitimised."

The motion backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, and opposition political parties.

Responding when the Green motion was passed, the Board of Deputies and Jewish Leadership Council said in a joint statement that "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".

Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote on the motion as he left the conference early to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election which was held days later.

He has since told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, he would not overturn the motion, which would be party policy until 2028.

News.title: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlists
News.content:
More music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services.

And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.

The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.

Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.

This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.

In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.

So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?

News.title: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands.

Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Thomas Markle in a letter that he would never meet his grandchildren.

It is understood the letter was sent to Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.

It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle had been found in his former home in the Philippines and UK police in 2019 told Meghan about claims of abuse against him. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations.

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. He pulled out of his daughter's royal wedding that year, citing ill health.

The letter sent in 2025 appears to be the end of what has been a troubled relationship between father and daughter.

It is understood details of the letter, first reported in the Sun on Sunday, external, include Meghan telling Markle that he would never meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lillibet, with Meghan making it clear she would never contact her father again.

She also apparently told her father that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.

Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed to the Sun on Friday he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home.

He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the US Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) about it in July.

The FBI has since confirmed it is aware of the allegations.

On Sunday Markle Jnr, 60, apologised to Meghan in an interview with the Sun for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement.

"I now know I have been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years," he said.

Philippines officials have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father, telling the BBC on Friday that its anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured Thomas Markle's computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meanwhile, Thomas Markle has given an interview to the Mail on Sunday, external in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines on past visits but denies sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.

News.title: Russia to host first Olympic federation world event since Ukraine invasion
News.content:
Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships - the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022.

The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced its decision on Sunday, four months after confirming Russian athletes would again be eligible to compete in its events.

In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted a suspension on the Russian Olympic Committee.

That suspension had been imposed following the country's invasion of Ukraine.

The IOC's subsequent decision potentially opened the way for Russian athletes to compete for their country at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

The IWF announced the host cities of four world championships at junior, youth and senior levels, awarding the 2029 senior event to Ahmedabad in India.

"All the bids we received were excellent and we are sure that the championships in your respective countries will be a huge success," said IWF general secretary Jose Quinones.

No world championships in an Olympic sport, summer or winter, have been held in Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine.

The 2025 World Aquatics Championships, initially awarded to the Russian city of Kazan, were instead moved to Singapore.

Moscow has not held the World Weightlifting Championships since 1983.

The Russian Weightlifting Federation said: "[We are] the first Olympic sports federation to succeed in bringing a top-level official competition back to the country in many years."

Federation president Aleksandr Vinokurov thanked the IWF in a post on Telegram "for their trust", with the championships also serving as a qualifying event for the 2032 Olympic Games in Brisbane, Australia.

"Russia has all the necessary experience and capabilities to host competitions of the highest level," he said.

"Moscow has repeatedly staged major international sporting events and has modern infrastructure."

In announcing its decision in July to provisionally lift Russia's suspension, the IOC said that no decision had been taken on whether Russia could display their flag, colours and anthem at the Olympic âGames.

The IOC said it would continue to "not organise IOC events in Russia or invite Russian government or state officials to its events".

Some Russian athletes competed at the 2024 Paris Olympic Games and this year's Winter Olympics in Milan as neutrals.

Ukraine filed an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) requesting that the IOC decision to lift its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee be annulled.

The IOC's move decision came after the International Paralympic Committee had already ended Russia's exile from global sports events, with the country's athletes allowed to compete under their national flag at the Winter Paralympics.

Five Ukrainian athletes are listed to compete in the 2026 IWF World Championships in Ningbo, China, which are scheduled to take place from 27 October to 8 November.

News.title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
News.content:
We're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.

That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.

Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around Â£24bn to as low as Â£11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.

The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.

At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.

Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.

BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money, external on Wednesday.

News.title: Budget to include £1bn for social and affordable housing
News.content:
Under the plans for the regions, an initial Â£285m in transitional seed funding will be allocated by the government next year to support mayors and local leaders - and reduce reliance on "fragmented bidding pots" in Whitehall, the Treasury said.

The government will also confirm that it will work with mayors to design a new Â£1.5bn borrowing facility from 2028, which would allow them to access capital needed to support local priorities.

The Treasury said this could be put towards new homes, bringing High Streets back to life, or improving transport links.

Healey said: "Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas."

Areas across the country which are not yet strategic authorities will be able to access a share of the Â£285m to "unlock projects which will contribute to growth in their areas".

The prime minister said: "I'm calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country."

Claire Ward, chairwoman of the UK Mayors Network and Labour's East Midlands mayor, said that having the "right powers and resources through increased devolution" would help turn "ambitious plans into reality and deliver real, lasting change" for communities.

Lord Sadiq Khan, Labour's mayor of London, said greater ability to invest could "help unlock transformational infrastructure projects" including the West London Orbital route, the extension of the Bakerloo Underground line and Docklands Light Railway, and the development of Stratford International station.

Departing Treasury entrepreneurship adviser, Alex Depledge, has criticised the government's treatment of start-ups ahead of her last day on Thursday - the day after the Budget.

She told the Sunday Times, external, that start-ups were being treated as a "sideshow" and should not be pushed to the "margins of economic policy".

"Keeping scale-ups on the fringes underestimates the contribution of our greatest companies, and we need to support and develop them on British shores at all costs," she said.

Leading up to the Budget, defence has also remained a key talking point. Healey resigned in June from his role as defence secretary in the previous government over the defence investment plan, which he claimed fell "well short" of what was needed to fund the armed forces.

He had called for defence spending to rise to 3% of the country's GDP by 2030, on the way to reaching a Nato target of 3.5% in 2035.

But urging him to commit to setting out plans to spend 3% of GDP on defence, the shadow chancellor said: "We are living in an era of extraordinary threats, and yet the chancellor is dithering over finding the money to pay the country's insurance premium... you cannot have a strong economy without a strong defence".

Responding to Andrew Griffith's comments, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Conservatives were to blame for failing to invest in the military while in office.

Streeting said the prime minister had made it clear that his government was "determined to give our armed forces the investment needed to keep us safe".

News.title: Why the King's Caribbean tour could be 'biggest risk of his reign'
News.content:
The King will make three significant speeches during the Caribbean trip and will follow government advice not to issue an official apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade.

A senior royal aide said that the King would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past" but stressed that decisions over apologies and reparations were matters for government.

The current Burnham administration, like those before it, will not pay reparations.

Buckingham Palace says that acknowledging the wrongs of the past will be built into the King's programme in all three countries.

But apologies, reparations, and republicanism are rich pickings for campaigners and protests are likely.

This is the reality for the King and Buckingham Palace, and they are accepting of it.

Those who've worked on the planning of the trip view protests as part of the open debate in the region and security preparations include their possibility.

Lurking in the back of Royal Household minds will also be memories of the last tour by senior royals to the Caribbean in the early part of 2022.

Then, as the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, William and Catherine found themselves facing criticism over the optics of the trip - images of the royal couple reaching out to touch the outstretched hands of Jamaican children through a wire fence looked clumsy. Engagements designed as tributes to past royal visits appeared outdated. And protests also caused the cancellation of a small part of the schedule.

Everything will have been done to avoid those kinds of missteps on the 2026 Caribbean tour.

News.title: Four-year-old girl dies after fall from tower block
News.content:
A four-year-old girl has died after falling from a tower block in east London.

The Metropolitan Police said officers were called to the scene at an address in St Paul's Road, Barking, at about 11:00 BST on Saturday morning, following reports that a child had fallen from height.

Paramedics from the London Ambulance Service gave first aid and the child was taken to hospital, but later died from her injuries.

A Met spokesperson said the incident was not believed to be suspicious.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the child's family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time," they said.

"An investigation into the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident is ongoing. However, at this time, the incident is not believed to be suspicious.

"We urge anyone with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting CAD 2424/24OCT."

News.title: Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget
News.content:
The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.

It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.

Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost Â£8.9bn.

A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a Â£9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.

But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).

Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said that while hosting an Olympic Games would "likely provide a positive boost for the country", the cost of proposals would require "careful scrutiny".

He said the chancellor should use the Budget to bring down everyday costs before looking to "spend millions in taxpayer cash on reheated announcements made by his predecessor".

French added: "The irony is that Labour's new tourism tax will create a cost barrier for sports fans wanting to visit the North of England for an Olympic Games."

The new feasibility study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.

Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.

"Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."

News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport.

"We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement.

"Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

News.title: Thousands of people gather in support of Drumcree Orangemen
News.content:
The first part of the parade was followed by a series of speeches, mainly from members of the Orange Order.

This was very much an Orange Order event and not a political rally but inevitably there was a political tone to many of the comments.

There was explicit criticism of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher, the secretary of state and the first minister, but also implicit criticism of the leaders of the two biggest unionist parties - the DUP and Ulster Unionist Party.

Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister was applauded but by far the loudest cheers were for the Orange Order's legal adviser Jamie Bryson and the local MP Lockhart.

She was invited on to the stage and presented with a special gift for her support of the Orangemen.

Lockhart was the only politician to take to the stage, where she repeated her challenge to the DUP leadership: "Profound consequences must mean profound consequences. Michelle O'Neill must go.

"That's where I stand, and this lady is not for turning."

Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson warned politicians that they could face consequences at the next election over the Drumcree dispute.

"Politicians need to remember that we put them into office and we can take them out of office," he said.

He added that the Orange Order had won the right "to return home via our traditional route and Portadown District intends to exercise that right on a date and time of our choosing, and if necessary, without further recourse".

Orange Order Deputy District Master Alistair Power said Drumcree must not be allowed to divide unionism.

"It should not be used by parties to attack each other publicly over differences of opinion," he added. "We need to stand united."

News.content:
