Meta is not the only tech company grappling with teen access to beauty filters. TikTok also restricts users under the age of 18 from using them. Snapchat does not restrict teen access to filters. Neither company responded to NPR's request for comment. YouTube told NPR it does not have any filters. But there's nothing stopping users from posting images or videos made with third party filters to the platform — or onto TikTok and Instagram, for that matter.

Meanwhile, state attorneys general are reaching the end of a two-month window they set themselves to provide Meta with guidance in the form of a letter on what constitutes a bannable filter — and what does not.

Evolving beauty standards

They face a moving target, as digital beauty standards evolve rapidly.

"If the states want to define what is a beauty filter, they should define what is beauty," said Florencia Solari, a creative technologist who has spent years developing AI and augmented reality experiences for global brands.

Sponsor Message

Solari noted that trend cycles move quickly. "Instagram face" is already falling out of favor. "People are starting to move away from that because it's starting to look a bit clownish," Solari said. "Now it's going towards extreme thinness. So that's another problem."

As a result, the tools that are used to achieve the latest look are therefore also changing. So what might be branded by lawmakers as an "extreme" beauty filter in 2026 will likely be different in 2027.

Technological changes

While beauty standards are changing quickly, so is technology.

Instead of sitting in boardrooms debating pixel thresholds for cheekbones, Kelly Frasier, the co-author of a recent study highlighting the negative impacts of social media on body issues in adolescents, said legislators should consider the fact that teens will soon be able to use AI to create entire fake universes around themselves, not just change the way they look. So they should focus on broader AI regulation for minors.

"I think that legislators are asking the wrong question if they're asking where to draw the line for beauty filters," said Frasier. "And to be honest, filters will probably become completely obsolete within the next few years."

Legal and regional challenges

On top of the technological and cultural challenges, legal experts warn that individual states may struggle to reach a consensus on what does and does not constitute what the settlement agreement describes as a "cosmetic procedure filter."

"What we don't really have a sense of is what happens if the states disagree with each other?" said David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. "What if one state finds, you know, eyebrow lifting to be completely acceptable and another one thinks it's awful?"

NPR reached out to the attorneys general offices in all four plaintiff states that led the trial — California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey — for an update on the guidelines. But officials either declined to comment or did not respond.

Sponsor Message

Beyond the U.S., some international regulators are hoping to avoid discussions around beauty filter definitions entirely.

In Europe, the proposed KIDS Act — designed to regulate youth social media usage — takes a sweeping approach.

In that plan, "Beauty filters – not extreme beauty filters; beauty filters full stop – are forbidden for minors," said European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier. Regnier said EU legislators are closely watching the implementation of the U.S. settlement. "We want child-friendly services for our children. A beauty filter has nothing to do with a child-friendly service," Regnier said.

Teens want to be heard

Meta says that it plans to enforce the ban on "cosmetic procedure filters" by early next year.

For youth activists like Lerner, the hope is that tech companies and regulators will include teens in these discussions. "So often it's just the government or these companies in these conversations," Lerner said. "The company should be asking us for our actual perspectives, like 'Are people actually using these extreme AI filters or is that not going to make a difference?' 'Do we need to target something else?'"

Meta said the company has partnered with teens over the years, but did not respond to NPR's question asking if it is doing so currently.

World.title: More dads taking paid family leave for a new baby, sometimes as much as moms are
World.content:
More dads taking paid family leave for a new baby, sometimes as much as moms are

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

Karlo Campana is usually outnumbered these days. He has three young kids under age 4.

On a recent Saturday, he played a mini-game of basketball with his two older kids in their Southern California home, shooting a ball into a hoop on the door, while his baby boy watched from his bouncy chair.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

Campana took paid time off in May after the birth of his son — just as he did for his daughters.

It's sometimes called "bonding" or "family" leave, to distinguish it from the paid leave ("maternity" or "disability" leave) that mothers can take to physically recover from childbirth.

"You need that adjustment period," he said. Campana, who works at an ad agency, said having the time off not to think about work — or worry about losing income during that time — was crucial for him and his family during a sleep-deprived period.

Sponsor Message

"My wife isn't doing it on her own," he said. "She doesn't feel like she's alone on this journey. She feels like she has support." He jokes that by kid No. 3, he thought he had nailed diaper changes without too much mess — but he was wrong.

"The benefits are I get to spend time with each of them when they were in the infant stage, the baby stage, and I get to hold them and, you know, change the poopy diapers," he said. " It's like the funny moments of, like, being a parent, like, 'This is it right here, you're in the thick of it.'"

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

Campana is among a growing number of fathers who take leave to bond with a new child in the states that offer paid family leave programs — and are part of a larger cultural shift that has seen dads handle more caregiving duties.

In California — as in several other states — men make up about half of bonding claim applications. Last year, men even surpassed women — as in Colorado and Washington — for the first time in the state's history. This trend comes at a time when the federal government has said it wants Americans to have more babies, and families report affordability is an obstacle in raising them.

Sponsor Message

There's no federal law guaranteeing paid parental leave, but California is one of 14 states, plus Washington, D.C., that have passed legislation to enact paid family leave programs — and in many of those places, more dads are opting in.

"We're in a very different place in terms of our understanding of gender roles, of paternity leave, of dads' roles than we were 20-plus years ago," said Molly Weston Williamson, policy director at Paid Leave for All, an organization that advocates for paid family leave policies.

California's program offers, within a year, up to eight weeks of paid bonding leave for parents after a birth, adoption, or foster care placement. That's on top of six to eight weeks of paid disability leave that moms get to recover after birth.

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

Campana said he initially wasn't sure if he should take paternity leave because of lingering gender stereotypes.

" I felt guilty, for sure," Campana said. " I think dads maybe feel they need to be the provider. They need to be the ones that are only helping their family by bringing money or working."

Campana said that when he was growing up, his father worked three jobs. "It was hard for him to be present, and I think that's the one thing now — it's like, 'No, be present. Be there for your kids.'"

Research has shown that paternity leave confers benefits beyond allowing a father extra time to bond with a new child: It has positive effects on the whole family, including better health outcomes for both parents.

Paid parental leave has also been linked to lower odds of postpartum depression and a decrease in infant mortality rates.

In California, men accounted for 51% of bonding claims filed in 2025. It's a massive shift from when the state program started in 2004, and men made up about 18% of claim applications.

Sponsor Message

States fund their paid family and medical leave programs with different combinations of employer and employee contributions; California is among six states where family leave is entirely funded by employee payroll deductions.

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

In addition to changing gender norms, Williamson said other factors are likely contributing to the increase in claims by men in the state: greater awareness about the program, and recent changes to the benefit.

In 2025, the state boosted the amount of income a worker can recoup while on family leave. Now, in California and in other states, the leave benefit can be as high as 90% of their regular salary.

"That makes it a realistic option for a lot more families, and I think we're seeing dads and moms responding to that change," Williamson said. Still, she said, there's a lot the new data about dads isn't telling us.

"We're getting one particular vantage point into this data, which is useful and valuable, but it's only telling us sort of part of the story, and we'd need other kinds of information to better understand the full picture," Williamson said.

"Is it that more dads are working and therefore are potentially eligible for these benefits? Is it that women are deciding not to take leave?"

While private employers can offer their own paid leave as a benefit, this data also reflects only people who took leave through California's paid family leave program.

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

A spokesperson for the California Employment Development Department, which administers the state's family leave program, said the department couldn't provide definitive reasons for the increase in male bonding claims.

One thing is clear: The growth in these states comes as more parents are feeling strained economically.

President Trump has said, "We want more babies," and has promoted policy initiatives like expanding access to in vitro fertilization and offering investment accounts for newborns.

Sponsor Message

"People really are very worried about the affordability of kids," said Jeremy Pope, a professor of political science at Brigham Young University, and a principal investigator of the American Family Survey.

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

According to the latest survey in 2025, 7 in 10 Americans said raising children had become unaffordable, according to the survey. It was the biggest single-year jump since the survey started more than a decade ago.

"I don't think they want government involved in the decision to have kids," Pope said. "But they worry a lot about how much it costs and they would like to see ways of making those costs smaller or getting help with those costs."

The Pew Research Center found in a recent survey of full-time working parents who are not self-employed, 84% said paid parental, family, or medical leave would be "extremely or very helpful" to them, but only half said it was available to them.

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with LAist and KFF Health News.

World.title: Independent candidates sense a moment. Some Democrats hope they're right.
World.content:
Independent candidates sense a moment. Some Democrats hope they're right.

toggle caption i Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images

BURWELL, NEBRASKA – Tucked in the rolling Sandhills, the largest sand dune formation in America, sits Morgan Ranch, a 15,000-acre, family-run operation home to 1,000 cows and thousands of offspring.

"There's a lot of mouths to feed — both animals and two-legged," laughed Dan Morgan. His ranch has one of the largest privately-owned Wagyu herds in the U.S.

He said his job has given him a front row seat to what he calls the "uncertainty" of President Trump's policies.

"To raise a piece of meat takes me three years," Morgan said. "Well, look at the changes in the past two years: costs, tariffs, reciprocal tariffs because half of our business is export — it's just hell," he said.

Sponsor Message

He's a Democrat — a self-described small blue dot in a sea of red, in a county and state that President Trump dominated two years ago.

There's no Democrat running for the Senate in Nebraska, but Morgan is excited by independent candidate Dan Osborn.

"Osborn makes the case that somebody needs to represent the working family," Morgan said. "And he can effectively do that."

Osborn is one of four independents running for Senate in states President Trump won handily, including Idaho, South Dakota and Montana. Buoyed by the president's sinking approval ratings and public frustration over affordability, independent candidates argue they bring a winning case to voters.

It is an argument that some Democrats hope will resonate with voters as the party looks to retake control of Congress, betting that these candidates can help topple Republicans in parts of the country where their own brand is hurting.

"I'm a partisan Democrat. I believe in the Democratic Party. I also believe in building coalitions so we can win elections and then do the work of the people," said Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic Party. "And if that means creating coalitions with independents in some of our states, then that's exactly what we need to do."

Sponsor Message

But while these independents are generally unified in their political philosophy that the two-party system is toxic and has led to legislative intransigence, the challenges they face in their respective races are different, in large part because of the role the Democratic Party has decided to play.

'Spoiler' accusations abound in Montana

Seth Bodnar, a former Green Beret running for Senate in Montana, said voters he talks to are fed up with politics as usual — and that he offers a viable alternative as an independent.

"When I go to Washington, D.C., I'm not going to put on a red jersey with an 'R' or a blue jersey with a 'D.' I'm going to have a jersey with an 'M' on it, and I'm going to work for Montana," Bodnar said in an interview from the homecoming parade at the University of Montana, where he used to be president.

Like Osborn, Bodnar said if elected, he won't caucus with either party. The current two independents in the Senate, Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine, both caucus with Democrats.

His theory of the case is that in a closely-divided Senate, an independent willing to work with either party — but beholden to neither — actually holds significant strength.

toggle caption i Mathew Brown/AP

"I think there is real power in an independent or multiple independents that can work together, even with people who maybe don't leave their caucus but form an independent-minded bloc, that can move forward common sense solutions that this country so desperately needs," Bodnar said.

The race has been marked by frustration among Democrats — at either Bodnar for not running as a Democrat himself, or at the Democratic nominee, Alani Bankhead, for not dropping out and creating a glide path for Bodnar.

"Had Bodnar run as a Democrat, he'd be leading in this election," said former Democratic Gov. Brian Schweitzer.

Sponsor Message

"At the end of the day, there will be a lot of people that look in the mirror and say, 'Oh, my God, if we would have just run a Democrat without an independent, we would have won this election,'" Schweitzer said.

Many prominent Montana Democrats — like former Sen. Jon Tester and former Gov. Steve Bullock — have endorsed Bodnar, setting up a divide between Democrats supporting their own party's nominee and those supporting the independent.

"It's just been really, really contentious and quite a bitter thing within the state party," said Rob Saldin, political science professor at the University of Montana.

Saldin said unlike states like Idaho, which has deep Republican entrenchment, Montana Democrats aren't as "beat down" and look at the election as a chance to rebuild the brand in the state.

"They want somebody who, for years into the future, is going to be able to help bring money into the state Democratic Party, to help down-ballot candidates for the legislature, to be the face of the party in the state," he said. "And when you've got an independent candidate who's saying, 'a pox on both your houses,' this is not the guy who's going to be able to do that work in the trenches for the party."

There was an effort to get Bankhead to exit the race before the August deadline. Bankhead said she and her family were harassed. She also said "white gloved politicians" were subtly trying to tell her to drop out of the race.

toggle caption i Clayton Murphy/Montana Public Radio

"They were very polite. They didn't ask me to drop out, but it was subtle — like, 'Well, what's the goal and what kind of job do you want down the road?'" she said, adding she heard from a sitting senator, sitting governor and former cabinet official. "Nobody from the [Democratic National Committee] was like, 'drop out' but that was certainly the nudge."

Sponsor Message

Bankhead claimed in an interview with Montana PBS that she was offered a DNC job if she dropped out of the race. The DNC denies this.

Bankhead said if Democrats want to support independents — there's a better way to do it.

"Nebraska was very transparent, right? The Democratic nominee said they would step aside in favor of the independent if the people voted for them. And that's very transparent — that's great."

Fending off 'Democrat Dan' label in Nebraska

Kleeb, the Nebraska Democratic Party chair and a DNC vice chair, said Nebraska Democrats were very conscious about being transparent regarding their intentions to support the independent on the ticket.

"We were very honest with voters," said Kleeb. "And I think if you're going to do this as a Democratic Party, that's what you have to do — you have to be honest with voters, explain the strategy and make sure that Democrats support that."

She said Democrats had high hopes for Osborn, a mechanic who got his start in politics leading a strike at the Kellogg's plant in 2021, and raised eyebrows two years ago when he came within seven points of incumbent Republican Sen. Deb Fischer.

The choice for Democrats to support Osborn led to the party running someone in the primary with the stated intention of having her drop out to clear the path for Osborn. There was then a lawsuit attempting to force the party to replace that winning primary candidate who dropped out.

toggle caption i Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images

Kleeb said the decision to back Osborn is part of a long-term goal, which includes repairing the damage to the Democratic brand in a redder state like Nebraska.

"It's right that people have pushed back on our brand – it's a problem. We are working on it," Kleeb said, adding there will be a time when Nebraska builds up its Democratic base so it's competitive statewide.

Sponsor Message

In the meantime, Democrats like Kleeb are hoping Osborn can help the party deny Republicans a majority in the Senate.

Osborn has been crisscrossing the state on a 93-county tour. His town halls have a distinctly populist pitch to voters denouncing money in politics.

"We are at a turning point in our country where we have to take it back for ourselves – for the workers, for the people," he said to a group of 30 in Taylor. "Because the powers that be — the money interests — have taken control."

In between stops in five counties on one day, Osborn said in an interview he's not only running against incumbent GOP. Sen Pete Ricketts.

"I'm running against the entire establishment that is stuck in this system that's working exactly the way it's supposed to work for them," he said. "I represent something that's going to throw a wrench in."

As Osborn travels the state, Ricketts has been working to convince constituents that the independent is actually a Democrat.

"Dan's a Democrat. Open borders, take our guns, higher taxes, that's no fun — vote for Osborn and you'll see, the Democrats will run D.C.," croons a radio ad from the Ricketts campaign. In their debate, Ricketts called Osborn "Democrat Dan" so many times the independent suggested they should bring out a third podium.

toggle caption i Nati Harnik/AP

Sue McNeil, a lifelong Republican voter in Loup County, said she doesn't like the nickname.

"I think they're just using that 'Democrat Dan' to scare people, because Nebraska is a Republican state and I feel like a lot of people are a little nervous about supporting a Democrat," she said. "But Dan Osborn is not a Democrat — he's an independent."

She's supporting Osborn, citing frustration with the Trump administration and GOP-controlled Congress.

"Why did we start the war with Iran? Our fuel prices have skyrocketed," she said, noting she recently paid $159 to fill up the pickup. "How are we supposed to make it?"

Sponsor Message

But other conservative voters say they agree with Ricketts.

"Osborn is a fraud," said Rich Sherbeck from Ansley. "He's not really an independent — he's a Democrat, DSA-aligned."

Casey Stengel, who said he always votes Republican, was curious about Osborn and came to a meet and greet at a coffee shop in Thedford. He told Osborn he was on the fence and asked him to convince him to vote for him.

Osborn launched into a discussion about uplifting workers and building bridges with both parties to bring about real change.

Once Osborn left, Stengel sighed.

"Yes, there's good ideas," he said. "But we all know one man ain't going to go fix the deal."

Sam Gringlas contributed to this report.

World.title: Who is B.C.'s new premier Lorne Doerkson?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson struck political gold Saturday night.

The former small-town newspaper publisher delivered a stunning defeat to David Eby's NDP and led the B.C. Conservatives to a commanding majority government.

Early Sunday morning, Doerkson's Conservatives were leading in 64 ridings, reducing the NDP to just 27 seats and toppling several cabinet ministers.

It's a remarkable turnaround for a political party that was in disarray just five weeks ago, days before a snap election was called.

But where his political opponents may have seen weakness, Doerkson said British Columbians chose instead to seize an opportunity.

"For a very long time, a lot of British Columbians have felt like Victoria forgot about them, like the map maybe stopped at Hope," Doerkson told a throng of more than 1,000 supporters at the Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver.

"But tonight the whole map counts."

WATCH | Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson gives victory speech: FULL SPEECH: Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson's victory speech | Duration closed caption 17:01

Rodeos to newspapers to politics

Born in New Westminster, Doerkson grew up in Surrey and the B.C. Interior, before settling in Williams Lake, where he raised a family.

He spent 20 years publishing community newspapers and volunteering with local business and community service groups before entering politics.

"That was a very good education for me," he told supporters. "You learn what’s really going on in a town: who’s hiring, who’s closing, who’s hoping."

Doerkson was first elected in Cariboo-Chilcotin as a B.C. Liberal in 2020, and later joined John Rustad's fledgling Conservative caucus.

His victory makes him the first premier from B.C.'s Interior since Bill Bennett left office in 1986.

Doerkson was on his way home from South Africa last month when he learned his Conservative caucus colleagues wanted him to take over the party as interim leader.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay had just resigned after months of scandals that led to the departure or expulsion of more than a dozen MLAs.

Doerkson admitted he needed convincing.

"Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," he said in a pre-election interview with CBC News.

Lorne Doerkson speaks to supporters in the crowd during provincial election night Saturday. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Promises to cut income taxes, red tape

Doerkson spent his victory speech Saturday night introducing himself to British Columbians at the same time as celebrating the "trailblazers" who came to the province searching for gold and a better life.

It's a spirit he told supporters that still animates the province, where people want to build something big, from resource communities through to the big metro areas.

"That is the trailblazing spirit of British Columbia and it never left, it just needs government that’s on its side," he said.

WATCH | CBC News projects a Conservative government: CBC News projects a B.C. Conservative majority government | Duration closed caption 1:59

Doerkson reiterated promises to cut red tape "like it’s never been cut before," speed up forestry and mining permits, and triple natural gas production by 2035.

"A province only works if all of it works," he said.

"A mill running in Quesnel keeps a trucker working in Surrey. A mine opening in the north keeps the port busy in Delta. It’s one economy and it runs through every town on our map."

Doerkson also pledged no new taxes and health care that is "fully and publicly funded."

Still, questions remain about how he'll pay for everything, including a promise to cut income taxes by $1,000 a year.

The province is already on track to see a $13.8-billion deficit in 2026-27.

The NDP spent their campaign warning that the Conservatives' platform could mean cuts to health care and education.

Speaking in Vancouver Saturday, Doerkson reiterated election promises, including to cut red tape 'like it’s never been cut before.' (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Overcoming divisions

As premier-designate, Doerkson now faces the challenge of not only governing but keeping together a coalition that includes social conservatives and more centrist, fiscal conservatives.

And though he has promised to repeal B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People’s Act, he appealed to First Nations communities as partners in the province’s development.

"This future is one we build together as partners with the certainty that all of us need," he said.

One source of division Doerkson won't need to deal with immediately will be the NDP.

With preliminary results showing New Democrats reduced to fewer than 30 seats, the Official Opposition's first priority will be choosing a new leader to replace David Eby who announced Saturday that he will step down.

World.title: Sgt. Morgan Wong remembered as loyal friend, dedicated soldier at funeral following CFB Wainwright tragedy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A funeral home in central Edmonton was full Sunday morning, with most in attendance wearing poppies over their hearts to honour the sergeant who died last weekend at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, in central Alberta.

Eight service members carried the casket of Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, draped in the Maple Leaf, to the front of the room as bagpipes played him in.

The flag was later replaced with a yellow descendants’ blanket — a traditional Chinese textile used during funerals — before a shrine, featuring a framed photo of Wong, fruit, rice and flowers, was placed in front of the casket and other Buddhist funeral customs were performed.

“Each one of us has our own special memories of Morgan, and I hope holding onto those memories will remind us to live our lives with courage and integrity, like he did,” his sister, Megan, said in a speech during the service.

“He was too young when he left us,” she said. “But I hope his life will be a reminder for each of us to use the time we have to achieve a life we would be proud of.”

Megan described her brother as brave, warm and hilarious, a loyal friend and dedicated soldier. She added that Wong was close to their mother — and that now they’re together again.

The family also offered their condolences to the other soldiers who died and were injured at CFB Wainwright.

A fire at CFB Wainwright on Oct. 17, resulting from a training exercise, was first reported in the base's grenade launcher range — a "permanent danger area" that base firefighters couldn't enter. Strong winds in the region that day spread the flames quickly, overwhelming service members and eventually burning beyond the base.

The fire caused dozens of casualties and killed four service members including Wong, a member from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment who served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“The love that Canadians have shown for Sgt. Wong means more to all of us than we could ever explain. We will always remember him, and his family will forever be part of our family,” Lt.-Col. Bryn Wright, commanding officer of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, said in a written statement to journalists Sunday.

In a statement issued earlier this week, Wong's family expressed their love for him and how proud he had made them. They said he joined the military in 2017 and was training at CFB Wainwright last weekend to prepare for a second deployment to Europe.

Since the news of his death, friends and people Wong volunteered with described him as a passionate volunteer and a mentor.

World.title: Venezuela's opposition leader Machado returns after months in exile
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado reappeared in Venezuela on Sunday for the first time since December, returning from exile at a time when doubts about the country's democratic future — and the role of the U.S. — are growing.

It was her first appearance since the U.S. military deposed the country's then-president Nicolás Maduro in January, replacing him with an interim president who has exceeded the time she was authorized to serve, with no election scheduled.

Machado announced her arrival on social media, writing: "I am here. With you."

Another leading figure in the Venezuelan opposition, Edmundo Gonzalez, wrote on X confirming that Machado had arrived and that he would be next to her "very soon."

"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" he wrote. "You know it, this is until the end."

Supporters greet Machado

On Sunday afternoon, Machado strode into a church in the state of Lara, west of Caracas, to the applause of dozens gathered there as they shook her hand and hugged her, with cellphones aloft to record her return.

"María! María!" someone cried out, as another shouted, "Welcome to Venezuela!"

"Long live freedom, damn it!" a man yelled.

One woman wiped away tears and called it "a miracle," while another woman's hands flew to her face as she saw Machado enter the church.

Asked by reporters Sunday about Machado's return to Venezuela, U.S. President Donald Trump said: "I don't know anything about it, but I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize. So how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe. She's a very nice woman. But we're doing really well in Venezuela."

No election scheduled

Since Maduro's ouster, Venezuela has been run by interim President Delcy Rodríguez, a longtime Maduro ally who received the Trump administration's blessing to succeed him.

Rodríguez was initially supposed to serve only 90 days as acting president, but has remained in office and has made no move to call an election.

Machado went into hiding in Venezuela for 11 months after being briefly detained following a protest in January 2025.

WATCH | Machado was awarded the Nobel peace prize last year: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader | Duration 1:51 The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Maria Corina Machado. Machado won 'for her tireless work promoting democratic rights for the people of Venezuela and for her struggle to achieve a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy,' the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in its citation.

After leaving the country in a clandestine escape, she reappeared that December in Norway, where she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her peaceful challenge to Maduro's authoritarian government.

Machado and her allies have been demanding a date for a presidential election in Venezuela, but U.S. officials have emphasized economic stabilization first.

Election integrity questioned

In October 2023, Machado won an opposition primary and intended to challenge Maduro in the 2024 presidential election, but the government barred her from running for office.

González took her place on the ballot, and ample credible evidence showed that he defeated Maduro by more than a 2 to 1 margin. But the National Electoral Council, which is stacked with ruling-party loyalists, declared Maduro the winner.

The lead-up and aftermath of the election were marked by widespread government repression, including forced disappearances, torture and other human rights violations. More than 2,000 people, including poll workers, were detained in the days after the vote.

WATCH | Detractors decry Maduro's 2024 election win: Upset Venezuelans react as Maduro claims presidency | Duration 1:04 Winning a third term with 51 per cent of the vote, incumbent Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro stated he would defend the democracy and people of Venezuela, while detractors voiced their unhappiness with the election results after multiple exit polls suggested the opposition would win.

In January, the U.S. military captured Maduro in Caracas and whisked him to New York to face drug-related charges, which he has denied. Many Venezuelans were stunned by the Trump administration's decision to work with Rodríguez, instead of Machado, to try to revitalize the crisis-racked country.

Machado had repeatedly vowed to return to Venezuela, and, according to her party, she made seven unsuccessful attempts.

One of the efforts would have seen her take a charter boat, but the operator cancelled the trip, alleging the vessel was unfit for navigation. In another attempt, her team said, Machado tried to fly to the Caribbean island of Curacao, from where she could take a speedboat to Venezuela, but her plane was denied landing permits.

Opposition activists have accused Venezuela's government of blocking Machado's return, a claim denied by Venezuelan authorities. Others have also questioned whether the Trump administration has also been involved in the efforts to stop her from returning.

Trump administration officials deny they are holding Machado back but have said that, on some occasions, they have advised her against returning due to safety concerns.

After Maduro was deposed, Venezuela's highest court said Rodríguez could serve as acting president for up to 90 days — an interim appointment that could be extended by the National Assembly for an additional 90 days. But the ruling party-controlled assembly never voted to extend her term.

WATCH | Who is interim President Delcy Rodríguez?: Who is Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodriguez? | Duration closed caption 4:00 With Nicolás Maduro removed from office, Delcy Rodriguez has become Venezuela’s interim president. CBC’s Lyndsay Duncombe breaks down Rodriguez’s rise and the complicated relationship she’s entered with the U.S. government.

Machado and her allies have demanded that the Rodríguez government set a date for a presidential election. Rodríguez told the UN General Assembly in September that Venezuelans will determine the "right moment" for the next election.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has argued that before holding new elections, Venezuela must stabilize its economy and rebuild its institutions, including its courts and electoral council. But he said in a news conference earlier this month that Machado has "every right to enter her country whenever she wants to return."

Supporters of Machado have held demonstrations in Caracas demanding her return.

World.title: Is this Quebec-developed fruit the 'apple of the future'?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Orléans apple — developed on Île d’Orléans, Que. — is hitting grocery store shelves this fall, but has been in the works for nearly 25 years.

Beginning back in 2002, producers handpicked pollen from Honeycrisps and Empire apple flowers, and then spent years crossbreeding them until they arrived at the bright red and crisp Orléans. While it has been available in Quebec orchards for about two years, it's only now hitting grocery store shelves.

"I have some clients coming here asking especially for that kind," says Karen Morin. She thinks it just might be "the apple of the future."

The co-owner of the Verger du Roy in Portneuf grows 57 different types of apples, but Morin says the Orléans is growing more and more popular this year with apple pickers.

"It's a mix of Honeycrisp and Empire, so these two together, it's like a bomb. It's really, really good, so sweet [and] still really crispy," says Morin. "In the future, our children, it won't be the Honeycrisp anymore that will be the top one, it will be the Orléans."

Morin says that, while apple preferences can vary from generation to generation, people are always looking for apples that stay crisper longer. She believes that's why the Orléans apple is increasing in popularity.

Karen Morin says the Orléans apple has been growing in popularity for the past two years with apple pickers, but many people still aren't aware of the latest apple varieties coming to the market. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)

"It's like on the top of the list for firmness, and it's almost top of the list for sugar content," says

Benoit Caron, the owner of La Maison de la Pomme. Caron planted 20,000 Orléans trees at his orchard in Frelighsburg about five years ago.

"It's not the first apple created in Quebec, but it's the first one that we can supply at least 10 months a year because of [its] conservation," says Caron.

He adds that this particular variety is great as a snack, "but it's also a really good apple for cooking. It will hold itself together. So if you do apple custard or apple pie, you will have the nice apple slice that will stay together."

More supply and more demand for Quebec produce

Jérôme-Antoine Brunelle, the executive director of the Producteurs de pommes du Québec, says it's good to have new varieties to appeal to all the different types of consumers, but that the demand for Quebec produce has also been growing recently.

"If these new varieties can help us gain market shares from imported apples and that we can source more of Quebec-grown apples to consumers, it's a win for everyone," he says.

Brunelle says recent tensions with the U.S. and tariff woes did have an impact. "Consumers had more of an interest in locally sourced food," he says, and apples were no exception.

There’s been a bigger interest for locally sourced apples for the past two years, "and it doesn't seem to be slowing down," says the executive director of the Producteurs de pommes du Québec, Jérôme-Antoine Brunelle. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)

"That interest for locally sourced fruit helps us out, and we see that Quebec consumers are more conscientious of where their food comes from," says Brunelle.

He says he is aware, however, that producers and grocery stores must make sure Quebec apples are clearly identified as such in produce aisles to attract more consumers .

Different regions, different apples, different ciders

Claude Jolicoeur, an author who's published three books about apples and cider production, wants to increase the number of apple varieties in Quebec, specifically for cider. "And eventually maybe to have an appellation ‘regional cider,'" he says.

Jolicoeur says this could bring Quebec cider production to another level, similar to wine production in Italy — where different grape varieties, grown in different regions, produce different types of wines, with distinct flavours.

Morin, for instance, says Quebec-grown apples can also taste like other fruits, such as bananas, pineapples, strawberries, and even chestnuts.

"You can compare apples with apples, but they're different," she says.

Regardless of their provenance or flavour, cider apples would not be the same ones as those picked in orchards, or bought at the grocery store, however. "When you want to sell apples in a grocery store, that apple has to be beautiful," says Jolicoeur.

In the cider context, however, he notes, "no one is going to see the apple, so what it looks like is not important at all."

Jolicoeur hopes Quebec cider and apple producers will grow more and more Quebec apple varieties in the coming years.

However, apple producers reiterate, in the meantime, several apple varieties are already available year round, not only in the fall — including the brand new Orléans.

World.title: People are using AI to 'dumb down' their smart TVs. Is that a good idea?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's a very 2026 paradox.

Some tech users, fed up with constant surveillance, ads and other distractions, are using artificial intelligence to "dumb down" their smart devices.

Viral social media posts are showing people how to use AI coding prompts to hack and "debloat" smart TVs by removing unnecessary apps and programs and disabling some tracking features in an effort to make them run more smoothly.

While some are rejoicing, others warn the AI solution can cause bigger problems — and say there are easier, safer ways to simplify a cluttered TV.

"My TV was updating all the time with different security features and that's because of all the apps and data collection that's required," Toronto-based tech analyst and cybersecurity expert Ritesh Kotak told CBC News.

"So yeah, here is a big push to make the TVs not as smart."

WATCH | Calgary researchers investigate if smart home devices are leaking private data: International team of researchers looked at how IoT devices interact with home networks | Duration 4:29 Joel Reardon, associate professor of computer science at the University of Calgary, was on CBC News at 6 to discuss his findings.

An easy fix?

Some people have posted their coding scripts — sets of programming instructions carried out by AI agents — on the internet for others to copy.

One, called "dumbtv," was created by its developer to fix a Fire TV that had "become painful to use" because of constant ads on the home screen and apps taking too long to open.

Kotak says people are essentially using AI agents to help them identify their TV's IP address, then blocking certain traffic, like ads on TV home screens and analytics that get sent back to the company that makes the TV.

Some say they had success with asking a Claude AI agent how to hack their TV and talk them through the process so they could do it themselves, an example of a process called "vibe coding."

introducing dumbtv - no spying - no ads from tv - fully customisable to setup just point your agent to this repo - https://t.co/prQLD17Wa4 https://t.co/c6R8EhljiA —DevMuzzammil

But that hasn't worked for everyone. Some users are skeptical that Claude would even respond to that suggestion, and one said his attempt actually made his Android TV unusable.

Experts have urged people not to use these AI solutions, warning they could cause bigger problems. They also point to existing apps like Kyu Launcher and AT4K Launcher that can achieve similar results without the risk.

People 'starting to get fed up'

Tech-savvy individuals have long been hacking devices to customize them, but vibe-coding has opened that capability to a much wider audience, says London, Ont.-based tech analyst and journalist Carmi Levy.

For example, some people have used similar strategies to dumb down their smartphones, with the goal of making them less distracting and addictive.

But Levy warns that vibe coding is not for the "faint of heart," because people can inadvertently destroy their devices, void warranties or install the wrong kind of software.

"It's definitely a 'your mileage may vary' type of scenario. Sometimes it'll work, sometimes it won't. Sometimes you'll end up breaking the very device that you're trying to update."

Levy says in the case of smart TVs, many of these changes can be made by simply tweaking the settings on the TV itself.

WATCH | One Canadian's warning about Meta's new AI agent: He used Meta’s AI agent Muse for Marketplace sales. Then it set one up behind his back | Duration closed caption 2:39 Matt Robb started using Muse, Meta’s AI agent, to handle Facebook Marketplace transactions. But after listing a keyboard for sale, he got more than he bargained for. One expert advises people to really look at what they’re letting Muse access.

While he doesn't necessarily recommend enlisting AI agents to do the job, Levy says this emerging trend is an understandable response to the surveillance and data collection that's increasingly invading consumer products.

"Every device that we buy has to be smart, every device we buy has to have an app and it has to collect all sorts of information," he said.

"I think, frankly, people are starting to get fed up with all of this data collection. And they're starting to react to this surveillance economy."

Security concerns

Kotak says one way to address these concerns is to use a Fire Stick or other multimedia streaming device loaded with the apps you want that plugs into a TV's HDMI port. Because these tools (which also include the Apple TV device) have their own Wi-Fi adapters, you can leave your TV offline so it will basically just function as a monitor for the streaming device.

He cautions that users should also consider that hacking their smart TV while leaving it connected to the internet could end up making them more vulnerable to outside attacks.

Those annoying updates that keep popping up on your TV, he notes, are usually security-related.

"It's important to understand that a lot of smart TVs now also have microphones in them … My fear would be that is it possible for hackers to take over some of those features on your television," Kotak said.

"If your TV is going to be connected to the internet, and you're blocking certain services and you're not doing those updates, you may be making yourself vulnerable."

World.title: Netanyahu 'fighting for his political life' in 1st Israeli vote since Oct. 7. He might still survive
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On the cusp of Israel's first election since Benjamin Netanyahu presided over the most devastating security failure in the country's history, the Israeli prime minister is still hawking himself as the security candidate of choice and counting on it to work.

And it might. There are few Israeli analysts willing to write off the country's longest-serving prime minister in Tuesday's vote, despite the catastrophic impact of the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed about 1,200 people and led to 251 being taken hostage.

In an election already short-handed in terms of pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs, opinion polls in the weeks ahead of the vote have consistently suggested neither side will win the 61 seats needed to form a majority in the Israeli Knesset.

"We are back to where we were Oct. 6 [2023] in terms of the fact that the nation is split almost in the middle, electorally speaking," Tamar Hermann, a senior research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) in Jerusalem, said in an interview with CBC News.

"This means that we might come out with indecisive results. We may also have a minority government, but [then] the question, if there is a minority government, how long will it last?"

Netanyahu greets supporters in Jerusalem. The deaths of more than 74,000 Palestinians in Israel’s war against Hamas — a figure from health officials in Gaza — have not been the subject of much debate in the mainstream of Israel's election campaign. (Nico Hameon/CBC)

It could also mean a lengthy period of coalition building, during which Netanyahu would serve as a caretaker prime minister.

"Israel has moved to the right ever since Oct. 7, and maybe that is part of the answer to why the current government in the polls hasn't collapsed completely," political scientist Reuven Hazan of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem said in an interview earlier this month.

Hazan doesn't believe that Netanyahu, 77, and his far-right coalition partners will ultimately regain power, but he also said that "they should be doing a heck of a lot worse in the polls than they are."

Well-documented allegations that Netanyahu was repeatedly warned by regional allies and members of his own intelligence services that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel but ignored them have filled newspaper columns and media broadcasts in Israel and abroad.

WATCH | What did Netanyahu know on Oct. 6?: What Netanyahu knew before the Oct. 7 attacks | Duration closed caption 6:03 New allegations are emerging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ignored warnings about the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas-led attacks, and as CBC senior international correspondent Margaret Evans explains, they come just weeks before a pivotal election.

The repeated pleas to Netanyahu by families and friends of Israeli hostages held in Gaza to agree to a deal with Hamas for their early release rather than insisting on "total victory" first have left Israel with some of its deepest scars.

The deaths of more than 74,000 Palestinians in Israel’s war against Hamas — a figure from health officials in Gaza — have not been the subject of much debate in the mainstream of Israel's election campaign. But the country's increasing isolation on the world stage has.

Israeli lawyer and longtime peace campaigner Daniel Seidemann said it's as surprising to many Israelis as it is to outsiders that Netanyahu might stand a chance of returning to office given the allegations stacked up against him.

Daniel Seidemann, an Israeli lawyer and longtime peace campaigner, estimates Netanyahu still has strong, core support of about 30 per cent of the population. (CBC)

"It's a function of a number of things," he said in an interview from his Jerusalem office. "Number one, Netanyahu's hard-core supporters have to be described as a cult."

"Absolutely nothing that can be discovered about Netanyahu will pierce the armour of their devotion to the cult leader. That is probably about 30 per cent of Israel."

Netanyahu is currently being tried on allegations of corruption , including fraud, bribery and breach of trust. And he's steadfastly refused to appoint a commission of inquiry into the failings of Oct. 7, despite public pressure.

Some question reliability of Oct. 7 warnings

The IDI's Hermann said Netanyahu supporters contend that any leader could have made similar mistakes. In polling done by the institute , she said, 43 to 46 per cent of Jewish Israelis questioned whether the warnings delivered to Netanyahu were reliable.

Hermann said 60 per cent of those surveyed about what the prime minister did or didn't know believe the allegations have surfaced close to the election as part of an agenda to topple him.

"He is honest," Monel Bercovich said at a campaign event in Jerusalem on Friday, when asked why she backs Netanyahu.

Monel Bercovich says she's backing Netanyahu in the election because he's 'honest' and has taken a tough stance on Iran. (CBC)

She also mentioned his tough stand on Iran amid speculation that Israel might launch another round of strikes against it.

"To go to Iran and to do all the wars and all the things with [U.S. President Donald] Trump."

Hermann agrees with Seidemann that Netanyahu — nicknamed Bibi by those both for and against him — enjoys an unusual relationship with core supporters.

"Some of Netanyahu's voters actually love him," she said. "I mean it is something that comes from their stomach or their heart if you wish. [It's] a phenomenon which we don't have on the centre and left."

Rival vows Oct. 7 review

There's very little of a "left" left in Israeli politics, and much of the anti-Netanyahu side — or "change bloc," as it's known — arrayed against him would be described as centre-right and right.

Netanyahu's strongest challenger in the general election is former Israel Defence Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot , whose political party is called Yashar, which means "straight" or "honest" in Hebrew.

Hazan, of Hebrew University, said Eisenkot's military background will appeal to voters concerned about security, particularly in the face of what many Israelis view as an existential threat posed by Iran.

"In other words: the security of this country, keep us safe in our homes. That's what they're looking for. But essentially, his entire campaign has not been on security issues. It's been on social issues, that this country is hemorrhaging, that we need to unite."

Gadi Eisenkot, centre, leader of the Yashar party and a former Israeli military chief, visits the Western Wall in Jerusalem's Old City on Thursday. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)

Eisenkot, 66, joined Netanyahu's unity government in the days immediately after Oct. 7, but resigned eight months later.

His youngest son, a master sergeant in the Israeli military, was killed in Gaza during the war, and, unlike Netanyahu, he has pledged to create an Oct. 7 commission of inquiry if elected.

Ultra-orthodox conscription issue

Eisenkot has also distinguished himself from Netanyahu by making compulsory conscription for Israel's sizable ultra-Orthodox community a campaign issue.

Military service is mandatory in Israel for Jewish men and women once they reach 18. Until recently, the ultra-Orthodox — or Haredi — community enjoyed an exemption dating back to the founding of the state in 1948.

Israel’s Supreme Court refused to extend the exemption two years ago, despite Netanyahu's efforts. He's relied on the support of ultra-Orthodox coalition partners to stay in power over the years, and their vote will be key next week.

WATCH | How Haredi draft dodgers became a key Israeli election issue: How Haredi draft dodgers became a key Israeli election issue | Duration closed caption 5:11 CBC’s senior international correspondent Margaret Evans explains how draft dodging by members of the ultra-Orthodox — or Haredi — community has become one of the defining issues of the upcoming Israel election, sharpened by the Oct. 7 attacks.

But the exemption is a much harder sell for the rest of the country in the wake of Oct. 7.

"I think for the last few years, we saw how tough it is and how our security situation is not as secure as we thought," said 27-year-old Yonatan Lambert, who was sent to serve in Gaza and will not vote for Netanyahu.

"If you decide that you want or don't wanna be part of the army — or part of the country — you shouldn't get anything from the country," Lambert said, a reference to subsidies paid by the Israeli government to yeshivas, where ultra-Orthodox men study full time.

"[The ultra-Orthodox] know that they will never have it so good as they do under Netanyahu," said lawyer and peace campaigner Seidemann, a view he shares of Netanyahu's other coalition partners: hardline Jewish nationalists underpinning Israel's settlement expansion in the Israeli-occupied territories.

Military exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox — or Haredi — community are a much harder sell for the rest of the country in the wake of Oct. 7. (CBC)

'Total devotion of the right-wing settler base'

Israeli settlements, including in the occupied West Bank, are considered illegal under international law.

Images of increased violence by Israeli settlers attacking Palestinians and their property as they seek to bring in their annual olive harvest have horrified onlookers and increased Israel’s isolation internationally.

"In the past, Netanyahu, with all of his bluster, was risk averse," Seidemann said. "He was attentive to international engagement in ways that he did not usually disclose, but he was capable of exhibiting restraint.

"That's not the Netanyahu that we have now. He is in a semi-messianic disgruntled mode. He is fighting for his political life, and he has decided that the way he can survive politically is by having the total devotion of the right-wing settler base."

A campaign poster for Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel's national security minister, shows him superimposed over the images of shackled Palestinian prisoners on their knees. (CBC)

That base includes Itamar Ben-Gvir , a Jewish settler from Hebron convicted in the past of incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organization.

Appointed by Netanyahu as the country's national security minister, Ben-Gvir's campaign posters show him superimposed over the images of shackled Palestinian prisoners on their knees.

Seidemann likens the increase in land appropriation and settler attacks in the West Bank over the past month to an "end-of-season fire sale" ahead of the election.

"There's a sense that ... let's do whatever we can now, because it's an opportunity that may not repeat itself," he said. Then again, depending on Tuesday's results, it might.

World.title: This Nova Scotian just ran his first marathon. He trained for it by eating donairs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Growing up in Cape Breton, David Wadden thought donairs were fixtures at pizza shops worldwide.

It wasn't until he moved to Halifax that he learned the beloved official food of the city — spiced meat served on a pita with onions, tomatoes and a sweet garlicky sauce — was not a global thing. Well, not yet at least.

This realization, coupled with the fact that he couldn't name a favourite donair spot to friends visiting from out of town, got him thinking about how to incorporate a journey of donair discovery, exercise and raising money for charity.

"Thinking of exercise, I went to running, donair and marathon, kind of shove those two words together, and then once we had the name Donair-Athon … the ball really started to roll," said Wadden, 29.

Wadden ran and biked to 59 donair shops in the Halifax area this year to eat donairs, rate them and post videos about the experiences. He's raised more than $2,200 for Feed Nova Scotia doing so.

But that wasn't the hard part. After eating the donair, he faced the ungodly task of running or biking back home.

David Wadden rated the donairs on factors such as meat and pita quality, and tracked the results in a publicly available spreadsheet. He even weighed the donairs to calculate the price per pound. (Submitted by David Wadden)

This unorthodox training regimen resulted in Wadden running a 42.2-kilometre marathon two weeks ago at the Valley Harvest Marathon in Nova Scotia's Annapolis Valley.

Wadden said after eating the donairs, sometimes he felt great, sometimes not.

"There was the odd time where I felt better after the donair, I don't know why," he said. "But most of the time I was a little sluggish getting back out and running. I didn't have any incidents, which was nice. I kind of expected maybe more bathroom breaks needed or, heaven forbid, a throw-up."

While running after eating a donair is an achievement on its own, even more impressive is that Wadden did not have a background in running prior to this. He used to do indoor rock climbing, but had to find a new outlet after a shoulder injury.

Wadden has an innate curiosity. He used to post videos to YouTube of himself learning new skills, such as how to juggle or cook the perfect steak, so this project is an extension of that attitude.

A rotating spit of donair meat is seen at a King Of Donair restaurant in Halifax on Tuesday, Nov. 14, 2017. (Andrew Vaughan/The Canadian Press)

Wadden said he selected Feed Nova Scotia because he wanted something food-related that was local.

"I think it's the broader idea of helping the community," said Wadden. "I was lucky enough never to have those issues myself, but I always had family that … would fundraise for these different charities."

Thomas Coldwell, Feed Nova Scotia's director of philanthropy and engagement, said every year there are hundreds of "third-party events" where people like Wadden fundraise for the charity or hold food drives. He said they're important for the charity.

Coldwell said he's not sure if others have pitched donair-themed events to the charity.

"Well, I love a donair, but I'm not sure I could happily bike after eating one, so it's great to see someone like David who's using their skills and putting out wonderful videos showcasing the Halifax donair … and also to tie it in with food insecurity and support fundraising," said Coldwell.

Besides the out-of-pocket costs for the donairs at roughly $12 each, Wadden said he also had to buy running equipment. Despite the social media views, he said he hasn't made any money from the project.

Wadden said he came up with the idea for the project about a year ago. Before he could actually do the Donair-Athon, though, he had to spend a few months training to get ready for it, dealing with complications such as shin splints and knee pain.

How Wadden prepared for the marathon

Starting in February, he'd do one donair excursion a week. In March, he upped the frequency, running two days a week and throwing in a third donair trip by bike, eventually landing on running three days a week.

On the off days, he'd supplement the regimen with things like yoga or strength training. All told, he said he ran more than 500 kilometres and biked more than 300 kilometres through the Donair-Athon.

Wadden said the highlight of the venture was meeting with people at the donair shops and doing the marathon itself.

His least favourite part was the shin splints.

"They were not fun one bit," he said.

Prior to the Donair-Athon, Wadden said he only ate donairs once every couple of months, which explains why he couldn't suggest a favourite place to out-of-towners.

Wadden said he's had enough donairs for 2026, but might resume eating them in the new year.

Future marathons?

While he rules out doing another full marathon, a half-marathon may be in the works.

"I told myself once I finished this, I'm done [running]," said Wadden. "And now that I've finished the marathon, I really want to get back out there.

"I'm going to see if I can fit it in because I do want to keep doing other stuff, but I definitely have a new love for running that I didn't think I would get."

World.title: A polarized Brazil heads to presidential vote with economy, corruption top of mind
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

During a recent Bible study service in the Río de Janeiro neighbourhood of Vila Isabel, the congregation recited a prayer about God and being faithful.

Regina da Silva Andrade, 38, one of the congregants, said that while she believed God was in charge of the universe, Brazil's elected officials had a duty to care for the country's citizens.

"We have ... expectations that our country’s leadership would be concerned with meeting essential needs — such as health care and education —and that, at the very least, these areas would be properly cared for," she said.

Still undecided about who to vote for, Andrade said she was leaning toward Flávio Bolsonaro, the 45 year-old senator son of Jair Bolsonaro, the former Brazilian president convicted of plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

WATCH | Jair Bolsonaro's son now running for president: Brazil's former president gets 27 years for plotting a coup in 2022 | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 4:41 Former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro was sentenced yesterday to 27 years and three months in prison, hours after being convicted of plotting a coup to remain in power after losing the 2022 election. The Associated Press's Mauricio Savarese breaks down the case and the reaction from the public following his conviction.

Andrade said Flávio Bolsonaro was a better candidate than his father.

"Bolsonaro … may waver between one extreme and the other at times, but I see a genuine interest on his part in finding balance," she said.

"I don't know if he'll succeed, but I'm not particularly concerned — his father engaged in corruption to the point of ending up in prison."

Regina da Silva Andrade, 38, centre, said that while she believed God was in charge of the universe, Brazil's elected officials had a duty to care for the country's citizens. (Douglas Engle/CBC)

Presidential race 'never this close,' journalist says

Flávio Bolsonaro — campaigning on tax cuts, a hard line on crime and family values — emerged from the first round of voting on Oct. 4 in Brazil's presidential election with about 2.2 million more votes than Lula, the 80-year-old incumbent.

Recent polls have shown the race between the two candidates tightening.

"It's really a toss of a coin," said Pedro Doria, editor of MEIO media group in Río de Janeiro.

Still, Doria said no presidential candidate who came in second after the first round of voting has ever won an election since 1989 — when the current electoral system was put in place.

"But it was never this close. Flávio's difference against Lula was 1.9 percentile points. This is basically nothing."

Doria said that the Brazilian population is heavily polarized, and some voters are more motivated to vote against a candidate than in support of someone they believe in.

"A third of Lula's voters are not voting for Lula, they are voting against Bolsonaro," said Doria. "Half of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's voters are voting against Lula, not for Flávio."

Marsílea Gombata, a researcher with the University of Sao Paulo's International Relations Research Center, said frustrations around corruption and feelings of personal financial stagnation have driven many voters to cast ballots for Bolsonaro. (Courtesy of Marsílea Gombata)

Marsílea Gombata, a researcher with the University of Sao Paulo's International Relations Research Center, said frustrations around corruption and feelings of personal financial stagnation have driven many voters to cast ballots for Bolsonaro despite the actions of his father and the candidate's own record of controversy.

Bolsonaro has in the past been tied to paramilitary groups — he praised them in a two decade-old speech while a state deputy, and his office once employed the mother and wife of the founder of a paramilitary group linked to the killing of a human rights activist.

Bolsonaro's father's coup-plotting conviction — which included allegations there were plans to assassinate Lula — and subsequent 27-year sentence has had limited impact on Flávio Bolsonaro's support, said Gombata.

"We can see that it doesn't matter to people."

While Lula, who previously served two presidential terms between 2003 and 2011, strengthened and reintroduced social programs in his last term to help the poor such as Bolsa Familia, which provides conditional direct cash transfers to families, a large swath of the population has felt left out, said Gombata.

The lower middle class, where many work a second job in the gig economy, has felt "betrayed" by Lula's promises of prosperity that, they believe, never materialized for them.

"They were hoping for a better life, for their children, but it didn't happen and today life is more difficult," said Gombata.

Bolsonaro's promises of tax cuts for fuel, electricity and transport, as well as reductions in government spending appeals to this segment of the population, she said.

Paulo Coelho, who runs the Cavacas Sporting Goods store in Río de Janeiro, 64, said he’s voting on the economy Sunday and his ballot will go to Bolsonaro. (Douglas Engle/CBC)

The 2014 Operation Carwash investigation, which ensnared several top officials in Lula's Workers Party and Lula himself — until the Supreme Court overturned his corruption-related conviction in 2021 — still casts a long shadow, Gombata said.

"We are still living those consequences … the theme of corruption is a big one."

Both candidates facing corruption probes

Bolsonaro has been side-swiped during the election campaign by his own corruption allegations.

It recently emerged that Bolsonaro requested and received millions of dollars for a documentary about Jair Bolosonaro from a key player in a major bank fraud case. Flávio is also under investigation in relation to the case.

However, Lula has faced his own troubles. His son is under a separate influence peddling and corruption probe ordered by the Supreme Court, Reuters reported.

Paulo Coelho, 64, who runs the Cavacas Sporting Goods store in Río de Janeiro, said he’s voting on the economy Sunday and his ballot will go to Bolsonaro.

"Everyone is worried about slowing economic activity in Brazil," he said.

"Flávio Bolsonaro has an economic plan and vision that I am more aligned with."

The Brazil election's U.S. factor

Aline Vieria, 38, who runs a community dance program for women, said she's voting for Lula because she worries a Bolsonaro government will sever the social safety nets that have kept many people from misery.

"I have three children, ages 15, 11 and five, and I don’t want to jeopardize their future," she said.

"There is a real risk to our population given the stances they've taken on social issues."

Aline Vieria, 38, who runs a community dance program for women, said she's voting for Lula because she worries that a Bolsonaro government will lead to a severing of social safety nets. (Douglas Engel/CBC)

Solange Marquez, vice-president of policy with the Canadian Council for the Americas, says Sunday's results could impact Brazil's relationship with the United States.

The close relationship between the Bolsonaro family — Flávio is one of three brothers — and the U.S. administration of Donald Trump could lead to an escalation of U.S. military involvement in South America through boots on the ground in Brazil in joint security operations against armed drug trafficking groups, said Marquez.

"I think [Flávio] Bolsonaro is eager to open the door to Donald Trump in exchange for a better economic, commercial relationship with Washington."

WATCH | From last summer: Trump weighs in: Trump threatens 50% tariff on Brazil over Bolsonaro trial | Duration closed caption 2:58 U.S. President Donald Trump singled out Brazil for import taxes of 50 per cent, saying the trial of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is charged with trying to overturn his 2022 election loss, 'should not be taking place.'

U.S. boots on Brazilian soil is something that worries retiree Carlos Vitor, 65, who voted twice for the elder Bolsonaro. This time, he says, he's voting for Lula.

"I’m afraid that the United States might invade Brazil because of the drug traffickers," he said.

Vitor said a Flávio win will magnify the deep divisions that currently exist within the country and possibly lead to violence.

"The left, they're going to fight. If Flávio wins, they're going to fight," he said.

"Will this place turn into a civil war? For sure."
