World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: María Corina Machado returns to Venezuela after ten months abroad and seven failed attempts
World.content:
María Corina Machado returns to Venezuela after ten months abroad and seven failed attempts

25th Sunday, October 2026 - 17:08 UTC Full article

Machado returns to a country transformed since Nicolás Maduro’s removal from power following the US military operation in January

Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado returned to Venezuela on Sunday after nearly ten months abroad and at least seven failed attempts to go back. “I am here. With you,” she wrote on X, shortly before reappearing at a Mass at the Divina Pastora sanctuary in Barquisimeto, Lara state, surrounded by supporters.

Former presidential candidate Edmundo González confirmed her return: “I am thrilled to announce that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil. Today is an important day for Venezuelans,” he wrote, adding that he too would return “very soon”. How she entered the country has not been disclosed. US network Newsmax said she came in from Colombia, while Spain’s ABC newspaper said her return was made possible by a diplomatic operation involving several countries.

Machado left Venezuela in early December 2025, after more than a year in hiding, to collect the Nobel Prize in Oslo. Between June and September she tried to return at least seven times, by boat, overland and on commercial and private flights from the United States, Panama and Curaçao. Several media outlets reported that US officials blocked some of those attempts, which President Donald Trump denied. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said she could return “like any Venezuelan citizen”.

Machado returns to a country transformed since Nicolás Maduro’s removal from power following the US military operation in January. The government of acting President Delcy Rodríguez has been negotiating since August with Dinorah Figuera, president of the National Assembly elected in 2015, a roadmap that includes renewing the Supreme Court and the National Electoral Council and holding regional elections before the presidential vote, a sequence Machado has rejected. The presidential election still has no date.

The government says it had not vetoed her return, although it accuses her of having promoted the US intervention, and Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello had warned he had “a surprise” in store for her. Machado, barred from the 2024 election, backed González’s candidacy, whom tally sheets collected by the opposition showed as the winner despite the victory claimed by the chavista government. An AtlasIntel poll for Bloomberg in August gave her 57.4% of voting intentions.

World.title: Montevideo cements its role as a staging port for Antarctic expeditions
World.content:
Montevideo cements its role as a staging port for Antarctic expeditions

25th Sunday, October 2026 - 13:32 UTC Full article

The vessels that arrived were the Expedition, Ocean Albatros, Ocean Nova, Sylvia Earle, Ocean Explorer, Seaventure and Sea Spirit, ships with reinforced hulls equipped to sail in polar waters

The port of Montevideo welcomed seven polar expedition ships this week at the start of the Antarctic season, reinforcing the Uruguayan capital’s role as a staging point for cruise ships heading to the frozen continent.

The vessels that arrived were the Expedition, Ocean Albatros, Ocean Nova, Sylvia Earle, Ocean Explorer, Seaventure and Sea Spirit, ships with reinforced hulls equipped to sail in polar waters. In Montevideo they carry out crew changes, take on provisions and drinking water and undergo repairs before starting their itineraries.

According to Uruguay’s National Ports Administration, the Expedition completed part of its preparation in Montevideo and embarked 123 passengers, in an operation overseen by the port captain, Luis Varela. Ruben Jokas, head of shipping agency Velmaren, said some passengers fly into Montevideo and stay in the city before boarding, generating demand for accommodation, restaurants, transport and shopping as well as port services.

From Montevideo, the Ocean Albatros will continue to Buenos Aires, while the Ocean Nova and Ocean Explorer will head to Ushuaia, the main departure port for Antarctica.

World.title: Falklands Government reminds 2026 Census latecomers to submit returns
World.content:
Falklands Government reminds 2026 Census latecomers to submit returns

25th Sunday, October 2026 - 09:37 UTC Full article

All households are legally required to complete the census

The Falkland Islands Government (FIG) has reminded residents who have not yet completed their 2026 Census to do so as soon as possible.

All households are legally required to take part unless exempt, and residents are encouraged to submit their returns promptly and to contact the Census Team if they need assistance. Forms in Spanish and Tagalog are available on request.

What the census covers

The questionnaire is divided into three parts. Part 1 collects information about the household and must be completed by every household. Residents who have registered other properties that will be unoccupied on census night must also fill in Part 1 for each of those properties.

Part 2 collects information about individuals. It must be completed by, or on behalf of, every person normally resident in the household, including students currently overseas, people away from the islands on holiday or work trips, and those receiving medical treatment overseas.

Part 3 covers temporary visitors. If anyone in the household is visiting the Falklands temporarily, for three months or less, the household should complete this part on their behalf.

The Census Team can be reached on 28422 or 28437, by email at census2026@sec.gov.fk, or in person at the Policy Office, Secretariat, in Stanley.

World.title: Defense and Falklands, PM Burnham call with Chilean president Kast
World.content:
Defense and Falklands, PM Burnham call with Chilean president Kast

25th Sunday, October 2026 - 09:36 UTC Full article

The leaders began by outlining their shared ambitions to strengthen the two nations’ relationship including on defense, security, science and trade.

Ten Downing Street reported on Friday that Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke to the President of Chile, Jose Antonio Kast on Friday 23 October.

The leaders began by outlining their shared ambitions to strengthen the two nations’ relationship including on defense, security, science and trade.

On defense, the leaders agreed on the need for the UK and Chile to work together to modernize defense capabilities.

The Prime Minister also raised the UK’s interests in ensuring the Falkland Islanders retain the ability to exercise the right of self-determination.

The two leaders discussed the growing cultural, scientific and people to people links between the two countries, and the positive impact this has had on investment and infrastructure opportunities.

The leaders recognized the untapped trade opportunities between the two nations and agreed on the need for closer trading.

They both look forward to speaking again.

Regarding defense, next December Chile will be holding its annual Naval Expo, focused on the new concepts for modern naval warfare, and air and seas power, based on drones and un-crewed systems which the Royal Navy is already working on and has been identified as the Hybrid Navy.

For the event in Chile, a naval delegation from UK has been announced headed by Retired Admiral, former First Sea Lord and Chief of the Defense Staff, Sir Antony Radakin who will be lecturing on Lessons for Industry from Contemporary Conflicts.

Likewise two academics from the renowned British RUSI think tank (Royal United Service Institute), John Griffiths and Dr. Andrew Gee will also be participating in the conferences event.

World.title: Trump’s favorite president and Argentina’s Economic Chainsaw Massacre
World.content:
Trump’s favorite president and Argentina’s Economic Chainsaw Massacre

25th Sunday, October 2026 - 09:34 UTC Full article

Milei and his chainsaw-wielding policies have established himself as the darling of the far right.

By Jeremy Adelman



Argentine President Javier Milei may currently be a lynchpin in US President Donald Trump’s geo-economic vision for Latin America; but he could soon become its weak link. With elections coming next year, he has achieved an economic recovery and relative price stability by driving millions of his people into destitution.

BUENOS AIRES— Nearly three years after Javier Milei became Argentina’s president, the chainsaw-wielding free-marketeer has established himself as the darling of the far right. Brazil’s right-wing presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, is promising an economic policy that would follow Milei’s lead, and US President Donald Trump calls him his “favorite president.” Last year, Trump extended Argentina an unprecedented $20 billion currency swap line to halt its currency’s free fall on the eve of legislative elections, and the gambit worked. Milei’s party won a surprising victory.

More than a mere symbol or role model for the far right, Milei plays a crucial role in Trump’s new “Shield of the Americas,” a security umbrella designed to ward off US rivals and turn Latin America into a resource-rich hinterland of US-compliant partners. But since Milei’s contributions to Trump’s hemispheric order depend on Argentina’s economic performance, one must ask how MAGA’s South American poster child has fared.

The “Chainsaw Plan” (Plan Motosierra) that Milei unveiled in June 2022 was more than a means to halt hyperinflation. The larger goal was to squeeze the life out of a public sector that had come to be seen as a source of political patronage, and to make Argentina great again as a primary goods exporter. This vision happily aligns with the Trump administration’s geo-economic worldview. Investments in lithium fields in the country’s north and hydrocarbons in Patagonia have fueled an economic recovery and bolstered Argentina’s strategic importance to the Shield of the Americas.

Meanwhile, the country has been plastered with billboards declaring that the Malvinas (better known as the Falkland Islands) belong to Argentina, not to the United Kingdom. Milei has no problem pandering to populist nationalism while also nursing claims to newly discovered South Atlantic oil fields.

But the immediate success of the Chainsaw Plan rests on austerity. It was Milei who provided the playbook for Elon Musk’s short-lived (and far from successful) DOGE effort. Upon taking office, he halved the number of Argentine government ministries to nine, froze public works, fired 51.218 federal employees (plus an additional 23,000 from state companies), and slashed welfare spending. Before long, chronic deficits turned into budget surpluses. After years of volatility and runaway price growth, the inflation rate fell from roughly 250% to 30%, and the economy bounced back.

In addition to reining in prices, Milei’s cuts drove capital into the private sector as his government offered tax incentives to foreign investors and promised a vast new private insurance regime to replace state functions. Austerity compelled workers to follow the money, triggering a flight to for-profit firms in the health, security, and education sectors. Argentina used to have world-class laboratories backed by its national science agency (CONICET); but following salary reductions and budget cuts in research, over 10% of CONICET scientists and technicians—primarily biologists, geologists, agronomists, and physicists under 40—have left for the private sector.

But the informal sector absorbs most displaced workers. The night before public trash collection, throngs of Argentines walk the streets looking for recyclable metal and paper. At dawn, caravans of shopping carts and horse-drawn carriages haul the scrap to depots where scavengers are rewarded with a few pesos.

Scavenging is but one activity in the informal sector—a traditional cushion in a labor market short on social protections. Without labor contracts, unemployment benefits, or pension contributions, informality serves as many Argentines’ only safety net. Once in it, workers tend not to return to formal jobs, with 40–50% of the labor force now surviving on precarious work.

Young people no longer hope for public-sector jobs or even formal work, and almost 70% of Argentines between 18 and 25 toil in informal jobs. When I taught recently at a university in a downwardly mobile district of outer Buenos Aires, all my students had jobs, but not promising prospects. If they were not teachers working for near-minimum wage, they were street vendors, Uber drivers, domestic workers, or food and medicine couriers.

In other words, Argentina’s great recovery is full of misery. By early 2026, urban poverty reached 32.3%, with extreme deprivation afflicting over 7% of the population. The extent of the destitution is staggering, especially when one considers how much of it has been masked by the equally staggering growth in personal indebtedness. Fintech apps, digital wallets, local moneylenders, emergency credit cards, and other products designed to help poor families make ends meet have proliferated. Delinquency rates are soaring. With almost six million Argentines at least 90 days behind on debt payments, central-bank officials are struggling to forestall a tidal wave of petty bankruptcies.

The chainsaw will continue to grind away. Driving inflation down from 30% will require more austerity, but there is less to cut. New commodity frontiers generate growth, but not many jobs, and poor households are running out of options. Yet Milei rushes on. The thought of government intervention to promote economic recovery is, in his characteristically nuanced estimation, “Keynesian garbage.”

Time is running out. With elections coming in 2027, Milei may not be able to count on a free-spending Trump stopgap. His political base is not to be dismissed, but it is dwarfed by the legions of people slipping into a low-income, low-productivity trap. Milei may be a lynchpin in Trump’s geo-economic vision for now; but he could soon become its weak link.

Jeremy Adelman is Director of the Global History Lab at the University of Cambridge and the author, most recently, of The Capitalist Era: The Making—and Unmaking—of the Global Mind (Princeton University Press, 2026).

World.title: Next Wednesday, Chancellor Healey delivers the Budget statement, PM Burnham’s first
World.content:
Next Wednesday, Chancellor Healey delivers the Budget statement, PM Burnham’s first

25th Sunday, October 2026 - 09:00 UTC Full article

The previous Labour Chancellor, Rachel Reeves holding the famous red Budget box

Each year UK’s Chancellor of the Exchequer makes the Budget statement to the House of Commons outlining the state of the economy and the Government's proposals for changes to taxation. The government of PM Andy Burnham has announced that the Budget will take place this week on Wednesday 28 October 2026 and delivered by Chancellor MP John Healey. The last Budget was delivered Wednesday, 26 November 2025.

The Budget, or Financial Statement, outlines the nation’s finances and the Government’s proposals for changes to taxation. The Budget also includes forecasts for the economy by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

The Budget and the Finance Bill are usually annual events, in part because income tax and corporation tax are annual taxes which have to be renewed by legislation each year. By contrast, most UK taxes including all indirect taxes, petroleum revenue tax and taxes on capital are ‘permanent’.

In election years, after a change of Government, a Budget will also usually be introduced by the incoming Chancellor of the Exchequer, even if the outgoing Chancellor has already delivered one.

Some measures, such as any changes to the rates of duty on alcohol and tobacco, come into effect on Budget day or soon after.

The power to make these changes on an interim basis, before the Finance Bill is passed, comes from the House of Commons approving a motion for the provisional collection of these taxes. After the Chancellor finishes the speech, but before the Leader of the Opposition responds, the Chairman of Ways and Means puts a single motion to the Commons asking for agreement to these changes.

This is called the 'Provisional Collection of Taxes' and is by convention agreed to by the House, meaning that the changes can come into effect at 6pm on Budget day.

Traditionally the Leader of the Opposition, rather than the Shadow Chancellor, replies to the Budget Speech.

The Budget is usually followed by four days of debate on the Budget Resolutions, these are the tax measures announced in the Budget. Each day of debate is led by a different Cabinet minister and focuses on a particular theme of the Budget. The Shadow Chancellor makes their response on the day after the Budget statement during the Budget debates.

Budget Resolutions can come into effect immediately if the House of Commons agree to them at the end of the four days of debate but they require the Finance Bill to give them permanent legal effect.

A new Finance Bill is presented to Parliament each year; it enacts the proposals for taxation made by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in the Budget statement and brings them into law.

Once the House of Commons has agreed the Budget Resolutions, the Finance Bill starts its passage through Parliament in the same way as any other bill.

The House of Lords has a limited role in respect of Finance Bills. The House of Commons has the sole right to initiate and amend bills whose main purpose is to levy taxes or authorize expenditure.

The House of Lords will have a second reading debate on the Finance Bill but they will not consider the Bill clause by clause and will not amend the Bill.

The Commons Treasury Select Committee is a cross-party committee of MPs whose role is to scrutinize the work of the Treasury.

Following each Budget statement the Treasury Committee conducts an inquiry into the Government’s proposals, gathering evidence from expert witnesses and publishing a report with its conclusions and recommendations.

The Government then produces a report in response to the Committee’s findings, often with a contribution from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Some history on the red Budget box The word Budget comes from an old French word ‘bougette’ meaning little bag. It was customary to bring the statement on financial policy to the House of Commons in a leather bag. The modern equivalent of the bag is the red despatch box or Budget box.

The distinctive red Budget Box which Chancellors used to carry their speech from 11 Downing Street to the House of Commons was in use for over one hundred consecutive years. The wooden box was hand-crafted for William Ewart Gladstone around 1860. It was lined with black satin and covered with scarlet leather.

Lord Callaghan was the first Chancellor to break with tradition in 1965 when he used a new box. In July 1997 Gordon Brown became the second Chancellor to use a new box for the Budget.

George Osborne used the Gladstone Box for his first Budget in 2010 but used a new box in 2011.

Traditionally the Chancellor is photographed on Budget day on the steps of 11 Downing Street, the official residence of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, holding up the Budget Box.

By tradition, the Chancellor, unlike Ministers at the despatch box at any other time of the year, may drink alcohol during the Budget Speech if they wish.

World.title: Brazil chooses between Lula and Bolsonaro in its tightest runoff in recent history
World.content:
Brazil chooses between Lula and Bolsonaro in its tightest runoff in recent history

25th Sunday, October 2026 - 07:02 UTC Full article

Bolsonaro won the first round on October 4 with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, a result that confounded the polls

Nearly 160 million Brazilians are called to vote on Sunday in the presidential runoff, in which President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, seeks a fourth term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. The two arrive level: the latest Datafolha poll gives each 50% of valid votes.

Polling stations open at 8 a.m. and close at 5 p.m. Brasília time across the country, and the electronic voting system allows results to be known the same night. Voting is compulsory for those aged 18 to 70 and optional for older voters and for 16- and 17-year-olds. Runoffs for governor are also being held in six states.

Bolsonaro won the first round on October 4 with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, a result that confounded the polls. Since Brazil returned to direct presidential elections in 1989, no candidate who came second in the first round has gone on to win. Both campaigns have concentrated on mobilising the roughly 33 million voters who stayed away then.

Lula, of the Workers’ Party, has defended the continuity of his government and stepped up announcements in the final stretch, including the 15% increase in the Bolsa Família social programme and the approval of the 40-hour working week. Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party, backed by almost all of the right, has focused on security and the cost of living, and promises to cut public spending while maintaining social programmes. He has also pledged to pardon his father, sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, and has announced a constitutional reform to “re-democratise Brazil”, according to the newspaper El País.

Whoever wins will govern with a Congress in which the Liberal Party won its largest-ever bloc in the Chamber of Deputies in October. The campaign has also been marked by the legal dispute with Meta, which both candidates accuse of unequal treatment on its platforms.

The election is being closely watched in the region. Argentine President Javier Milei has backed Bolsonaro and accused Lula of seeking to “steal” the election, while the Brazilian president used Milei as an argument against his rival in both campaign debates. Lula turns 81 on Tuesday.

World.title: Burnham tells Trump of the “economic consequences” of Argentina’s Falklands measures
World.content:
Burnham tells Trump of the “economic consequences” of Argentina’s Falklands measures

24th Saturday, October 2026 - 08:32 UTC Full article

Trump has said in recent weeks that the US position of neutrality on sovereignty over the archipelago is under review

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham set out to US President Donald Trump on Friday “the economic consequences that Argentina’s coercive measures have for the United Kingdom and the United States”, in a phone call focused on the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, according to a Downing Street statement quoted by the EFE news agency. Burnham reiterated the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources.

The call came a day after US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau acknowledged in Buenos Aires that Washington is closely watching the impact Argentina’s National Sovereignty Defence bill could have on its companies. The bill, still stalled in the Chamber of Deputies, extends sanctions to affiliates, shareholders, financiers and suppliers of companies operating in the islands. Trump has said in recent weeks that the US position of neutrality on sovereignty over the archipelago is under review.

The same day, Burnham spoke with Chilean President José Antonio Kast, to whom he raised “the UK’s interest in ensuring that Falkland Islanders retain the ability to exercise their right to self-determination”, according to Downing Street. The two agreed on the need to work together to modernise their defence capabilities and that there are “untapped trade opportunities” between their countries. Kast reiterated Chile’s support for Argentina’s sovereignty claim during a state visit to Buenos Aires in April, while his government described the new commercial route between Punta Arenas and Stanley in September as “a business between private parties”.

Argentina launched sanctions proceedings in September against dozens of people and companies linked to Sea Lion, operated by Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, and asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to the project. The tribunal will hold its hearing on November 10 and 11 in Hamburg. The United Kingdom has announced measures to protect its companies from Argentine sanctions and maintains that the islanders’ decision to remain British, expressed by 99.8% of voters in the 2013 referendum, must be respected.

World.title: Mezcal production, Mother Earth and the enduring spirit of the Zapotecs
World.content:
Nestled between the Pan-American Highway and the Rio Grande, all along the Ruta Caminos del Mezcal, exist hundreds of palenques, or small farms that carry the ancient practice of mezcal production. Tourists come in droves to watch the mules pull the great stone wheel of the tahona in slow circles, crushing roasted agave before it is fermented, distilled and enjoyed.

I had the pleasure of learning about this age-old practice firsthand, a practice that existed long before it became a spectacle for curious travelers, while living and volunteering at one of these fabled farms.

How community and ecology sustain mezcal production

The land once belonged to the Zapotecs, an ancient civilization known for its profound connection to the natural and spiritual worlds. Inhabiting the land for more than 2,500 years, the Zapotecs were first overtaken by the Aztecs beginning in the late 15th century, and subsequently by the infamous Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés.

Although the group suffered decimation from disease and invasion, around 500,000 Zapotec speakers remain in the Oaxaca region. That air of tradition survives in the people and culture of Oaxaca today: in the emphasis on community, in farming and ecological initiatives, in spiritual practice and myth, and most notably, in mezcal.

Oaxaca, the mezcal capital of the world, is also known for its ecological initiatives and Earth-centered culture, and remains a place of continual education and philosophy for anyone passionate about a lifestyle that benefits the planet.

Indigenous and mestizo communities own nearly 82% of the state’s 6.1 million hectares of forest, managing them collectively rather than as private property. Zapotec is still spoken in several municipalities, and local mythology and spiritually driven land stewardship make the state an example of an ecologically sustainable community.

First sip goes to the Earth and ancestors

In Zapotec tradition, mezcal brings people closer to the spirits. Across Oaxaca, it is common to pour the first sip for the thirsty earth and for ancestors long gone.

As the glasses are raised and the offering given, participants speak the word “Dixeebe” over the anointed ground. Dixeebe is a Zapotec salutation used to express deep reverence for the spirit of Earth. The gesture is small, but it is a daily reminder to put the needs of the Earth, and of those no longer living on it, before one’s own. Repeated across a community, it builds a culture devoted to a better planet for all of us.

This inherent reverence and respect for the Earth reverberates through small, traditional mezcal-producing palenques across the Oaxacan region.

1 of 13

Protecting the land is protecting mezcal

For Miguel Ángel Zamora, mezcal maestro at Casa Cabrón in Unión Zapata, protecting the land and protecting mezcal are inextricably linked. Casa Cabrón is one of many family-run palenques in Unión Zapata that remain true to the traditional culture of mezcal production.

Regarding his production process, Zamora says, “That connection (to the Earth) is so important for life in general, and can also be achieved through mezcal. But first, we must be conscious of producing it in a conscious way.”

He goes on to say, “We must care for Mother Earth, because from her flows the medicine that heals our soul, mind, body and life.”

‘Revealing a bit of life’s magic’

The mezcal production process begins on monthly cycles.

During harvest day, jimadores use machetes to cut and carve the agave plants’ core and prepare them for pickup. After the batch is cut and ready, workers from the palenque or neighboring farms retrieve the haul from the mountains and bring it back to the palenques for production.

“For me, producing mezcal means revealing a bit of life’s magic, the magic of transformation,” Zamora says. “It means showing the world that processes rooted in great love and respect for Mother Earth foster life, enjoyment, bliss and joy.”

The following day the crew and I headed back to the harvesting site promptly at 4:45 a.m. to pick up the agave and deliver it. The trip to the Sierra Mixe mountains was a generous three hours, even with our skilled, quick driver.

As we maneuvered the mountains’ impressive turns, the men talked of the prior night’s full moon, healthy horses and newly bought motorcycles. My traveling companions would point out edible plants, dangerous cacti or friends’ palenques, all the while passing snacks over my shoulder.

Once we arrived at the agave harvesting site, beverages were shared over small coolers, while the workers formed assembly lines — one man lifted the cut-down plant, tossed it to the next, and finally threw it into the back of the exporting truck.

Despite the physically demanding work and intense heat, there was no shortage of laughter. It was easy to mistake our hard work for a friendly reunion.

Navigating the tradition-modernity divide

Although larger mezcal corporations have pitched their tent along the mezcal route in recent years, family-run mezcal farms remain, with their beliefs intact and traditions upheld. Contrasts between old and new, nature and machines, are everywhere in Oaxaca. Local ruins exist amongst modern towns. Spanish churches are built upon ancient Zapotec temples.

Nowhere is this divide clearer than at the Church of San Pablo in Mitla. An ancient Zapotec ceremonial site, this once-great temple was torn down and rebuilt by Spanish Dominican friars, turning the structure into a Catholic institution. However, the original Zapotec foundations remain, creating a haunting visual representation of religious syncretism within the region and the enduring Indigenous presence.

As I walked through the ruins, our guide, a local Zapotec historian and teacher, led us past fallen walls and shrunken tombs that once sheltered a people defined by their relationship to the natural world. Spirals of life and death decorated the low-hanging frames, and old women passed, the numinous melody of the Zapotec language drifting in their wake.

We had brought our guide freshly distilled mezcal to taste, and he insisted we pour the first sip for the thirsty ground and the ancestors. We stood together, surrounded by the imposing walls of the temple’s spiritual resilience, and poured the first sip of mezcal onto the ancient stone floors.

We saluted using the Zapotec word dixeebe, while remembering all those who had been at this very spot before us.

The Zapotec civilization may have been nearly lost to time, but its beliefs and the spirit of its people live on in Oaxaca and, evidently, around the world, carried in the smoky, sultry, handmade spirit of mezcal.

Abigail Rose is a journalist, archaeologist and storyteller with a hands-on, in-the-field approach to journalism. She reports on local environmental initiatives, cultural stories and frontline conflict through writing, photography and video. Her work has taken her across Colombia, Peru, Oman, Greece, Mexico, Ecuador, Germany, Italy and the U.S., with her next project bringing her to Oaxaca, Mexico.

World.title: Mexico Well-Read: A review of Sofía Robleda’s ‘The Other Moctezuma Girls’
World.content:
Anyone who has stood in Mexico City’s Zócalo has felt the weight of history; beneath the cathedral and the crowds lie Tenochtitlán and the blood and bones of conquest. The city has spent the succeeding five centuries deciding which parts of that story to tell. The usual cast is familiar: Moctezuma, Cortés, Cuauhtémoc and a Malinche as contested now as she was in 1519.

Rarely, however, does anyone linger on Tecuichpoch, Moctezuma’s favored daughter, baptized Isabel. She was consort to two Mexica emperors, Cuitláhuac and Cuauhtémoc, bore a daughter to Cortés, and later married three other Spaniards. Her life ran through nearly every famous name of the Conquest, yet she barely registers in the popular telling.

‘A disturbing tapestry’

Robleda decided to address that lack in her new novel, “The Other Moctezuma Girls,” an ambitious, often moving romp across history and the fascinating cultural geography of the Valley of Mexico.

The story opens in Tenochtitlán in 1551, 30 years after the Spanish Conquest, as Tecuichpoch’s will is read aloud after her death. Her daughter Isabel suspects that a second account of her mother’s life may be hidden, chapter by chapter. The clues to that inheritance are found in a disturbing tapestry bequeathed to Isabel and her younger sister in the will. Isabel sets out to follow them with her favorite siblings and a handsome young cook.

Alongside Isabel’s journey runs her mother’s own testimony, delivered in the first person by a woman who knows her time is short:

“Moctezuma, Cuauhtemoc, Cortés, Malintzin … they reshaped the order of the entire world. They may be dead, but by God, they are known. Yet no one but you will know me. I may be mentioned in passing as the child, the wife, the mistress … Listen to me, rambling on. Trying to carve out a pinprick of light in the darkness these people have cast over my life. It is very difficult, for I was also taught not to exalt myself, not to seek attention, lest I be judged, or mocked, or worse, publicly shamed. As my mother would say, Tlacoqualli in monequi — moderation is a must.”

Nearing death, Tecuichpoch wants to be known; she declares that she will not die silent. In a line that could serve as the book’s thesis, she observes that “men would leave us nameless, if they could.” That premise gives the novel real moral force.

‘Pure adventure’

Tecuichpoch recalls being married off three times by the age of 12. She was raised, as Nahua women of the age were, to keep her face serene, and she credits that discipline with her survival. The empress describes her father’s love as a weapon that cut both ways: She was Moctezuma’s cherished child, and he still handed her to his enemies. Yet she insists he was neither fool nor coward, and that he read the Spanish correctly, as men rather than gods, and as the vanguard of an innumerable and therefore unstoppable horde. It is a humane portrait, and it lets Moctezuma be a father without excusing him.

The domestic details do much of the work. There is the tank of axolotls that Tecuichpoch kept in her father’s zoo, the pranks she played on her father’s other wives, and the beloved brother who collected obsidian and volcanic stones in a wooden box. Anyone who has wandered the Museo Nacional de Antropología will understand why these touches matter. The Mexica are usually presented as a catalog of gods, glyphs and sacrifices, while here they are real people with siblings, grudges and favorite pets. Tecuichpoch’s prose is formal and lightly ornate, sprinkled with Nahuatl as well as Spanish.

Her daughter’s half of the book is more conventional but livelier. One of Isabel’s siblings, Catina, lost her hearing after an illness, and the siblings communicate through sign language, a welcome touch that keeps the teens from becoming a mere chorus of clue-solvers. The quest itself is pure adventure. It takes the young people through the viceregal court and then the chinampas of Xochimilco, into tunnels beneath the ancient pyramids of Teotihuacán, and even up the icy slopes of Iztaccíhuatl as nearby Popocatépetl threatens to erupt.

A highly entertaining mix of history and drama

Since Robleda is writing about a woman forced to live in two worlds at once, it is fitting that the book itself straddles these two modes. While guiding us through an exciting adventure — a deadly scavenger hunt — she also provides fascinating historical information about the colonial caste system, constraints on women, slavery and the lasting consequences of conquest. The country’s mestizo identity, after all, began in the negotiations, marriages and coercions that Tecuichpoch lived through.

Robleda assigns a high degree of respect to la Malinche, or Malintzin, from Tecuichpoch, who is said to have admired her spirit, her brilliance, and the long game this noblewoman-turned-slave-turned-noblewoman managed to play:

“(Malintzin), too, had been reshaped. Cortés had married her off to another of his captains, Juan Jaramillo, and she was no longer a slave but a free noblewoman again. This is what she had desired most in the whole world. Freedom for herself and her children—the young son she’d had with Cortés and Jaramillo’s newborn girl in her arms, who were now peers of the New World aristocracy.”

“The Other Moctezuma Girls” is not a scholarly reckoning, and it does not pretend to be. It is a novel of reclamation, intent on sharing the story of this utterly fascinating woman, the last Mexica empress. It is best suited to readers who enjoy their history with a mystery, a map and a pounding pulse. Take it with you on your next visit to Mexico City, and you may find yourself absorbing the history around you more energetically.

Ann Marie Jackson is a book editor and the award-winning author of “The Broken Hummingbird.” She lives in San Miguel de Allende and can be reached through her website: annmariejacksonauthor.com.

Oaxaca held its first Afro Guelaguetza in the coastal community of Chacahua Isla, bringing together 12 delegations to celebrate Afro-Mexican heritage through music, masked dances and traditional performances. World.title: Full speed ahead: The 39th Carrera Panamericana lives up to its billing
World.content:
“Mexico is the only place in the world where you can pass the police while going 180 mph, and they’ll smile and wave at you,” said Jan Bednar, a professional race car driver who made his debut in Mexico. “I love it. I’m having the best time.”

A few days prior, Bednar had arrived in Mexico from Czechia to compete in the legendary La Carrera Panamericana, or the Pan-American Race.

The Czech driver brought a restored 1969 BMW 3.0 CS that once competed in the Pan-Am over a decade ago. He even gathered the original team that had once raced in Mexico with the same vehicle — a classic German speedster that he said he found collecting dust in a forlorn garage in Eastern Europe. He was inspired when, after asking around, he found out about its former days in the Pan-Am.

Bednar was one of many international motorists from 15 countries to have saved up enough resources — upwards of $75,000 — to race in the 39th edition of La Carrera Panamericana.

A deadly origin story on the open highway

The race has developed a notorious reputation as one of the most dangerous, even deadly, open-road endurance rallies in the world. It launched in 1950 as part of an initiative from the Mexican government to highlight its completion of the Pan-American Highway.

The highway itself, which spans 19,000 miles, was proposed by the United States as a railroad in 1889. In 1923, that idea evolved into an automobile thoroughfare and was revisited at the International Conference of American States in Santiago, Chile.

It took 13 years for the 21 involved nations to sign on to build their respective sections, a sprawling agreement finalized at the Convention on the Pan-American Highway in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

In 1936, the highway — heralded as an international diplomatic success — announced the completion of its first section from Laredo, Texas, to Mexico City. Eventually, Mexico became the first country to finish its border-to-border commitment, prompting the idea for the inaugural Pan-Am race.

The race has since had a controversial, albeit exhilarating, history that brings professional racers, amateurs and hobbyists to Mexico for the landmark event. Known for its high death toll, with more than 30 fatalities in the first five years of its existence, the race was canceled in 1955 and remained dormant until 1988, when it returned in a modernized and regulated format.

A modern course winding through mountain passes

Today, the course extends from Chiapas to Chihuahua, covering eight states and nearly 2,400 miles for a seven-day haul across Mexico’s public roads. It is sectioned into timed portions and various classifications.

While Mexican road conditions have significantly improved since the 1950s, the race is still seen as a perilous task and offers a highly coveted trophy.

After kicking off on Friday, Oct. 16, in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the 50 registered crews and their vehicles — mostly vintage Porsches, Fords, Studebakers and Chevrolets — flock northward along the coast of Veracruz and up to the state’s port city before banking inland and ascending up the rainy highway into the Sierra Madre mountains toward Puebla.

The 100 drivers made a colorful pit stop in Xalapa, where hundreds of local fans gathered in the parking lot of a science museum to cheer on the competitors, who drove through the city’s avenues as a caravan. Many drivers got out to mingle with supporters and took a smoke break before blazing off in an impressive procession of throttling engines.

The loudest applause came when Xalapa’s first local team, Don Justo, made its anticipated debut. Its two Mexican drivers, Iván Martínez and Salvador Aburto, received a hero’s welcome on their home turf.

Local fandom and international drivers unite

Fans of all ages gathered to witness La Carrera Panamericana in person, which has only passed through Veracruz a handful of times because the route continuously shifts with each edition.

“Motorsports have had a major boom in Mexico since Checo Pérez (debuted in Formula One in 2013),” said Arturo Ibáñez Gómez, a fan from Xalapa. “But it’s not common to always see these racers up close, especially in smaller cities.”

Despite a busy work schedule, Ibáñez Gómez said he wouldn’t miss the rare chance to see the race cars up close, even braving the scattered rain and high winds that morning.

He certainly wasn’t alone in his dedicated fandom. Ramsés López and his father, Alejandro, were in attendance among hundreds of others as car enthusiasts and vintage collectors. For them, having the race in their hometown was a blessing.

For others, being in Xalapa — let alone Mexico — was an unlikely yet thrilling moment. Carter Fournier of Dallas, Texas, entered the race with his 1970 Porsche 911. Like many participants, it was his first time racing south of the U.S. border.

“This is the last road race like this of its kind in the world. It’s special,” Fournier said. “There’s nothing like it left. This is the best of the best. It doesn’t get any better.”

A timeless tradition in North American racing

Notable racers included former Production World Rally Championship champion Benito Guerra Jr., a Mexican legend who was swarmed by fans in his 1983 Porsche 911. His small but muscular car was tailored with RSR specs built specifically for tarmac rally racing.

Though the race has lost some of its universal fame over the decades, it still evokes a sense of romantic timelessness from a renegade era of Mexican motorsports.

For those in the know, it’s a holy grail event in North American racing lore — and worth standing around in inclement weather as part of a large crowd just to give a driver a thumbs-up (trust me, they’ll always give you one back).

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: From the archive: What’s inside that piñata? A guide to Mexican candy
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in June 2025 — is a humorous yet informative look at the candies waiting to be liberated inside Mexico’s iconic piñatas.

If you’ve been in Mexico for a while, chances are you’ve been invited to — and perhaps attended — a few children’s parties.

Whether or not you know the child being celebrated is truly irrelevant. A party is something their parents throw, and they get a big say in who attends. This is only right because parties are expensive.

Sure, at least some of the kid’s friends will be there too. But you’d be forgiven for peeking into a salón de fiesta and wondering why a bunch of beer-drinking grown-ups rented a bouncy house.

A central feature of the Mexican kid’s party — and Christmas party, and New Year’s party — is, of course, the piñata.

Piñatas, as you might guess, have been around for quite a while. Before the papier-mâché varieties of today, for example, piñatas were literally clay pots. (For an informative read on the history of piñatas, check out MND’s excellent article on the subject.)

As a parent, I have watched as my daughter and other guests take turns trying to smash many a piñata to smithereens. My voice has gone hoarse from singing the “dale dale” song; thankfully, I usually have a beer to soothe it. And of course, my heart has stopped many times as I watched particularly enthusiastic children swing with all their might, even as others rushed toward them, one or two pieces of candy on the ground already.

Piñata candy-collecting is not a sport for the weak. You either rush in there and scoop up candy as fast as you can — or you don’t get candy. My daughter, whom I’ve infected with some of my gringa sensibilities, tends to hang back and grab stragglers, often sharing with smaller kids. This is kind, yes, but it’s also safe: She knows she’ll get a gift bag at the end of the party too. Under no circumstances will she go without.

You might think that once your kids get candy, you’ll get candy. This is true. There’s usually plenty to go around, along with — thank goodness — a big supply of local dentists.

Some of the candy is what we’re already familiar with, like chocolate. There are paletas (suckers) too, of course, and the little pieces of hard candy called caramelos.

But, oh, the variety. Everyone seems to love these things around here, so let’s have a look at what some of the less-familiar ones are!

Miguelitos

I have not met a Mexican who does not love miguelitos. My daughter loves them too. I, myself, would rather eat paint chips.

What are miguelitos, you may ask? Well, they’re little paper or plastic packets of powder that, since they’re sold as candy, you would think would be sweet. Basically, it’s a chamoy-flavored powder.

And what is chamoy, you may ask? It’s the stuff on the rim of your glass if you have a michelada, for one. It’s sweet, sour, salty and spicy all at the same time, and Mexicans go nuts for it. In powder or sauce, it goes on fruit, candy, popcorn, the rims of glasses or straight into the mouth. For a fascinating history of chamoy in Mexico, check out this video.

Pelón Pelo Rico

This is another favorite of pretty much every kid I know, including my daughter, and is in the tamarind candy category. Its presentation is silly: it’s a push-up goo made to look like a little green fellow’s red hair. It’s tangy and spicy, and also a little … salty? Not my bag, but it doesn’t have to be: It’s got tons of fans.

Tamarind is the featured flavor in a few other popular Mexican candies as well, like Pulparindo, which my partner calls his personal favorite. This one is just a bit heavier on the spiciness and saltiness — and it’s chewy, like a fruit roll-up. Salty fruit roll-ups, anyone? There’s also a kind of tamarind pulp sold in an actual plastic spoon to lick off!

Mazapán

Now that we’ve talked about some of the many things they put salt and chile in, let’s move on to something, in my opinion, much tastier. Mazapán — De la Rosa is the brand — is a round disk of ground peanuts and sugar pressed together. It’s technically a solid, but it has a way of both breaking off and then melting in your mouth that’s just so satisfying.

Obleas

I was very confused the first time someone handed me one of these. “Are these two body-of-Christ wafers with caramel in the middle?” That’s exactly what they are.

The cream in the middle is cajeta, a gooey caramel made from goat’s milk (the similar dulce de leche is made from cow’s milk). There are also cajeta suckers, which are delicious, and rollos de guayaba filled with cajeta, which are also worth seeking out, though they can’t typically be found in a piñata. I just wanted to mention them because I love them.

Paleta payaso

If you’re lucky, there will be a few of these in the piñata. The paleta payaso is a chocolate-covered marshmallow on a stick with a candied smiley face.

Unwrapping one is always a comical event, because the face is always misshapen. I remember frowning for a good five seconds the first time someone handed me one. But it’s pretty good.

Which Mexican candies do you like?

This article isn’t a complete list — obviously. I tried to stick mostly to things that might seem foreign to … well, foreigners.

Even after 23 years, there are some of these candies that I just don’t like: chile and salt with sweet and sour, for example, will never be okay in my book. But most candies, I do like.

So come on, out with it: What are your Mexican faves?

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Trade optimism holds despite a CIA-linked treason case
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico and the United States were “very close” to a trade deal, both presidents said this week — but lower tariffs were still a negotiating goal, not an agreement. Meanwhile, the arrest of Chihuahua’s former attorney general over alleged unauthorized CIA involvement in a drug raid sharpened the dispute over foreign agents operating in Mexico.

At home, Sheinbaum acknowledged that fuel seized in a much-publicized bust was not stolen, while Guadalajara residents continued to march for clean water. Water is on the mind of many outside Jalisco as well, as recent rains have proven insufficient to ease drought across areas of the country. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Tariff talks and sovereignty

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Monday that Mexico hoped for U.S. tariff reductions before year-end. Steel and aluminum face 50% duties, while vehicle tariffs include exemptions for U.S. content. USMCA remains in effect despite Washington’s July decision not to extend it another 16 years.

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum outlined the remaining obstacles to a trade agreement: Washington was offering tariff reductions in exchange for concessions Mexico had not fully accepted. She said Mexico would not accept terms that run contrary to its laws or that damage the economy or jobs.

Meanwhile, former Chihuahua Attorney General César Jáuregui was arrested for treason over allegations he authorized CIA participation in an April drug-lab raid without federal approval. On Friday, Sheinbaum recounted how Chihuahua Gov. Maru Campos denied authorizing foreign agents, accusing Jáuregui during a tense private meeting in September.

Mexico also announced plans to file a complaint over Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias’ death in ICE custody. The Foreign Ministry counted 18 Mexican deaths in custody or during immigration operations since Trump’s second term began. At the same time, U.S. authorization to test a heat ray along the Mexico-U.S. border raised concerns about possible burn injuries to targets on both sides of the border.

Security claims under scrutiny

On Tuesday, the U.N. Committee on Enforced Disappearances’ chairman urged General Assembly consideration of Mexico’s disappearances crisis. Mexico rejects the committee’s crimes-against-humanity characterization.

Wednesday brought official figures of 2,539 fuel-related arrests since October 2024, but also a qualification: Sheinbaum said 59 million liters confiscated in Guanajuato were not stolen or illegally imported. The company from which the fuel was confiscated had produced documentation establishing the facility’s legal operation, while the federal prosecutor in Guanajuato was fired and placed under investigation over irregularities in the bust.

Friday’s urban security survey found 58.1% of adults in surveyed cities felt unsafe, the lowest proportion in the series begun in 2013.

Water protests and persistent drought

Guadalajara’s contaminated-water crisis drew another mass protest a week after a similar protest ended with arrests and accusations of police brutality. This past Sunday, some 10,000 people marched. Participants blamed masked infiltrators for violence along the route, but their affiliations remained unestablished. Residents’ demands for clean tap water remained unresolved.

Nationally, rainfall had not erased accumulated drought deficits. Moderate-to-severe drought covered 12.7% of Mexico on Oct. 15, compared with 7.5% a year earlier. Rain helped some northern areas but failed to reverse earlier shortfalls in the south and southeast.

Economy and labor

The peso closed Thursday at 18.71 per dollar, depreciating 9.7% since Sept. 4. A narrower Mexico-U.S. interest-rate gap and trade uncertainty contributed to the slide.

Also on Thursday, the government announced 20 additional industrial parks, bringing Plan México’s operating total to 40.

In labor news, healthcare workers’ protests appear to be winding down after the union representing IMSS workers negotiated a new pay agreement. The package combines 4% more base pay with 4% in housing assistance, below the requested 10% base-pay increase; demonstrators also demanded medicines and better conditions. While protesters have promised to keep pressing for a better deal, attendance at the most recent marches dwindled following the improved pay offer.

Healthcare was not the only public service under examination: MND’s education deep dive found that more young adults are completing upper secondary education, even as education spending as a share of GDP and student test scores declined over the periods reviewed.

Politics and legislation

The Morena party’s dominance in Mexican politics appears to be holding strong, with early polling showing Morena as the overwhelming favorite in next year’s 2027 midterm elections. The party is preferred by 46% of Mexicans, although 31% expressed no preference and party preferences for gubernatorial contests were more varied.

Senators approved legislation that would allow the Finance Ministry to require digital payments in designated sectors, with gas stations and highway tollbooths expected to be among the first affected. Supporters say the measure would combat tax evasion; opponents warn it could exclude people who rely on cash

Congress also approved the so-called “anti-meme law,” penalizing misuse of official government logos. Supporters say it targets fraud; opponents warn ambiguous wording could threaten satire and political criticism.

Culture

In San Cristóbal de las Casas, a new textile conservation laboratory will repair damaged garments and protect the Maya World Textile Center’s 3,400-piece collection from insects and fungi. Other traditions found an audience onstage: 12 delegations brought music and masked dances to Oaxaca’s first Afro Guelaguetza, a dedicated celebration of Afro-Mexican heritage in Chacahua Isla. Further afield, Ballet Folklórico will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a 24-city U.S. tour, featuring regional dances and live music.

Other news from across Mexico

Looking ahead

The week ends with tariff relief still unresolved and new payments legislation awaiting promulgation. The Federal Reserve’s Oct. 27–28 meeting, followed by Banxico’s Nov. 5 decision, will put interest rates back in focus after the peso’s recent slide. Businesses and consumers will also be watching for Hacienda’s designation of sectors facing cash-payment restrictions once the legislation takes effect. Meanwhile, across Mexico, families and communities are preparing to remember their dead on Nov. 1–2.
