World.title: 20 years of ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’: 5 facts about Del Toro’s masterpiece
World.content:
Two decades after its theatrical release, “El Laberinto del Fauno” (“Pan’s Labyrinth”) remains Guillermo del Toro’s magnum opus and a timeless classic of popular culture. What began as a modest, independent project between Mexico and Spain ended up breaking records and conventions on a global scale: It moved the Cannes Film Festival with a legendary 20-minute standing ovation, grossed over US $80 million worldwide at the box office, and cemented its critical success by winning three Oscars and numerous awards at national and international ceremonies.

Set in the postwar period of 1944, this R-rated film follows Ofelia (Ivana Baquero), a young girl sent to an oppressive military camp controlled by her violent stepfather, Captain Vidal (Sergi López), a Francoist officer obsessed with eradicating the guerrilla resistance. In this hostile environment, Ofelia discovers a labyrinth where an ancient faun (Doug Jones) reveals a delicate truth to her: She is Princess Moanna, ruler of the underground kingdom, and must complete supernatural tasks to reclaim her throne.

Weaving historical horrors with fantasy, “El Laberinto del Fauno” serves as a profound allegory about the loss of innocence and the importance of ethical disobedience in the face of injustice and oppression.

To mark its 20th anniversary and re-release in theaters, we’re delving into the depths of this legendary labyrinth to bring you the most amazing and unexpected behind-the-scenes facts: from its original conception and its connection to “El Espinazo del Diablo” (“The Devil’s Backbone”), to how the story managed to make Stephen King himself squirm in his seat.

1. The original script was darker and more sexual

Little Ofelia’s journey — forced to overcome dangerous, fantastical challenges after moving to a military setting — did not always have the tone or the ending that we have come to love and admire. Few people know that, in its early stages of development, “El Laberinto del Fauno” did not feature a young girl as the protagonist, nor was it set in postwar Spain.

In the original version, Guillermo del Toro wrote a much rawer, darker and more erotically charged draft set in the Victorian era. The protagonist was an adult, pregnant woman who discovered the labyrinth after moving with her husband into an old mansion. There she met the faun, but instead of undertaking fantastical tasks to reclaim her throne, she became entangled in a dark, passionate relationship with the creature.

In the official DVD commentary, the director shares details of this concept: “They made passionate love, she fell in love with him, and he asked for the blood of the firstborn in return for the labyrinth to open and for her to go to the magical kingdom with him.”

By shifting his focus to childhood, Del Toro transformed that idea of adult horror into the fascinating gem of innocence, resilience and rebellion that made it to the big screen. Fortunately for the history of cinema, the Mexican director changed his mind just in time.

2. Two films connected

“El Laberinto del Fauno” was conceived by Del Toro as a companion piece to his 2001 film “El Espinazo del Diablo” (“The Devil’s Backbone”). Although they lack a direct narrative connection or shared characters, the director has formally defined them as “mirror films” due to their profound parallels. Together, they function as a diptych that explores the horror of war through the vulnerable and unspoiled eyes of childhood.

Beyond the historical context — with “El Espinazo del Diablo” set in 1939 during the Spanish Civil War and “El Laberinto del Fauno” in 1944 during the postwar Franco era — the closest connection between the two films is that neither uses horror in a superficial way.

The supernatural appears in Del Toro’s films from a profound and metaphorical dimension to help us process social tragedies and shed light on the darkest corners of the human condition. As the filmmaker explained to Voices of Monterey Bay: “In fairy tales, monsters exist to be a manifestation of something we need to understand, not just a problem we need to overcome.”

Like its predecessor, “El Laberinto del Fauno” demonstrates that true monstrosity does not stem from the supernatural realm — symbolized by the faun and the creatures of the underworld — but rather from the cruelty of human beings.

In both stories, the authentic villains are bloodthirsty, heartless men — such as Jacinto and Captain Vidal — who are obsessed with money, weapons and absolute control. It is in the face of these oppressors’ brutality that the child protagonists use their imagination and sensitivity to come to terms with the world they find themselves living in, defy the tyrants and defend their very existence.

3. The origin of the faun

Long before becoming an iconic figure in modern fantasy, the faun was already haunting Guillermo del Toro’s mind. During his childhood, the director used to have intense lucid dreams in which this creature came to life, emerging from the back of an old family wardrobe.

“I used to sleep at my grandmother’s house … And every night, right at midnight, in my bedroom, a faun would come out of the armoire. It must have been lucid dreaming, but for a child, it was as if it were real,” he told The Guardian. “I would see the faun’s human hand emerge from the armoire, then the smiling face of a goat, and then the hairy leg of a goat. I could clearly see him pulling his body out of the armoire, and I would start screaming.”

For Del Toro, bringing the monster that made him scream at night to the big screen was his way of coming to terms with his childhood fears. Although the faun we see in the film underwent countless changes in appearance, the idea was born from that peculiar childhood experience. Who would have thought that those terrifying sleepless nights would be the origin of the fantastical universe that would ultimately establish him as an international star?

4. The bold rejection of Hollywood that preserved the film’s identity

When the major studios read the story of “El Laberinto del Fauno,” they tried to entice Guillermo del Toro by offering to double the budget, on the condition that he relocate the story to the U.S. market.

However, true to his artistic vision, the filmmaker flatly refused. He believed that if he accepted the change in language and setting, the story would lose all its political power, its historical context and its authentic identity.

During an interview with KPBS, he clarified the direction the film would have taken under the industry’s commercial demands: “I never would have attempted to make ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ in Hollywood because we would have audience-tested it, and we would have had a super-happy ending with dancing little creatures.”

5. The movie terrified the ‘master of horror’ himself

Sharing your work with an icon like Stephen King is a dream come true for any filmmaker, but to make the master of horror himself squirm with fear at your own movie is an achievement reserved for very few. That’s exactly what Del Toro experienced in New England during a special screening of “El Laberinto del Fauno.”

During the iconic scene where the unsettling Pale Man comes to life to chase Ofelia, the Mexican director noticed that the celebrated writer began shifting uncomfortably in his seat, completely overwhelmed by the tension.

As you can imagine, witnessing the obvious unease of one of his greatest artistic influences was one of the most significant moments of recognition in his entire career.

As Del Toro explains in the film’s official commentary: “I must say, it remains the single best screening experience of my life — sitting next to Stephen King and watching him squirm during the Pale Man sequence. That, for me, is an Oscar. That’s absolutely the best thing that ever happened to me in my life.”

Disobedience as a legacy

Two decades have passed since Ofelia first entered the labyrinth, and the good news is that this dark fairy tale retains its ability to delight and unsettle us. Beyond its global box office success and a historic awards season — in which it won three Oscars (art direction, cinematography and makeup), three BAFTAs, seven Goya Awards, and nine Ariel Awards, among others — the deepest impact of Guillermo del Toro’s masterpiece lies in its power to engage with the challenges of modern times.

Far from being a childish escapist fable, this film stands as a manifesto on individual sovereignty and civil disobedience in the face of the dangers of blind, mechanical and unconditional submission. The lesson the film continues to impart to us today is that, in the face of overwhelming and dehumanizing authority, dissent is not an act of immature rebellion, but rather a moral virtue and an indispensable tool for survival.

As Dr. Ferreiro so aptly put it before his execution: “To obey just like that, for the sake of obeying, without questioning … That’s something only people like you can do, Captain.”

Twenty years later, that call to think for oneself and to challenge tyrants — both on and off the screen — remains more alive and urgent than ever.

Carolina Alvarado is a Venezuelan journalist who has devoted much of her career to creative writing, university teaching and social work. She has been published in Lady Science, Latina Media, Global Comment, Psiquide, Cinetopic, Get Me Giddy and Reader’s Digest, among others.

World.title: Brazilians Abroad Split in Runoff Count
World.content:
Voters queue at the Colégio Leonardo da Vinci polling station in Brasília during Brazil's first round on 4 October 2026. Photo: Lula Marques/Agência Brasil

Published Sunday, 25 October 2026, 1:58 p.m. ET · Unofficial press tallies of ballot-box reports

Brazilians living abroad voted first in Sunday’s presidential runoff, and their early count is split: Flávio Bolsonaro leads the overseas total, while Lula leads in more countries. These are press tallies, not official results, and the electoral court publishes its first numbers from 4 p.m. ET.

Key Facts — Who Brazilians abroad voted first in the runoff between Lula, Brazil’s president, and Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator.

— Count At 1:42 p.m. ET the early overseas tally gave Flávio Bolsonaro 45,720 votes to Lula’s 41,101 (52.7%), while Lula led in 30 places to 12.

— Why Japan supplies 62% of Flávio’s votes; without it, Lula would lead the overseas count.

— Electorate 918,876 registered voters abroad, about 0.6% of the total, 265,437 of them in the United States.

— Official numbers The electoral court (TSE) publishes results from 4 p.m. ET; the last US and Canadian polls close at 8 p.m. ET.

— Prediction markets Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 83% and Kalshi at 81% (Lula: 18% and 20% ), as of 25 October, 1:40 pm ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

— Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Live results Brazil Election Data Room Runoff poll average: Flávio Bolsonaro 51.0 %, Lula 49.0 % 45 national polls from 21 pollsters since 4 October, updated hourly. Every poll, free to download. Open the Data Room · Download the CSV · Embed the chart Follow Brazil’s runoff count on our results page Official TSE numbers, state by state, as soon as the electoral court publishes them from 4 p.m. ET. Open the live results page →

Exame, a Brazilian business magazine, adds up the ballot-box reports posted from 42 places abroad. Its running count at 1:42 p.m. ET gave Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative senator for Rio de Janeiro, 45,720 votes (52.66% of valid votes, which exclude blank and spoiled ballots) and Lula, the left-wing president, 41,101 (47.34%).

The overseas vote is a tiny slice of the runoff results guide explains when and where official numbers arrive.

In Plain English Runoff: the second round between the top two candidates, held because nobody won more than half of the valid votes on 4 October.

the second round between the top two candidates, held because nobody won more than half of the valid votes on 4 October. Ballot-box report: the results sheet each voting machine prints when its polls close, which news sites add up before any official count.

the results sheet each voting machine prints when its polls close, which news sites add up before any official count. TSE: the Superior Electoral Court, Brazil’s election authority, which publishes the official results.

Where Brazilians Voted First

Voting abroad runs from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. local time, so Asia and Oceania finish first and Europe follows hours later. Brazilians in the United States and Canada vote last: the final polls in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Vancouver close at 9 p.m. in Brasília, which is 8 p.m. ET.

The Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Brazil’s election authority, counts 918,876 registered voters abroad in 186 cities. The United States is the largest bloc with 265,437 (28.9%), followed by Portugal (134,797), Japan (88,366), Canada (46,488) and Germany (41,551).

We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What the Early Polling-Station Tallies Show

Japan decides the early sum. Metrópoles, a Brasília news site, counts 28,538 votes for Flávio Bolsonaro and 7,098 for Lula there (80.08% to 19.92%), from ballot-box reports posted in Japan.

Japan’s 28,538 votes make up 62% of everything Flávio Bolsonaro has collected abroad so far, Exame calculates. Without Japan, Exame says, Lula would lead the overseas count.

A Brazilian electronic voting machine of the kind used at polling stations. File photo, not from a polling station abroad.

Exame reports Lula ahead in 30 places and Flávio Bolsonaro in 12. Metrópoles reports Flávio ahead in Taiwan, Malaysia and the Philippines, and Lula ahead in Australia and China; Exame adds Lula ahead in Singapore. Terra also lists Flávio ahead in Israel, Indonesia and South Africa.

In Europe, Exame lists Lula ahead in the Netherlands, Switzerland, Poland, the Czech Republic and Finland. Terra, a Brazilian news portal, gives him 85.06% in Denmark and 78.26% in Sweden, while Flávio Bolsonaro won Greece with 311 votes to 255 (54.95%).

The gap has narrowed as more places reported. Metrópoles’ count at 1:29 p.m. ET, covering 37 countries, gave Flávio Bolsonaro 58.43% of 66,131 valid votes; Exame’s count 13 minutes later, with 86,821 valid votes, gave him 52.66%. Exame also says Malaysia, which Lula won on 4 October, went to Flávio this time.

We could not find reported counts for Portugal, the second-largest overseas bloc, or for the United Kingdom. Germany and France were only partly counted in the tallies we saw.

Why Overseas Votes Are Not a Forecast

Brazilians abroad are about 0.6% of the roughly 158.7 million voters, so even a lopsided overseas result moves the national total very little. The count is also lumpy: one country, Japan, outweighs dozens of smaller ones, and each country leans differently.

World.title: Serbia Probes Care Home Incident at Polls
World.content:
Key Facts Care home: Unknown people entered a polling station inside a care home in Mladenovac, a town near Belgrade.

Who says: Vladimir Dimitrijević chairs the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), Serbia’s election authority.

Claim: He said the intruders posed as observers and pressured residents who cannot move around.

Second case: Prosecutors in Sombor, a northern city, are probing a laptop and documents found in Deronje.

Prediction markets: Kalshi, a US-regulated market, prices President Vučić’s ruling Progressive Party (SNS) list 54%, the protest-born student list 48% (1:43 p.m. ET).

Serbia’s election authority said on Sunday that unknown people burst into a care home that doubles as a polling station in Mladenovac, a town near Belgrade. The Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) chair said they claimed to be observers and pressured residents who cannot move around.

Polls in the snap parliamentary election close at 20:00 CET (Central European Time; 3:00 p.m. ET). Follow every development in our Serbia Election 2026 coverage, and see our earlier turnout report.

RIK Chair Describes Care Home Intrusion

RIK chair Vladimir Dimitrijević told a press conference at 17:00 CET (12:00 p.m. ET) that “unknown persons” entered the care home, claiming to be observers. He said they exerted “impermissible pressure” on residents, including people who cannot move.

Police were alerted and were at the scene, he said, and he promised more information at the next RIK press conference. He said it happened just before the briefing, so he had no further detail.

Dimitrijević said voting was otherwise proceeding regularly, based on reports from local election commissions and polling boards. He described the other problems as minor and said polling boards resolved them, with the Interior Ministry (MUP) stepping in where they could not.

File photo: Serbian police on a Belgrade square.

Prosecutors Probe Laptop and Documents

The Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office in Sombor, a city in northern Serbia, said a laptop and several A4 documents were found in a hospitality venue in Deronje, a village in the north of the country. It said they are suspected of being linked to the election process and were handed to police in Odžaci, a town in northern Serbia.

Prosecutors told police to gather information without delay and to file a report so they can decide on further steps in the early preliminary stage. The office has not said what the documents contain or who left them.

In a separate statement, Sombor prosecutors said that shortly before 15:00 CET they received two electronic messages from the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office, a more senior body, in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city. The messages passed on citizens’ reports of alleged irregularities at polling stations on two streets in Sombor and in Apatin, a town near Sombor.

Checks found that no polling stations exist at those addresses, and neither do the local communities named in the reports. Prosecutors also said there were no irregularities at the polling stations with the reported numbers, 39 and 13.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Kalshi, the SNS-led list, President Aleksandar Vučić’s ruling Serbian Progressive Party, was priced at 54% to win the parliamentary election and the student-backed Student List at 48%, at 1:43 p.m. ET on 25 October. The market had 97,961 contracts traded; the two prices do not add to 100% because each is a separate last-traded bet.

Our earlier Sunday report had the SNS-led list at 75% and the Student List at 26% at 4:27 a.m. ET. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and its prices are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Why Election-Day Pressure Claims Matter

The vote is mainly a contest between Vučić’s ruling camp and the student-backed Student List, born of nearly two years of protests, as our election-day report explained. Both sides have claimed to be ahead, and the integrity of the vote is a central issue, as our Saturday report noted.

The Mladenovac claim concerns residents who cannot move around, and police have not yet reported what they found. The Sombor checks, by contrast, found no irregularities at the two reported polling stations.

What It Means for You

If you follow European politics from the United States, these cases show how contested the integrity of Serbia’s vote already is before any result. Allegations on election day often shape how voters, observers and foreign governments judge the outcome.

If you are travelling to Serbia, expect heavy attention around the count in Belgrade and check your government’s travel advice. See also our report on the vote-silence period.

What Is Not Known

Dimitrijević did not say who the intruders were, which group they claimed to represent or whether anyone has been detained. The RIK chair gave no estimate of how many residents were affected.

Prosecutors have not said whether the Deronje laptop and documents relate to any party or list. It is unclear whether the two cases are connected, and no result or official turnout figure is part of this report.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened at the polling station in Mladenovac?

What did prosecutors find in Deronje?

The Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office in Sombor said a laptop and several A4 documents were found in a hospitality venue in Deronje. It suspects a link to the election process and ordered police to gather information.

When do polls close in Serbia’s election?

Polls close at 20:00 CET on Sunday 25 October 2026, which is 3:00 p.m. ET. The vote fills all 250 seats of the National Assembly.

What does RIK do in Serbia’s election?

World.content:

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Published Sunday, 25 October, 1:43 p.m. ET · Source: Poder360 (a Brazilian political news site), Metrópoles (a Brasília news outlet), Folha de S.Paulo (a São Paulo daily)

Key Facts The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest country, holds its presidential runoff today between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of a former president.

What happened Lula’s campaign says it will ask the electoral court (TSE) to extend voting after reports of bus cuts.

The claims The campaign says São Paulo runs 60% of its buses, and Salvador kept at least 75 buses in garages.

Still open The TSE had not ruled when we published, and officials dispute why buses were late.

Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Prediction markets Polymarket, a prediction market, gives Flávio Bolsonaro an 81.8% chance of winning today’s runoff (25 October, 1:43 p.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 83% and Kalshi at 81% (Lula: 18% and 20% ), as of 25 October, 1:40 pm ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

Lula’s presidential campaign said on Sunday it will ask Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE), the country’s top election authority, to keep polling stations open past 4 p.m. ET (5 p.m. in Brasília). Poder360 reported the announcement at 1:36 p.m. ET (2:36 p.m. in Brasília), during the Brazil election 2026 runoff between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Brazil Election Data Room Runoff poll average: Flávio Bolsonaro 51.0 %, Lula 49.0 % 45 national polls from 21 pollsters since 4 October, updated hourly. Every poll, free to download. Open the Data Room · Download the CSV · Embed the chart

Marco Aurélio de Carvalho, a lawyer who coordinates Lula’s legal team, said voters in São Paulo and Salvador faced long waits because of reduced bus services. As of publication, no ruling on the request had been reported.

What the Lula Campaign Is Asking For

Carvalho spoke to reporters outside Lula’s home in western São Paulo and said the party expects the full TSE bench to meet urgently, Poder360 reported. “We will ask, yes, for the hours to be extended so that everyone can vote,” he said.

Earlier, Lula’s party federation, which groups the Workers’ Party (PT) with two allies, filed a request to extend voting until 6 p.m. ET (7 p.m. in Brasília) in Salvador, Feira de Santana and Lauro de Freitas, Metrópoles reported. As of 1:28 p.m. ET, TSE president Kássio Nunes Marques had not yet analysed it, the outlet said.

Bus Cuts in São Paulo

The campaign told São Paulo’s 1st Electoral Zone that buses were running with only 60% of the fleet, despite a court order for full service, Folha de S.Paulo reported. Carvalho said some voters had waited “more than an hour, an hour and a half” for a bus on a Sunday, according to Poder360.

São Paulo’s city hall said it told all bus companies on Saturday to run weekday schedules with at least a 10% reserve, after an order from the regional electoral court (TRE-SP), Poder360 reported. The campaign’s filing also asks for the arrest of the city’s mobility secretary and the president of SPTrans, the city’s bus agency, which are allegations, not findings.

The Dispute in Salvador

In Salvador, the capital of Bahia state, at least 75 public buses were kept from leaving their garages on Sunday, Poder360 reported. The city’s mobility department said the stop followed a dispute over Lula stickers that union members had put on the vehicles.

Mayor Bruno Reis, of the União Brasil party, said buses of one operator only began running after stickers with the number 13, Lula’s ballot number, were removed. He called the situation an electoral crime, while the mobility department says it has ordered all buses released.

Bahia’s regional electoral court (TRE-BA), led by Mauricio Kertzman Szporer, ordered the full fleet restored immediately, with a fine of R$1 million (about US$200,000 at 4.97 reais per dollar) per hour for non-compliance, according to Poder360. Folha reported that the same court ordered the arrest of mobility secretary Pablo Souza.

What It Means for US Readers

A dispute over turnout in a close runoff can sharpen market nerves and fuel claims about the legitimacy of the result. Brazil’s currency and stocks, and US-listed shares of Brazilian companies, can react to such uncertainty.

For anyone following US relations with Latin America’s largest economy, the TSE’s answer will be a test of how the court handles pressure on election day. Our guide to the Brazil runoff date explains when results are due.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, an online prediction market, traders give Flávio Bolsonaro an 81.8% chance of winning today’s runoff and Lula 18.5% (25 October, 1:43 p.m. ET). The “Brazil Presidential Election” market has seen about US$198.8 million in bets, and our Brazil election odds page tracks both Polymarket and Kalshi, an prediction market regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

What Is Not Known

The TSE has not said whether it will extend voting, or whether any extension would cover only parts of Bahia or also São Paulo. It is also unclear how many voters were kept from the polls, and no court has tested the claims about the bus fleets.

Accounts of why buses were late differ between the campaign, city officials and the courts. We have not independently verified any of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Lula’s campaign want longer voting hours?

It says bus cuts in São Paulo and Salvador kept people from reaching polling stations. Officials dispute why the buses were late.

When do polls close in Brazil?

Voting is scheduled to end at 5 p.m. in Brasília, which is 4 p.m. ET. The TSE had not changed that when we published.

Who decides whether voting is extended?

The Superior Electoral Court (TSE), led by Kássio Nunes Marques, receives national requests, while regional electoral courts handle local orders, such as the one in Bahia.

What did the Bahia court order?

It ordered Salvador’s full bus fleet restored at once, with a fine of R$1 million (about US$200,000) per hour. Folha also reported an arrest order for the city’s mobility secretary.

Polymarket gives Flávio Bolsonaro 81.8% and Lula 18.5% (25 October, 1:43 p.m. ET). These are bets, not polls.

World.title: Serbia Turnout Tops 56% With Four Hours Left
World.content:
The House of the National Assembly in Belgrade. File photo. (Photo: Kallerna, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts Turnout: 56.38% of registered voters had voted by 16:00 Central European Time, CET (11:00 a.m. ET).

Pace: Turnout was 46.53% at 14:00 CET, against about 32% at the same hour in December 2023.

Polling stations: Close at 20:00 CET (3:00 p.m. ET) for 250 parliamentary seats, with 6,450,523 voters registered.

Incidents: Serbian media reported attacks on people heading to vote near a polling station in central Belgrade.

Prediction markets: Kalshi, a US-regulated prediction market, prices President Vučić’s ruling list at 55% and the student-led list at 46% (12:43 p.m. ET).

Published Sunday, 25 October, 12:43 p.m. ET · Source: Republic Electoral Commission of Serbia, the state body that runs the vote

More than half of Serbia’s registered voters had cast a ballot by 16:00 CET (11:00 a.m. ET) in Sunday’s snap parliamentary election. The Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) put turnout at 56.38%.

Polling stations stay open until 20:00 CET (3:00 p.m. ET). We covered the build-up in our Saturday preview, the campaign ban before the vote, the 6.45 million voter register and the final opinion polls.

Turnout Runs Well Above 2023

RIK reported 46.53% of registered voters at 14:00 CET, so turnout rose by about 9.9 points in two hours. At 16:00 CET in December 2023, turnout was 42.36%, according to N1, a Serbian news channel, and Vreme, a Belgrade weekly.

That puts this vote about 14 points ahead of the last parliamentary election at the same hour. A final figure will come only after polling stations close at 20:00 CET.

File photo: Serbian flags at a night protest in central Belgrade.

Incidents Reported on Voting Day

Mašina.rs, an independent Serbian news site, reported at 15:00 CET that a group of men first verbally and then physically attacked people heading to vote near a polling station in central Belgrade. 021.rs, a news portal in Novi Sad, led its live coverage with the report that a woman was attacked in the city centre.

Danas, a Belgrade daily, also headlined incidents across the country. We have not been able to confirm the number of incidents, and no official response was available at the time of writing.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Kalshi, the ruling list led by the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), President Aleksandar Vučić’s party, was priced at 55% to win, and the Student List, a list backed by the student protest movement, at 46%, at 12:43 p.m. ET. The two contracts are priced separately, so they need not add to 100%, and 86,940 contracts had traded.

At 4:27 a.m. ET, in our earlier report, Kalshi priced the ruling list at 75% and the Student List at 26%. Kalshi also priced at least 46% of the vote for the Student List at 51%, and at least 50% at 29%.

On Polymarket, a global prediction market, a turnout contract with US$121,123 traded priced a final turnout of 70% or more at 69.5% and 66% to 70% at 26.0%, at 12:40 p.m. ET. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and all of these prices are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

For readers in the United States, high turnout makes this vote harder to call, and traders have narrowed the gap between the two lists since the morning. The result will show whether a long-dominant leader can hold off a student-led protest movement in a Balkan country.

If you travel to Serbia, check your government’s travel advice, because incidents were reported in Belgrade today. Final official results can take days after polling stations close.

What Is Not Known

No result or projection is available, and the winner and the size of any majority are unknown. We could not independently check how turnout will move before the count ends.

The scale of the reported incidents is unclear. The final turnout is not yet known.

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

When He expects the result between 8:30 and 9 p.m. in Brasília, the capital, which is 7:30 to 8 p.m. ET.

World.title: Nigeria Attack Kills 40, Amnesty Says
World.content:
A Nigeria Police armoured vehicle in Lagos. Archive photo, not from the attack site. Photo: satanoid, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Published Sunday, 25 October, 11:35 AM ET · Source: Amnesty International via Premium Times

Amnesty International, the global human rights group, says at least 40 people were killed when armed men attacked a village in Taraba State, northeastern Nigeria, on Friday, 23 October 2026. Police initially confirmed 10 deaths, and more bodies were found later, according to Premium Times, a Nigerian news outlet.

Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country and a major oil producer, and its security crises reach US investors and travellers.

Key Facts Who. Armed men, not yet identified, and residents of Binnari village in Taraba State.

What. Amnesty International, a global human rights group, says at least 40 people were killed.

Where. Binnari, in Karim Lamido district (a local government area), Taraba State, northeastern Nigeria.

When. Friday, 23 October 2026; Amnesty’s toll of 40 was reported by 25 October.

Why it matters. Police confirmed only 10 deaths at first, so the true toll is still unclear.

What Amnesty and Police Say

Amnesty International’s Nigeria office said gunmen attacked Binnari in the Karim Lamido local government area on Friday. It said at least 40 people died as additional bodies were discovered.

“The community is now littered with dead bodies, some burnt beyond recognition, as families declare many still missing,” Amnesty said, according to Premium Times. The attackers also burned houses, shops, goods and motorcycles.

Police first confirmed 10 deaths. Victor Mshelizah, spokesperson for the Taraba police command, said officers were deployed to restore order, Premium Times reports.

The attackers entered through a border area with neighbouring Plateau State, according to the same report. A local government area is Nigeria’s third tier of government, similar to a county.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Amnesty’s Criticism of Authorities

Amnesty accused Nigerian authorities of a “consistent failure” to prosecute suspected perpetrators of such attacks. It said this was “clearly emboldening impunity,” meaning attackers expect no punishment.

The group called for an impartial investigation and adequate reparations for survivors. We have not seen a government response to those demands.

In plain English Amnesty International: a London-based human rights organisation with a Nigeria office that tracks killings and abuses. Taraba State: a state in Nigeria’s northeast; Karim Lamido is one of its local government areas. Plateau State: the neighbouring state through whose border area the attackers reportedly entered.

What Is Not Known

The 40 figure comes from Amnesty. In the reports we reviewed, police have confirmed only 10 deaths, and we have seen no official total.

Reports we reviewed do not name the attackers or give a motive. The number of missing residents, and whether more bodies remain to be found, has not been stated.

What It Means for US Readers

A toll this large in one night keeps Nigeria’s northeast on the security agenda for investors, aid groups and travellers. The gap between Amnesty’s count and the police count will matter for any official response.

Travellers should check the US State Department’s current Nigeria advisory. Earlier details are in our report Gunmen Kill 10 in Nigeria’s Taraba State, and wider context is in our Nigeria coverage and the story on Nigeria’s state police bill.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people died in the Taraba attack?

Amnesty International says at least 40 were killed in Binnari on 23 October 2026. Police initially confirmed 10, and no official total has been reported.

Where is Binnari?

Binnari is a village in the Karim Lamido local government area of Taraba State, in northeastern Nigeria. Attackers reportedly entered through a border area with Plateau State.

Who carried out the attack?

Reports we reviewed do not identify the attackers or a motive. Police said officers were deployed to restore order.

What does Amnesty want?

Amnesty called for an impartial investigation and adequate reparations for survivors. It accused authorities of failing to prosecute perpetrators.

World.title: Colombia Says Bombing Killed 10 Rebels
World.content:
Colombian military personnel on a Black Hawk helicopter. File photo, not from this operation.

Published Sunday, 25 October, 11:35 AM ET · Source: Colombian presidency via Infobae, El Colombiano, El Heraldo

Colombia’s president says a military bombing in the southwestern department of Cauca killed 10 members of the ELN, a guerrilla group, including two of its commanders. The strike happened before dawn on Thursday, 22 October 2026, and the government announced it on Sunday, 25 October.

For readers in the United States, the ELN (National Liberation Army) is a rebel group the US government lists as a foreign terrorist organisation. Colombia is also a major US security partner, so a shift in how Bogotá fights armed groups matters in Washington.

Key Facts Who. Colombia’s military and police against ten ELN guerrillas, the National Liberation Army, a rebel group.

What. President Abelardo De la Espriella says the “Operation Ónix” bombing killed 10 ELN members.

Where. Rural El Tambo, a municipality in Cauca, a department in Colombia’s southwest.

When. Before dawn on Thursday, 22 October 2026; announced Sunday, 25 October.

Why it matters. It is the government’s fifth bombing of armed groups, a tactic under political fire.

What Colombia’s President Announced

President Abelardo De la Espriella announced the result on Sunday in a post on X. He said troops and police carried out “Operation Ónix” in rural El Tambo and that ten ELN members died.

Among the dead, he said, were two of the group’s main leaders, known by the aliases “Marcos Pacífico” and “Ochenta” (also called “Murillo”).

He called it “the hardest blow in eight years” against the ELN, according to El Colombiano and El Heraldo, two Colombian daily newspapers. EFE, the Spanish news agency, quoted him saying the strike weakens the group’s chain of command and combat capacity.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Security forces seized seven rifles, a pistol and two grenades, the president said. They also found a camp able to hold about 25 fighters, according to EFE via Infobae, a Latin American news site.

A Contested Military Tactic

Colombian media count this as the fifth bombing the government has ordered against illegal armed groups. The tactic has drawn criticism because armed groups recruit children, who can be present in camps.

The debate began after the second bombing, in late August in the southern department of Guaviare. Colombian outlets report that three of the 10 people killed there were minors: two aged 15 and one aged 16.

A fourth bombing, on 10 October in the Catatumbo region of Norte de Santander near the Venezuelan border, killed a 16-year-old girl, according to La Silla Vacía, a Colombian news site. The reports we reviewed do not say whether any minors were among the dead in El Tambo.

In plain English ELN: the National Liberation Army, a left-wing guerrilla group that has fought the Colombian state since the 1960s. Cauca: a department (state-level region) in southwestern Colombia with routes toward the Pacific coast. Bombing: Colombian officials use the word for military strikes on rebel camps.

What Is Not Known

The announcement came three days after the operation. Colombian media first reported nine dead on 22 October, and the president’s account raised the toll to ten.

The identities of the dead rest on the government’s account, and the reports we reviewed carry no reply from the ELN. Whether any minors died has not been stated.

What It Means for US Readers

The strike shows Bogotá leaning on air power against armed groups even as scrutiny over child recruits grows. How the government answers questions about civilian and minor casualties will shape its standing with partners, including the United States.

Travellers should check the US State Department’s current advisory for Cauca before planning any trip there. For wider background, see our Colombia coverage and our report on Colombia’s repeal of 15 mining districts.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in El Tambo, Colombia?

President Abelardo De la Espriella says a military bombing killed 10 ELN members in rural El Tambo, Cauca. The strike took place before dawn on 22 October 2026.

Who are the ELN?

The ELN, or National Liberation Army, is a Colombian guerrilla group active since the 1960s. The US government lists it as a foreign terrorist organisation.

Which ELN leaders were killed?

The president named aliases “Marcos Pacífico” and “Ochenta,” also called “Murillo.” Identification of the dead rests on the government’s account.

Were minors among the dead?

The reports do not say. Earlier bombings drew criticism after minors died, including three in Guaviare in August.

World.title: Kenya Bus Crash Kills 22 on Mombasa Road
World.content:
The Nairobi skyline seen from Nairobi National Park, photographed in May 2019. It is a general view of the city, not of the race weekend. Photo: Timothy A. Gonsalves / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

KENYA · MAKUENI COUNTY · BREAKING

A passenger bus and a lorry collided head-on on Kenya’s main road from Nairobi to Mombasa on Sunday morning, and at least 22 people died.

Published Sunday, 25 October, 11:20 a.m. ET · Source: Kenyan press reports and the EFE news agency

Key Facts Toll: At least 22 dead, up from 20 after two injured people died.

Where: Kanga, near the town of Mtito Andei, in Makueni County, southern Kenya.

When: Sunday morning, 25 October, at about 7:00 a.m. Kenya time (around midnight Eastern Time).

Why it matters: The road links Kenya’s capital to its main seaport, Mombasa.

Cause: Not yet established; Kenya’s road-safety regulator suspects improper overtaking.

At least 22 people died on Sunday 25 October 2026 when a bus and a lorry collided head-on at Kanga, in Makueni County in southern Kenya, officials said. The crash happened on Sunday morning, at around 7:00 a.m. local time, on the highway between the capital, Nairobi, and the Indian Ocean port of Mombasa.

Abdullahi Khalif, the government’s commissioner for Makueni County, first confirmed 20 deaths, according to a report from EFE, Spain’s national news agency, carried by the Latin American news site Infobae. The toll rose to 22 after two injured passengers died, the report said.

The Star, a Nairobi newspaper, and Capital FM, a Kenyan radio and news outlet, also reported 22 dead.

What We Know About the Crash

The bus was carrying people home from a burial ceremony, according to The Star and Capital FM. The injured were taken to Mtito Andei Sub-County Hospital.

Dr Kevin Wamalwa, the hospital’s medical superintendent, told reporters: “It is a serious accident. We are attending to those who have survived.”

He said some people died while receiving treatment, and that staff were compiling a list of the victims.

In Plain English Makueni County: a county in southern Kenya that the Nairobi-Mombasa highway crosses.

a county in southern Kenya that the Nairobi-Mombasa highway crosses. Mtito Andei: a town on the highway whose hospital treated the injured.

a town on the highway whose hospital treated the injured. Lorry: the British word for a heavy truck.

Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Investigators Look at Overtaking

The National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA), Kenya’s road-safety regulator, said in a statement that preliminary information indicates the two vehicles collided head-on and suggests improper overtaking may have contributed, according to the EFE report. It said its accident investigation team is working with police to establish the full circumstances.

The Star reported that the cause had not been determined when it published, and accounts of how the crash unfolded differ. The death toll could still change as the injured are treated, and the number of injured has not been confirmed.

File photo: lorries carrying shipping containers at Mombasa port, at the coastal end of the route.

A Road With a Deadly Record

The crash comes weeks after another deadly collision in Makueni County. EFE reported that at least 17 people died in early October in a crash involving two lorries, a minibus and several cars.

EFE noted that Kenya as a whole suffers a high number of fatal road accidents, partly because of poor vehicle and road conditions. The Star reported that the police and the NTSA are running road-safety campaigns ahead of the December festive season.

The Associated Press reported that the NTSA lists this stretch as an accident black spot.

What It Means for You

The highway links Kenya’s capital with Mombasa, the country’s main seaport, and it is a main route for people and freight between the coast and the interior. Travellers planning road journeys on this corridor should check with their operators, as the cause of the crash is still under investigation.

Officials have not yet named the victims, the bus operator or the final cause. Those details usually emerge from the police and NTSA investigations over the coming days.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people died in the Kenya bus crash?

At least 22 people died, according to The Star and Capital FM, after the toll rose from 20.

Where did the crash happen?

At Kanga, near Mtito Andei in Makueni County, on the highway between Nairobi and Mombasa.

What caused the collision?

The cause is not confirmed. The road-safety regulator’s preliminary information suggests improper overtaking may have contributed.

Who was on the bus?

The bus was carrying people returning from a burial ceremony, according to The Star and Capital FM.

Has this road had other deadly crashes recently?

Yes. EFE reported that at least 17 people died in another Makueni County crash in early October.

Sources: The Star (Nairobi), Capital FM (Nairobi), Infobae (EFE), as of Sunday 25 October 2026. More from us: Eastern Africa.

World.title: Canadian Says She Lost $350,000 to Costa Rica Community Now Under Fraud Investigation
World.content:
A Canadian woman says she sold everything she owned and lost about $350,000 to a religious community in the southern area of Pérez Zeledón, where four Americans, including the community’s alleged leader, are now under investigation on suspicion of defrauding foreigners.

The woman, who lived at the community known as EarthWaking Village and spoke to local media under a pseudonym, said she arrived in November 2024, paid $22,000 for two lots in a planned expansion area and lent $325,000 to the leader at 7% annual interest for one year. She says that money has not been repaid.

Investigators estimate that at least 11 foreigners lost about $600,000 to the group. OIJ director Michael Soto said most of the alleged victims are U.S. citizens. Investigators described the estimate as preliminary, and a lawyer for several of the alleged victims has said the real figure could be higher.

Agents of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) raided properties in Platanillo and Barú on Oct. 6, working with prosecutors and the U.S. Embassy’s investigations department, and seized money and documents. They detained two men and two women identified by their surnames: England, 44, described as the community’s leader; Hallman, 44; McDow, 63; and Gingras, 62.

None of the four has been charged. They were released under six-month precautionary measures that require them to report to the local prosecutor’s office every 15 days, surrender their passports and remain here, vacate their declared residence by Oct. 20 and refrain from intimidating or harassing the alleged victims.

EarthWaking Village describes itself as a Christian eco-village and has promoted its way of life, as a self-sufficient “Garden of Eden,” on social media and YouTube. A listing in an international directory of intentional communities says members began living together on the property in January 2019, with about 25 full-time residents on roughly 2 hectares (5 acres).

The group says it is not a sect. Former residents describe a community led by Americans, in which members were taught that the outside world, which they called “Babylon,” would collapse and that only those inside would be saved. Most residents were foreigners, and several families with young children lived there.

According to investigators, the suspects advertised extended stays and spiritual retreats, and recruits deposited money that the group then managed. Some allegedly handed over property and vehicles as well.

Former residents say newcomers were offered land parcels for $11,000, but that the terms later changed to require that land be donated to the leader. They also say the leaders claimed the settlement was sovereign territory, exempt from both Costa Rican and U.S. taxes, where residents settled their own disputes.

The Canadian woman said the atmosphere toward her changed after she began questioning the leaders, and that she was ridiculed, accused of being possessed by demons, spat on and pushed. She said a council within the group voted for her to leave, which she did on May 5, and that she now fears for her safety.

An American woman whose son, now 27, spent more than two years in the community told local media that members were told to hand over their money, cut contact with their families and, in some cases, max out their credit cards. She said her son spent five months in a mental health facility in the United States after leaving.

Javier Chaverri Ross, a lawyer who represents several of the alleged victims, said the group seeks out people at vulnerable moments, often after a family tragedy, and encourages them to cut ties with loved ones. Some residents who remain in the community declined to comment, saying their lawyer had advised them not to speak while the investigation is under way.

The case follows the recent collapse of a teak investment scheme that has left thousands of European investors fearing losses in Costa Rica. The investigation remains open. Until it concludes, the four remain in Costa Rica under court supervision, while the alleged victims wait to learn whether any of the money they handed over can be recovered.

World.title: Puerto Rico’s Yannik Álvarez Makes History at 2026 Junior Tennis Finals
World.content:
Puerto Rican tennis player Yannik Álvarez has made history by becoming the first player from the island to qualify for the ITF World Tennis Tour Junior Finals, placing him among eight of the world’s leading junior competitors at one of the sport’s most prestigious youth tournaments.

The 18-year-old earned his place in the season-ending competition following a strong 2026 campaign that included three international singles titles and his first successful appearances on the professional circuit. The tournament, held October 21–25 at the Sichuan International Tennis Center in Chengdu, China, brings together eight boys and eight girls who have earned their places through results over the previous 12 months.

It is considered the junior equivalent of the ATP and WTA Finals, giving some of tennis’s most promising young players an opportunity to compete against one another before moving into the professional ranks. For Álvarez, simply qualifying represented a milestone for Puerto Rican tennis.

He entered the competition near the top 10 of the International Tennis Federation’s junior boys’ rankings, having built his standing through victories at tournaments in Brazil, Paraguay and Italy. His biggest junior title of the season came at the J500 tournament in Gaspar, Brazil. He also won J300 events in Asunción, Paraguay, and Santa Croce sull’Arno, Italy.

Those results demonstrated his ability to compete internationally and provided the ranking points needed to reach the elite eight-player field in Chengdu. Although Álvarez struggled against the strong competition in China, his participation marked another step in a season of significant progress.

He lost all three of his round-robin matches, finishing fourth in a group that included American Jordan Lee, Slovenia’s Ziga Sesko and Germany’s Jamie Mackenzie. The Puerto Rican then lost his opening placement match against Austria’s Thilo Behrmann, leaving him to face Mackenzie in Sunday’s seventh-place match.

The result of that final placement match had not been independently confirmed at publication time. Despite those defeats, Álvarez’s development has extended well beyond the junior circuit this year. In April, he made an impressive start in professional competition, reaching the semifinals of an ITF M15 tournament in Boca Raton, Florida.

He followed that performance with a quarterfinal appearance at another M15 tournament in Orlando the following week. At the Orlando event, he also captured a professional doubles title alongside American Ryan Cozad. Those performances are particularly important because the transition from junior to professional tennis can be difficult. Young players must begin competing against older, more experienced opponents while adapting to the physical demands and financial pressures of the professional circuit.

Álvarez has also gained experience representing Puerto Rico internationally. He was part of the country’s Davis Cup team as Puerto Rico earned promotion to the 2027 World Group II Play-offs, another encouraging development for tennis on the island. His junior Grand Slam appearances have provided additional opportunities to compete against leading players from around the world.

At the 2026 French Open, Álvarez reached the boys’ doubles semifinals. He had previously reached the same stage of the junior doubles competition at the 2025 US Open. In September, he competed in the US Open junior singles draw, defeating Japan’s Hyu Kawanishi in the opening round before losing to Kirill Filaretov.

Those experiences, combined with his success in junior tournaments and early professional results, have helped establish him as one of Puerto Rico’s most promising young tennis players. The Junior Finals also provide practical benefits for players preparing to move into professional tennis.

The ITF has allocated more than $220,000 in travel grants to participants, with payments determined by their finishing positions. The grants are intended to help young competitors cover the costs of future tournaments. Higher year-end junior rankings can also provide access to professional events through the ITF’s Junior Accelerator Programme, which helps leading juniors gain opportunities on the men’s and women’s circuits.

For Álvarez, those opportunities could become increasingly important as he continues his transition into professional competition in 2027. Puerto Rico has produced internationally recognized tennis players, most notably Olympic gold medalist Monica Puig, but establishing a consistent presence on the professional men’s tour has proved more difficult.

Álvarez’s qualification for the Junior Finals does not guarantee future success at the ATP level. However, his achievements across junior tournaments, professional events and Davis Cup competition show that he has already begun building experience beyond his age group. Whatever his final position in Chengdu, the 2026 season has given Puerto Rican tennis a new milestone and Álvarez a foundation for the next stage of his career.

World.title: International News: Florida cop accused of stealing dead man’s identity and moving into his home
World.content:
International News: Florida cop accused of stealing dead man’s identity and moving into his home

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A police officer in Florida is accused of finding a man dead during a welfare check, then taking over his identity and his house.

Brian Louis Sguros, 35, an officer with the Lauderhill Police Department, was arrested this week by the Broward County Sheriff’s Office, according to the BBC.

Investigators say that in 2022, Sguros was called in as backup for a welfare check on 71 year old Dennis West, who was found dead of natural causes.

Authorities allege Sguros then told the medical examiner he was West’s friend and that West had no living relatives. Investigators say neither claim was true. West’s body was later cremated.

Sguros allegedly moved into the two storey home in August 2022, paid utilities in the dead man’s name and renovated the property, claiming he spent more than US$214,000.

The scheme was uncovered when West’s heirs tried to sell the property.

Sguros faces charges including official misconduct and criminal use of a deceased person’s identification. He was released on a US$25,000 bond and placed on paid administrative leave. He has not commented on the charges.

World.title: Rosado Got To Go: House Speaker calls for removal of Alexis Rosado — ‘Unconscionable form of gaslighting’ for complainant; ‘Powerful men are protected, they matter more’
World.content:
Rosado Got To Go: House Speaker calls for removal of Alexis Rosado — ‘Unconscionable form of gaslighting’ for complainant; ‘Powerful men are protected, they matter more’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: In an extraordinary public statement that puts her directly at odds with Prime Minister John Briceño and Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca, Speaker of the House of Representatives Valerie Woods has made a forceful case for Ambassador Alexis Rosado’s removal as Belize’s Co-Agent before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), arguing that his continued appointment while facing serious sexual offence charges compromises the country’s credibility and inflicts further distress on the complainant.

Woods, a longtime member of the People’s United Party (PUP), has publicly challenged the position of her own party’s leadership, questioning whether Rosado’s continued appointment represents an exception being made for a powerful individual.

In her statement titled “The Co-Agent Exception,” Woods writes:

“If, at this stage, there is still an insistence on his keeping the position, it raises the question whether the high-profile title is being used as a kind of unspoken influence.”

She goes further, stating:

“The message to anyone who is observing is that Mr. Rosado is an extremely important person in the eyes of the state and exceptions should be made for him.”

Her remarks follow Prime Minister Briceño’s public defence of Rosado earlier this week, when he declared that removing the ambassador at this critical stage would not be in Belize’s national interest.

“The ‘existential’ nature of Belize’s ICJ case cannot be used to justify keeping him as Co-Agent,” Woods counters.

She maintains that removing or replacing Rosado, based on the information publicly available, would not prejudice Belize’s territorial case against Guatemala.

Woods also directly challenges Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca’s explanation that the Government is following the advice of Belize’s lead agent, Assad Shoman, who considers Rosado vital to the ongoing preparation of the case.

“Whatever value Mr. Rosado brought to the preparation of the case is largely spent. He is not the lead Co-Agent and will not argue the case,” Woods states.

She argues that Belize’s written submissions have already been filed, hearing dates have been established, and responsibility for presenting the case rests with experienced international lawyers.

She consequently describes claims that Rosado is indispensable to the country’s case as exaggerated.

But perhaps the most striking aspect of the Speaker’s intervention is her defence of the complainant and her criticism of the message being sent to women and girls by the Government’s continued support for Rosado.

“For the complainant, this must be an unconscionable form of gaslighting that is unfolding publicly and compounding the distress of the proceedings,” Woods declares.

She warns that retaining Rosado in such a prominent position undermines the country’s efforts to confront sexual violence.

“It sends troubling messages, particularly to women and girls, that high ranking, powerful men are protected, they matter more, they are shielded from institutional consequences.”

Woods also invokes Belize’s commitments under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, the 2022 national parliamentary Domestic Violence in Belize Motion, the 2026 Blue Teddy Bear campaign and the annual 16 Days of Activism to End Gender-Based Violence.

She questions how the Government can reconcile those commitments with its decision to maintain Rosado in his prominent international assignment while he faces serious criminal charges. Her argument raises questions about the consistency of Belize’s commitments rather than establishing a legal violation of any convention.

The Speaker further points out that Rosado resigned from his diplomatic postings after being charged in April 2022, arguing that the same considerations that justified protecting the integrity of those offices should apply to his continued ICJ appointment.

Woods acknowledges that Rosado remains innocent until proven guilty, but maintains that the presumption of innocence does not prevent a public official from stepping aside while criminal proceedings are pending.

The intervention comes just hours after Breaking Belize News raised this very issue in a public discussion on Saturday morning, comparing Rosado’s continued professional appointment with the situation involving Pastor Kevin Tzib, founder of Dunamis Ministries, who was recently charged with seven sexual offences and subsequently released on bail.

BBN asked whether Tzib should similarly be allowed to continue his ministry if Rosado can remain in his ICJ role with the support of the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, and questioned what distinguishes the two situations. Dunamis Ministries has announced that it will take administrative measures, although the precise restrictions on Tzib’s ministerial duties have not been publicly established.

Woods’ statement addresses the broader questions of the presumption of innocence, public accountability and whether individuals facing serious criminal allegations should remain in positions of trust.

The statement is especially significant because it places the Speaker of the House in direct public disagreement with the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister on a matter involving Belize’s most consequential international legal proceedings.

Woods concludes by rejecting the suggestion that the importance of the ICJ case should shield any individual appointment from reconsideration.

“No individual appointment is beyond recall,” she declares.

“The importance of Belize’s case before the ICJ is not a reason to tolerate the avoidable reputational risk of retaining Mr. Rosado in the position of Co-Agent.”

She maintains that, as Belize prepares to present its case before the ICJ, it is precisely the importance of those proceedings that demands a rethink of Rosado’s continued appointment.

Mayor of Belmopan, councilors complete Good Governance Training at Galen University
