World.title: International News: Thousands rally for Lula and Bolsonaro as Brazil braces for tight Presidential runoff
World.content:
International News: Thousands rally for Lula and Bolsonaro as Brazil braces for tight Presidential runoff

By Zoila Palma: Thousands of supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro took to the streets today as the candidates made their final appeals ahead of a closely contested presidential runoff election. Lula supporters filled Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana beach with the red colours of his Workers’ Party, while hundreds of bikers and other supporters rallied behind Bolsonaro in Belo Horizonte.

The rallies capped a bitter campaign that has deepened political divisions in Latin America’s largest country, AFP reports.

Lula, who turns 81 next week, waved a large Brazilian flag from a campaign truck as he addressed the crowd in Rio de Janeiro. He urged voters to choose between someone who respects Brazil’s national flag and someone who embraces the American flag.

Meanwhile, Bolsonaro’s supporters expressed confidence in his chances after he secured 47 percent of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula’s 45 percent.

A Datafolha Institute poll released during the week showed the candidates tied at 50 percent of voting intentions.

The election has drawn attention across the region as Brazil considers whether to continue under left-wing leadership or join a broader political shift toward the right.

World.title: Jamaica hit Sri Lanka for six at U15 World Cup
World.content:
File photo (Photo JFF)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica extended their historic run to three wins at the FIFA Under-15 World Cup, beating Sri Lanka 6-0 in Baku, Azerbaijan on Sunday.

This is the first time that Jamaica has registered a win against a non-Concacaf team at a FIFA World Cup since 1998, when the Reggae Boyz beat Japan at the 1998 FIFA Men’s World Cup in France.

The Jamaican team opened their schedule on Saturday with a 9-0 win over the US Virgin Islands and then beat Cuba 1-0 in their first of two games on Sunday.

Jamaica have now recorded three wins in a row for the first time ever at a FIFA World Cup.

They will next face Togo and the Czech Republic on Monday, and if they top their first-round group, will advance to the round of 32 of the competition.

— Paul A Reid

World.title: Jamaican DJ Kovert dies at 19 following car crash
World.content:
DJ Kovert gets into his set at an event. The up-and-coming disc jock, real name Matthew Nelson, has died aged 19 after a car crash on Washington Boulevard in St Andrew.

Popular disc jock, DJ Kovert, real name Matthew Nelson, has died.

The 19-year-old passed away at the University of the Hospital of the West Indies on Saturday, following complications from a motor vehicle crash which took place a few days earlier on the Washington Boulevard in St Andrew.

DJ Kovert, who was one of the shining lights in the new generation of music connoisseurs, had been playing music professionally since 2024 when he won the SunCity High School DJ Competition.

A former student at Ardenne High, he was a first-year management studies student at the University of the West Indies, Mona. He also co-promoted a bi-weekly series over the summer called FWD.

News of his passing has rocked the entertainment fraternity. Several of his musical peers took to social media to share their condolences.

In an interview with Observer Online on Saturday night, DJ Russ Buss shared his fondest memory of his late colleague.

“My fondest memory by far of Kovert, was the first time seeing him playing in the SunCity High School DJ competition during the preliminary rounds, and I listened to his transitions and how he played; I knew he would have won,” said Russ Buss. “I was impressed the first time that I saw him play. He reminded me so much of myself when I started playing music, how much he loved it, his humility and he had a lot of manners. He loved the craft and had such a bright future ahead of him.”

DJ Zacky, a close friend of DJ Kovert, shared his condolences and reflected on their friendship in a detailed post on Instagram.

“One DM turned us from strangers to brothers. From practice sessions to site visits, to bookings and even just going out for drinks, you became more than a friend to me. Every Friday, you would call me and say “Wah time yah play tonight”, and once I told you, it was always “Live, me a fwd.” Every room you waked into, you lit it up, and that’s something I’ll never forget,” DJ Zacky wrote, adding “One thing I’ll always remember about you is how you always found the positive in every situation, even when we were late for bookings. No matter what was happening, you always found a way to make the best of it. That’s the kind of person you were, and I’ll truly miss that about you.”

In an emotional post on Instagram, DJ TZ recalled when he learnt about DJ Kovert’s crash.

“I saw you the night of and we did a laugh and a run bare jokes a Ribbiz, to then get a call in the morning seh yuh crash bro. Mnk (Mi nuh know) how fi function rn bro. You was one of the realest, happiest, talented and down to earth niggas I’ve ever met,” the post read. “You was my brother and I got so much love for you gang. I promise to keep your name and legacy alive and to take you with me everywhere I go. I promise to never let you be forgotten and to keep going and to push through bcs ik that is what you would want. Love you family and rest easy.”

Meanwhile, DJ JJ Deadlock wrote on his whatsapp status, “Dawg Kovert sooo humble and jovial. We had this event together and my laptop wasn’t connecting and he easily gave me his laptop to DJ half of my set.”

Others who commented publicly include Fyahman, DJ Hibby, DJ Alpha C and emerging recording artiste Kong Magic.

The circumstances surrounding the fatal crash involving Nelson are still unclear. However, it is understood that Nelson had been driving home in the wee hours Thursday when the incident occurred.

The impact of the crash damaged electrical infrastructure and left sections of Molynes Road and nearby communities without electricity.

World.title: British ‘heirs of slavery’ back reparations
World.content:
(FILES) People calling for slavery reparations, protest outside the entrance of the British High Commission in Kingston, Jamaica on March 22, 2022, during the visit of the Britain's Duke and Duchess of Cambridge. Caribbean nations stepping up their campaign for slavery reparations have won support from an unexpected source -- the descendants of some of Britain's most prominent families to have benefitted from the slave trade. As prime ministers, courtiers and aristocrats, the names of the Gladstone, Lascelles and Trevelyan families were at the heart of the governing elite down the decades. (Photo by Ricardo Makyn / AFP)

LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP) — Caribbean nations campaigning for slavery reparations have won support from an unexpected source — the descendants of some of Britain’s most prominent families to have benefitted from the slave trade.

As prime ministers, courtiers and aristocrats, the Gladstone, Lascelles and Trevelyan families were at the heart of the governing elite down the decades.

They accumulated significant wealth from slavery through the ownership of plantations in the West Indies and South America.

Laura Trevelyan, a former BBC journalist, told AFP she had been unaware of her family’s involvement until hearing about an archive listing compensation payments to plantation owners triggered by the British parliament’s abolition of slavery in 1833.

“I was clueless,” she told AFP.

“I looked at the database and saw this small island in the eastern Caribbean called Grenada that various members of the Trevelyan family had claimed compensation for the loss of what was termed their property.”

The revelation spurred Trevelyan, who made a public apology in Grenada in 2023, to co-found the Heirs of Slavery group which supports “reparative justice”.

With other members of her family she has paid voluntary personal reparations of around £100,000 ($133,000) earmarked for educational projects.

“Everybody I met, I asked them ‘should I apologise for what my ancestors did and do you think that I personally should pay reparations?’ and the answer came back a resounding ‘yes’,” she said.

Co-founder Charlie Gladstone, a direct descendant of reforming 19th century prime minister William Gladstone whose father John was one of the largest slave owners in the British West Indies, followed suit by making a public apology in Guyana in 2023.

Another group member is aristocrat David Lascelles, the Earl of Harewood, whose family has close links to the royal family.

A portrait of the actor David Harewood hangs at the family’s stately home, Harewood House in northern England, after it was discovered that his ancestors had worked on Lascelles family sugar plantations in Barbados.

The UK government in September reiterated its rejection of calls for slavery reparations.

Modern British royals have expressed remorse, but like the government have not issued an official apology.

The issue is likely to be raised during a Caribbean tour by King Charles III which begins Tuesday when he travels to the Bahamas, then Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda where he will address the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting.

A Buckingham Palace spokesman said the king would acknowledge the “darkest days” of colonial rule and slavery during the trip.

Ahead of the visit, Guyana’s President Irfaan Ali said his country would continue to champion the reparation issue “because slavery was the worst indignity to humankind”.

He called for a “mature” discussion on an apology and reparations, pointing to differing measures from debt relief, to finance for education and healthcare, and even climate adaptation.

The Reparations Commission of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) has called for “monetary compensation” alongside debt cancellation and a full apology as part of its “Ten-Point plan”.

Meanwhile, Britain’s Privy Council — the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories — will next year hear a petition for slavery reparations filed by Jamaica.

The petition asks the court to rule on whether the capture, transport and enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was ever legal under English law, and whether the UK owes the people of Jamaica a “reparatory remedy”.

Not all families who benefitted from slavery, however, have agreed with the Heirs group approach.

Caricom Reparations Commission chair Hilary Beckles has repeatedly spoken out about ex-Conservative Party lawmaker and UK landowner Richard Drax, 68, whose ancestors established Drax Hall Estate in Barbados in the mid-17th century.

Beckles has estimated up to 30,000 slaves died at Drax plantations in Barbados and Jamaica over 200 years.

Drax has remained staunchly opposed to reparations. He has said that while the role his ancestors played in the slave trade was “deeply, deeply regrettable … no-one can be held responsible today for what happened many hundreds of years ago”.

The Draxes are unique in that “they’re the only family that still owns a plantation that was set up in the beginning”, said Paul Lashmar, author of “Drax of Drax Hall: How One British Family Got Rich (and Stayed rich) from Sugar and Slavery”.

But he said it was increasingly difficult to see how Drax’s position could prevail.

“If you are very wealthy and a lot of your wealth comes from those years then it’s not something you can wash your hands of,” he said.

World.title: Heartless!
World.content:
HAVANA, Cuba — A woman carries water containers during a blackout in Havana, on July 7, 2026. Cubans were gradually getting power back on July 7 after the third nationwide power outage since the start of the year, causing mounting despair in the face of an energy collapse precipitated by a US fuel blockade. (Photo: AFP)

Ten former Caricom leaders are urging the global community to support the upcoming United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) resolution that calls for an end to America’s embargo against Cuba, denouncing the long-running sanction as inhumane and contrary to international law.

“The unilateral, coercive actions of the USA against Cuba represent the law of the jungle and can in no way be justified by the Charter of the United Nations or any other source of international law and justice,” the former Caricom heads of State and Government argued in an open letter to all nations of the world dated October 24, 2026.

They pointed out that every year since 1992, the UNGA has been “adopting overwhelmingly” a resolution on this subject. “Yet the USA has been ignoring the clear voice of the international community, the requisites of international law, and the most elemental of civilising principles.”

The 10 leaders are Freundel Stuart, former prime minister of Barbados; Dean Barrow and Said Musa, former prime ministers of Belize; Keith Mitchell and Tillman Thomas, former prime ministers of Grenada; Donald Ramotar, former president of Guyana; Bruce Golding and PJ Patterson, former prime ministers of Jamaica; Kenny Anthony, former prime minister of St Lucia; and Ralph Gonsalves, former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines.

Noting that the vote is scheduled for October 28, the 10 leaders said they were “strongly and unequivocally” urging all nations to vote in favour of the resolution as the imposition of the embargo is contrary to “every civilised precept of life and living”.

Their appeal came a day after the US Government, in its latest bid to increase pressure on the Cuban Government, urged Cubans to make “discreet” contact with America’s Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).

“To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post.

“The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA,” Rubio added.

French news service Agence France Presse (AFP), in its report on the development, said the unusual post appeared to confirm that the CIA is currently active in Cuba after a long history of covert operations, including backing the disastrous Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961.

According to AFP, Rubio’s call was mocked by Cuban officials.

“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.

“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”

AFP reported that the CIA later uploaded a video to X offering instructions in Spanish for those who believe they have information of interest to the intelligence agency, encouraging them to first and foremost visit an official US installation in person if they can safely travel to one.

For those hoping to contact the CIA online via the cia.gov website, the agency instructed users to access the Internet on a secure network, like a VPN, using a private browser and a ‘burner’ e-mail account unassociated with any personal details.

Those sharing information should be prepared to include their city, job, level of access, and contact information with their message, AFP reported.

For months, US President Donald Trump and other senior officials of his Government have openly hinted at a military intervention or takeover of Cuba, ramping up economic, political, and legal pressure on the Spanish-speaking country.

Trump, speaking at a rally in Florida on Friday, underlined his ambitions to impose regime change in Cuba.

“Those beautiful [US military] ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast,” he said. “They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez quickly dismissed Trump’s threats.

“Our coastline is full of beautiful beaches, but there are also razor-sharp limestone spikes, an inhospitable environment for those who make it to our shores with hostile purposes and lust for domination,” he posted on social media.

In another move against the Cuban leadership, Florida’s top prosecutor last week announced an arrest warrant for former President Raul Castro on State murder charges that echo a federal indictment unveiled earlier this year.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said Castro, 95, is wanted in connection with the 1996 shooting down of two civilian aircraft from Brothers to the Rescue, an organisation assisting Cubans fleeing to Florida by sea.

“Raul Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,” Uthmeier said in a statement.

Castro, brother of the late revolutionary leader and US nemesis Fidel Castro, was indicted on federal charges related to the incident in May.

Trump previously seized on a US indictment to justify military action that toppled Venezuela’s then-president Nicolas Maduro, a staunch ally of the Cuban authorities.

Current Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel has said the US federal indictment against Castro has “no legal basis” and was an attempt “to justify the folly of a military aggression against Cuba”.

The US indictment has also been denounced by China and Russia, which both have close ties with Cuba.

On Wednesday, Beijing urged Washington to cease “all forms of coercion and pressure against Cuba”.

“China has consistently opposed the abuse of judicial measures to exert pressure on Cuba, and firmly supports Cuba in safeguarding its national sovereignty and resisting foreign interference,” foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters at a news conference.

“Comrade Raul is a highly respected leader of the Cuban Revolution who enjoys great prestige internationally,” she added.

A day earlier, Russia said in a statement that it “categorically” rejected and “strongly” condemned the Florida arrest warrant, and reaffirmed Moscow’s “unwavering solidarity” with Cuba.

“Bringing a baseless and contrived accusation more than 30 years after the events can only be seen as an act of vengeance by the anti-Cuban lobby in Miami,” Russia’s foreign ministry charged.

In January this year, Trump began imposing a crippling fuel blockade on Cuba, intensifying the island’s severe economic crisis. Washington has since piled more sanctions on Cuba, cutting off nearly all its sources of revenue.

The island of just over nine million people has endured constant power cuts due to the poor state of its ageing thermoelectric plants. That has worsened significantly since the US action in January in its bid to pressure Havana’s communist Government.

A severe lack of fuel makes it difficult to supply Cuba’s power plants and backup generators, which typically run on imported diesel.

In recent weeks, blackouts have lasted more than 30 hours in the capital, while in outlying provinces they have sometimes stretched past 60 hours.

The cuts have also affected the island’s water supply and mobile phone network, adding to extremely tough general living conditions for residents.

Havana blames the crisis on the array of US-imposed punitive measures, while Washington attributes the hardship to poor internal management.

The embargo was first imposed in 1962 by then US President John F Kennedy, who invoked the Trading with the Enemy Act, which allows Washington to restrict trade with countries it considers foes.

Since 1978 every single US leader has renewed the provision annually.

In August this year the US extended the trade embargo by another year, drawing fury from the Cuban Government.

Foreign Minister Rodriguez called the embargo “a genocidal policy” and accused Washington of being “intent on suffocating an entire nation”.

“This extension comes at the cruellest moment of the US offensive against Cuba in recent years,” he said in a post on X.

Trump has claimed that Cuba, located 150 kilometres (90 miles) off Florida’s coast, represents an “extraordinary threat” to US national security.

However, the former Caricom leaders, in their open letter on Saturday, stated that “Cuba is not a threat to any nation or any person on planet Earth”.

They argued that the embargo “continues to be a threat to hemispheric and international peace and security…is a brazen violation of Cuba’s right to sovereignty and independence, [and] derogates from the most elemental human rights of a people established and declared by international law.

“The vote on this UNGA resolution this year is more urgent and important than ever before. In recent months, the US Government has further ramped up its illegal embargo against Cuba in an attempt to starve the Cuban people into submission through the imposition of third-party sanctions against any Government or entity which grants, sells, or transports energy products, including gasoline and diesel, to Cuba. Surely, such US conduct is inhumane, and undoubtedly contrary to international law,” the 10 leaders wrote.

“Accordingly, it is imperative that the blandishments and pressures currently being deployed by the USA to derail and defeat the proposed UNGA resolution must be resisted,” they added.

“Let us all contribute to the healing of the hemispheric fracture between the United States of America and Cuba by supporting the UNGA resolution on October 28, 2026. Let us all stand with Cuba and humanity on this matter,” the leaders said.

World.title: Shake-up ahead for underperforming hospital management
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton is speaking with patients waiting to see a doctor at the Noel Holmes Hospital outpatient area on Friday. (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

FORT CHARLOTTE, Hanover — Strong action will be taken against the management teams of non-performing public health institutions warns Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton following a national patient complaints report showing that long wait times remain a primary grievance across the island’s hospital network.

“I am just giving a notice that we are going to be taking stronger action around throughput and the quality of throughput, and Noel Holmes is not going to be an exception. All institutions are going to have that,” stated Tufton during a press conference at the Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover on Friday afternoon.

Before the press briefing, the minister toured the Type-C facility, which is currently being rehabilitated following Hurricane Melissa last October. During the tour, several patients raised concerns about lengthy wait times.

“Coming here and hearing that five people are waiting at an outpatient area from 9:30 or 10:00 this morning until 12:00, and the doctor has not yet seen the patient — the five or six people — not a good thing. Nobody should wait three or four hours and you haven’t seen one patient yet. Sorry. We are going to have to call these things out when they happen,” stated Tufton.

The minister highlighted that staff numbers at Noel Holmes Hospital increased significantly from 189 before the hurricane to 270, including specialist doctors. He stressed that this expanded workforce must translate into enhanced service delivery, improved throughput, and shorter wait times.

Moving forward, the ministry will closely evaluate staff counts against productivity and patient throughput across the entire public health sector.

Tufton added that the recently completed national patient complaints report will be released publicly within three weeks.

“The number one reason why people complain is access to service — timely access to service. And I know that there’s a default mode that says, ‘It’s because we don’t have this,’ or, ‘We don’t have that.’ But if we hire more doctors, the least that can happen is that the doctor must turn up and deal with the patient on time. Patients are not supposed to wait long if you have more doctors working. I can’t put it any plainer,” said Tufton.

Tufton warned institutional and regional leaders that they will be held accountable for administrative and operational failures.

“Hiring more people means greater levels of productivity, more efficient throughput, and less wait time. People see their doctors more on time. Management, leadership, and supervisors must ensure that it happens, and they must be at their posts to ensure that it happens.

“And I’m charging the regions — this regional [acting] director [Deveta McLaren] is on the line now because I’m here in Noel Holmes, but when I go to the other places I do the same thing — they must ensure that their reports reflect that, because we’re ranking institutions now on levels of performance and on complaints. And if you fall below the satisfactory rank, a team is going to come in and they’re going to start with leadership: Are you the suitable person to run this institution or to provide leadership? Because, ultimately, the buck stops with leaders,” warned Tufton.

When asked by the Jamaica Observer what specific administrative actions could be taken, Tufton explained that measures would range from performance warnings to removal from leadership posts.

“It starts with appraisal; it starts with the board. The board is going to put the region under pressure, and the region will have to relate to your parish managers. Parish managers will have to look at the key performance indicators at the level of the institutions, and people will have to be spoken to,” argued Tufton.

He cited a recent example in which a non-performing hospital chief executive officer (CEO) was removed from his post, two weeks ago, following a written directive to the board.

“The board was told to find another place to put him, because he was not providing leadership in the hospital. And we’re going to get more of that. The board has the authority to do it. I appoint the board, and you know, the truth is I appoint or remove them at my discretion. They, ultimately, have responsibility, and they must ask for these reports,” stated Tufton.

To avoid the perception of a totalitarian regime, Tufton said training and technology will be used to provide support to employees.

“Where we need to train and retrain, it has to be a critical part of the culture going forward, and technology is an important thing — using technology to give support. Things like registration, follow-ups, those sorts of things have to be a critical part. It’s not just about the human component; it’s about the ecosystem that you build out around them,” he explained.

World.title: Legendary Derrick Harriott ‘checks out’
World.content:
Derrick Harriott (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Derrick Clifton Harriott, who excelled as a singer, producer, and record label owner, died at his St Andrew home on October 24.

He was 87.

Lorna Thomas, his friend of over 60 years, confirmed his passing in an interview with the Jamaica Observer. She said he died just after midnight, less than one week after leaving Medical Associates Hospital in St Andrew.

Thomas disclosed that Harriott had been ailing for some time, but his condition deteriorated since August when he was hospitalised twice.

The youngest of six children, Harriott was born in Kingston and attended Excelsior High School. He got his start in music during the late 1950s as a member of The Jiving Juniors, a harmony quartet that recorded mainly American-inspired ballads.

That was followed by a successful solo career that produced songs like Walk The Streets, Solomon, The Loser, Born to Love You, and the 1984-released Checkin’ Out.

Harriott also established himself as a producer with his Crystal label, which released hit songs by Keith and Tex (Stop That Train, Tonight), The Kingstonians (Singer Man), The Federals (Penny For Your Song) and Dennis Brown (Lips Of Wine, Silhouette).

Lips Of Wine, released in 1968, was Dennis Brown’s first song. Harriott also directed Brown on a 1973 album that includes covers of Glen Campell’s Wichita Lineman and Let Me Down Easy, originally done by Van McKoy.

Since the early 1970s, Harriott operated the Chariot record store in Twin Gates Plaza in Ha;f-Way-Tree, St Andrew. It was a hub for fans seeking hard-to-find vinyl records, as well as dances, shows, and roots plays on VHS.

One of the artistes whose careers Harriott impacted was singer McAnuff. He produced Pick Hits to Click, McAnuff’s first album, which was released in 1977.

“Derrick was like mi father, one of di nicest people yuh could ever meet. Him was a lesson in humility,” said McAnuff.

For his contribution to Jamaican music, Harriott was honoured by the Jamaican Government with an investiture into the Order of Distinction in 2009.

Minister of Culture and Entertainment Olivia Grange said that with the death of Harriott, Jamaica, sadly, has lost another of the icons who helped to shape the trajectory and reach of the country’s musical genres.

“Derrick was a true pioneer of Jamaican music, and it is interesting that February 6, his birthday anniversary, is the same as that of reggae legend Bob Marley,” she shared. “Through his music and his record store, he nurtured talent and preserved our music over many years.”

He is the latest entertainment industry stalwart to die in 2026. Drummer Sly Dunbar, guitarist Stephen “Cat” Coore, singer Stranger Cole, guitarist Rupert Bent II (who played on Lips of Wine), and bass guitarist Jackie Jackson predeceased him.

Derrick Harriott is survived by his 97 year-old sister, Loy Shegog; eight children, grandchildren, and great grandchildren.

World.title: 80 years for one, retrial for second in 2015 family massacre
World.content:
A Jamaica Observer file photo of inside a courtroom at the Court of Appeal building in downtown Kingston.

AN appeal from two men serving life behind bars for the “brutal execution-type slaying” of six members of one family and the arson of the family home, which left four survivors severely burnt, has resulted in one felon losing his bid to overturn his conviction and his 80-year pre-parole period being affirmed, while the other is heading to a retrial for the six murders. The Appeal Court, however, affirmed the sentences for that man on five other counts.

The men, Mikhail Campbell and Errol Clarke, had been jointly charged, tried, and convicted on an indictment containing 11 counts for the offences of arson (count one), murder (counts two to seven), and causing grievous bodily harm with intent (counts eight to 11) before Supreme Court Judge Justice Martin Gayle and a jury in the Hanover Circuit Court in November 2018. The jury convicted both men on all 11 counts, unanimously in the case of Campbell and by a majority of five to two in the case of Clarke.

Campbell and Clarke were sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment for arson and 20 years’ imprisonment for each count of causing grievous bodily harm with intent. Campbell was sentenced to life imprisonment on each of the six counts of murder, with the stipulation that he would not be eligible for parole until after serving 43 years for the first three counts of murder and 40 years for the remaining three. Clarke was also sentenced to life imprisonment for each of the six counts of murder; however, it was stipulated that he should serve 40 years before becoming eligible for parole on each count. For both men, Justice Gayle ruled that counts one to four and counts five to 11 were to be served concurrently, while counts five to 11 were to be served consecutively to counts one to four, resulting in a total minimum sentence of 80 years’ imprisonment before eligibility for parole.

In what was described by the court as “an unimaginable act of cruelty and brutality” on the night of October 8, 2015, perpetrators forcefully entered the home — which had just hours before been the scene of a celebration to welcome the mother and daughter who had returned from an overseas visit — and despite desperate pleas, shot and killed a 62-year-old matriarch, a pregnant 36-year-old woman, two men in the prime of their lives (40 and 29 years old), a young woman who had just attained the age of majority, and a minor aged 15 years.

They then set the house on fire, resulting in the deceased being burned beyond recognition and the four survivors being left with thermal injuries affecting 13 to 25 per cent of their bodies during their desperate fight to escape the flames.

The crime, according to prosecution witnesses, was premeditated and motivated by revenge on the part of Campbell, described as a “close, trusted family friend of the deceased” who had been present at the homecoming celebrations earlier in the day. Campbell, the court was told, took men to the house to exact vengeance on one of the family members for “disrespecting” him. After the family members failed to disclose the whereabouts of the man who was being sought, they were executed by Campbell and Clarke.

Ironically, that family member, who was one of the six Crown witnesses to testify during the trial, had taken refuge under a bed in one of the rooms in the house.

The men, following their convictions, appealed.

Campbell challenged his convictions and sentences, arguing, among other things, that the prosecution’s case against him should have been thrown out since it hinged entirely on voice identification evidence which he contended “was inconsistent, insufficient, and unreliable”.

Campbell did not challenge the sentences imposed for the offences of arson and causing grievous bodily harm with intent, but insisted that the sentences for the murders were “manifestly excessive”.

Clarke, on the other hand, in appealing his convictions, maintained that the jury was deprived of its statutorily mandated time for deliberating the six counts of murder against him, as such rendering the murder convictions “unsafe” and the trial a nullity.

According to the court’s record, on November 30, 2018, the seven jurors retired at 12:16 pm to deliberate and reach a verdict for Clarke and returned 58 minutes later at 1:14 pm; the foreman indicated that they had not arrived at a unanimous verdict. The trial judge directed them to continue deliberating. The jury retired again at 1:18 pm and returned 40 minutes later at 1:58 pm to announce their majority verdict. The total time of deliberation was one hour and 38 minutes. Section 44 of the Jury (Amendment) Act, 2016 stipulates that a jury deliberate for two hours before returning a majority verdict.

The Appeal Court, in considering the argument that the sentences for the murders were “manifestly excessive”, said “it cannot be denied that this matter could be regarded as an exceptional case and represented…‘the worst of the worst’ for this type of offending”. In fact, the Appeal Court said it was “worth recognising…that the prosecution could have, at the very least, sought the death penalty with respect to the second and subsequent murders”.

It, however, said, “In light of the errors identified in the learned trial judge’s approach to sentencing…it is fair to say that his sentencing approach lacked the required structure and clarity essential in a case of this magnitude, thereby entitling this court to embark on its own sentencing exercise.”

The judges of the appeal, while declaring that “the magnitude of the brutality and callousness surrounding the killing of all six deceased cannot be overemphasised”, admitted that “the learned trial judge did not employ the structured methodology that has since become well established for determining appropriate minimum pre-parole periods, nor did he otherwise demonstrate how he arrived at those periods”.

“In the absence of comparable cases to provide guidance, it was especially important for the basis of those periods to be apparent from his reasoning. The learned trial judge also failed to consider each count separately, and he imposed lesser sentences on the latter counts of murder,” they stated.

The Appeal Court panel, however, following a resentencing exercise for Campbell, said there actually was an increase in the aggregate minimum pre-parole period he was to serve. It, however, said since based on case law there can be no increase in a convicted person’s sentence on appeal without notice to him and/or his counsel of the court’s intention to do so, and given the absence of any such notice, “Campbell shall serve an aggregate minimum term of 80 years’ imprisonment before eligibility for parole, as ordered by the learned trial judge”.

“The learned trial judge did not err in rejecting the submission of no case to answer that was made on Mr Campbell’s behalf. The quality of the evidence was sufficient for the learned trial judge to determine that it merited the jury’s consideration. He also gave the jury all the appropriate directions on voice identification and on inconsistencies and discrepancies. It was for the jury, the judges of credibility, having heard the evidence and being properly and adequately directed, to determine the weight to be attached to the evidence and arrive at the verdicts they considered appropriate. It is pellucid from their unanimous verdicts that they were convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr Campbell was guilty as charged. The application for leave to appeal conviction is, therefore, refused,” the judges of the appeal ruled.

In respect of Clarke, the judges of the appeal said the trial court was obliged to observe and uphold the law which mandates that a majority verdict in a murder case may be received only after “the lapse of two hours from the retirement of the jury”.

“As a result, Mr Clarke’s trial, conviction, and sentence on counts two to seven of the indictment amount to a nullity. Therefore, the convictions on those counts will be quashed and the sentences set aside…a retrial of those counts of the indictment will be ordered in the interest of justice,” the judges of the appeal ruled.

In the meantime, however, the court said, the aggregate sentence of 40 years’ imprisonment — comprising two 20-year terms ordered to run consecutively — was neither manifestly excessive nor disproportionate, and did not breach the totality principle in Clarke’s case even though the learned trial judge erred in failing to deduct the three months Clarke spent in pre-sentence remand.

“In accordance with the authorities, this period will be deducted from the sentence imposed on count one of the indictment. This will result in a sentence of 19 years’ and nine months’ imprisonment at hard labour. This is the only basis for interfering with the sentences imposed by the learned trial judge,” the Appeal Court said in allowing the appeal against the sentence, in part.

“The sentence of 20 years’ imprisonment at hard labour on count one of the indictment is set aside and substituted therefor is a sentence of 19 years’ and nine months’ imprisonment at hard labour, with three months spent on pre-sentence remand being fully credited. The sentences on counts eight to 11 are affirmed. The sentences on counts eight to 11 are to run concurrently but consecutively to the sentence on count one as imposed by the learned trial judge. The appellant shall, therefore, serve an aggregate term of 39 years and nine months’ imprisonment at hard labour,” the judges of the appeal ruled in respect of Clarke.

“The sentence on count one is to be reckoned as having commenced on December 14, 2018, the date on which it was imposed. The sentences on counts eight to 11 are to commence after completion of the sentence on count one,” the court said further.

World.title: WHO WANTS IT?
World.content:
Colorado Murray of Waterhouse celebrates after scoring against Molynes United in their Jamaica Premier League match played at Constant Spring Sports Complex on Wednesday, March 18. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

The lead in the Legend Jamaica Premier League will be up for grabs on Sunday, with Montego Bay United not playing until Monday and Racing United, Waterhouse FC and Tivoli Gardens all having a chance to move ahead of the leaders.

Three points separate the top five teams in the standings. Montego Bay United lead with 14 points from six games, followed by Racing United on 13, Waterhouse FC on 12, and Tivoli Gardens and Tru-Juice FC on 11 each.

Racing United, who are unbeaten in their last three games and have scored 10 of their 14 goals over that period, will start favourites to extend Humble Lion’s winless run to seven games. Racing are away to the bottom-placed team, who have yet to win this season.

Despite being held 0-0 by Waterhouse on Monday, Racing United remain one of the competition’s top-scoring teams. They will face a Humble Lion defence that has conceded 17 goals, five more than the next-worst team, Molynes United, with 12.

Nickyle Ellis and Tajay Grant have combined to score seven of Racing United’s goals, with each having scored more goals than Humble Lion’s entire team.

Waterhouse FC have drawn their last three games after opening the season with three wins. They will host Dunbeholden FC, who are 12th in the standings with three points.

Waterhouse have scored just two goals in their last three games, a sharp decline from the 13 they netted in their first three matches. They will hope to rediscover their scoring touch against Dunbeholden.

Colorado Murray and Mario Simms have scored three goals each for Waterhouse.

Tivoli Gardens could also move ahead of Montego Bay United on goal difference. They travel to face Cavalier FC, who are winless in their last three games and are coming off a loss to Molynes United.

Tivoli have scored 13 goals this season, with Leaunghn Williams leading the way with three. Steve Clarke and Ajuma Johnson have scored two each.

Tru-Juice FC will be looking for back-to-back wins when they visit winless Treasure Beach at the STETHS Sports Complex. It will be the first meeting between the teams in the Jamaica Premier League.

Tru-Juice are coming off a 4-0 win over Humble Lion, while Treasure Beach have scored just four goals in five games.

Defending champions Portmore United, who have played just three games because of their Concacaf Caribbean Cup commitments, will host Chapelton Maroons at the Ferdie Neita Sports Complex.

Portmore are ninth with five points after drawing their two most recent games and will be looking for a win. Chapelton, however, will be seeking back-to-back victories after edging Treasure Beach 1-0 last weekend.

World.title: Burnham open to return of free movement between UK and EU
World.content:
“But at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now]. Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

Burnham said at the Labour Party Conference in September that he is weighing different options for a reset of relations with the 27-country bloc.

He did not elaborate in his conference speech on the options he would present — but different figures within Labour have argued for joining the EU single market, the customs union, or rejoining the bloc wholesale. Rejoining the single market would require the U.K. to sign up to the EU’s rules permitting free movement of people.

His stance on freedom of movement marks a significant shift from the Labour Party’s 2024 manifesto, which ruled out a return to the single market, customs union or free movement, and comes one month ahead of a Nov. 20 summit where the EU and the U.K. hope to sign off on a set of agreements ranging from trade to climate regulations.

In his interview with the Sunday Times, he set out his own red lines, adding that he “can’t see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen.”

World.title: Leaked emails show AfD co-leader’s U-turn on ‘explosive’ nationalist colleague
World.content:
The revelations come from more than 420,000 emails and roughly 48,000 documents released by hackers this week, providing a rare glimpse inside Germany’s largest far-right party. An anonymous spokesperson for the hackers told Die Zeit the attack was not “politically” motivated “in the sense that [they] support another party,” but that they published the allegedly stolen material to promote “transparency and public accountability.”

The AfD confirmed the breach, saying hackers had attacked a hosting provider in late September. It condemned the leak as “an attack on the German party system and therefore on democracy itself.”

WELT, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, examined emails from one of Weidel’s accounts between 2015 and 2017, when she was a relatively junior figure in the party’s leadership.

Asked by WELT to explain the contrast between her warnings at the time and her present position, Weidel declined to comment through a spokesperson.

A spokesperson for Höcke did not respond to a request for comment sent by POLITICO on Saturday.

‘Deeply problematic’

The messages seen by WELT show a politician deeply alarmed by the growing influence of Höcke, who championed an ethnically defined German nationalism drawing on ideas associated with the Nazi era.

World.title: Security Sunday: Bringen Frankreichs Proteste Marine Le Pen an die Macht? – mit Martina Meister
World.content:
Brennende Mülltonnen, verbarrikadierte Schaufenster und eine unübersichtliche Mischung aus Gelbwesten, Anarchisten und Banlieue-Jugendlichen auf den Straßen. Was als Schülerprotest in Frankreich begann, hat sich an steigenden Energiepreisen zu einer radikalen Bewegung entzündet. Präsident Emmanuel Macron verliert zunehmend die Kontrolle und wirkt in der Krise wie ein Pilot ohne Cockpit.

Inmitten der Eskalation positioniert sich Marine Le Pen geschickt als Kandidatin der Ordnung, während die politische Mitte zerbröselt und eine erdrückende Staatsverschuldung den Handlungsspielraum raubt.

Was ein möglicher Rechtsruck für die europäische Sicherheitsarchitektur und das ohnehin angespannte deutsch-französische Verhältnis bedeutet, analysiert Welt-Korrespondentin Martina Meister im Gespräch mit Rixa Fürsen.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

World.title: Tensions flare up across France as marches come to an end
World.content:
Authorities said the march in Paris, which drew 110,000 people, remained calm through Saturday afternoon, but tensions flared as demonstrations came to an end in multiple cities.

In Lyon, France’s third-largest city where gatherings were banned in parts of the city, the police used tear gas to disperse protesters. Forty people were arrested in Nice, where the protests were banned, while tear gas was used against protestors in Marseille, French broadcaster BFMTV reported.

Tensions also escalated during the afternoon in Toulouse, Lille, Nantes and Rennes, according to media reports, with protestors throwing projectiles at police and officers using water cannons to disperse them. Authorities in Lille, where about 15,000 people protested according to early estimates, extended their curfews for minors through Monday.

Nuñez, the interior minister, told police forces to be “uncompromising” with potential rioters earlier on Saturday, ahead of a day of protests that is leaving the country on edge.

“Today’s key words will be mobility, responsiveness and adaptability, so we can really act against high-risk groups… We must be absolutely uncompromising and hyper, hyper, hyper-responsive,” he said during a visit Saturday morning to the National Police Academy in Vincennes.

Nuñez was heavily criticized for his handling of last Saturday’s protests, and has been accused of underestimating both the number of protesters and the potential for violent incidents. He announced on Friday that 70,000 police officers would be deployed, 10,000 more than last weekend.

World.title: Starlink connection restored at high speed in Ukraine, defense minister says
World.content:
The antenna of a Starlink satellite-based broadband system is seen in the Kharkiv region of Ukraine on Sept. 25, 2022. | Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images

SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services have been restored in Ukraine, allowing the country's forces to operate drones at high speed, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on Saturday.

"The Ministry of Defense's monitoring systems indicate that Starlink/Starshield speeds have been restored," Khmara told reporters in WhatsApp messages. "We are recording speeds exceeding 400 km/h, and the connection is stable."

Since last week, Kyiv had been reporting speed limits on Starshield, Starlink's military-grade service, affecting Ukraine's ability to use drones and carry out defensive strikes. The throttling came amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump blaming President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for the continuation of the war with Russia.

World.title: Inside the cyber flaw scramble that brought the AI threat to life
World.content:
While no major hacking damage was immediately apparent, the way the incident unfolded over 72 hours showed how easily cybersecurity processes can break down and the outsized consequences of cyber risks in the AI era.

The man who set off the chain reaction with the early release — Chainguard’s CEO Dan Lorenc — quickly apologized in a LinkedIn post. But on Thursday, in an interview with POLITICO, Lorenc said he’d shared the information ahead of time because the flaw was already being exploited. Though others disputed that, Lorenc said he believed he’d seen enough evidence to invalidate an embargo set up to allow time to find a fix for the flaws.

While he disputed that his actions would have caused problems for other defenders, Lorenc conceded that the evidential threshold in these coordinated cyber defense systems is a “grey area.”

The revelation of the PHP flaw brings out into the open what cyber officials have been bracing for since the arrival of the most powerful tools of artificial intelligence, which not only can be used to discover vulnerabilities but also to exploit them at scale.

The cybersecurity world’s long-established protocols helped prevent disaster scenarios, in which hackers would have successfully exploited the vulnerabilities to take control of numerous websites and access their data. But now the scale and end-of-days potential of AI-driven cyber risks are visible for the world to see.

This “is what happens when AI turns up a flaw that’s been hiding for years,” said Eylam Milner, co-founder and chief technology officer at cybersecurity start-up Echo. The vulnerabilities, he added, are “about as serious as it gets for the web.”

World.title: What’s not on the ballot in Israel: Peace
World.content:
But campaigns by both the Arab parties and Jewish politicians have avoided talking about what the outcome might actually mean for Jewish-Arab relations in the region, for the possibility of a two-state solution and even for U.S. President Donald Trump’s vision for a comprehensive peace-through-prosperity deal between Israelis and the Palestinians.

“The election campaign has been bizarre,” said Michael Milshtein, a retired Israeli army colonel and former head of Palestinian affairs in Israel’s military intelligence agency. “The campaign has been focused on domestic and personal issues, and on Netanyahu.”

That means it hasn’t included “the very deep complicated issue of the critical relations between us and the Palestinians, and what kind of scenarios or solutions are left after the Oct. 7 Hamas attack and the Gaza War — for any kind of political settlement,” Milshtein said.

But outside of Israel there’s alarm — especially among Arab leaders — over the absence of any serious debate about how to end the multi-front conflicts Israel is engaged in and what that might foretell, said HA Hellyer, a geopolitical scholar specializing in the region.

“Netanyahu, or not, the Israelis are on a particular trajectory when it comes to foreign and security policies,”Hellyer told POLITICO.

“Opposition politicians blame Netanyahu for Israel’s increasing diplomatic isolation and loss of support in parts of Europe and North America. But when you look at what they’re actually saying, they’re not arguing with the policies when it comes to Gaza. They support the overall settlement project in the West Bank. They support the incursion in Southern Lebanon. Their proposition is that they could have done things in a better way,” said Hellyer, who’s a fellow at Britain’s Royal United Services Institute.

World.title: EU and China weigh next sectors for trade curbs
World.content:
After a scheduled January videoconference with his counterpart Wang Wentao, Šefčovič said he hopes the two can deliver results in March 2027 at their next round of in-person talks in Brussels.

“I would like to see that we both have an understanding of what sectors we are going to focus on next,” he said.

The intense engagement with China comes as the bloc seeks to rebalance mutual economic ties, which EU officials say have been distorted by Chinese subsidies, market barriers and a surge in imports. Šefčovič stressed the urgency of the task, given that the EU’s trade deficit with China “reached almost €197 billion in the first half of this year. At this rate, we could break the 2022 record” of €397.3 billion.

“A part of our team is working on implementing all what we agreed, and [another] part of the team is talking to our Chinese counterparts on what should be the next sectors, next areas on what we want to focus the work on. Hopefully with another [Trade and Investment Consultation] in Brussels we can actually deliver the results,” he added.

“The primary objective for us ... is to rebalance the trade.”

At a press conference on Friday, the trade chief said the European Commission was looking to shield more sectors from Chinese overcapacity, with plastics the leading candidate for safeguard measures — a mix of quotas and tariffs.

World.title: Brazil: long queues and river journeys mark decisive presidential vote
World.content:
Across Brazil, voters made their way to polling stations on Sunday 25 October as President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva faced Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff election.

 

In the Amazon rainforest, residents of the isolated Lago do Catalão community travelled by canoe and motorboat to cast their ballots, relying on waterways to access polling facilities.

In Rio de Janeiro's Rocinha favela, long queues formed as residents waited to vote, reflecting the deep divisions surrounding the election.

In Brasília, voters showed passionate support for both candidates, highlighting the stark choices facing the electorate.

The official result is expected tonight between 23:30–00:00 CET (around 20:30–21:00 Brasília time).

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 25th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Storms batter northern Europe, cutting power to more than 150,000 homes and disrupting road and air transport
World.content:
Storms battered northern Europe on Sunday cutting power to more than 150,000 homes, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights and silencing phone networks.

 

Winds of up to 135 kilometres an hour were recorded in Argyll and Bute in western Scotland and fallen trees and power cables blocked roads and rail lines across the country.

Storm Boelo, the second of two storms to hit the UK this weekend brought widespread travel disruptions and power outages to Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England on Sunday. The Met Office, the UK's national forecaster, said Storm Boelo will bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.

A car drives on the flooded A8 in Port Glasgow, Scotland, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026, after Storm Boelo passed through the area. (Jane Barlow/PA via AP) Press Association

Flood warnings are also in place, while airports, ferries, railways and roads have seen disruptions. Power outages have affected some 82,000 homes in Britain, nearly 60,000 in France and at least 10,000 in Germany. Boelo, pronounced “Boo-Loh”, has followed hard on the heels of storm Austen, which battered southern England, in particular, on Friday, before continuing across northern continental Europe

Hundreds of flights were cancelled or diverted because

As the storm moved eastward into continental Europe, Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport warned travelers of cancellations and delays of flights to and from the busy aviation hub caused by strong winds that were battering the Netherlands. Belgium also took a battering - falling trees injured four people in Brussels on Saturday.

A tourist takes pictures on the Roemerberg square in Frankfurt, Germany, during rain falls on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Michael Probst) Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Two people were seriously hurt Saturday by scaffolding blown away by storm Austen's winds during an autumn market at the town of Nastaetten near Frankfurt, German police said. Germany's weather agency DWD predicted more powerful winds of up to 100 kilometres an hour on the northern coast on Sunday.

High wind and rain were expected in Denmark, Norway and parts of Sweden. Some ferries in the region were canceled, train services were suspended on some Swedish lines as a precaution and some trailers were barred from Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge.

World.title: María Corina Machado back in Venezuela after 10 months in exile
World.content:
Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado is back in her home country following a series of failed attempts to return and nearly a year in exile.

 

Machado announced her return via a post on social media site X, in which she wrote "I am here. With you".

Machado had covertly left Venezuela in December 2025 to receive her Nobel Peace Prize. Just weeks later, US forces seized the country's longtime leader Nicolás Maduro and flew him to New York to face criminal charges.

Machado has heaped praise on US President Donald Trump for launching the risky operation, though Washington has allowed Maduro's deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, to rule as interim president.

According to her party, Machado attempted to return seven times in the past three months, from the United States, Panama and Curaçao. They say she was repeatedly blocked by Venezuelan authorities.

Many believed Washington played a role in blocking Machado's return, given Trump's repeated expressions of satisfaction with Rodríguez.

That claim has been denied by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Machado setting the stage for her return

Machado has spent the last few months trying to regain her place on Venezuela's political stage while talks on the country's future moved forward without her being able to take part directly from within.

This past week, she called on Venezuelans to take to the streets and demanded that a date be set for the presidential elections, one of her main demands of Delcy Rodríguez's government.

She had accused Rodríguez's government of being afraid of her return. Now, with the opposition leader back in Venezuela, the question is no longer when she will manage to return, but what role she will be able to play in a political landscape shaped by negotiations between Chavismo, different sectors of the opposition and the United States.

Rodríguez did not immediately react to the news of Machado's return.

World.title: Thousands of sheep take over Madrid's streets for Transhumance Festival
World.content:
The flock of 1,250 sheep and 160 goats set off from Casa de Campo before crossing the Puente del Rey and making its way through the historic centre. Bells chimed and animals bleated as crowds of residents and tourists lined the streets to watch, take photographs and follow the procession.

 

Several shepherds wore traditional dress, while others carried young lambs or offered treats to their animals. Folk musicians added to the festive atmosphere as the flocks filled streets and squares normally dominated by traffic.

The event marks transhumance, the centuries-old practice of moving livestock between summer and winter pastures along vías pecuarias (drovers’ routes). At Plaza de la Villa, officials staged the traditional payment of 50 maravedís per thousand animals, a symbolic ceremony dating from 1418.

This year’s route was altered to avoid Puerta del Sol, where housing campaigners have set up a protest camp following the eviction and subsequent death of an 87-year-old local resident.

Beyond celebrating rural heritage, the festival highlights the environmental value of traditional grazing: by consuming vegetation, the animals help reduce flammable undergrowth and lower wildfire risks.

World.title: Off the Record: Yalta 2.0 spells bad news for Europe in desperate need of a plan
World.content:
Welcome back to Off the Record, coming to you from Brussels.

 

This week, a story made my jaw hit the floor.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has floated a three-way meeting with Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping to discuss a way out of the war in Ukraine, which he started. Trump seemed to confirm the pitch, without putting a date on it, suggesting it could be good for the world if it included denuclearisation.

If you’re not alarmed by this, you should be.

Putin wants a Yalta 2.0 moment. One that would restore his international stature and present Russia as a great power, much like the three-way summit that helped shape the post-WWII order 81 years ago in the resort city of Yalta.

In 1945, as victory over Nazi Germany drew closer, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin gathered in Yalta to divvy up the post-war world. The conference helped lay the groundwork for spheres of influence across Europe, with the Soviets subsequently cementing their control over practically all of Eastern Europe.

Churchill was an imperfect man, but nonetheless the war hero Great Britain needed at the time. He walked away from the whole affair disenchanted.

He knew the Soviets would engulf half of Europe, leaving the continent divided by an Iron Curtain for decades to come. In the midst of it all, Poland would be sacrificed, alongside the Baltic states, much of Central Europe and parts of the Balkans. And he was right. But he still had to accept the deal.

Yalta dictated the terms of a new world order, but also set the stage for the Cold War. Of course, the echoes of history can be cruel: Yalta has been under Russian occupation since 2014, following Moscow’s illegal annexation of Crimea.

If you follow that logic, the modern-day triumvirate of Trump, Xi and Putin would get together and split up the world for the next 100 years. One piece for you, another for me — you get the gist of it.

Presumably, the talks would focus on Ukraine and Taiwan. If Yalta 2.0 works anything like the 1945 conference, the three would cut a backroom deal and the rest of the world would have no choice but to go along with it. Putin would emerge as the winner, which explains why he’s pitching it in the first place.

Russia is a nuclear power, but it is no longer a great power. Putin, who once called the collapse of the Soviet Union “the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the century” for Russia, has long sought to restore Moscow’s lost sphere of influence.

If Trump joins that meeting, he would be handing the Russian leader his biggest strategic victory since the Soviet Union’s collapse.

Along the way, the US President would alienate America’s friends. Trump may not think much of his allies, but they are crucial. Policing the world has brought Washington lucrative deals, enormous influence and military bases that it needs for its own security, whether Trump likes to admit it or not.

A new Yalta without his allies would certify the death of the West as we know it.

The Europeans should be very concerned, as they too are on the chopping board in this dangerous ménage à trois. A backroom deal over Kyiv’s head would also spell the end of the transatlantic relationship and erode NATO’s deterrence.

​Brussels may insist it is in the game, but it’s clear that much is happening behind its back already. The Europeans need their own peace plan and a clear definition of what a good outcome truly entails — for Ukraine and for Europe.

Inevitably, this will force the EU to confront uncomfortable questions it has long avoided, from the territories Ukraine may not get back to the security guarantees it will need to provide in exchange for a US backstop. That means boots on the ground to ensure peace, and it can’t just be France and the UK.

The EU will also need to ring-fence funding for Ukraine as the political cycle turns against continued support. Let’s face it: it is expensive, and it’s becoming unpopular as protests over the cost of living mount.

Our politicians need to do a much better job of explaining that our security is at stake too, with more than 4,000 kilometres of Europe’s eastern flank at play. It is in Europe’s interest to reach a fair deal in Ukraine. The opposite will come back to haunt us.

Europe needs its own peace plan, starting with the appointment of an envoy who can secure a seat at the negotiating table, set out a clear negotiating position and report back. This should have been done a year ago. Enough with the Trump whisperer strategy. It doesn’t work. It is futile as long as Europe is not represented by someone who can speak with a political mandate.

If you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu. Serve it while it’s hot.

Thank you for reading Off The Record make sure to subscribe here.

World.title: Demonstrators wounded as police break up Lisbon and Porto housing protest camps
World.content:
Protesters chanted "smells like a dictatorship" overnight into Sunday as police hit desmonstrators with batons in both the capital Lisbon and and the city of Porto, in an operation to dismantle tents set up to protest against skyrocketing housing prices.

 

In a message posted on X, the police said officers had "intervened early this morning... to put an end to these illegal encampments".

"Once dialogue ended, the operation led to 31 arrests for disobedience," the police added.

A spokeswoman for the protest camp in Porto told the Portuguese news agency Lusa there were 37 minor injuries and two arrests.

"It is the third night in which we are being repressed with a method of total intimidation that one would never expect in a democratic country governed by the rule of law," said Catarina dos Santos, speaking to reporters.

The Public Security Police (PSP) had warned earlier in the afternoon that it would not allow tents to remain overnight in Rossio.

Protest camps in main public squares a point of friction for weeks

The presence of tents in Rossio Square and Praça D. João I (in Porto) have been the main points of friction with the police during the past weeks of protest. As night fell, the demonstrators decided by majority to put up tents and stay overnight.

Around 130 tents were erected in Rossio Square in Lisbon.

130 tents erected in Rossio Square, Lisbon. Manuel Ribeiro/Euronews

The operation to remove the tents began at around 1 am in both cities, after protesters started to notice what they called "disproportionate" police reinforcement, with canine units gathering in the squares in both locations.

"There were at least 20 crowd-control dogs, clearly agitated, and and a number of weapons pointed at us, and if this is not intimidating and serious, I don't know what is," lamented Catarina Santos, quoted by Lusa.

Shortly before 2 am on Sunday, the police contingent had both squares cordoned off and began moving in against the demonstrators, who had formed a human chain. Police used batons, while firecrackers were heard causing considerable confusion. In Praça D. João I, bystanders criticised the PSP's conduct and began to sing "Grândola Vila Morena", a song associated with the revolution of the 25 April that ended decades of dictatorship in 1974.

The "clean-up" operation in the squares was swift: the tents were removed immediately by the authorities and the protesters, who say they will return, dispersed to nearby squares.

A banner placed on the statue of D. Pedro IV, in Rossio Square, reads, in Portuguese, 'The fight goes on until nobody sleeps on the streets'. Lisbon, 24.10.2026 Manuel Ribeiro/Euronews

Protesters demand changes in new tenancy law and a cap on rents

The Lisbon and Porto camp movements are calling for measures such as the reversal of the tenancy law, an end to evictions of people with no housing alternative, limits on the purchase of property by real-estate funds, the rehabilitation of vacant buildings and a ceiling on rents.

People march during a protest to demand affordable housing in Lisbon, Portugal, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Ana Brigida) Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Large crowds had turned out the previous day for peaceful demonstrations, accusing the government of failing to act to tackle Portugal's housing crisis

World.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine kill four and injure 28, authorities say
World.content:
Russian strikes on Ukraine's eastern Dnipro region on Saturday night left four people dead and 22 injured, authorities have announced, with a separate attack on Vinnytsia in west-central Ukraine injuring another six people.

 

Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, said Russian forces had targeted the Dnipro area with drones and aerial bombs, striking three districts more than 20 times.

The attacks damaged infrastructure in Dnipro city and destroyed private homes, apartment buildings, stores and cars in the Synelnykivskyi district, he said. A private home was also damaged in the Nikopol district, he added.

In a post on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian drone had also hit a high-rise apartment building in Vinnytsia, while a hypermarket had been targeted in Kharkiv in the northeast of the country.

"In Kharkiv, the Russians first struck a home improvement hypermarket and then carried out a cynical double-tap strike on the emergency services that arrived at the scene," he wrote, adding that an unspecified number of emergency responders had been injured.

The Ukrainian leader also reported overnight strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities, including a thermal power plant and substations.

According to Zelenskyy, Russia has launched roughly 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones against Ukraine over the past week.

Ukrainian forces hit back on Saturday and overnight with their own strikes against Russian targets, including army radar stations, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.

Ukraine's military also struck command posts as well as Russian "personnel concentrations," per the General Staff.

"Striking radars creates gaps in the enemy’s radar coverage and expands the Defence Forces of Ukraine’s ability to employ unmanned systems at all levels," it said.

Starlink access restored

It comes after Kyiv announced on Saturday that its forces had re-established a "stable" connection to Elon Musk's Starlink network amid a dispute with the US.

"The speeds are now where they need to be. The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient," Zelenskyy said. "This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered 'shaheds.'"

Starlink, and its military version Starshield, have proved crucial to the Ukrainian military's operations as it has continued to battle Russian President Vladimir Putin's invading forces, providing resilient internet and communications over the battlefield.

World.title: Azerbaijan hijab ban exposes strain in ‘brotherly’ ties with Turkey
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch advocate of Muslim rights, has been notably silent on Azerbaijan’s recent hijab ban in schools. For years, Erdogan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev have shared a close alliance, but the ban is putting the Turkish president in a tight spot.

Advertising

School uniform rules introduced in September in predominantly Muslim Azerbaijan, which is a secular state, have been used to bar pupils wearing the hijab. Teachers have also reported being excluded. The new rules do not explicitly mention hijabs, but prohibit clothing deemed incompatible with school uniforms or secular education.

With Turkish social media awash with videos of Azerbaijani children wearing hijabs and pleading to be let into their schools, the ban has sparked outrage among Turkey’s religious conservatives.

Yet Erdogan, a vocal defender of Muslim rights both at home and on the world stage, has remained silent on the issue.

"He's unusually muted because Azerbaijan and Turkey, of course, had this extremely good relationship,“ said Turkish political analyst Sezin Oney. "If it were another country, he would have had a harsher reaction.”

‘We're fighting a daily battle': Iranian women dare to shed hijab in public

Baku's response

Erdogan, who is religiously conservative, rose to political prominence in the 1990s by challenging a similar ban in Turkish universities, and went on to become a global advocate of Muslim rights.

Oney predicts his silence on Azerbaijan will damage this reputation.

"[It's] a far cry from the days when Erdogan could stand up against the powerful of the world. That was the image he projected, and now he cannot even stand up to Aliyev."

Aliyev has publicly dismissed criticism of the hijab ban by one of the Turkish president’s advisors and Baku has issued international arrest warrants for several prominent Turkish Islamist and conservative figures, along with banning others from entering the country after similar criticism.

Azerbaijani officials accuse the critics of threatening its sovereignty and national security.

Shifting status

Aliyev and Erdogan have enjoyed close ties for more than two decades, built on economic and defence cooperation, with the mantra of ‘two states, one nation’.

“Erdogan and Turkey [still] see Azerbaijan as a little brother,” explains Tbilisi-based defence and security expert Eugene Kogan.

“I think that's not the perspective that comes from Baku because they say quite clearly that their relationship is no longer between a big brother and a little brother, and their relationship is now of equals.”

He added: “I think this phrase 'equal' is not fully accepted in Ankara. So that puts a strain on bilateral relations between the two countries."

Energy-rich Azerbaijan is growing in economic importance, in comparison with Turkey’s struggling economy. It is also among Turkey’s largest foreign investors.

Earlier this month, the two countries signed arms agreements worth more than $500 million. Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR says it has invested around $19.5 billion in Turkey.

“SOCAR is the flagship of investments in Turkey – it's huge," said Turkish analyst Atilla Yesilada of Global Source Investments.

“Turkey has a chronic deficit in plastics and petrochemicals. In fact, there are plans to establish a huge petrochemical complex in the Adana or Antalya area with a cost of $10 billion. I don’t think domestic capital has that kind of funding. Eventually, if Turkey wants to cover its petrochemical deficit, it needs SOCAR to get involved."

Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea

Relations with Israel

Azerbaijan’s deepening relationship with Israel, despite its Turkish ally’s condemnation of Israel’s war in Gaza and broader escalating tensions, is another source of friction with Ankara.

International media reported that Azerbaijan signed a $235 million arms deal with Israel’s Elbit Systems this month, although neither side has commented on the reports.

Azerbaijan also remains a key oil supplier to Israel, with oil piped through Turkey and shipped from the Turkish Ceyhan port. In 2024, Erdogan moved swiftly to suppress mounting protests against these exports – protests led largely by religious conservatives who form a crucial part of his political support.

However, Kogan believes Israel will not try to exploit any rift between Baku and Ankara. “The stability of relations between Ankara, Baku and Tel Aviv is very, very important for Tel Aviv,” Kogan said.

Turkey-Azerbaijan alliance strained by opposing stances on Israel

Baku last year hosted talks between Turkey and Israel aimed at defusing tensions over Syria.

'[Isreal] understands that it could come to war [with Turkey] and Baku can still act as a meeting point for both countries. I cannot really think of another meeting point between Ankara and Tel Aviv at the moment,” Kogan said.

With Turkey the main export route for Azerbaijan’s oil and gas, mutual dependency remains a powerful means to contain any tensions.

Gasimov suggests the current rift is part of a learning process.

“I wouldn’t read it as reshuffling or rebalancing, but rather as a new chapter that may have opened up now, if the two sides learn from it and are ready to accept these kinds of differences."

As Turkey wrestles with mounting financial and economic woes, Erdogan is expected to look for ways to smooth things over with his affluent neighbour. But the full impact on their ties of this dispute remains to be seen.
