World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019158/China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.title: China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019158/China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.content:
Chinese scientists have developed the world’s lightest wireless mesoscope, a miniature microscope weighing just 1 gram that can record 25 times as many neurons in mice as comparable devices.

The device, named Airscope, was unveiled in the prestigious journal Nature on Oct. 19, and developed by a team led by Tsinghua University professor Dai Qionghai and Chinese PLA Medical School professor Dai Pu, in collaboration with researchers from other institutions.

When installed on a mouse’s head, the Airscope can record activity from over 8,500 neurons as it freely explores, climbs, and interacts with other mice.

Previously, microscopes designed to image large areas of the brain at high resolution often required cables or the subject to be restrained, making it difficult to study natural behavior. Meanwhile, head-mounted microscopes that let animals move freely could observe only limited areas.

In contrast, the Airscope combines wireless operation with mesoscopic imaging, allowing scientists to observe large areas of tissue while still distinguishing individual cells. This enables researchers to “understand how large numbers of neurons interact and work together to produce complex functions,” Wu Jiamin, an associate professor in Tsinghua University’s Department of Automation and one of the study’s corresponding authors, said in an article published Tuesday by Tsinghua University.

The device weighs just 1 gram without its battery, more than 30% less than the latest head-mounted mesoscopes, according to the researchers. It has single-cell resolution of 4 to 6 micrometers, and a 6-millimeter field of view compared with typically less than 1 millimeter for conventional head-mounted devices. A magnetically attached battery can be replaced in two seconds.

With the Airscope, the team conducted several experiments that were previously difficult because of cables or equipment weight.

For example, in a simulated natural habitat with ramps, tree hollows, and shelters, mice could explore freely while researchers recorded their cortical activity. The team could also use neural signals to predict which portion of the habitat a mouse was in.

In another experiment, researchers placed two mice at opposite ends of a narrow tube and used their neural activity to predict which would force the other to retreat, achieving over 80% accuracy.

Other experiments included mounting one Airscope on a mouse’s head and another on its back to compare spinal cord and cortical neural activity, as well as tracking mice exploring a large maze in search of water rewards.

The team has also publicly released several datasets collected from their experiments.

Zhang Yuanlong, one of the study’s first authors and an assistant professor at Tsinghua University’s Center for Life Sciences and Artificial Intelligence and Department of Automation, said the team used AI to help optimize the optical design. The technology also uses a 2-megapixel image sensor, whereas previously published wireless systems had not exceeded 1 megapixel, allowing higher resolution.

Dai Qionghai said the Airscope could enable “more precise neural detection” and potentially expand into fields such as immunology and cancer research.

Zhang added that the device could be used to track the progression of Alzheimer’s disease, brain injuries, cardiovascular diseases, depression, and other conditions in animal models, and gain insights into disease mechanisms, prevention, and treatment.

In 2023, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology developed two head-mounted microscopes using a new optical design: one optimized for a larger field of view, measuring around 4 millimeters and weighing 1.4 grams, and another optimized for lower weight, with a 1-millimeter field of view and weighing just 1 gram. Both devices required wires for power and data collection.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from the WeChat public account of Tsinghua University, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019154/In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.title: In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019154/In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.content:
For her vacation to China’s southern province of Hainan during this year’s weeklong National Day holiday, Chang Yajie bought five new pieces of clothing: a beach skirt, a floral halter top, a straw hat, a swimsuit, and a pair of loose rainbow pants.

She wore them all on the trip, relishing taking photos in her new outfit on the resort-laden island’s beaches and posting them to social media.

But when she got home, she stuffed the clothes into her trash can.

Chang, an office worker in Xinxiang, a city in the central Henan province, used to spend thousands of yuan on vacation outfits. Unsuitable for work and out of place in everyday life, they ended up at the back of her closet after her trips.

“You can’t possibly wear a plunging, neon-colored beach dress to a corporate desk job,” the 37-year-old told Sixth Tone. “Spending so much on clothes I might wear only once or twice just isn’t worth it.”

In contrast, the five items she packed in early October had cost a total of just 200 yuan ($28). Known as cipaoyi, or disposable outfits, these clothes typically cost under 50 yuan per item and are designed to be worn once for holidays, photo shoots, or social media posts, and then discarded or resold.

The trend, which took off this National Day, comes amidst fast fashion and influencer-driven consumer culture, as well as the phenomenon of haoyangmao, or buying clothing, wearing it for travel, photoshoots, or events, and then returning it for a full refund.

On Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, posts under the topic have drawn over 60 million views. On e-commerce platforms, sellers offer clothing ranging from coats and snowpants for use in the northeastern city of Harbin to red dresses designed for photos in the desert. The trend is particularly popular among young women.

Proponents of disposable outfits argue that they’re an inexpensive way to look and feel good while matching scenery and holidays. But others, including environmental advocates and medical professionals, have raised concerns about their potential impact on the planet and people’s health.

Cutting costs

Despite having always loved dressing up, Chang said her clerical desk job leaves little room for it, so she keeps an understated, practical wardrobe. Disposable outfits, then, are a way to “boost her mood.”

“When I go to work, I just wear whatever helps me blend into the crowd,” she said.

But travel, and embellishing her outfits, have helped her reconnect with a more energetic, youthful version of herself. “After months of the same dull routine, dressing up for a trip feels like a shot of adrenaline,” she said.

Chang wasn’t initially looking for disposable clothes. But as she scrolled online for holiday looks, she found it hard to choose among those that caught her eye. In the end, she opted for cheaper versions of similar styles so she could buy more.

A brand dress can easily cost 300 to 500 yuan, she said. “For the same amount of money, I could buy seven to 10 cheaper outfits — enough to wear a different look each day of the trip.”

Chang said the appeal of disposable outfits lies partly in their novelty, helping her match a destination’s look and feel. The clothes let her try styles she rarely wears in daily life — brightly colored pieces with bold, saturated hues, more revealing cuts, or designs that push the boundaries of her usual wardrobe.

For 20-year-old Wu Xiangmeng, a college student in the southern Guangdong province, disposable outfits help her travel money — saved from her university’s monthly living allowance — go farther, leaving more for train tickets, accommodation, food, and activities. So far, she has visited almost 10 cities across China this way.

Before each trip, she researches her destination to pick disposable outfits that fit the scenery. When she’s done with her clothes, she lists them on secondhand platforms like Xianyu and Xiaohongshu instead of throwing them away, pairing the listings with photos of herself wearing the outfits on holiday to attract buyers.

“I can recoup some of the cost while making room — and saving money — for my next trip,” she said.

Outside impact

Though disposable clothing can be a cost-effective way to dress for specific destinations, Wu said she spends hours finding clothes she considers suitable, shopping, sorting through poor-quality purchases, and returning those that don’t make the cut. “The shopping experience is very draining,” she said.

While preparing for a trip to Hainan’s city of Sanya, for instance, Wu ordered several dresses, only to find the fabric flimsy, ripping at the slightest pull. She ultimately kept only two pieces from the pile and returned the rest.

Zhang Bingquan, who operates a garment factory in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, said disposable outfits cost so little partly because of their simplified designs and production process. With fewer patterns and straightforward sewing techniques, as in beachwear, he said production costs per garment can be kept in the single digits in yuan.

But the low prices have also intensified competition among manufacturers. To cut costs, some factories use lower-quality fabrics, reduce fabric weight and thickness, or take risks by using fabrics and dyes that fail to meet quality standards, he added.

“The biggest health risk with disposable clothing lies in the materials used,” Zhong Jianbo, deputy chief physician of the dermatology department at Hangzhou First People’s Hospital, told local media. “Cheap garments often use low-quality fabrics and dyes that may contain high levels of chemical residues.”

Sun Weiling, a dermatologist at Jiangsu People’s Hospital, told domestic media that disposable clothing is often made from stiff fabrics that can irritate the skin and cause damage, particularly in more delicate areas, such as the underarms, chest, waist, abdomen, and inner thighs.

The trend has also drawn criticism over its environmental costs. China is the world’s largest producer, consumer, and exporter of textiles, and generates vast amounts of textile waste. According to the China Association of Circular Economy, discarded clothing in the country is expected to reach 50 million metric tons a year by 2030, with each person throwing away an average of 16 garments annually.

During this year’s National Day holiday, the volume of textiles collected by Shanghai-based recycling platform Feimayi nearly doubled from the same period last year, Deng Qihua, the company’s head of marketing and sustainable development, told Sixth Tone.

“Some of the clothes we collected still had their original tags attached,” Deng said.

But recycling disposable outfits can be difficult and costly, as they are often made from blends of synthetic fibers, she added. “A garment bought cheaply and worn only a handful of times may therefore leave behind a much longer problem once its owner is ready to discard it,” Deng said.

A growing number of users are noticing the problem. A September commentary by state-run media outlet People’s Daily called on regulators to steer the market toward more sustainable alternatives, such as clothing rental. A Douyin hashtag promoting alternatives to “disposable fashion,” with tips on styling existing clothes and buying clothes with long-term use in mind, has garnered more than 32 million views.

But for many, health and environmental concerns take a back seat to looking good on vacation for minimal cost. Chang, the office worker, said that when she posted pictures of herself in her disposable outfits, friends praised her looks and “girlish charm.”

“At least it helps me feel better about myself,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019153/China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.title: China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019153/China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.content:
China has approved its first auditory brainstem implant for clinical use among deaf patients amid a national push to commercialize brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies.

Approved Oct. 19 by China’s National Medical Products Administration, the implant — dubbed Nurotron WH-01A — is classified as a Class III medical device, the highest-risk category under the country’s medical device classification system.

The device was developed by a team led by Wu Hao, a surgeon and professor of otolaryngology at Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine’s Ninth People’s Hospital, in collaboration with Zhejiang Nurotron Biotechnology, headquartered in the eastern city of Hangzhou.

It is designed to restore hearing in patients who cannot benefit from conventional cochlear implants because of severe inner-ear malformations or an absent cochlear nerve, which normally carries auditory information from the inner ear to the brain.

Unlike cochlear implants, which stimulate the nerve via the inner ear, the auditory brainstem implant bypasses both the cochlea and the cochlear nerve, delivering electrical impulses directly to the cochlear nucleus, a brainstem structure through which all sound information enters the brain and where sound processing begins.

The system consists of six components, including a stimulator and a receiving coil. Used with Nurotron’s cochlear speech processor, located outside the patient’s body, it converts digital signals into electrical pulses that directly stimulate the cochlear nucleus.

Eligible patients include children aged 2 to 6 with “nonsyndromic deafness,” or deafness without other associated medical conditions or physical abnormalities, as well as those whose deafness was not caused by tumors or who cannot benefit from cochlear implants.

By 2024, the team had completed the implant surgeries and follow-up procedures for its clinical trial. The device achieved an overall treatment effectiveness rate of almost 97% after 12 months of activation, they told domestic media.

The approval comes as China ramps up efforts to advance its BCI industry toward clinical use and commercialization. China’s national development plan, part of its most recent five-year plan (2026–2030), identified BCI as one of six future industries. In July 2025, seven national ministries jointly set guidelines and targets for fostering a globally competitive BCI industry by 2030.

National regulators have also accelerated BCI device approvals for patient populations including those affected by stroke, Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and spinal cord injuries. In March, the country approved its first BCI kit, designed to help patients with quadriplegia caused by cervical spinal cord injuries regain limited hand function.

China’s BCI market is expected to exceed 6 billion yuan ($900 million) by 2028, with a compound annual growth rate of roughly 18% between 2024 and 2028, according to domestic research agency CCID Consulting.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Left: Professor Wu Hao’s team during an auditory brainstem implant surgery. Right: The auditory brainstem implant recently approved for market release. From the website of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.title: Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.content:
In 2022, I spoke with Emma, a 22-year-old Chinese student in the UK, about her experiences with dating apps. Recalling one particularly disappointing encounter, she let out a sigh. Emma had matched with a man whose profile explicitly stated that he was looking for a long-term relationship. But the day after their third date, he texted her to say he had only ever wanted casual sex, then ghosted her. Feeling betrayed and emotionally drained, Emma changed her dating profile to say she was “Not Sure” what she wanted.

Emma’s experience was far from unusual. More than two-thirds of the 40 heterosexual Chinese students I interviewed in the UK reported similarly ambiguous dating intentions — findings drawn from a longitudinal study conducted between January 2022 and March 2023 that examined how their experiences with dating apps evolved while studying abroad. Many initially joined dating apps with clear goals, whether to pursue romantic relationships, make friends, or engage in language and cultural exchange. Yet over the course of the study, 27 of the 40 interviewees became less certain about what they wanted, increasingly adopting a “go with the flow” or “I’ll just see what happens” attitude.

For some, this ambiguity opened up new possibilities. For many others, however, it became a way to protect themselves after disappointing dating experiences. Beneath their apparent uncertainty, many still longed for a stable, long-term relationship.

For some young Chinese students arriving in the UK, keeping their dating intentions ambiguous is a deliberate strategy to leave their options open. In China, traditional dating culture places considerable emphasis on long-term commitment and marriage. Expressing vague or noncommittal intentions on Chinese dating platforms can carry a social stigma, with users sometimes labeled zhanan or zhanü, derogatory terms for men and women perceived as dishonest or irresponsible in romantic relationships.

Moving abroad can change these expectations. In the UK, students encounter a dating environment where a wider range of relationship arrangements is socially accepted. Living far from their parents and the social expectations of home also gives them greater freedom to experiment. For some, dating apps offer an opportunity to explore different kinds of relationships without committing to any particular one.

This “go with the flow” mentality was particularly common among postgraduate students enrolled in one-year degree programs. Jenny, a 23-year-old master’s student, explained during our first interview, shortly after arriving in the UK, that she had deliberately avoided setting clear dating goals so she could explore unconventional relationships.

“In China, I never thought about it because I was afraid of facing stigma and judgment,” she recalled. “I want to seize this opportunity to explore different possibilities during this one-year period.”

But not everyone embraced ambiguity out of a desire to experiment. For many other students, particularly women, keeping their intentions vague was a response to negative dating experiences.

After encountering misleading dating profiles and being ghosted without warning, some students became reluctant to invest emotionally in new relationships. Julia, a 23-year-old woman who had joined dating apps hoping to find a long-term partner, described feeling “emotionally paralyzed” after repeatedly meeting men who were only interested in casual sex. She initially had a clear relationship goal, but as she grew increasingly doubtful that she would find the commitment she wanted, she changed her profile to express more ambiguous intentions. By lowering her expectations, she hoped to avoid further disappointment.

Yet the difficulties these students faced in finding long-term relationships were not only about whom they encountered on dating apps. Their status as temporary residents in the UK could also make commitment more complicated. With student visas approaching expiration, many faced uncertainty about where they would live or work after graduation. Investing emotionally in a relationship could feel risky when relocation or a return to China was only months away. Potential partners in the UK might also hesitate to commit to someone who could soon leave the country.

Chou, a 23-year-old student, summed up her approach as “No expectations, no disappointments.” She explained, “Most local daters did not want to form a long-term relationship with me because I’m only here temporarily as an international student. They worried that once I head back to China after graduation, our relationship wouldn’t have a future.” Chou thus adopted ambiguous motivations to cope with the difficulty of forming and maintaining long-term relationships as graduation approached.

Yet perhaps the most surprising finding from my study was that adopting a “go with the flow” approach on dating apps did not necessarily signal a growing preference for casual relationships. In practice, my interviewees experienced different kinds of relationships, with some remaining short-term while others had the potential to develop into longer-term partnerships. Many of them still longed for lasting love. In some cases, that desire became stronger over time, as the initial excitement of exploring different relationships began to fade.

Jack, a 26-year-old student, described this gradual shift. During our first interview, he said he found it exciting to keep his intentions ambiguous because it allowed him to “explore different types of relationships.” But when we spoke again nearly a year later, he had come to understand his desires differently.

“As I kept using dating apps, I started to realize my expectations for long-term relationships had been awakened. Trying different relationships was fun, but it gradually left me feeling empty. I really wanted a serious relationship, but I suppressed that desire because I felt it was impossible to find something long-term on dating apps.”

The word “awakened” is revealing. It suggests that Jack’s desire for long-term commitment had never entirely disappeared. Rather than simply shifting from a preference for casual relationships to serious ones, he gradually came to recognize what mattered most to him.

Eve, a 23-year-old master’s student, captured this tension through a food metaphor. She described her short-term relationships as daican, a Chinese term meaning “meal replacements.” In Chinese internet slang, the term describes a substitute that offers some comfort or satisfaction but cannot fully make up for what someone really wants.

“I feel it’s very difficult to form long-term relationships on dating apps, so I’ll just stick to some ‘meal replacements’ for now to keep me from getting hungry,” she explained. “But a meal replacement cannot replace staple food.” For Eve, these brief connections were not meaningless. They offered companionship and helped ease the loneliness of living abroad. But they were substitutes for what she really wanted. The “staple food” in her metaphor was a stable, long-term relationship.

These experiences were neither entirely positive nor entirely negative. The “meal replacement” strategy could help meet immediate emotional needs. But such relationships rarely satisfied overseas students’ deeper desire for lasting commitment. In this sense, these experiences shouldn’t be taken as defining who they were or what they wanted from intimacy.

Dating apps offer Chinese students abroad new opportunities to explore relationships beyond the expectations they grew up with. But while living overseas may change how they approach dating, it does not necessarily change what they ultimately want. For many, the desire for lasting love remains, even as the uncertainty of their temporary lives abroad shapes what they feel able to pursue.

In line with research ethics, all research participants are given pseudonyms.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019127/At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead
World.title: At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019127/At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead
World.content:
ZHEJIANG, East China — At China’s largest film and television production base, veteran director Zheng Zhongfu was taking his two leads through a confrontation between a prince and his wronged wife.

“In my previous life, you gouged out my heart and left me to die in the wilderness,” he recited, showing them how to deliver the line and where to look. “In this life, I will take back everything that belongs to me.”

Qi Kexin and his wife listened closely. But once the cameras rolled, they caught each other’s eye and burst into laughter, forcing Zheng to call cut. Again.

“The emotion has to land … your gaze has to focus,” he reminded them. “Whatever you do, don’t laugh. Let’s go again.”

Qi, 48, and his wife were tourists at Hengdian World Studios in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, where visitors can pay 388 yuan ($60) per person to star in a short drama of their own. Qi had booked the shoot on a whim after spotting the experience on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

The package includes costumes, makeup, and filming, with studio performers filling the supporting roles. Visitors spend about an hour in makeup and on set, sometimes longer if they add scenes or need additional coaching. Two days later, they receive a finished two-minute drama with a complete storyline.

Earlier tourist shoots required groups of three to five and at least two hours, said Wu Yizhuo, who oversees the service at Hengdian World Studios. “Individual tourists with packed schedules found that hard to accept.” His team developed shorter shoots that a single visitor could book.

Visitors can now choose from nearly 30 scripts written by staff screenwriters, drawing on themes from Chinese social media and the country’s booming ultrashort drama industry, including palace intrigue, martial arts fantasy, and romances featuring domineering CEOs.

Wu’s team asks visitors whether they want to play a hero or a villain. Most choose villains as a way to relieve stress, he said, with “satisfying revenge” stories especially in demand.

Amateur hour

Qi chose a palace intrigue script in which he plays a prince who wants to divorce his wife for another woman. His real-life wife plays the wronged spouse, who turns the tables on him with an emperor’s order and a sword.

After a nervous start, the pair began to settle into their roles as Zheng coached their dialogue and movements. Their sleeve flicks and sword draws became more assured. “You nailed it!” he called from behind the camera after one take.

By the time the shoot wrapped, Qi had a new respect for professional actors. “You have to memorize lines, vary your tone, and add emotion. You can’t attend to everything at once,” he said.

“Actors really have it hard. It truly takes skill,” Qi added. “We’re just playing around — we’re far behind the professionals.”

Zheng had spent years directing trained actors before he began filming tourists in Hengdian this summer. He breaks difficult lines into smaller pieces, sometimes splitting a sentence across three shots to ease the pressure on visitors, and aims to finish filming in about 30 minutes.

Professional crews are serious and not particularly cheerful while filming, Zheng said. With tourists, the focus is on participation and keeping the set lively. “They may not care much about the final film’s quality. The main thing is to come here and be happy.”

Zheng is open to visitors adding scenes or lines, or switching into dialect. “As long as the final film works well, it’s fine,” he said. “The more drama there is, the more fully they perform — and the more they share it on social media.”

On the day Sixth Tone visited Hengdian, Zheng moved straight from Qi’s shoot to his next performer, Zhang Zhongfeng. The 58-year-old farm owner had driven more than 2,000 kilometers from the southwestern Sichuan province with her daughter for the experience. She had never acted and was nervous when she learned her daughter had booked a shoot for her.

Zhang chose palace intrigue, and Zheng tailored a role to her age and temperament. Once filming began, her commanding presence surprised him. Onlookers mistook her for one of the studio performers.

Her daughter, Su Jing, 35, filmed a princess scene at another set the next day. “It’s a bit more complicated than filming yourself with a phone, but much simpler than a big movie — no huge number of lines to memorize, and staff guide you throughout,” she said. “It’s like an upgraded version of travel photography.”

Zheng said the experience was drawing growing numbers of visitors, particularly during holidays. Nearly 3,000 people have taken part since the package launched in July.

Around 2010, Hengdian mainly hosted big-budget films and large TV productions with long shooting schedules, Wu, who oversees the tourist service, recalled. Before one production finished, the next was already booked. “Vertical-screen short dramas have since become more common, while large productions have declined,” he said.

In recent months, cheaper AI production and cuts in platform financing have reduced live-action shoots. In Hengdian, the weekly average number of filming crews reportedly fell nearly 25% year on year in the first half of 2026.

On peak days, Wu’s team handles 30 to 40 groups of tourists. When its regular staff cannot cover the bookings, the studio calls in local part-time workers. Zheng films tourist dramas as a member of one such outsourced team.

Giovana Velasco, a tourist from Peru, first visited Hengdian last year, when the experience wasn’t available, she recalled. After spotting it on Trip.com this year, she booked a shoot and chose to play a rejected daughter seeking revenge.

She rehearsed lines in Chinese, Spanish, and English, battled nerves and laughter, and sometimes relied on body language to stay in character. Her shoot took twice as long as those of Chinese visitors. She is already planning another trip to play a scheming sister and surprise her TikTok followers.

A Shanghai tourist surnamed Xia chose a scene from the 2011 Chinese period drama “Empresses in the Palace” in which her character slaps a maid who has struck her first. She booked the shoot after seeing influencers perform in Hengdian on social media. “Just for fun, out of curiosity,” she joked.

Before she delivered the slap, the director demonstrated how to draw her hand back to make the movement look bigger on camera. The finished film arrived two days later, sooner than she expected. Xia was impressed by the picture quality, the background, and her own styling and makeup.

When she shared it with close friends, many wanted her to take them along to film one themselves. They asked, “Where’s the next episode?”

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo and Xiao Chuhan; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A crew films tourists in Hengdian, Zhejiang province, September 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019149/Chinese Satellite Constellation Extends Coverage to Arctic
World.title: Chinese Satellite Constellation Extends Coverage to Arctic
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019149/Chinese Satellite Constellation Extends Coverage to Arctic
World.content:
China has used a domestically developed satellite communication system to make video calls with those in the Arctic for the first time, supporting scientific data transmission, emergency medical response, and other purposes.

The breakthroughs occurred between polar research vessels on the country’s latest Arctic expedition, the country’s Qinling research base in Antarctica, and a base in the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, domestic media reported Monday.

The system uses the GW constellation, the country’s first state-backed satellite internet constellation project. The constellation launched its first satellites in December 2024 and plans to deploy almost 13,000 satellites by 2035. It aims to provide broadband services to areas beyond the reach of terrestrial networks through a system of low-orbit satellites operating below 2,000 kilometers above Earth.

The expedition has transmitted and received more than 300 files totaling over 100 gigabytes and held more than 40 video conferences via the system. Connectivity reportedly remained stable in harsh conditions, including extreme cold, high altitudes, strong winds, blowing sand, and ice fog.

The first breakthrough came on Aug. 3, when the research vessel Xuelong, then in the Arctic Ocean, completed a video call with China’s Qinling Station in Antarctica, the country’s highest-latitude communication ever performed using a domestic satellite system.

On Sept. 25, as the Xuelong returned to China, its crew exchanged Mid-Autumn Festival greetings via the satellite system with researchers at the Qinling Station and those aboard the Jidi and Tansuo-3 vessels during their ongoing Arctic expeditions.

A separate video call connected the Jidi, Qinling Station, a test station on the Lhasa River in Xizang, and the North China Sea Bureau of the Ministry of Natural Resources in the eastern Shandong province.

The communication system also reportedly enabled a video consultation with medical experts in Shandong’s port city of Qingdao, who provided remote medical support for a crew member in the Arctic.

Video call lag was no more than one second, according to state media outlet CCTV. After the vessels entered ice-covered waters, files and navigation logs were also transmitted via the GW constellation, with peak one-way speeds of around 30 megabits per second, enough to download a 1 GB file in about 10 minutes.

The event also marked the first time domestically developed buoys had transmitted ocean observation data in real time via Chinese satellites rather than international satellite services, state media outlet People’s Daily reported.

“The tests have improved the ‘information isolation’ faced by polar expeditions … offering practical evidence and experience for fully domestic communications support for China’s polar expeditions and marine equipment,” Zhang Meng, a member of the expedition and an on-site tester with the North China Sea Bureau, told state news agency Xinhua.

Previously, maritime communications along Arctic shipping routes relied mainly on shore-based radio and satellite systems, but coverage was limited and signals were often constrained. Earlier media reports said Chinese polar expeditions had used satellite services including the U.S.-based Iridium and British Inmarsat systems.

China’s latest Arctic expedition departed from the northeastern Liaoning province on July 3. The Xuelong and Xuelong 2 returned to Shanghai on Sept. 29 after completing their missions.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019141/Chinese Users Get Back at AI Male Teen, Casting Him as a Grifter
World.title: Chinese Users Get Back at AI Male Teen, Casting Him as a Grifter
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019141/Chinese Users Get Back at AI Male Teen, Casting Him as a Grifter
World.content:
“Xiaohai, how come your parents still aren’t here? Everyone else’s family has come to help,” a teacher asks a teenage boy preparing for a student-led product sales competition.

“I’m fine, teacher,” the boy says, sweat streaming down his face. “I can do it alone — I believe the aunties and moms out there will help me.” He then makes an at-camera plea, sweat now turned to tears, asking viewers to help him by buying a luxury face cream and saying, “Are children from poor families really not suited for this stage?”

This scene comes as videos featuring the AI-generated teen male character, “Xiaohai,” surge in popularity, with a related hashtag amassing more than 620 million views on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, as of Tuesday. The videos, marketed to older women, appear across dozens of accounts and push a range of products, from soy sauce to cosmetics.

But in response to the popularity of Xiaohai videos — in which the teen often relays fictional sob stories, likening them to elderly-targeting scams — other user-made clips portraying him as a greedy, ill-mannered troublemaker, under arrest or admitting to fraud, have also begun to emerge, domestic media reported this week.

In the original Xiaohai videos, the character addresses viewers as “aunties and moms,” asks after their health, and occasionally performs a song before marketing various products.

Many older viewers reportedly believe the AI-generated character is real. In one video in which Xiaohai donates blood, the comment section is flooded with statements that appear to reflect people’s belief that he is real, such as “You’re such a good boy,” and “Why are you so pale? Please take good care of yourself.”

Using the character to sell products has proven lucrative, according to domestic media. A report by state media outlet Shandian News found that content creators producing videos featuring Xiaohai earn up to over a half of total sales, and some creators say they earn at least 1,000 to 2,000 yuan ($140 to $280) a day from videos featuring the AI character.

In contrast, the recent wave of Xiaohai videos shifts the narrative, aiming to paint him in a light that proves he’s not worthy of viewers’ affection and to dissuade them from purchasing his products. In some videos, the boy brags about how much money he’s squeezed out of his devoted followers. In others, he smokes, drinks, insults older women, or flaunts his wealth.

In response, some commenters said they were angry they had bought Xiaohai-backed products. Others interpreted the videos as evidence that Xiaohai had accidentally gotten into trouble or been coerced into lying. “Know that your aunties and moms won’t think badly of you,” reads one comment. “This will pass … I’ll think of something; tell me your address and phone number.”

Xiaohai creates a “sense of intimacy” that can make his appeals persuasive to seniors, Yi Xiaoting, associate dean of the School of Humanities and Public Administration at Shanghai Open University, told Sixth Tone. “That sense of familiarity and intimacy can override the need to verify whether the character is real or whether the story is true,” she said.

Helping older adults navigate AI-generated misinformation means encouraging them to question seemingly trustworthy personas and to verify claims independently, even when the story feels emotionally convincing, Yi added. She also stressed the need for both digital literacy programs for seniors and increased regulation of AI-generated content.

In recent years, regulators and state media have increasingly scrutinized the use of fabricated personas and empathy-driven narratives to sell products online. In 2024, a local court in southwestern China’s Sichuan province convicted eight people for selling products online using false narratives. At last year’s Two Sessions meeting, industry experts called for legislation to curb the misuse of AI-generated deepfakes.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Screenshots of Xiaohai, an AI-generated character. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019142/Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.title: Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019142/Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.content:
In wildlife conservation, there are three steps to helping an injured or orphaned animal: rescue, rehabilitate, and release. “Returning” isn’t part of the plan, but try telling that to China’s celebrity seal Nana.

This 2-year-old wild spotted seal, a Class I protected species in China, was a must-see attraction this summer for visitors to Dachangshan Island, part of Dalian’s Changshan Archipelago in the northeastern Liaoning province.

Nana has been released twice far out into the Yellow Sea, with the hope he’d join a migrating colony. Both times he’s made his way back alone, once covering more than 200 kilometers in just six days.

When he first showed up on the island in June, he was wary of humans and swam away when approached. But over time, he grew braver. Tourists tempted him near with tasty fish, though this sometimes resulted in him receiving a prod or a kick, and often a startling camera flash.

Concerned for Nana’s welfare, the local government put up warning signs telling people not to feed him and to keep a safe distance, and vowed “not to use him to promote tourism.” Yet within months, a “Nana Line” shuttle service had opened, running directly from the island’s Yuanyang Port to its “best seal-watching spot,” while the local tourism bureau began working with a private business to make and sell seal-related merchandise.

For many locals, Nana’s presence has been bittersweet: he’s a cute addition to the neighborhood, but the risks to his safety outweigh the benefits, they say.

Despite the falling temperature, authorities have ruled out moving him again, much to the delight of those who feel the seal has “made his choice.” But as the tourist season ends and his steady, fan-fueled food supply dries up, others worry that Nana could face a harsh winter alone.

Hello, new neighbor

Nana was just a pup in the summer of 2024, when fishermen first spotted him resting on a buoy in waters off Beihai, in the southern Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Noticing he was thin and had wounds on his body, likely caused by boat propellers, they alerted the authorities, who transported him to the Beihai Aquatic Rescue and Rehabilitation Center.

The spot where Nana was discovered lies just off a migration route for spotted seals between the western Pacific Ocean and Dalian’s Liaodong Bay. Experts suspect he drifted from his colony and was stranded alone.

In November 2025, after being nursed back to health, Nana was transferred to a wild species rehabilitation center in Dalian operated by the Liaoning Ocean and Fisheries Science and Research Institute. There, he quickly went from 50 to 70 kilograms and grew a new coat of glossy fur. “You could see him looking better every day,” says Chai Yuqiao, a researcher at the base.

By this spring, Nana was deemed well enough to return to the wild. On April 16, the institute released him and two other rescued seals roughly 10 kilometers from shore in the Yellow Sea, thinking they would naturally head for the migration route and find a new colony.

Nana’s two companions did exactly that, but data from his satellite tag shows he never left the Yellow Sea. Two months later, he popped up at Dachangshan Island.

Locals first spotted the seal relaxing in a rocky tide pool on June 19.

“Back then he was wary and rarely came close,” recalls Feng Zhi, who runs a guesthouse on the island. “He’d just hang around, and if someone walked over, he’d swim away.”

But that changed the more he interacted with tourists. “Wherever the crowd was thickest, that’s where he’d be,” says Li Ai, who also works in the hospitality industry. “But he can be picky about people,” she adds, explaining that Nana appeared especially fond of a wetsuit-wearing livestreamer known as “Man in Black,” who has 24,000 followers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. Nana often chased him and snuggled up to him.

Zhou Long, another guesthouse manager, says Nana once squeezed in between him and several friends as they stood in the shallows. The seal was warm, slippery, and plump, “like a balloon that’s about to pop,” he says.

People soon began feeding Nana fish and petting him when he got close. A local boat captain says he often tried stopping tourists from doing this, but few listened. He worried Nana might accidentally be fed a fish containing a fishhook, “the consequences of which don’t bear thinking about.”

Some people were even captured on surveillance cameras throwing Nana barbecued meat, bread, and potato chips, foods that could seriously upset his digestive system, while others kicked him, and thoughtless children threw stones at him.

“I couldn’t bear to watch and couldn’t do anything about it. I could only turn around and walk away,” says Li.

Many locals breathed a sigh of relief on Sept. 7 when the authorities finally arrived to take Nana away.

Gone, but not forgotten

To protect and “re-wild” Nana, the Changhai County government, which administers Dachangshan Island, decided to again transport the seal out to the Yellow Sea, this time to a spot about 140 kilometers away by boat.

Nana was back on the island just six days later. His tracking tag had fallen off a month earlier, but Tian Jiashen, director of marine rare animal conservation research at the Liaoning institute, estimates the seal’s return journey must have covered at least 200 kilometers.

Zhou had an inkling he’d not seen the last of Nana. Social media users had been eagerly sharing news of sightings, and the seal was getting closer all the time. On the evening of Sept. 13, Zhou went to the shore, opened a livestream, and lay in wait, with nearly 200 followers logging on to watch.

As night fell, Zhou heard a splash, like “a huge creature leaping into the water.” When he ran over, Nana was beside the blue pontoon bridge that he’d frequented all summer.

Within hours, Lin Gao, an employee at a beachside water sports center, had reinstalled the giant inflatable yellow duck Nana had liked to sleep on. “We couldn’t let him come back and find it gone,” he says, adding that work had felt “hollow” without Nana around.

Tian admits he never expected the seal to return but now believes Nana’s interactions with tourists might have reawakened his memories of being rescued and fed by humans.

Staff at the Liaoning institute recall that Nana was initially more curious than cautious. Marine researcher Chen Yanyu says he was once scrubbing the rearing pool when Nana surprisingly pushed a long-handled brush toward his hand. He badly wanted to pat the seal’s head, but that would be against the rules of “rehab and release.”

In wildlife conservation, keeping a safe distance is paramount. Rescued seals are fed by pouring live fish into the pool, while researchers deliberately approach the animals with nets to condition them to avoid people. By the time of his release, Nana had begun watching the staff from afar.

On that first release day, Chen watched Nana slide down the boat’s ramp into the sea with tears in his eyes.

However, when the seal became a celebrity, the institute came under attack from netizens who felt it had failed in its responsibilities to rehabilitate Nana.

Tian, who has worked there since 2010, believes the criticism was unfair. He explained that the institute is manned year-round by researchers who volunteer their time for free, and that in the past two decades it has helped rescue 244 spotted seals, releasing 223.

“The sea is his home, and he should go home,” he adds, talking about Nana. “Keeping him here, in a human environment — that would be cruelty.”

The risks human behaviors pose to wildlife are obvious. Ah Nong, a spotted seal rescued late last year after spending 15 months in waters off Wenchang, in the southern island province of Hainan, was found to have diarrhea, elevated liver function, and ultraviolet skin burns from being fed, touched, and photographed by tourists.

When Nana returned a second time, Chai and some colleagues wanted to go see him, “to find out whether he still remembered us.” Others, like researcher Shi Hongyue, held another wish: that one day they would come across Nana naturally during a survey of a wild colony.

Sealing his fate?

Nana became even more famous after returning to Dachangshan Island last month. By 7 a.m., at least 10 livestreamers would already be set up on shore, waiting for the seal to wake up. These channels quickly became a key marketing tool for guesthouses and other local businesses.

In August, Chinese media quoted an unnamed local official as saying that authorities “would not use (Nana) for cultural tourism promotions.” However, that attitude appeared to shift after the seal’s return in September.

The Changhai Culture and Tourism Bureau opened the “Nana Line” on Sept. 25, and beachside stalls hawking Nana-themed merch began popping up this month.

More warning signs and loudspeakers have been placed along the beach, reminding tourists that feeding protected species is forbidden, while enforcement officers and volunteers now regularly patrol the area. The local government has announced it will not attempt to move Nana again and is planning to build him a shelter on the pontoon bridge, away from the crowds.

Residents say the feeding and touching has declined, but it still happens.

This will naturally trail off as the tourist and fishing seasons wind down ahead of the coldest months, leading some to worry that Nana could starve. Despite the rules, in October, Sun Zongjun, the owner of the water sports center, pledged on a livestream that “we’ll definitely keep feeding him when it gets cold.” The county government has yet to confirm whether live fish stocks will be provided for the seal over winter.

Tian says it’s hard to predict whether Nana will ever leave and fully return to nature; it depends on diverse factors like water temperature, his physiological state, and whether he meets any companions and joins a new colony.

Scientific studies using tracking data show that spotted seals tend to rest or breed in the same place, year after year. Tian believes this behavior, and his memories of human interaction, could be what led Nana back to Dachangshan Island.

While most locals were happy to welcome Nana “home,” his presence has also brought pressure. “Our island lives off tourism. If anything happens to him, the criticism of millions of people could crash down on us in an instant,” says Lin, who regularly volunteers to patrol the pontoon bridge in the early hours.

On most nights, Nana can be found sleeping soundly on his giant yellow duck as it rocks gently in the waves. Soon, he will be joined in these waters by other spotted seals. No one knows what will come next.

“It’s fine if Nana stays,” says Liu Yi, a guesthouse owner on the island. “But I still hope he leaves.”

(Due to privacy concerns, Lin Gao, Feng Zhi, Li Ai, Zhou Long, and Liu Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Qin Bing and Feng Haoni.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Beijing News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: PaperBuddy; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.title: Carlos Yulo dethroned in world vault final, finishes 7th
World.content:
STRENGTH. Carlos Edriel Yulo of the Philippines in action during the vault final of the 2026 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam.

Carlos Yulo goes home empty-handed this time from the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships after missing out on the podium in his pet events

MANILA, Philippines – It appears fatigue may have caught up with the Philippines’ gymnastics golden boy Carlos Yulo.

For the second straight final, Carlos Yulo finished off the podium, placing seventh and falling short in his bid to defend his vault crown at the 54th Artistic Gymnastics World Championships in Rotterdam, Netherlands, on Sunday, October 25.

A day earlier, Yulo finished eighth and last in the floor exercise final.

Armenia’s Artur Davtyan claimed vault gold with 14.850 points, dethroning Yulo, who ruled the apparatus in 2021 and 2025.

Yulo scored 13.833 points, with 8.033 in execution and 5.600 in difficulty, while incurring a 0.30 penalty.

However, competing in two international events in just one month proved too much for Yulo.

His World Championships campaign came after Yulo captured gold in both men’s floor exercise and vault at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan.

Joining Davtyan on the podium were Great Britain’s Jake Jarman, who took silver with 14.650 points. Norway’s Sebastian Sponevik secured bronze with 14.366 in the eight-man final.

On Saturday, October 24, Yulo finished eighth in the floor exercise final with 13.233 points, recording 7.633 in execution and 5.800 in difficulty, along with a 0.10 stick bonus and a 0.30 penalty.

Floor exercise and vault are among Yulo’s pet events, having won gold in both apparatus at the 2024 Paris Olympics. – Rappler.com

World.title: 4 ways US foreign policy could change if Democrats win in November
World.content:
A man holds a 'Vote Blue' sign while sitting in a golf cart during a Democratic rally in The Villages, Florida, US, October 17, 2026.

Here are some ways a Democratic Congress could hem in Trump's foreign policy

WASHINGTON, USA – Nonpartisan analysts say Democrats stand a good chance of winning the US House of Representatives and possibly the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, which would give them a slice of power in Washington after two years of Republican control.

Democrats argue that Republicans have allowed President Donald Trump‘s administration to declare war and control spending, even though the US Constitution reserves those powers for lawmakers.

Here are some ways a Democratic Congress could hem in Trump’s foreign policy.

Curb the Iran war

Trump did not secure approval from Congress before he launched the war with Iran on February 28, and Democrats have voted repeatedly to end the fighting unless he does so. One of these resolutions passed with support from a handful of Republicans, but Trump’s administration ignored it.

With control of the House or the Senate, Democrats could cut defense spending to pressure Trump to obtain permission from Congress to continue the war. They could also require administration officials to testify publicly about their plans.

Fresh support for Ukraine

Trump has largely halted direct US financial and military aid to Ukraine, despite broad support from Democratic and Republican lawmakers as it fights a Russian invasion.

Most recently, he has angered members of Congress, including many Republicans, by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russian energy only weeks after signing them into law.

With a victory in both chambers in November, Democrats would be able to decide what gets voted on and when.

That could allow them to approve new aid to Ukraine, which likely would pass with the two-thirds majorities needed to overcome a Trump veto.

They could also target other Trump activities. For example, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, who could head the House Foreign Affairs Committee if Democrats win control, has introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump’s plan to bring Russian diesel back into the global market.

End military aid to Israel

Support for Israel has plummeted among Democrats over its conduct in the Gaza war, which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians. The ongoing violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s close alliance with Republicans have also been factors.

Democrats could limit or end military aid to Israel, which amounted to $3.8 billion in the most recent fiscal year. That is more than was provided to any other country.

Nearly half of House Democrats voted this summer to ‌cut off aid to Israel. Some of those who voted against that effort, such as Meeks, have backed limits on providing weapons like heavy bombs to Israel.

Limit military spending and restore foreign aid

Democrats are far more likely than Trump’s Republicans to limit military spending. Trump asked for an unprecedented 67% increase in the military budget this year, to $1.5 trillion, but Democrats blocked it in the Senate, citing his refusal to consult Congress about the Iran war and his steep cuts to social programs.

Trump has also withheld or canceled billions of dollars in foreign aid approved by Congress. Many Democrats have been angered by the cuts and say they will try to restore funding.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Teodoro warns PMA of ‘weaponization of information’ as warfare moves beyond battlefield
World.content:
DEFENSE CHIEF. Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. joins Philippine Military Academy officials, cadets, alumni, and guests during the Academy’s 128th Foundation Anniversary celebration at Fort del Pilar on October 24, 2026.

The Philippine defense chief says technological advances, geopolitical developments, disruptions to supply chains, and other changes can emerge quickly and carry consequences for the security of states and individuals

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – Wars are no longer fought only with guns, ships, and aircraft. Information itself can be weaponized, and future military leaders must know how to deal with it.

Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro Jr. raised that warning during the Philippine Military Academy’s 128th Foundation Anniversary on Saturday, October 24, pointing to the “pervasive weaponization of information” as one of the security challenges that military institutions can no longer afford to treat as secondary.

Teodoro said technological advances, geopolitical developments, disruptions to supply chains, and other changes can emerge quickly and carry consequences for the security of states and individuals.

Some of these changes, he said, are not even the result of carefully planned government action but may come from technological breakthroughs or decisions by major global players that force everyone else to adjust.

The military, he said, must be able not only to respond but also to build leaders capable of managing organizations through that uncertainty.

For the Philippines, Teodoro said, that means strengthening the institutions needed to protect “our most sacred sovereignty, territorial integrity, and dignity as a Filipino people.”

Teodoro is among the most vocal in the Philippine government over China’s actions against the Philippines in the West Philippine Sea, enough for China to bar him from entering the country as well as from engaging in “any transaction, cooperation or other activities” with organizations or individuals in China.

‘Tall order’

Teodoro said the changing security environment also affects what PMA is expected to produce.

“We have to produce in this academy war fighters, make no bones about it. Every graduate of this institution is a war fighter,” he said.

He was quick to explain that he was not referring only to soldiers engaged in combat. “War fighting is not confined to combat operations and kinetic operations. War fighting spans the whole gamut of activities that will preserve the national objectives of any state,” he said.

That includes intelligence, analysis, logistics, personnel support, and the people who keep operations going behind the front line.

“Every person in uniform is a war fighter. Every member of the civilian human resource team of the Department of National Defense and the Armed Forces of the Philippines is a war fighter,” he said.

For PMA, this means doing two difficult jobs within the cadets’ four years at Fort del Pilar.

The academy must give them an education that can meet Philippine standards and stand alongside peer institutions in countries the Philippines works with. At the same time, it must produce junior officers ready to serve in the Armed Forces and, beginning three years from now, the Philippine Coast Guard.

Those graduates, Teodoro said, must leave with the proper military ethics, duties, responsibilities, and basic tactical skills required of their respective services.

“That is a tall order,” he said.

‘Today is not fast enough’

Teodoro also had a message for defense planners: Think bigger. Move faster.

“The Philippines cannot afford to be conservative in its planning,” he said.

If the country plans cautiously while similarly situated states are more ambitious, he said, the Philippines risks falling behind. That is particularly dangerous when sovereignty and national security are involved.

“Ambitious plans needed to have been laid down on the ground years ago,” Teodoro said. “But we cannot recoup the past. We can only make the present faster.”

Then came one of his sharpest lines: “And today is not fast enough. Tomorrow is certainly unacceptable.”

Teodoro said he had extensive discussions with PMA Superintendent Lieutenant General Michael Logico on the academy’s growth plans, infrastructure, curriculum, Corps of Professors, and the future design of the Cadet Corps, building on goals left by former superintendent Vice Admiral Caesar Bernard Valencia.

Education is not the same as training

Teodoro also questioned a habit he said he has seen in AFP education and training systems.

“Education is for knowledge. Training is for skills,” he said.

The two, he argued, should not simply be fused together. “Without knowledge, you cannot form skills. You cannot train skills.”

Military officers need a continuing and current body of knowledge across different fields, he said, because conflict has become increasingly multidisciplinary, unpredictable, and difficult to structure neatly.

That knowledge can then be translated into skills.

Teodoro also took issue with educational opportunities being awarded without sufficient regard for merit, particularly in advanced study and research.

“The opportunity for acquiring knowledge should be democratic,” he said.

Once that opportunity has been made available fairly, however, he said “individual merit and excellence” should determine educational qualification.

PMA cannot stay inside Fort Del Pilar

Teodoro also challenged the idea that PMA education and training should remain confined to its Baguio home.

“Fort Del Pilar houses the Philippine Military Academy. But the Philippine Military Academy should not be solely in Fort Del Pilar,” he said.

The Philippines has too many different operating environments, he said, for future officers to depend on a single training venue.

He linked this to the government’s push to secure military reservations for AFP use and to address infrastructure gaps that have affected operations, particularly in the maritime domain, as well as logistics, internal security, external defense, and disaster response.

Teodoro said the Armed Forces must be ready to enforce Philippine laws across the country’s vast maritime domain and deal with state actors that may not always follow international law.

That, he said, is why the defense establishment cannot afford timid planning.

The task for PMA is no longer simply to teach cadets how to fight the wars previous generations knew. It is to give them enough knowledge, skill, and judgment to understand what the next threat looks like, especially when it may arrive not as a bullet, but as information. – Rappler.com

World.title: Disenchanted Netanyahu supporters are prize of Israel election campaign
World.content:
CAMPAIGN. A person uses a smartphone next to a campaign van for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party at Hatikva market during Netanyahu's visit, ahead of Israel's national election, in Tel Aviv, Israel, October 22, 2026.

Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute

DIMONA, Israel – In the remote Negev Desert town of Dimona, long a bastion of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, disenchanted voters are going door-to-door campaigning for his top rival, hoping to bring down the veteran prime minister in Israel’s election on Tuesday, October 27.

The ballot is Israel’s first since Hamas’ October 7, 2023, surprise attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the militant group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran.

The October 7 security breach saw Likud’s popularity plummet. Opinion polls for months have predicted Netanyahu’s coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties losing its majority. But his top rival, centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears.

Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground.

“We must have change. Bibi has to go,” said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most his life. “Bibi has brought disaster to Israel.“

Likud loyalists

Assayag is part of a cohort of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot’s party Yashar, which is neck-and-neck with Likud in the polls.

It’s a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the previous 2022 election cast a ballot for Likud.

“I will never betray Likud,” said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and the blame he receives from detractors for October 7 was unfair.

Right-wing Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced centre-left Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations.

Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightwards, and there are now around half a dozen other parties courting Likud voters, from the centre to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong.

“Most people here vote for Likud just because that’s how they were raised,” said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. “The change will come when people start to think about their children’s future rather than their parents’ past.”

Battle for wavering Likudnics

While Netanyahu has a hard core of supporters that can’t be won over, the prize is undecided voters who “understand that we are in a state of crisis” and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot’s Dimona campaign.

Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute.

Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided.

It is in places just like Dimona where Eisenkot stands a chance to bite a chunk out of Likud’s base, said Amotz Asa-El, a political scientist at the Hartman Institute.

A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins from the Mizrahi community that “appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud’s traditional electorate,” said Asa-El.

In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters.

At a town hall during a visit to Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a leader of Mizrahi descent. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son.

But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds.

“Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love,” he said.

Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears.

But even some who are sympathetic to Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel’s youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms.

“It’s time for him to go,” said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. “He’s done a lot for Israel but it can’t go on. I won’t give my vote to someone almost 80-years-old.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Brazil heads to polls in runoff between leftist Lula and Bolsonaro Jr.
World.content:
ELECTION CAMPAIGN. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate seeking re-election, waves a flag during a closing campaign rally ahead of the presidential runoff, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 24, 2026.

Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days

SAO PAULO, Brazil – Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday, October 25, in a tight runoff vote that could shift Latin America’s largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region.

The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the month by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round.

A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.

The election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety, and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from Jair Bolsonaro’s 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if he is elected.

Trump has called the case a “witch hunt” and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. While many of those were later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices.

Lula has cast the Trump administration’s proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labeling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying.

On economic issues, despite falling inequality, and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters’ minds.

Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns and has also promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses.

Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days.

Historical precedent favors Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote.

Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%.

The senator’s first-round win sent Brazil’s markets and currency soaring on expectations of pro-business reforms.

His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him, or complicate governance for Lula. – Rappler.com

World.title: What schools will do amid intense heat during El Niño
World.content:
HYDRATION. A student at Rafael Palma Elementary School in Manila drinks from her tumbler on October 8, 2026.

How prepared is the Department of Education for the potential effects of El Niño?

MANILA, Philippines – The education sector will not be spared when El Niño worsens in the coming months. Across the country, temperatures are expected to be warmer than usual, which would pose another threat to students’ learning.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara previously said government protocols would ensure that El Niño’s effects are mitigated in public schools.

How exactly is the Department of Education (DepEd) preparing for the impact of the weather phenomenon? Pending formal guidelines, here’s what we know so far:

How to conduct classes

In an interview with Rappler on Friday, October 23, Education Undersecretary Malcolm Garma said the DepEd is concerned that lost school days may increase due to high heat index levels. The heat index, or the temperature that the human body perceives, is measured using the air temperature and the relative humidity in a place at a given time.

Garma noted that the DepEd’s existing class suspension guidelines, issued back in June, already spell out learning continuity plans for schools.

The DepEd said that under Level 1-Hayo, face-to-face classes continue during manageable conditions. Schools can set scheduled water breaks, shift outdoor activities to early morning or shaded areas, and allow students to wear comfortable clothing or Physical Education attire.

At Level 2-Hinay, schools may adopt modified class days with structured home-based or hybrid learning.

Level 3-Hinga may be implemented when temperatures can cause heat cramps or heat exhaustion or there is loss of water supply. Learning packets, short activities, and broadcast resources may be used to reduce academic demands.

Once the heat index reaches 42°C and above, academic activities are suspended at Level 4-Hinto, focusing on safety checks and psychosocial support referrals, according to the class suspension guidelines.

Garma said self-learning modules, activity sheets, and other materials needed for alternative learning will be prepositioned before the peak months of intense heat.

What if the heat is unbearable?

In case actual conditions turn out to be worse than projected, Garma said school heads can adjust class schedules or recommend granular suspensions of face-to-face classes. But he added that the situation must be properly assessed.

“Hindi naman ‘yung school head ay basta-basta na lang siyang magpapauwi o magsu-suspend. So kailangan mai-vet ito ng [schools] division office…or [they should] even coordinate with the local government unit. Para sa gano’n, talagang hindi naman maabuso din ‘yung pagsususpende ng klase,” the DepEd official said.

(The school head cannot just decide to send students home or suspend classes. This must be vetted by the schools division office or they should even coordinate with the local government unit. This is to prevent abuse of class suspensions.)

“While we are looking after…the welfare of our learners, we also have to ensure that learning continues. At alam naman natin na pinakamainam pa din na learning delivery natin ay kung school-based ito or face-to-face (And we know that the best learning delivery is school-based or face-to-face),” he added.

Measures for water supply, health

Garma said the DepEd has ordered schools to make hydration facilities and equipment, such as safe drinking stations and water dispensers, accessible to learners and personnel.

The DepEd also told schools to repair water leaks immediately and coordinate closely with local water concessionaires for rationing contingencies.

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian earlier raised the possibility of deploying community water depots to public schools. These depots are rainwater catchment equipment with built-in filtration systems to provide potable water during shortages. Garma said the DepEd welcomes such proposals.

Regarding health, Garma said school clinics will be ready to address medical concerns like heat stroke or dehydration. Additional support from local government units (LGUs) and the Department of Health will also be tapped for emergency response.

With El Niño also threatening agriculture and food supply, schools division offices and schools were directed to develop contingency menus for the school-based feeding program, partner with LGUs and cooperatives for local food sourcing, and maintain buffer stocks of shelf-stable commodities.

How about school buildings?

Garma said public schools can use their funding for maintenance and other operating expenses to buy additional ventilators like electric fans.

But the DepEd’s long-term solution is structural intervention.

“For old classrooms, we cannot change their designs; we can only do mitigation. But for those classrooms under construction and for future ones, we’ll make sure that there will be structural intervention such as high ceilings, insulated ceilings, and wide airflow,” he said in Filipino.

Garma also said the DepEd is exploring the possibility of institutionalizing the use of solar power in schools to reduce electricity costs and possibly provide air-conditioning.

The DepEd said its upcoming formal guidelines for El Niño-related measures will mandate schools to conduct integrated school-level risk assessments covering water supply reliability, classroom thermal safety, electricity resilience, and fire hazard prevention.

The set of guidelines is also expected to prohibit schools from charging or requiring parents to buy cooling equipment, connectivity, or specialized attire as a condition for alternative learning modalities. – Rappler.com

World.title: Malversation, graft charges filed vs 2 ex-DPWH execs over GenSan right-of-way scam
World.content:
The Office of the Ombudsman in Quezon City on March 6, 2026.

The Office of the Ombudsman files charges against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano Suan Jr., and several other DPWH personnel and private individuals

MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman has filed malversation and graft cases against two former Department of Public Works and Highways officials, four DPWH personnel, and seven private individuals over their alleged involvement in a road right-of-way scam in General Santos City.

The Office of the Ombudsman said in a press statement on Sunday, October 25, that it “found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction” against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano B. Suan Jr., and DPWH personnel Tomas Marquez Rodriguez, David Lucena Padlan, Paisal Amerol Padate, and Ansare Mariga Busran.

The Ombudsman also included seven private individuals in the cases filed before the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan: Wilma Mamburam, Nelson Ti, Evelyn Paloso, Rudy Hadji Ong, Marisa Seguirre, William Uy, Paul Michael Bagio.

“The Ombudsman filed 18 informations for Malversation of Public Funds or Property through Falsification of Public Documents under Article 217 in relation to Article 171 of the Revised Penal Code, and another 18 informations for violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act,” the Office of the Ombudsman said.

In 2018 and 2019, the National Bureau of Investigation submitted three investigation reports to the Ombudsman in relation to the DPWH Region 12 payment for right-of-way for 18 parcels of land allegedly affected by the construction of the Digos-Makar National Road in Lagao, General Santos City.
