World.title: The economic outlook for 2027 is stark. Ordinary workers will wear the costs
World.content:
A boss earning more than a million dollars a year urging staff to accept a pay cut.

A street of power poles that cost $3 billion.

A bank cutting thousands of jobs just weeks before Christmas.

The likelihood of the economy getting tighter.

You've got questions about what 2027 will feel like? You don't need to wait, we've got economic dislocation and fear in stark view.

Take one for the team

Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Michele Bullock is one of the most highly paid people in Australia.

Michele Bullock manages Australia's central bank and more than 2,000 staff. (ABC News: John Gunn)

In 2025-2026, she received total remuneration of $1.22 million. Her salary increased by 2.4 per cent and is set by the independent Remuneration Tribunal. Good on her.

Bullock is vastly experienced, manages 2,039 staff in 11 offices and has so much money to manage she needs to carefully enunciate her "b"s and "m"s so that all the illions don't get mixed up.

But she wants her staff to take, effectively, a pay cut.

Last week, RBA staff again rejected a pay offer that would see their real wages, the growth in wages minus the impact of inflation, fall immediately. (Bullock's pay rise is also below inflation).

In the rejected three-year deal, staff would have got a 3.7 per cent increase in the first year, then 3 per cent in 2028 and 2.8 per cent for the subsequent year.

The consumer price index (CPI), which measures the speed of price rises, says costs are going up 4 per cent a year. This means the deal would be a cut to their purchasing power, an erosion of real wages.

RBA warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' As markets put the chance of a rate hike in November at more than 50 per cent, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser warns of a "central banker's nightmare".

In its own words, the bank acknowledges its people would be going backwards at a high speed.

"Underlying inflation is expected to remain above 3 per cent until mid-2027, before declining to the midpoint of the 2-3 per cent target range in 2028," the bank's statement on monetary policy declared in August, before inflation kicked up another gear.

And there's a further sting.

The bank prefers to use a measure of "underlying" inflation called the trimmed mean, and who can blame them. The trimmed mean reduces the spiking impact on inflation of volatile items, like the rocketing oil price, which makes filling up vehicles more expensive.

People don't have that luxury. When fuel goes up they can't simply exclude it. They wear it.

Fragile AI eco-system

Sanderson Street in Yarraville, in Melbourne's inner west, has a creek up one end, a cemetery at the other and now a curious mantle: greatest destroyer of capital on the stock exchange by a single street this year.

Yarraville residents parked cars along a street in protest about large power poles being installed for a data centre. (ABC News: Norman Hermant)

Residents saw the march of industrial-sized concrete power poles heading towards NEXTDC's mammoth data centre, near their homes. When they parked cars in the street to stall the installation they set in train events that focused attention on the fragility of the trillion-dollar build-out of AI infrastructure.

In a small act of civil disobedience, they wiped $4 billion off the value of one of our biggest listed companies.

People power in suburbs exposes fragility of AI boom A neighbourhood dispute over power poles has wiped $3 billion from a listed company in a day and made the AI boom a little shakier.

With bolshie residents in the streets and a furious local member of parliament on the phone, electricity distributor Jemena did a swift reverse ferret, filling in the already-drilled holes and announcing the commencement of "engag(ing) with the local community". How timely!

In the tightly leveraged world of AI and data centre financing, this delay shook the company to its core.

Forget its score of existing and proposed centres across the nation, in an announcement to the market NEXTDC revealed projected revenue would drop by one-third, it would stop building some centres and consider selling land-banked sites it held.

All of which explains why NEXTDC started the week as a $7 billion company and ended it valued at closer to $4.1 billion.

What it doesn't explain, yet, is how fragile the entire eco-system of AI-powered companies appear to be.

As a multi-trillion-dollar hyper-scaler race goes on here, in the US and around the world, there could be other suburban streets that inadvertently crush what's seen as the future of capitalism.

Loading

NAB's job cuts not not about AI

Into this deepening chasm between people and capital strolls NAB, the third most valuable company in the nation (after BHP and Commonwealth Bank).

It revealed it would cut 2,500 jobs, most by Christmas, as well as an unknown number of consultants and contractors, to "simplify its operating model".

There was no direct reference to AI in what NAB told the market, although it did refer to "rapid technological change". Staff being pushed out were more direct about why they were cut.

As Swinburne University of Technology governance expert Helen Bird told me: "What the bank fails to explain to its investors is how it is going to achieve these cited benefits."

As if you need more scaring, senior NASA engineer and manager Jeevan Perera told ABC's The Business that every human is pretty doomed anyway.

"With the capabilities I've seen in AI and automation, I can't think of a position or a job that can't eventually go away to full automation," he said.

And that's all before we careen into the next meeting of the Reserve Bank's monetary policy board, better known as "the people who set interest rates".

ABC Business Daily podcast The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. Analysing the stories moving share markets, shaping industries and affecting the Australian economy.

A rise in the rate on Melbourne Cup Day is now a coin flip, with the coin weighted towards a rise. If the board chooses to lift rates it makes money more expensive. People can borrow less and those with debts face bigger repayments. (Let's note that those who have paid off their housing and have money in the bank, deposits, see increases in their returns as well).

Even though unemployment has lifted, RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser worried he's facing the "central banker's nightmare", where businesses start to expect inflation to stay above 3 per cent a year. They raise prices. Workers demand wage rises to deal with it (and generally don't get them). Consumer spending and business confidence slump.

All these things happen at the same time. Companies make decisions. Leaders make choices. Poles sometimes don't go up on time. Ordinary workers and investors are left in a swirl.

Right now, some of our largest and most visible institutions are trimming or fighting with employees, in an economy that's powered by the build-out of job-changing technology that is both gargantuan and seemingly brittle at the same time.

It's not here yet, but 2027 feels shaky already.

World.title: Educators weighing pluses and minuses of a 'digital detox' in school
World.content:
Federal Education Minister Jason Clare says a "digital detox" for schools will be on the agenda at a meeting with his state counterparts expected early next month.

It follows efforts by some governments overseas to reduce screen time in classrooms, and growing scrutiny of the impact of digital devices on learning.

Mr Clare has said results from the recent Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) show there is a "need to wind back the amount of screen time in schools — a digital detox".

Jason Clare has thrown his support behind a "digital detox" for schools. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Sweden has made one of the most high-profile efforts to replace screens with paper and books in classrooms since 2023.

However, like many other high-income nations, its results in PISA last year showed further declines, especially in reading and maths.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) report on the 2025 PISA results last month said the impact of digital devices on learning depended on how they were used.

Global results show Aussie students' struggles Australian students have recorded their lowest-ever scores in maths and reading in international testing, but improved on their science results.

"Across OECD countries, moderate use of digital devices for learning is associated with stronger science performance, while excessive use and digital distraction are associated with weaker outcomes," it said.

Neil Selwyn, a Monash University professor and expert on digital education, said some countries pushing ahead with digital technology in schools had done well in PISA.

"If we take things like PISA seriously — and there are a lot of reasons to treat them with a pinch of salt — then whether a school system is tech-centred or not doesn't seem to be a clear determining factor," he said.

So what do Sweden's efforts to remove screens from classrooms teach other countries such as Australia? And how do countries that performed well in PISA, including in Asia Pacific, use digital devices in schools?

Sweden's 'extreme' shift on screens

Sweden's approach to digital learning has "shifted extremely" in the past decade, according to Ingrid Forsler, an associate professor and researcher in media technologies in education at Södertörn University.

"We have gone from being very pro-digitalisation to having, at least on the surface, a very extreme de-digitalisation approach," she said.

This was partly a response to research into how digital devices caused distractions in learning, while politicians had also received popular support for reducing screen time in classrooms, Dr Forsler said.

Sweden once embraced digital technology in classrooms. (AFP: Karol Kozlowski/Robert Harding)

Sweden's government has started work on new curricula that would make compulsory schooling largely screen-free, particularly in early and middle years, and it has banned mobile phones in schools.

Simona Mohamsson, Sweden's education minister, said it had also funded new books for schools since it began pursuing a "back to basics" policy focusing on teaching reading, writing and maths.

She said its approach was consistent with research showing children learned these skills most effectively using "analogue tools in analogue environments".

Simona Mohamsson is pushing for less screen time in Sweden's schools. (AFP: Fredrik Sandberg/TT News Agency)

"It will take some time for all these reforms to be fully implemented and have an impact," Ms Mohamsson said.

Some studies have indicated that young people may comprehend texts better on paper rather than screens, although experts say the evidence on whether digital technology benefits overall learning is mixed and depends on how it is used.

Dr Forsler said Sweden's so-called "screen to binder" reforms have, in some ways, been superficial so far.

"The Swedish school is still very digitalised … schools have [digital] learning platforms," she said.

"What is limited is mainly the use of private devices for students and also laptops and tablets for younger students.

"It's too early to say if there are any successes, so to speak."

Sweden's recent PISA test results were among the lowest ever for the country.

Loading...

Dr Forsler said supporters of "screen to binder" policies had seen this as reason to push harder in removing digital learning from schools.

Professor Selwyn, from Monash University, said Sweden's teachers and schools had received "a huge amount of work" scrambling to adjust to the policy change.

"At the moment the main lesson that we can take from Sweden is that it is extremely difficult to 'turn off' technology in schools at the whim of a minister," he said.

" If we are serious about de-escalating the use of digital tech in schools then we need a considered, planned approach. "

Meanwhile, nearby Estonia achieved strong PISA results without banning mobile phones in schools and was embracing artificial intelligence tools in secondary schools, Professor Selwyn said.

"The Estonian government put their success down to a history of trusting schools and teachers to make their own decisions, having high expectations of students, consulting with students and parents, and properly evaluating what they do with tech as they go along," he said.

"They would argue that their success is down to a system-wide set of factors — and that tech use is part of this, not a driving factor."

Where China wants to go

Students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang — some of China's most economically developed regions — also had strong PISA results on reading, science and maths.

Hongzhi Zhang, a senior lecturer on education at Monash University, said exams throughout China were still paper-based, and students did much of their work in handwriting rather than on digital devices.

Students hand write much of their schoolwork in China. (AFP: CFoto)

Schools still taught digital skills in IT classrooms but managed how devices were used, considering how they would enhance student learning, he said.

"If not, they just put it away," Dr Zhang said.

However, Yong Zhao, a professor and expert on technology in education at the University of Kansas, said in some ways China was moving in a different direction from countries trying to reduce digital learning.

"I would encourage [people] to look hard at where China wants to go," he said.

Education authorities in Shanghai and Beijing are experimenting with AI-based education in schools.

The global AI race is moving into Asia's schools Countries in Asia are emerging as the world's early adopters of AI in education, as the global race to lead in the technology accelerates.

"They're not trying to detox that way," Dr Zhao said.

Meanwhile, he said education authorities also wanted students spending more time exercising and staying healthy, with less focus on test scores.

He also argued that the focus on PISA results risked losing sight of other aspects of education, such as helping students develop an interest in solving problems that matter to others.

Professor Zhao said students would need to learn how to use digital technology critically.

"They will live in a world that's dominated by these devices."

Japan's digital pushback

Japan was another of the top performers in last year's PISA, although it also recorded declines in reading results.

Government efforts to bring devices such as digital textbooks into schools had faced some resistance, according to Adelaide University professor and education scholar Keita Takayama.

"Parents and teachers were not fully on board with it," he said.

Japan recorded some of the world's best results in PISA. (AP: Hiro Komae)

"They were concerned about the amount of time the kids would be spending looking at the digital devices.

'"The government ended up not pushing it too far."

Professor Takayama said the government had pursued the changes believing they would help give students digital technology skills they would need at work.

" But I think the question is, does it need to be introduced early in primary school, for example? Could it wait until secondary school or even university? "

Among the strengths of Japan's education system, he pointed to the huge efforts teachers made to create a sense of belonging among students.

"It's so centrally related to students' academic or cognitive development," Professor Takayama said.

He supported reducing screen time in Australian schools, but said it was too early to say whether it would immediately improve student performance.

"It's important for students to be able to engage in a relationship of learning that is not necessarily mediated by technological tools," he said.

"The minimum you could say in terms of the benefit of this digital detoxing in schools is that it could potentially have health benefits."

World.title: Albanese faces stark choice if Trump escalates Iran war
World.content:
Twenty-three years ago, Anthony Albanese was a newish opposition frontbencher. That year was significant, not for the contribution he made as shadow minister for employment services and training (though he may argue otherwise), but for speaking out against a war he thought was wrong.

Albanese wasn't alone in his opposition; his colleague and longtime leadership rival Tanya Plibersek also said the Iraq war set a dangerous precedent for the world. Together they joined more than 40 senators and Labor MPs who signed an open letter to then US president George W Bush.

Admittedly these Labor MPs were in opposition, but it wasn't just one lone voice breaking ranks. It was 41 MPs. Imagine these same MPs and how they would respond if Donald Trump were around and said we "may ‌do another little ‌Epic ⁠Fury", as he did last week, as if it was a trivial game.

Running a government has required the PM to blunt parts of the old brawler. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Blunting parts of the old brawler

Plibersek said at the time: "We wanted to let him know that there were many people in Australia, including the Labor Party, who didn't support the war in Iraq and we wanted him to know the reasons why."

The letter, which said the pre-emptive military action made the world more dangerous, rather than more secure, was not the only example of Albanese speaking out against the conflict.

During the first month of the conflict, in March 2003, Albanese delivered a speech in parliament that reflected his aggressive, left-wing pugilist style that earned him the nickname "the Marrickville Brawler".

"Our government is about to redefine us in the eyes of the world as willing backers of US militarism. The prime minister took a phone call and immediately said yes to President Bush, because we all know that that decision was made many months ago, before the pre-deployment of troops. We were not even at the meeting where the decision was made."

He went on to say: "We are, with this decision, supporting a pre-emptive strike, which changes forever the way that international politics works."

Albanese did acknowledge the need for regime change; it was the method that Labor opposed, not the sentiment.

Now Albanese is prime minister and a lot has changed. He begins this parliamentary sitting week with Trump saying the US may carry out another military operation against ‌Iran at a time when the war is nearing its eighth month, and rising fuel prices dominate the US midterm elections.

Farmers turn on Trump Farmers are usually a reliable voting bloc for Donald Trump. But amid a "man-made" farming crisis, Republicans can no longer take their loyalties for granted.

"We may ‌do another little ‌Epic ⁠Fury," the president said at a rally in Florida last week as he spoke about the war. He did not elaborate. Operation Epic Fury is the name used by the US military for its war ⁠against Iran.

As John Maynard Keynes is often credited with saying: "When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?"

Everyone grows up, grows older and learns in Canberra that the politics of passion give way to the business of governing and pragmatism.

Those around Albanese know the prime ministership is a job he has wanted for a long time, and one he almost never had after Bill Shorten defeated him in Labor's leadership ballot in 2013.

And while Albanese loves being PM, and loves reminding the media, the opposition and his own colleagues of the record 94-seat majority he secured at the last election, running a government has required him to blunt parts of the old brawler.

Now, another American president is threatening to escalate a war that is smashing the economy, and this time Albanese has his phone number and doesn't have to sign a letter to get his views across.

The Labor backbench has been muted during the past eight months of this war, but will it remain muted if Trump escalates the war again?

The government supported the action against Iran in February. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Ongoing war Labor's next pinch point

In the past few weeks, the Labor backbench has become slightly more vocal, although this is coming off a low base. But a new escalation in this ongoing war is likely to be the next pinch point.

When Trump launched a joint offensive with Israel attacking Iran in February, Albanese, supported by Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Defence Minister Richard Marles, issued a statement supporting the action. The statement cited the need to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and a need to protect Australians living in the region.

Back in February, the language was about a short, sharp attack. Like countless conflicts before it, this invasion has dragged on and even senior government figures admit to having no clue when it will end.

As it has dragged on, the cost hasn't just been felt in the Middle East. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent our government into a panic with low domestic fuel supplies and high bowser prices.

Some MPs will want Albanese to condemn Trump over Iran and get some distance from an unpopular president. Labor's strategy at the last election was a veiled signalling that they were the anti-Trump party, that Peter Dutton was a Trump-like figure.

But without stronger language and action, that case will be hard to argue twice. The world is becoming less safe, and Australians are angry about it.

Loading

Every sign we're in uncharted waters

A feeling that the world is spinning out of control is fuelled by a sense of being the recipients of chaos and rarely the decision makers. A more forceful position on Iran and the US is something Labor MPs have increasingly been hoping for.

In the UK, the fallout from wars in Ukraine and Iran and cyber attacks have led the government to change its language and warn that the uncertainty abroad must be planned for at a household level. This messaging is about control and a sense of agency. People feel they have no control, and some governments are trying to lean into accepting that reality.

A new government "be ready" campaign in the UK is urging the public to prepare for the disruption of everyday services and to stockpile three days of key supplies.

The checklist advises stocking up with bottled water and non-perishable food, a battery or wind-up FM radio to receive updates during outages, and cash in case electronic payments or cash machines are disrupted.

Political analysis that matters The ABC's politics podcast, Politics Now, dives into the biggest stories, giving you a balanced look inside the strategies and decisions behind the headlines.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that there was not a "specific thing" in mind when it comes to potential emergency incidents, but said the advice might help during power cuts or if a local shop was subject to a cyber attack and was a matter of "everyday national resilience".

Put to him by an audience member that it could be "scaremongering" and push people towards panic buying like during the COVID-19 pandemic, he said: "We want people to be alert but not alarmed, and the truth is we looked around the rest of Europe, what are our friends doing across the continent? They are way ahead of us on some of this stuff."

If Europe is ahead, where are we? We may be geographically isolated but we are not immune to a more unsafe world both economically and strategically.

Our government hasn't told us to start stockpiling yet, but there is every sign that we are in uncharted waters.

Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly, and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

World.title: One in three homicides fuelled by psychosis, as doctors fear growing crisis
World.content:
A fourfold increase in the number of homicides committed by people with psychotic disorders in Victoria is the result of catastrophic failings in the mental health system that are exposing the community to dangerous levels of risk, experts have warned.

Frustrated psychiatrists say the alarming uptick in killings by people with psychosis is a triple tragedy for perpetrators, victims and the wider public because many of the recent deaths could have been prevented had the offenders received proper treatment.

Some are also concerned the homicides are just the tip of an iceberg — the most extreme, most visible symptom of a deepening crisis that the mental health royal commission should have addressed but hasn't, and on some fronts may have exacerbated.

Data compiled by consultant forensic psychiatrist Dr Rajan Darjee suggests 43 out of an estimated 126 homicides in Victoria in 2024 and 2025 — about one in three — were committed by people with psychosis, a significant increase from a decade ago, when one in 10 homicides per year were perpetrated by people with psychotic disorders.

Half of all stranger homicides in Victoria in the same period were committed by people with psychosis, Dr Darjee's research shows, as were two in three intimate partner and family homicides, raising questions about the adequacy of domestic violence prevention policies which emphasise addressing gender inequality and "disrespectful" attitudes.

"I remember looking at the raw number" — 43 homicides in two years, with 45 victims — "going, this is astounding," said Dr Darjee, clinical director of psychiatry at Forensic Behavioural Assessment and Consultation Services and adjunct professor at Swinburne University's Centre for Behavioural Science.

But perhaps the most important finding, he said, is that almost 84 per cent of homicide offenders in the sample had previously received treatment by mental health services, while half were connected with a service at the time of the incident.

'The public should not feel safe'

Psychosis is a set of psychological symptoms that impair a person's sense of reality. A central feature of schizophrenia spectrum disorders, it usually occurs in episodes that last days, months or even years and can include hallucinations, delusions, disordered thinking and disordered behaviour.

Though most people with psychotic disorders are never violent, there is a clear association between psychosis and violence. Australian and international studies also show people with psychotic illness are more likely to perpetrate homicide than people in the general population — a major reason why experts have long stressed the importance of effectively treating psychosis to reduce and prevent violence.

Aussie mothers with postpartum psychosis 'falling through cracks' Many Australian women with postpartum psychosis actively seek help despite not understanding what is wrong with them, research finds.

"If you treat people with psychosis early and effectively, you prevent poor outcomes later, including chronic mental ill-health, disengagement from family, not being able to work, homelessness … but also violence and aggression," Dr Darjee said.

Dr Darjee and his colleagues designed the study — which is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal — to understand whether their anecdotal observations were reflected in formal data.

He surveyed nine forensic psychiatrists who write defence reports for courts in Victoria about how many people they assessed in 2024 or 2025 who were charged with murder or manslaughter and diagnosed with psychosis, and whether they were connected with mental health services, among other details.

"It's terrible that 45 people have died, especially when you think the majority of those were probably preventable deaths," Dr Darjee said. "But the homicides are the tip of the iceberg. The bigger [part of the] iceberg underneath means that people with mental illness and their families are living lives that are much worse than they need to be."

Professor Patrick McGorry chaired the expert advisory committee for the Royal Commission into Victoria's Mental Health System. (Supplied: Orygen)

Professor Patrick McGorry, a psychiatrist who chaired the expert advisory committee for the Royal Commission into Victoria's Mental Health System, said the homicide data was the result of a "public policy failure" to build a modern system of care to replace the state's old psychiatric hospitals, which were decommissioned in the 1990s.

"What it shows is that people have had ineffective contact with mental health services," Professor McGorry said. "They've either tried to get access but have failed, or they've gained access but haven't been able to get effective treatment, which is what people with serious mental illness need. They get episodes of care rather than sustained, safety net-type treatment."

The royal commission, which ran from 2018 to 2021, was "largely a successful blueprint" to fix the system, he said, but the government "has not really invested properly in implementing its recommendations — every single one has been delayed or poorly implemented".

"I thought for sure the royal commission … would have led to a once-in-a-generation transformational reform — I was wrong," Professor McGorry said. "So I think the only thing … that will actually galvanise the public into demanding something is done is if they themselves don't feel safe. And the public should not feel safe in the context of the current mental health system."

Crucially, he added, most people with psychosis pose no harm when they are well. "It's the acute illness that has made them dangerous and so that's a tragedy — not just for their victims but for them personally — that they've been allowed to harm other people. And it's not a character problem, it's a health problem."

Compulsory treatment can be 'life-saving'

Several experts told ABC News they were particularly concerned about an anecdotal increase in the number of short-term admissions to mental health units when longer stays are generally required to stabilise patients with psychosis.

Many are also worried a royal commission recommendation to reduce the use and duration of compulsory treatment orders has contributed to a system-wide reluctance to use them, including in cases where they ought to be.

"With the best of intentions we've instigated these least restrictive care policies but they've become negligent," Dr Darjee said. "I don't like compelling people [into treatment], I always do it reluctantly, but sometimes it's life saving."

Brendan Nugent's mental health Once known as a passionate environmentalist, neighbours and family say Brendan Nugent became increasingly isolated in the years before Monday's alleged attack.

Forensicare chief executive and Swinburne University Adjunct Professor Colmán O'Driscoll agreed people should ideally be compelled to take psychiatric treatment only as a last resort. But he said the mental health system was at risk of "swinging the pendulum too far the other way" if people with psychosis aren't being put on compulsory treatment orders when they need to be.

"We always think about these orders as a compulsion on the individual to receive care. In my view, a significant part of their benefit is that they compel the system to provide the care you deserve as a member of our community," Professor O'Driscoll said.

And given psychosis can affect people's ability to make "good decisions", he said, maintaining their engagement with treatment is crucial, and leads to better outcomes.

Australian studies have found people with psychosis are much more likely to be convicted of a violent criminal offence than the general population, but that early and frequent contact with mental health services reduces their risk of reoffending — and those on community treatment orders are less likely to reoffend than those who receive punitive sanctions.

"The starting point is finding a way to conceptualise violence among people with psychosis as a complication of their illness and therefore we should have a health system that sees the prevention of it as core to its work, not separate from it," Professor O'Driscoll said.

He said Victoria should be invest more in programs that divert people with psychosis away from the criminal justice system into treatment programs, focus on improving patient engagement with such programs, and upskill the mental health workforce in violence risk assessment and management.

Dr Darjee believes there should be a "wholesale review" of the royal commission's recommendations. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Some doctors also believe there is a trend in Victoria, particularly since the introduction of the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act in 2022, to view a wide spectrum of mental health and "wellbeing" issues as equally important, but that severe mental illness must be prioritised.

"I genuinely think that, even though the royal commission and what came after it hasn't been fully implemented, we need a wholesale review and almost a reversal of some of its recommendations," Dr Darjee said. "And I think in mental health policy and care there needs to be more emphasis on people with severe mental illness."

So long as nothing changes, he added, "we're just going to carry on having lots of people dying unnecessarily".

"I just don't think it's right for a relatively well-off jurisdiction like Victoria to be neglecting people with mental illness as much as we're neglecting them."

Minister for Mental Health Ingrid Stitt did not respond to specific questions but a government spokesperson told ABC News that Victoria's mental health system was focused on ensuring people with serious mental illness can access safe, compassionate treatment.

"Every homicide is a tragedy and while these incidents are rare, it's vital they're not used to stigmatise people living with mental ill-health," they said.

"The Mental Health and Wellbeing Act provides for compulsory assessment and treatment where the legal criteria are met, while recognising that compulsory treatment should only be used as a last resort."

World.title: Donald Trump labels Obama 'incompetent' in post rally retaliation
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has retaliated after his Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama delivered scathing criticisms of the incumbent during rallies in Ohio and Michigan.

Mr Trump labelled the former leader "incompetent" during his own rally in Michigan, which came one day after Mr Obama campaigned alongside Democratic Party candidate Abdul El-Sayed in the same state.

"Obama was a grossly incompetent President! He paid off Iran with $Billions, and gave them a road to a Nuclear Weapon." Mr Trump wrote in a post on social media.

The US president also slammed Mr Obama for supporting US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

The back and forth unfolded after both parties campaigned across Michigan and Ohio one day apart. (AFP: Roberto Schmidt)

The hit at Mr El-Sayed comes after Mr Trump and Republican candidate Mike Rogers have repeatedly tried to tie Mr El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, falsely branding the Democrat a "jihadist."

In the same post on social media, Mr Trump called Mr El-Sayed a "Fake Doctor, who runs what is considered to be the WORST CLINIC IN AMERICA."

"Michigan doesn't want an arrogant, Open Borders, Fake Doctor, Jihadist, whose reputation will only get worse as more information is revealed."

Mr Trump has been telling voters to view the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot, and on Saturday Mr Obama did just that.

Obama unleashes

Ten days out from the November 3 elections that will determine control of the closely divided Congress, Barack Obama took to the campaign trail to accuse the Republican president of corruption.

Mr Obama used Democrat campaign rallies as a stage for criticism of the current President. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Mr Obama spared no mercy when it came to criticism surrounding Mr Trump's strategy for Iran, and skewered the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations.

Taking aim at new renovation projects across the US capital, including the National Mall's Reflecting Pool and the construction of a White House Ballroom.

The decorations added to the Oval Office during Mr Trumps second tenure were also not safe from critique.

"He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Mr Obama said.

Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office. (Truth Social: Donald Trump)

The former president has retained considerable popularity among the Democratic base, which he is keen to leverage to support his party's candidates.

In both states, Mr Obama blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, one of the top voter concerns.

"The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions," Mr Obama said in Cleveland, Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown.

"Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for."

The war on Iran has sent oil prices soaring as Tehran effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz after being attacked.

"After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, enough is enough," Mr Obama said.

Why Michigan was a crucial Democrat primary Abdul El-Sayed's victory in the Democrats' Michigan primary race could shape the party's messaging to voters and how it responds to Donald Trump ahead of November's crucial midterms.

Later, in Michigan he campaigned for Abdul El-Sayed, from the party's left wing, who is in a close race with Republican Mike Rogers for the US Senate.

"Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa," Mr Obama said, referring to the incumbent Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, who is not up for election this year.

" You got a Muslim man, you got a Jewish woman fighting for you in the United States Senate. That's something, Michigan, you can be proud of. "

Obama says 'don't procrastinate'

The former president also urged voters to cast their ballots as soon as possible since early voting is already open in both states.

"Don't procrastinate, don't equivocate," Mr Obama said.

Polls in Ohio give Democrats a slight lead in both races, but results are expected to be close.

Nationally, polls also suggest that Democrats could regain control of the House of Representatives but face a much more competitive contest for the Senate.

AP/AFP

World.title: Iran says resumption of war with US would not change its mind
World.content:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.

The remarks on Sunday came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on February 28.

Mr Araghchi said a fresh attack would not yield a different outcome.

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," Mr Araghchi said during a televised event in Tehran.

" They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past. "

A plume of smoke rises after a US strike in Tehran in March. (AP: Vahid Salemi)

An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the US put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

These military flare-ups have lulled in recent weeks.

Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation, moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region.

In response, the US has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

In June, Iran agreed with the US to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.

Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.

"The current war has changed everything," Mr Araghchi said.

"We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same.

"To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces."

Ten ballistic missiles intercepted over Riyadh

The Houthis have warned they could again target Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh's airport "a military target". (Reuters: Mohammed al-Mahdi)

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles over its capital Riyadh and southern areas on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said, as fighting with the Iran-aligned Houthis persisted.

The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising front in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.

On Sunday, Saudi civil defence authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh, Abha and Khamis Mushait, before announcing minutes later that the danger had passed.

The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait.

Travellers were told that the King Khalid International Airport was again operating normally. (AP Photo)

It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis warned they could again target Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday after a deadly attack earlier this month.

The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the airport remained a "military target" and warned all airlines, airport staffers and travellers against using it.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Kangaroos escape with World Cup win after Fiji threatens upset
World.content:
The Kangaroos have locked in their semifinal spot at the Rugby League World Cup, beating Fiji 36-22 after receiving an almighty scare in Brisbane.

Tom Trbojevic's second-half hat-trick helped Australia over the line after the Bati twice took the lead either side of half-time at Lang Park.

Fijian five-eighth Kurt Donoghoe was rightly named player of the match after laying on three tries and dictating terms for much of the game.

"I think we need more from everyone," Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters said after the game.

"We know we can play better but let's give Fiji a lot of credit. At times it seemed like we were getting on top and they pulled themselves back into the game."

Taane Milne's try gave Fiji an early lead. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Despite coming into the game as 50-1 outsiders, making three early errors and conceding the first try of the night, Fiji hit back through Semi Valemei and Taane Milne to lead 10-6 after half an hour.

For the second straight game, Kevin Walters's side looked vulnerable in defence and struggled with their last-tackle options, but still led at half-time after some James Tedesco brilliance led to a try for Sam Walker on debut.

But again the Fijians hit back, with Valemei's second retaking the lead for the underdogs just after the break and Solomone Saukuru appearing to extend soon after, only for the bunker to rule a line-ball obstruction.

The Kangaroos immediately went up the other end and Tom Trbojevic dove in for his first of three straight tries to snuff out the Fijian challenge.

Valemei completed his hat-trick late on before Jacob Preston added Australia's sixth shortly before full-time to lock in their semifinal berth, playing a double-header with the similarly undefeated Jillaroos at the Sydney Football Stadium next Sunday.

Fiji will have a chance to push for a surprise final-four spot if it can pull off an upset win over New Zealand next week, which suddenly does not seem so far-fetched.

World.title: Hand-delivered death threat, being spat at among abuse ACT politicians cop
World.content:
A hand-delivered death threat, being spat at and misogynistic abuse are just some of the incidents ACT politicians say they've experienced.

Several members of the ACT Legislative Assembly have spoken out about the abuse they've been subjected to, following the attack on federal independent MP Helen Haines outside her Victorian electorate office on Monday.

It's not yet clear what motivated Brendan Nugent, 43, to allegedly run her down in the incident that led to both her legs being amputated.

But the incident has renewed concerns about the safety of elected representatives across Australia, and highlighted the risks that come with their jobs.

Canberra Liberals MLA and former ACT opposition leader Elizabeth Lee said she has had to contact police twice over "very serious threats" she received.

"I had a death threat that named my daughter and my partner, and it was actually dropped at my front gate, so it came to my house," Ms Lee recalled.

"That was a pretty scary moment, and it does actually question, to me, as a parent especially, whether it's worth it.

"I have got this duty to ensure that I am prosecuting the issues that are really important to the community, but does that come at the cost of safety to my family?"

Elizabeth Lee says threats against her family have left her questioning whether to stay in politics.

The incident came on top of the many sexist and racist comments she has received online over the past decade of representing her community.

"Belittling criticism on a personal level. Criticisms on my weight and my body shape as well, what I'm wearing sometimes," she said.

The mother of two daughters, Ms Lee said she tried to find the balance between ignoring the comments and calling them out to show her girls that such behaviour was unacceptable.

"I try and ignore it on the whole, but at the same time I know that there are people who need to know that it's not okay," she said.

"So, every now and then I will take that and make an example out of it to call it out."

'Disturbing part of the job'

ACT Health Minister Marisa Paterson has also had some "pretty horrible" encounters with constituents.

"Yelling abuse at you, names at you," Ms Paterson said.

" I've been spat at; I've had things like that happen, standing outside the front of the shops and I've had people make violent threats to me face-to-face. "

Marisa Paterson says that while most of her interactions with constituents are positive, some recent encounters have been "pretty horrible". (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie )

Ms Paterson said she enjoyed meeting and greeting Canberrans at local shops and community events, and that "97 per cent of interactions" were "amazing".

But she said the abuse she received, both in person and online, was a "disturbing part of the job" that made her "feel very vulnerable".

"It's predominantly men. In fact, all of my examples are men," she said.

" And I don't know … why they feel they can say these things to me and speak to me like that. But that is what happens. It's really disturbing. "

Online, Ms Paterson said the abuse had "ramped up" over the past 18 months "very, very significantly", particularly with misogynistic, violent and hateful comments.

"The online world is a very unhappy place at the moment, I think," she said.

"Aside from having this job and needing to be there, other than that, I would have no part of it.

"It is a pretty awful environment with the online comments."

'Tough being a woman in politics'

For Greens MLA Laura Nuttall, it's her sexuality, gender and appearance that are often targeted on social media.

"You'll get some pretty nasty comments, which are often nothing to do with the debate [of the social media post], and everything to do with your appearance, your political leanings," Ms Nuttall said.

"I have had my sexuality speculated on and then sort of taken through the mud. I've copped a bit of queerphobic abuse, which is never fun.

"It is tough … being a woman in politics, particularly right now."

Laura Nuttall says that while most of her interactions with the public are positive, some encounters have been genuinely frightening. (ABC News)

Ms Nuttall said the comments she received could be demoralising and that she "would be lying" if she said the attack on Ms Haines hadn't scared her.

"I have occasionally … felt the impact of that in my personal life in terms of just a loss of confidence," she said.

"And at times, even though it's momentary, a little bit of loss of faith in humanity, that people could be so mean and so remorseless about it."

'Rage gets clicks'

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said he had seen his female counterparts cop far more abuse, particularly online, than he and his male colleagues did.

"Some of the men get criticised as well, but I think criticism on the basis of policy or disagreeing is really critical, that's part of our democracy and that's what a good, vibrant democracy looks like," Mr Emerson said.

"We should be able to disagree and disagree respectfully, debate those ideas. But when that flips into just abuse that's got nothing to do with the issue at hand, it is concerning."

Thomas Emerson acknowledges that his female colleagues are having "very different experiences as politicians" to his own. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

He said there was a lot more political leaders could do to lead by example.

"Every time we allow policy disagreement to devolve into denigrating the people we're disagreeing with, we're basically saying to the people we're supposed to be representing, and leading in some ways, that actually this is the right way to conduct yourself," he said.

"So there's some blame there for politicians.

"We know that rage gets clicks and it gets picked up in traditional media, on social media, and that can lead to some pretty perverse incentives for politicians themselves and for people out in that community."

Ms Lee agreed that "we all need to take responsibility as a society".

"Political leaders particularly have a role, but it's anyone who has a public voice including the media and the big companies that obviously are responsible for social media," she said.

"Anyone who has the opportunity and the privilege to be able to shape public discourse and debate has a responsibility."

Laura Nuttall says she wants to continue meeting with Canberra constituents at local shops. (ABC News)

As politicians across the country review their security measures, these ACT MLAs are determined to remain publicly available to constituents as part of a healthy democracy.

"It is absolutely the key part of my job that I love," Ms Paterson said.

"It is my job to be out and about talking to people, listening to people, listening to what their concerns are."

Ms Nuttall agreed that she did not want the pockets of aggression, venom and vitriol to detrimentally impact the way she did her job.

"The whole point of being a representative is to be as accessible as humanly possible," she said.

World.title: How mother-daughter dates became the red carpet trend of the year
World.content:
Exclusive LifestyleFashionSpring racing carnival How mother-daughter dates became the red carpet trend of the year Gyan Yankovich October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The morning of a special event, there are several things you should never leave home without: a fully charged phone, a hydrating lip balm and – as per the celebrity trend of the year – your daughter. At this year’s Met Gala, Nicole Kidman, dressed in custom Chanel by Matthieu Blazy, walked the carpet with daughter Sunday Rose, in Dior. “My daughter is blooming, and what she wore shows that,” Kidman told Vogue. In October, at Paris Fashion Week, Kidman swapped daughters and took Faith Urban as her date to the Chanel show, proving that the best date isn’t your long-term partner, a fling or someone you’ve just met on an app. Sunday Rose and Nicole Kidman attend the 2026 Met Gala (right); Faith Urban and Nicole Kidman attend Paris Fashion Week. Getty Images Why daughters make the best dates



It’s a trend already promising to be replicated at this year’s Melbourne Cup Carnival, with Lexus welcoming internationally acclaimed costume and production designer Catherine Martin Luhrmann AC and daughter Lilly Luhrmann to Crown Oaks Day on November 5. Catherine, the four-time Academy Award winner and wife of Baz Luhrmann, best known for her work on The Great Gatsby, Elvis and Moulin Rouge!, said attending the event with Lilly will add a deeply personal element to the occasion. Four-time Academy Award-winning designer Catherine Martin Luhrmann AC and her daughter Lilly Luhrmann will join Lexus at the 2026 Melbourne Cup Carnival, reflecting the brand’s celebration of masters of their craft and the next generation of creative talent. Yvonne Tnt/BFA.com/Shutterstock But Kidman and Martin aren’t the only celebrities reminding us why a daughter – especially a well-dressed one – is the perfect accessory. Kate Moss attended the Burberry show at London Fashion Week with daughter Lila Moss. And at last year’s Golden Globes, Angelina Jolie walked the carpet with her daughter Zahara, both dressed in Alexander McQueen.



The art of mother-daughter dressing The big difference between dressing for a red carpet and dressing for a raceday? Millinery. Related Article Caulfield Cup A lesson in elegance: The Caulfield Cup fashion winners When it comes to mother-daughter dressing, the best styling trick, according to Natalie Bikicki, award-winning milliner and founder of Natalie Bikicki Designs, is to find one connecting element, whether it’s a colour, texture or detail. “For example, a daughter’s floral dress might feature a shade that her mother picks up in her millinery,” says Bikicki. “That creates a lovely connection without needing to match everything. Neither woman should feel she has to dress older or younger to make the pairing work.”



Bikicki suggests women try on outfits together before the event – especially if they’re hoping for a nice photo – to check balance and ensure nobody’s face will be obscured by the other’s hat. Leo Lin, founder and creative director at Leo Lin, says he loves seeing women interpret the Crown Oaks Day dress code – soft pastels and florals – together. “One might choose a new silhouette in the same floral print; another might pair a floral with a soft pink drawn from the print.” “Vary the shape or scale, so each look feels personal but connected,” he says. Angelina Jolie attends the 2025 Golden Globes with daughter Zahara (right); Kate Moss and Lila Moss attend London Fashion Week. Getty The next generation



The theme for this year’s LANDMARK by Lexus – the brand’s pavilion inside Flemington’s exclusive Birdcage enclosure – is A New Dawn, exploring what happens when “experience meets fresh thinking, and when enduring traditions are carried forward in new ways”. It’s a concept that resonates deeply with Catherine, who sees Lilly as an example of the next generation of creative talent. “I’ve always believed that great design comes from a combination of technical mastery, collaboration and a willingness to explore new ideas,” she said. “Being able to share that appreciation for creativity with Lilly makes attending Crown Oaks Day together with Lexus particularly special.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: I’m no funnier, but improv comedy somehow made me a better traveller
World.content:
Reviews & adviceTravel tips Opinion I’m no funnier, but improv comedy somehow made me a better traveller Paul Marshall Travel writer October 26, 2026 — 5:00am

October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

My wife thinks I’m funny, which is about as close to a joke as I get these days. Unless, of course, you consider my bank account, which is hilarious to everyone but me. This is all to say that while my years of improv comedy did nothing to sharpen my sense of humour, they did wonders for me as an open-minded traveller, and it all comes down to this golden rule. Yes, and … The cornerstone of any good performance, ‘yes, and …’ is about more than accepting the offer, as it’s known in the parlance. It’s about creating a scene where there are no closed doors and no dead ends. Although it’s been a long time since I’ve done any actual improv comedy, you’d be amazed at how much this rule has echoed through my travels, where invitations are accepted and going off script is all part of my poorly laid plans.



When your flight plan falls apart in Myanmar, the road trip of a lifetime begins. iStock 



Related Article Opinion

Travel tips My husband wore budgie smugglers in the US. The locals were shocked Kate Allman Writer and broadcaster This definitely wasn’t in our script but I’ll be damned if it didn’t heighten the scene, and make our trip look so much better on the stage. This is what makes the “and …” so important. It’s how you pursue the unexpected and transform the mundane into the magical. It’s easy to think of the 15th hour into what was supposed to be an eight-hour bus ride as torture. It’s a lot harder to treat that torture as an opportunity to befriend fellow passengers, accepting that even the best-laid plans are no match for a bus timetable in Laos. I’m not saying that you should start watching reruns of Whose Line Is It Anyway? to make yourself a better traveller, although there are worse ways to spend an afternoon. I’m saying that when you accept your role as a player in this performance we call travel, then you become more than just a passenger on a trip. And while no good travel story ends with “and everything went according to plan”, I can think of quite a few that started with “yes, and…”

World.title: These luxe last-minute trips go all out for Christmas
World.content:
Travel newsTravel tips These luxe last-minute trips go all out for Christmas Julietta Jameson October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. If the prospect of peeling potatoes – or prawns – has lost its appeal, it’s not too late to make other plans for Christmas. Travelling offers a chance to swap the usual festive arrangements for something less demanding. And leaving the country needn’t mean leaving Christmas behind. You can still embrace old traditions, invent new ones or simply let somebody else take care of the hosting. European river cruises stop at towns that take traditional Christmas very seriously. iStock If you’ve always dreamt of a white Christmas, the traditional northern hemisphere festivities await on APT’s Magnificent Europe cruises, which travel between Amsterdam and Budapest along the Rhine, Main and Danube, passing through historic cities and towns that don’t do Christmas-lite. If it’s decorations, markets and centuries-old rituals you’re after, this is a rather luxurious portal to the mother lode. Tootle along the river in sublime comfort aboard APT’s luxury river ships, admiring the twinkling lights, then immerse yourself in places that epitomise the yuletide spirit.



Some departures encompass Christmas Day itself. On the Christmas and New Year’s Eve sailing, Christmas Eve is spent in Bamberg, Christmas Day in Nuremberg and Boxing Day in Regensburg, with festive dining and celebrations aboard. 



Outrigger Fiji Beach Resort on Viti Levu’s Coral Coast always combines local traditions with family fun, but Christmas is an especially big occasion. Christmas Eve brings carols by candlelight with a village choir, while Christmas Day begins with a church service before Santa makes his grand entrance on the beach. A giant gingerbread house is cracked open on the beachfront lawn, and families gather for a festive buffet or sunset dinner. Complimentary children’s clubs, activities for teenagers and a nanny service for younger guests mean parents might even find some time to themselves. At Phuket’s Sri Panwa the festivities include a six-course celebration dinner at Baba Poolclub on December 24 and 25. If you’d rather Christmas itself were a more low-key affair, Sri Panwa in Phuket offers a more relaxed approach, with panoramic Andaman Sea views and a six-course celebration dinner at Baba Poolclub on December 24 and 25.

Travel tips Ten overseas Christmas traditions Australia should adopt Ben Groundwater Travel writer Here, there’s no need to organise your day around a packed calendar of festive activities. Spend the day enjoying the resort’s pools, restaurants and spectacular oceanfront setting, then dress up for dinner. The serious partying can wait until New Year’s Eve, when silver-themed celebrations spread across the resort’s venues, with sunset drinks, a gala dinner, live entertainment and a countdown to the new year. Wherever you choose to celebrate, at least someone else is doing the dishes – and the peeling. See aptouring.com; jaresortshotels.com; outrigger.com; sripanwa.com

World.title: Three Blue Ducks up for first major award at tonight’s Good Food Guide awards
World.content:
Eating outGood Food Guide Three Blue Ducks up for first major award at tonight’s Good Food Guide awards Plus, will a new three-hatter be announced? Follow the action and announcements, including Best Chef and Restaurant of the Year via the live blog from 3pm. Sarah Norris October 26, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When the 500-strong crowd of leading industry figures meets for the 42nd Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide awards at Carriageworks tonight, it will be the first time Three Blue Ducks has been up for a major award. In fact, the group’s $210 per person farm-to-table Three Blue Ducks Burradoo in the Southern Highlands has been nominated for two awards: Regional Restaurant of the Year and Best New Restaurant of the Year. The ambitious farmhouse restaurant, located just outside Bowral, opened at Easter within billionaire Annie Cannon-Brookes-backed Burradoo Park, with the former co-head chef of Sydney’s three-hatted Quay, Troy Crisante, at the helm. Three Blue Ducks Burradoo chefs (from left) Rhys Connell, Darren Robertson, Andy Allen and Troy Crisante. Kitti Gould Callan Boys, co-editor of the Herald Good Food Guide, reviewed it in September, giving it a score of 16.5 and two hats, making it the highest scoring restaurant of the year at that time.



“With the chef talent involved, I knew it would be good,” says Boys, “but I wasn’t expecting such a cohesive tasting menu of finely tuned dishes. It’s a long way from avocado toast and slow-cooked lamb shoulder.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up While Three Blue Ducks has been important in the evolution of NSW’s dining scene – it helped redefine breakfast cafe food in Sydney and made paddock-to-plate dining a more accessible, everyday concept – it’s never been up for a major Good Food Guide award. The Three Blue Ducks story began in 2010 at the now-closed Bronte cafe, and has grown across the state, including an elaborate farm venture in Byron Bay and now the restaurant in Bowral. Part of its success was applying cheffing techniques to casual and cafe food – a concept that is much more common these days – led by two former fine-dining Tetsuya’s chefs, Mark LaBrooy (who is no longer involved) and Darren Robertson. The Three Blue Ducks at Burradoo is in a restored 1823 heritage farmhouse. Jennifer Soo



Along with Regional Restaurant of the Year and New Restaurant of the Year, presented by Aurum Poultry Co., tonight’s ceremony will also feature the announcement of 15 other awards, including T2 Tea Restaurant of the Year, Oceania Cruises Chef of the Year, T2 Tea Cafe of the Year and Oceania Cruises Service Excellence. The coveted Good Food Guide hats will also be announced. “Since Quay and Oncore closed this is the first time since the 1980s that the Guide has started the reviewing season with only two three-hatted restaurants,” says David Matthews, co-editor of the Guide. “Tonight we get to see whether any other contenders have made the leap.” The Good Food hat rating system – from one to the pinnacle of three – was created by the Good Food Guide more than 40 years ago to give readers a sense of what to expect in terms of food, service, experience and value for money. It’s been the cornerstone of Good Food’s rating system since. The main goal of this system, and the reviews in general, isn’t to tell readers whether reviewers like a restaurant. It’s to paint a picture of the experience, so readers can decide whether they might like it, and to explain how it sits within Australia’s dining landscape. Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide editors Callan Boys and David Matthews. Sitthixay Ditthavong



This year’s Guide, presented by Oceania Cruises and T2 Tea, features more than 500 independent reviews of restaurants, bars, pubs, clubs and cafes in regional NSW, Canberra and Sydney across various price points, cuisines, styles and suburbs, making it the largest Guide published to date. A new signature list will be launched this year: the 100 Essential Restaurants. These are the places that define dining out in NSW and the ACT right now. Diversity of cuisine, menu, geography and price point were considered when curating the list, which includes some hatted venues. The 100 Essential Restaurants list responds to the changing needs of Australian diners – recommending everything from fine-dining restaurants to food-court favourites – and also reflects how our food scene is evolving. The free 56-page Good Food Guide magazine liftout. Dion Georgopoulos This collection will be published in a free 56-page liftout in tomorrow’s Herald, and the list will be available in the Good Food app and on the web.



Since launching in 2024, the app is considered the home of the Good Food Guide and is where readers can search the full A-Z list of reviews using map and filtering functionality. The app has more than 3000 reviews and recommendations. All reviews go live on the app tonight after the conclusion of the ceremony, at about 8pm. The event will also be live blogged from 3pm, so you can follow the action. The winners of the 42nd Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide Awards will be announced on Monday, October 26, presented by Oceania Cruises and T2 Tea. The awards ceremony will be live-blogged via the Herald from 3pm; the Guide reviews will be available on the Good Food app from 8pm. Pick up a free 56-page Good Food Guide liftout in the Herald on Tuesday, October 27. The Good Food app is free for premium subscribers of the Sydney Morning Herald and also available as a standalone subscription. You can download the Good Food app here.

World.title: The best (and worst) cheeses for your gut health
World.content:
Tips & adviceGut health The best (and worst) cheeses for your gut health From cheddar to camembert, some of our favourite varieties of cheese harbour a surprising secret to better digestion. Damon Syson October 26, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We are a nation of cheese lovers, but it may come as a surprise to discover that this household staple is also a secret superfood. A recent study has revealed that the microbes in different cheeses could also offer a surprising boost for gut health. Scientists from the University of Reading tracked the microbial and biochemical changes that took place as three cheeses matured. Their findings suggest that some of the bacteria responsible for developing each cheese’s unique flavour profile may also be beneficial, “potentially producing compounds linked to reduced inflammation, cholesterol regulation and appetite control”. Not all cheeses are created equal, gut health-wise. Getty Images “The theory is that cheese acts as a kind of carrier and protector for [good] bacteria,” says Stephanie Moore, a clinical nutritionist, health coach and author of Eat Your Brain Happy. “Certain families of microbes found in cheeses – the Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus families in particular – are likely to be having a positive influence as they pass through the digestive system.” The process of making cheese invariably begins with microbes being added to milk. Depending on the type of cheese the cheesemaker wants to produce, they inoculate the milk with different moulds, yeasts and bacteria. After that, the environment the cheese is stored in for ageing, what it’s wrapped in and anything else that’s been added to the milk will determine the course of the fermentation, encouraging different microbial families to bloom. It’s a complex process, with many variables, which is why there are so many different varieties of cheese.



But which varieties are best for your gut? The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Cheddar cheese is good for your gut. iStock The best cheeses for gut health Cheddar Cheddar is the most consumed cheese in Australia and it’s excellent for gut health.



A mature cheddar will have gone through around six months of maturation through the work of helpful bacteria. “Generally speaking, the longer it is matured, the more intense and complex the flavour,” says Moore. “This tends to directly correlate with the diversity of microbes and other compounds that have developed naturally through the process.” A very mild cheddar may not have as much complexity of flavour or variety of microbes, but that doesn’t make it bad for you. “Even standard supermarket cheddar has to have gone through the milk-to-cheese maturation process,” says Moore. Parmesan “has helpful microbes”. Fudio Parmesan Parmesan has to be matured for a minimum of 12 months, with some being aged for up to two years, making it one of the longest-fermented cheeses. “That doesn’t automatically correlate with more helpful microbes, but it does tend to,” says Moore.



There’s also evidence that hard cheeses’ dense structure and high fat content help protect bacteria from the stomach’s harsh, acidic environment, meaning a lot of the good bacteria can actually reach the gut. A landmark study published in Nature Communications by researchers at the University of Parma found that the microbial communities (such as the gut-friendly Bifidobacterium strains) present in Parmigiano Reggiano could survive digestion and be detected in the human gut. Gut-friendly? You better brie-lieve it. Getty Images Brie and camembert Soft cheeses like brie and camembert are relatively young compared to cheddar and parmesan, as they’re usually aged for up to two months. However, they’re still fermented cheeses, so can contain gut-friendly microbes. The white mould Penicillium candidum, which forms the characteristic rind on brie and camembert, produces a substance called chitin that’s unique to this type of cheese.



“Chitin contains a prebiotic fibre that feeds beneficial gut bacteria,” Moore explains. A small 2022 study found that 4.5g of chitin per day improved gut diversity over three weeks, though it is worth noting that the amount of chitin found in cheese is significantly less than the amount in the study. Highly processed cheese slices have little health benefit. Getty Images The worst Burger cheese slices Moore cites burger cheese slices and cheese strings as the worst examples. “These highly processed products [contain no beneficial microbes],” she says. “There’s hardly any actual dairy in them, apart from maybe a bit of milk powder. With real cheese, once you’ve opened it, it changes over time. It gets mouldier or changes consistency. Whereas these ultra-processed cheeses can sit in your fridge for ages and barely change in appearance.”



Anything in a tube or a triangle “So-called ‘squeezy cheese’ is an ultra-processed food [UPF] containing artificial colourings and additives,” says Moore. UPFs have been found to have a detrimental effect on gut health, with a 2025 study concluding that these foods decrease the amount of good bacteria in the gut, damage the gut lining and contribute to inflammation. Soft cheese triangles like Laughing Cow are also classified as a “processed cheese spread”. Babybel, on the other hand, is not a UPF. “Babybel is fine,” says Moore. “It’s a traditional Edam-style cheese; it’s just very mild, which is why kids like it.” Babybel’s are not a UPF. iStock In the middle



Boursin Boursin is made with pasteurised cow’s milk and cream, but is unaged – it’s more like a fromage frais than a cheese. It’s relatively high in calories and saturated fat but low in protein compared with hard cheeses. “Boursin has gone through the [maturation] process, but not for very long,” says Moore. “It has then had cultures added to it, along with garlic and chopped herbs or basil and chives, which is what provides its flavour. It’s by no means microbiologically complex, but nor is it ultra-processed.” Blue cheese a good source of a compound called spermidine. Blue cheeses



The blue veins in Stilton, Roquefort and Gorgonzola are grown using a mould called Penicillium roqueforti, but that doesn’t make it a probiotic. However, blue cheese can be a good source of a compound called spermidine, which, says Moore, “is having a moment as a longevity molecule. Spermidine performs several actions that support gut health. And cheeses like Roquefort contain far more of it than non-blue cheeses.” Mozzarella and ricotta Ricotta and mozzarella are “young” cheeses. They haven’t been matured, so they won’t have a strong flavour or bacterial complexity. “Ricotta is made from the whey left over after cheesemaking and then heated,” Moore explains, “so nothing very microbial survives. Mozzarella goes through a fermentation process, but it’s then heated to make it stretchable, so not many of the live microbes remain. Mozzarella di Bufala Campana PDO, on the other hand, specifies it has to be fermented using a very specific starter culture, which creates a much richer microbial ecosystem before the curd is stretched.”



Feta Feta contains a particularly high amount of salt, with up to 3g per 100g (in contrast, mature cheddar usually contains less than 2g). A 2024 review of studies found that a diet high in salt can have a negative impact on our gut bacteria. “Feta is kept in brine, which is what makes it salty, though you can wash it before eating to get some of the salt off,” says Moore. Choose ‘cultured’ cottage cheese for better gut health. iStock Cottage cheese



Because cottage cheese is a young cheese, like ricotta or mozzarella, it doesn’t develop the more intense flavour and microbial complexity of mature cheeses. Standard supermarket versions are often heated during production, which can destroy beneficial bacteria. By contrast, “cultured” cottage cheese is inoculated with live bacterial cultures, which contribute to microbial diversity. Look for varieties with wording such as “contains live and active cultures” on the label. “A decent cottage cheese, meaning a cultured one that’s traditionally made, is a good option for gut health,” says Moore. “It’s tasty, microbially rich and a great source of protein.” The Telegraph, London Related Article The healthy, humble cheese that dietitians, shoppers and TikTokers can’t get enough of Related Article A dietitian ranks seven popular supermarket yoghurts (and reveals her top picks)

World.title: Judgment day looms for Star casino as court decides size of fine
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCasinos Judgment day looms for Star casino as court decides size of fine Colin Kruger October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
