The Federal Court is scheduled to hand down its decision this week on how big a penalty Star Entertainment should pay for repeated breaches of anti-money laundering laws that led to the suspension of its casino licences in NSW and Queensland. Star has acknowledged in its most recent annual report the existential threat the fine may pose for its business. “AUSTRAC submitted that a penalty of $400 million would be appropriate while The Star submitted that a penalty of greater than $100 million, payable in the 12 months following the hearing, would be challenging based on available liquidity options, including accessing equity markets. The Star is awaiting the court’s judgment,” it told investors in August. Star Entertainment chief executive Bruce Mathieson jnr has the job of rehabilitating the casino operator so it can regain its licence to operate the business. Monique Westermann Justice Cameron Moore is due to hand down his judgment on Wednesday morning, a day after shareholders gather for the casino operator’s annual meeting in Sydney.



It will be shareholders’ first, and possibly last, chance to meet new chairman Soo Kim, and chief executive Bruce Mathieson Jnr, who led the $300 million rescue package that saved Star from financial collapse last year. If the fine is too hefty, the company could end up in administration. The rescue handed control of the casino business to Kim’s US casino operator Bally’s and the Mathieson family pub empire also emerged with a significant stake after contributing $100 million to the deal. Star’s troubles started in 2021, when an investigation by The Age, The Sydney Morning Herald and 60 Minutes alleged Star had enabled suspected money laundering, organised crime, large-scale fraud and foreign interference in its Australian casinos for years, even though its board had been warned its anti-money-laundering controls were failing. Further inquiries led to the loss of its casino licences, a legal battle with the corporate regulator, as well as legal action by financial crime regulator AUSTRAC over the money-laundering breaches. Gambling revenue has fallen, and the casino group’s regulatory costs have mounted following the run of scandals.



Star got into more hot water this year following an investigation by this publication and the Australian Financial Review that raised questions about Star’s commitment to reforms to help it regain its casino licence, as its top executives try to make the casino operator financially viable under new regulatory restraints in NSW and Queensland. A leaked recording of Star Entertainment Group’s most senior executives has captured its Sydney casino boss and Mathieson Jnr complaining of the risk and compliance measures forced on to the group. Star Entertainment chairman Soo Kim. Dominic Lorrimer “We get these fines, which I think are just disproportionate to what is happening, and … all we’re doing is existing to pay a fine,” Mathieson Jnr said. “We keep on restricting ourselves tighter and tighter. We’re coming to a pretty critical time with obviously licences and all that sort of stuff, but it should be quite obvious to everyone that unless we can breathe … every time we get up to breathe, we cop another hit.”



Mathieson Jnr was conciliatory to the regulators in his letter to fellow shareholders via the annual report in August. Related Article Casinos Star’s Sydney casino licence to stay suspended “I would like to acknowledge and thank our regulators and other key stakeholders for their ongoing engagement, guidance and collaboration throughout this period of significant transformation. Their commitment and constructive involvement have been important in supporting our ongoing remediation and progress towards returning The Star to suitability.” He later told staff the new management team is “working to change” the problems inherited from previous management. Last month NSW Independent Casino Commission chief Philip Crawford extended the suspension of Star’s licence, saying questions remained over the casino’s progress in improving its governance, leadership and culture.



“There is no doubt that The Star has come a long way in addressing the matters which led to the suspension of its casino licence in 2022,” Crawford said. “However, recent allegations regarding governance, leadership and culture at the casino are serious and are being treated as such by both the manager and the NICC. It is disappointing that despite the progress made by the Sydney casino, the Group company continues to experience problems that affect each of its properties.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: ‘I’m the boss, not an employee’: The Sydney strip club owner fighting his ban from Kings Cross
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Papadopoulos had provided the tribunal with supporting statements and affidavits from his wife, Liana Papadopoulos, his mother Cleopatra Papadopoulos and his son, Dimitrios Papadopoulos, as well as a letter from his accountant, Michael Angelopoulos.

The order prevents him from entering “any high-risk venue in the Kings Cross and Sydney CBD entertainment precincts”.

Last week, the NSW Civil and Administrative Appeals Tribunal knocked back an application from the Cyprus-born 53-year-old to review a decision of the Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority to slap him with a Long-Term Banning Order.

It took two alleged violent assaults on women working at his club, one of which involved alleged choking, another where he allegedly slapped his penis in the face of one of the women, as well as a separate alleged assault on a man who visited the club, before Papadopoulos was finally prohibited by authorities.

But Papadopoulos’ colourful legal history proved no impediment to his subsequently owning and operating two clubs, Sydney Elements and Showgirls, on the same Kings Cross stretch notorious for its history of sleaze, crime and brutality.

In 2005, his sentence served, he was the subject of bankruptcy proceedings.

On March 15, Papadopoulos was arrested and charged with seven offences which allegedly had taken place in and around the club, including the serious indictable charge of “intentionally choke a person without consent” involving a female employee of the club whom the married man appears to have been involved with .

It was Sydney Elements, which bills itself as “Sydney’s Premier Stripclub and Nightclub”, and where “VIP packages” start at $1000, where all the trouble started.

As Papadopoulos told the tribunal, through his barrister Greg James KC, a former judge, the ban prejudices his business interests and represents a restriction of his “fundamental rights”.

Such a ban presents a problem for a man who owns two Kings Cross strip clubs. His wife told this masthead he is a good man, husband and father who is innocent.

But none of it made a difference. Dr Tahlia Gordon, the Senior Tribunal member who heard the case, said she was satisfied “that if Mr Papadopoulos attended Sydney Elements or Showgirls, there is a sufficient risk that he could engage in trouble-making behaviour and cause a problem”.

It also raises questions about the safety of strip club workers in a red-light district that has been somewhat cleaned up over the past decade.

The tribunal’s decision, handed down last week, contains extraordinary detail about the apparent operation of the club and the alleged violence at least two of its employees had been subjected to.

In filing his application to reverse the ban, Papadopoulos said “the order has an immediate and substantial impact on my livelihood”.

Still, the accused nightclub owner told police they should drop the ban application. He was entitled to the presumption of innocence. He was “of good character with no prior convictions for matters of violence”, and his bail conditions did not prohibit him from going to Sydney Elements.

It is understood Papadopoulos will defend all the charges against him.

Things got even worse for Papadopoulos on March 28, when he was charged with “assault occasioning actual bodily harm” in relation to an incident at Sydney Elements on March 10.

Six days later, NSW Police informed Papadopoulos they would be applying to the Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority for the ban order on him.

Papadopoulos then allegedly grabbed Victim 1 under her armpits and pulled her away from the bar.

Cut to 2am on January 9 this year, when Papadopoulos and Victim 1 were behind the main bar at Sydney Elements. They argued, and he allegedly placed his left hand on her head, grabbed a handful of her hair, and yanked her from the chair, snapping her head back with the force of the pull.

Embarrassed, Victim 1 wanted to leave the apartment, but Papadopoulos told her if she left, he would kill her.

According to police, “Victim 1 was confused as she did not remember what had happened, and the accused stated, ‘It was probably because I put my penis in your face’.”

A short time later, police say, Victim 1 was with Papadopoulos at his nearby Potts Point residence, when he told her that “multiple staff members had been traumatised by what happened earlier at Sydney Elements”.

It was 3am and Victim 1 was “highly intoxicated and lying on the ground” when, according to police, the accused kneeled next to her, pulled his penis from his pants and “used his penis to slap the side of Victim 1’s face”.

According to police facts, on September 29, 2025, the accused and “Victim 1”, a female employee of the club, were in a private room at Sydney Elements with about 10 other staff members.

He stopped, only to go through her phone to find evidence of her cheating on him. She later took a photograph of her bruised neck.

At about 2am on March 9, Victim 1 was again at the accused’s Potts Point home, lying next to him in bed, when he straddled her and placed his hands around her neck, restricting her breathing.

Yet more alleged violence was to come.

Victim 1 tried to leave, but he grabbed her and pinned her arms behind her back, while pushing her into an office. When Victim 2 tried to intervene, Papadopoulos placed his hand around her throat and moved her away. This alleged assault was also captured on CCTV.

A short time later, another assault is alleged to have occurred when Papadopoulos dragged Victim 1 and another employee, Victim 2, to the basement of the club.

The whole thing was captured on CCTV but the accused later told police the footage was “AI-generated and a conspiracy”.

Things came to a head on March 11, at about 9.30 pm, when Victim 1 and Papadopoulos began arguing while together at Sydney Elements.

She told him she was going to quit on the spot, which allegedly made Papadopoulos angry, and he allegedly pushed her face with force, then grabbed her by the neck and pinned her against a wall, holding her there for about a minute.

He took her phone and locked it in a safe, police allege.

Later that night, he was charged with three offences including common assault, and stalk or intimidate with intent to cause fear of physical or mental harm (domestic violence). Then on March 15, he was charged with another seven offences including the “intentionally choke a person without consent” rap.

A fortnight later, Papadopoulos copped yet another charge, for the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

This charge related to an incident that occurred about 3pm on March 10, when Papadopoulos allegedly beat up a man unknown to him, dubbed Victim 3, who came into Sydney Elements.

According to police, Papadopoulos grabbed the man, whose “body language appeared passive”, shoved him into a wall, dragged and threw him onto the ground, punched and stomped on his torso, and then “kicked Victim 3 directly in the face with such force, causing Victim 3 to fall back on the ground, immediately unconscious and motionless”.

The man suffered concussion, bleeding from a large cut to his lip, bruising to his neck and soreness over his body.

Some of the charges will be heard in November. The remainder will be heard in March next year. Papadopoulos is expected to plead not guilty.

When contacted this week, Papadopoulos’ wife Liana Papadopoulos said: “I know he is innocent and he is fighting for his rights.

“I am not saying that because he’s my partner, I’m saying the truth.

“He is a very good man, good husband and good father.”

Papadopoulos did not respond to attempts to contact him.

These charges are not the 53-year-old’s first tango with the law. In 1998, Papadopoulos passed $1500 to a local cop, when he was operating a different nightclub on the Kings Cross strip.

Back then, Papadopoulos was a 25-year-old with “strong family ties and real prospects of rehabilitation”, or so said his lawyer in a submission to the NSW Court of Appeal in 2000.

Papadopoulos wanted his jail time cut; after all, his sentencing judge had said he “apparently ran a place of entertainment which was otherwise within the law”. His appeal was denied.

Once his time was served, Papadopoulos’ name popped up in the Federal Court list in 2005, as the respondent in bankruptcy proceedings brought by lawyer Victor Berger, who was struck off in 2018 for overcharging an elderly woman by $137,543.

The bankruptcy application against him was granted in September that year.

‘I’m the boss, not an employee’

The goals of the Liquor Act are to regulate the sale of liquor “in a way that is consistent with the expectations, needs and aspirations of the community”, and to “facilitate the balanced development, in the public interest, of the liquor industry”.

The legislation is supposed to minimise harm associated with the misuse and abuse of liquor and ensure that the sale, supply and consumption of liquor contributes to the amenity of community life, as opposed to detracting from it.

Under the act, a Long-Term Banning Order can be imposed if a person has been charged with, or found guilty of a serious, violent indictable offence, and is also the licensee or manager of the premises, or is either working on the premises as an employee, or in a volunteer capacity.

Papadopoulos did not dispute he had been charged with serious indictable offences, namely, two counts of intentionally choke a person without consent, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and stalk or intimidate intending to cause fear of physical or mental harm.

But through his barrister Greg James KC, Papadopoulos submitted that it would be “unjust” to impose an LTBO on someone who may ultimately be found not guilty, and that if the tribunal could not be satisfied the evidence supported the charges, it should not uphold the ban.

But the most creative argument put by Papadopoulos’ barrister was that the ban should not apply because his client was not employed by Sydney Elements.

He was the boss.

James told the tribunal that “at the time of the alleged serious indictable offence, Mr Papadopoulos was at Sydney Elements as the sole director, secretary and shareholder of MLP Investments (NSW) Pty Ltd and Element MP Pty Ltd, the owner of the premises”.

Papadopoulos’s company interests have owned the Potts Point venue since 2013, when it last traded for $4.55 million.

The tribunal heard he has since invested $17 million in Sydney Elements.

It has clearly been a lucrative business. Papadopoulos also owns a Sutherland Shire property with a swimming pool that fronts a private-title beach. A Sylvania property is also registered to his name, and Papadopoulos’ second company, MGM Ventures, owns an inner-west property that is the registered home of his mother.

But the “mere fact” that he was owner and director of Sydney Elements didn’t mean Papadopoulos was an employee, working there or performing services of any kind.

His barrister argued that his client had “overall responsibility for the day-to-day operations of Sydney Elements”, which included tasks like managing staff and overseeing staff rosters.

He works full-time and “needs to be on call to deal with issues at the venues, as and when they arise”.

Furthermore, he did not have a responsible service of alcohol certificate, and as such, was not qualified to serve alcohol. He doesn’t receive a wage.

The iconic Coke sign in Kings Cross. Flavio Brancaleone

Papadopoulos’ “fundamental rights”

The respondents, the NSW Police and the Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority, counter-argued that Papadopoulos was, for the purposes of the act, a volunteer.

Further, they told the tribunal “that it would be an unusual lacuna in the Liquor Act if someone in the position of Mr Papadopoulos, who on his own evidence asserts day-to-day control over a high-risk venue, was found to be outside of reach of [the act] because he was not the licensee or manager, was not a volunteer, or did not have a written contract of employment”.

The tribunal rejected Papadopoulos’ narrative. Dr Gordon found that “Mr Papadopoulos plays an essential role in managing two high-risk venues in the Kings Cross precinct”.

If he was not technically a worker at the venue, then he was a volunteer.

Papadopoulos argued that his absence from Sydney Elements “has caused significant prejudice” to the operation of the business, and was “untenable because of the issues arising at the premises”, such as “staff conflicts and stock controls”.

The ban would also harm his plans to develop the venue into a five-storey hotel.

Most importantly, the ban restricted his “fundamental rights”.

He was so desperate to have it lifted that he even proposed a compromise: that he could be at Sydney Elements only between 11am and 11pm.

The tribunal rejected it all, and upheld the ban. Dr Gordon said that it “sends a clear message” to “troublemakers”.

A former manager of the now defunct but once popular nightspot Sapphire Lounge, who did not want to be named, said Papadopoulos was “the worst fucking operator in the Cross”.

The former club manager said the LTBO would be pretty useless, seeing as Papadopoulos’ other club, Showgirls, is across the road.

“So he can just stand there, and walk past and do what he wants.”

There is some consolation for Papadopoulos: the ban applies for only 12 months.

And the clock started ticking down on July 8 this year, when it was issued.

As of July 7 next year, depending on the outcome of his criminal proceedings, Papadopoulos will be at liberty to go wherever he likes on the King Cross strip, including into his own clubs.

Exclusive BusinessCompaniesRetail ASIC won’t sue Super Retail board over scandal that led to CEO’s sacking, says company Colin Kruger October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Rebel Sport owner Super Retail Group says the corporate regulator does not plan to take any further action over the alleged illicit executive relationship that will see its former chief executive, Anthony Heraghty, face court this week. But the group behind well-known brands also including Supercheap Auto, MacPac and BCF, says it will face further legal bills funding his defence against the legal action by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. Former Super Retail group CEO Anthony Heraghty. Dominic Lorrimer “Following the conclusion of its investigation, ASIC has confirmed that it is not taking enforcement action against Super Retail Group, its related entities, or any current or former director, officer, employee, agent or representative of Super Retail Group, other than Mr Heraghty,” a spokesman said. ASIC declined to comment.



Super Retail sacked Heraghty in September last year and stripped him of multimillion-dollar bonuses after he admitted providing misleading information to fellow board members about his alleged relationship with HR boss Jane Kelly. Jane Kelly. “In light of this new information, the board has concluded Mr Heraghty’s prior disclosures were not satisfactory,” the company told the ASX in the statement announcing his sacking last year. ASIC instigated an investigation into Super Retail after Heraghty’s sacking and sued him last month for allegedly breaching his directors’ duties and providing misleading information to the board and financial market about his alleged relationship with Kelly. Super Retail had already spent more than $40 million in a bitter legal battle with its two former top lawyers, who claimed they were bullied and harassed over a matter centred on Heraghty’s alleged relationship.



The confirmation is timely for Super Retail’s current board, which faces shareholders on Thursday morning. ASIC’s case against Heraghty goes before the Federal Court as the meeting commences. The case is expected to raise fresh questions at the AGM about Heraghty, the board’s response, and just how much it will have to pay to defend the former CEO in this legal battle with ASIC. The retailer will have to fund his legal defence on the basis that he was a director of the group at the time the alleged conduct is said to have occurred. “As you would expect of a listed entity, Mr Heraghty is the beneficiary of a deed of indemnity, insurance and access,” the Super Retail spokesman said. ASIC chair Sarah Court says the case is not about personal relationships but “whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders”. AAP The potential issue for Heraghty is that this indemnity drops if he is found in contravention of the law, and Super Retail can force him to repay these legal expenses.



“Under this deed, Mr Heraghty will be required to repay any costs within 90 days if it is found and determined that he was not entitled to be indemnified,” the spokesman said. In its legal action, ASIC alleges Heraghty – who was recently hired by appliance group Winnings for an expected billion-dollar float on the ASX – failed to disclose and manage conflicts of interest arising from the alleged undisclosed relationship. Related Article Retail Corporate cop makes explosive claims about former Super Retail boss’ ‘intimate’ relationship ASIC alleges Heraghty continued to supervise Kelly and took part in decisions affecting her employment, remuneration, incentives, rewards and redundancy package. He also allegedly participated in board and committee discussions of complaints and anticipated legal proceedings concerning the alleged relationship.



“This case is not about private relationships, but whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders,” ASIC chair Sarah Court said. Heraghty faces a potential ban from managing companies if found in contravention of the law, and fines for breaches of the Corporations Act that can attract a penalty of up to $1.56 million per breach. Heraghty was approached for comment via his new employer, Winnings. He will have the opportunity to file a defence to ASIC’s allegations in due course. World.title: How mother-daughter dates became the red carpet trend of the year
World.content:
Exclusive LifestyleFashionSpring racing carnival How mother-daughter dates became the red carpet trend of the year Gyan Yankovich October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The morning of a special event, there are several things you should never leave home without: a fully charged phone, a hydrating lip balm and – as per the celebrity trend of the year – your daughter. At this year’s Met Gala, Nicole Kidman, dressed in custom Chanel by Matthieu Blazy, walked the carpet with daughter Sunday Rose, in Dior. “My daughter is blooming, and what she wore shows that,” Kidman told Vogue. In October, at Paris Fashion Week, Kidman swapped daughters and took Faith Urban as her date to the Chanel show, proving that the best date isn’t your long-term partner, a fling or someone you’ve just met on an app. Sunday Rose and Nicole Kidman attend the 2026 Met Gala (right); Faith Urban and Nicole Kidman attend Paris Fashion Week. Getty Images Why daughters make the best dates



It’s a trend already promising to be replicated at this year’s Melbourne Cup Carnival, with Lexus welcoming internationally acclaimed costume and production designer Catherine Martin Luhrmann AC and daughter Lilly Luhrmann to Crown Oaks Day on November 5. Catherine, the four-time Academy Award winner and wife of Baz Luhrmann, best known for her work on The Great Gatsby, Elvis and Moulin Rouge!, said attending the event with Lilly will add a deeply personal element to the occasion. Four-time Academy Award-winning designer Catherine Martin Luhrmann AC and her daughter Lilly Luhrmann will join Lexus at the 2026 Melbourne Cup Carnival, reflecting the brand’s celebration of masters of their craft and the next generation of creative talent. Yvonne Tnt/BFA.com/Shutterstock But Kidman and Martin aren’t the only celebrities reminding us why a daughter – especially a well-dressed one – is the perfect accessory. Kate Moss attended the Burberry show at London Fashion Week with daughter Lila Moss. And at last year’s Golden Globes, Angelina Jolie walked the carpet with her daughter Zahara, both dressed in Alexander McQueen.



The art of mother-daughter dressing The big difference between dressing for a red carpet and dressing for a raceday? Millinery. Related Article Caulfield Cup A lesson in elegance: The Caulfield Cup fashion winners When it comes to mother-daughter dressing, the best styling trick, according to Natalie Bikicki, award-winning milliner and founder of Natalie Bikicki Designs, is to find one connecting element, whether it’s a colour, texture or detail. “For example, a daughter’s floral dress might feature a shade that her mother picks up in her millinery,” says Bikicki. “That creates a lovely connection without needing to match everything. Neither woman should feel she has to dress older or younger to make the pairing work.”



Bikicki suggests women try on outfits together before the event – especially if they’re hoping for a nice photo – to check balance and ensure nobody’s face will be obscured by the other’s hat. Leo Lin, founder and creative director at Leo Lin, says he loves seeing women interpret the Crown Oaks Day dress code – soft pastels and florals – together. “One might choose a new silhouette in the same floral print; another might pair a floral with a soft pink drawn from the print.” “Vary the shape or scale, so each look feels personal but connected,” he says. Angelina Jolie attends the 2025 Golden Globes with daughter Zahara (right); Kate Moss and Lila Moss attend London Fashion Week. Getty The next generation



The theme for this year’s LANDMARK by Lexus – the brand’s pavilion inside Flemington’s exclusive Birdcage enclosure – is A New Dawn, exploring what happens when “experience meets fresh thinking, and when enduring traditions are carried forward in new ways”. It’s a concept that resonates deeply with Catherine, who sees Lilly as an example of the next generation of creative talent. “I’ve always believed that great design comes from a combination of technical mastery, collaboration and a willingness to explore new ideas,” she said. “Being able to share that appreciation for creativity with Lilly makes attending Crown Oaks Day together with Lexus particularly special.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: I’m no funnier, but improv comedy somehow made me a better traveller
World.content:
Reviews & adviceTravel tips Opinion I’m no funnier, but improv comedy somehow made me a better traveller Paul Marshall Travel writer October 26, 2026 — 5:00am

October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

My wife thinks I’m funny, which is about as close to a joke as I get these days. Unless, of course, you consider my bank account, which is hilarious to everyone but me. This is all to say that while my years of improv comedy did nothing to sharpen my sense of humour, they did wonders for me as an open-minded traveller, and it all comes down to this golden rule. Yes, and … The cornerstone of any good performance, ‘yes, and …’ is about more than accepting the offer, as it’s known in the parlance. It’s about creating a scene where there are no closed doors and no dead ends. Although it’s been a long time since I’ve done any actual improv comedy, you’d be amazed at how much this rule has echoed through my travels, where invitations are accepted and going off script is all part of my poorly laid plans.



When your flight plan falls apart in Myanmar, the road trip of a lifetime begins. iStock 



Related Article Opinion

Travel tips My husband wore budgie smugglers in the US. The locals were shocked Kate Allman Writer and broadcaster This definitely wasn’t in our script but I’ll be damned if it didn’t heighten the scene, and make our trip look so much better on the stage. This is what makes the “and …” so important. It’s how you pursue the unexpected and transform the mundane into the magical. It’s easy to think of the 15th hour into what was supposed to be an eight-hour bus ride as torture. It’s a lot harder to treat that torture as an opportunity to befriend fellow passengers, accepting that even the best-laid plans are no match for a bus timetable in Laos. I’m not saying that you should start watching reruns of Whose Line Is It Anyway? to make yourself a better traveller, although there are worse ways to spend an afternoon. I’m saying that when you accept your role as a player in this performance we call travel, then you become more than just a passenger on a trip. And while no good travel story ends with “and everything went according to plan”, I can think of quite a few that started with “yes, and…”

Travel newsTravel tips These luxe last-minute trips go all out for Christmas Julietta Jameson October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. If the prospect of peeling potatoes – or prawns – has lost its appeal, it’s not too late to make other plans for Christmas. Travelling offers a chance to swap the usual festive arrangements for something less demanding. And leaving the country needn’t mean leaving Christmas behind. You can still embrace old traditions, invent new ones or simply let somebody else take care of the hosting. European river cruises stop at towns that take traditional Christmas very seriously. iStock If you’ve always dreamt of a white Christmas, the traditional northern hemisphere festivities await on APT’s Magnificent Europe cruises, which travel between Amsterdam and Budapest along the Rhine, Main and Danube, passing through historic cities and towns that don’t do Christmas-lite. If it’s decorations, markets and centuries-old rituals you’re after, this is a rather luxurious portal to the mother lode. Tootle along the river in sublime comfort aboard APT’s luxury river ships, admiring the twinkling lights, then immerse yourself in places that epitomise the yuletide spirit.



Some departures encompass Christmas Day itself. On the Christmas and New Year’s Eve sailing, Christmas Eve is spent in Bamberg, Christmas Day in Nuremberg and Boxing Day in Regensburg, with festive dining and celebrations aboard. 



Outrigger Fiji Beach Resort on Viti Levu’s Coral Coast always combines local traditions with family fun, but Christmas is an especially big occasion. Christmas Eve brings carols by candlelight with a village choir, while Christmas Day begins with a church service before Santa makes his grand entrance on the beach. A giant gingerbread house is cracked open on the beachfront lawn, and families gather for a festive buffet or sunset dinner. Complimentary children’s clubs, activities for teenagers and a nanny service for younger guests mean parents might even find some time to themselves. At Phuket’s Sri Panwa the festivities include a six-course celebration dinner at Baba Poolclub on December 24 and 25. If you’d rather Christmas itself were a more low-key affair, Sri Panwa in Phuket offers a more relaxed approach, with panoramic Andaman Sea views and a six-course celebration dinner at Baba Poolclub on December 24 and 25.



Related Article Opinion

Travel tips Ten overseas Christmas traditions Australia should adopt Ben Groundwater Travel writer Here, there’s no need to organise your day around a packed calendar of festive activities. Spend the day enjoying the resort’s pools, restaurants and spectacular oceanfront setting, then dress up for dinner. The serious partying can wait until New Year’s Eve, when silver-themed celebrations spread across the resort’s venues, with sunset drinks, a gala dinner, live entertainment and a countdown to the new year. Wherever you choose to celebrate, at least someone else is doing the dishes – and the peeling. See aptouring.com; jaresortshotels.com; outrigger.com; sripanwa.com

World.title: Three Blue Ducks up for first major award at tonight’s Good Food Guide awards
World.content:
Eating outGood Food Guide Three Blue Ducks up for first major award at tonight’s Good Food Guide awards Plus, will a new three-hatter be announced? Follow the action and announcements, including Best Chef and Restaurant of the Year via the live blog from 3pm. Sarah Norris October 26, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. When the 500-strong crowd of leading industry figures meets for the 42nd Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide awards at Carriageworks tonight, it will be the first time Three Blue Ducks has been up for a major award. In fact, the group’s $210 per person farm-to-table Three Blue Ducks Burradoo in the Southern Highlands has been nominated for two awards: Regional Restaurant of the Year and Best New Restaurant of the Year. The ambitious farmhouse restaurant, located just outside Bowral, opened at Easter within billionaire Annie Cannon-Brookes-backed Burradoo Park, with the former co-head chef of Sydney’s three-hatted Quay, Troy Crisante, at the helm. Three Blue Ducks Burradoo chefs (from left) Rhys Connell, Darren Robertson, Andy Allen and Troy Crisante. Kitti Gould Callan Boys, co-editor of the Herald Good Food Guide, reviewed it in September, giving it a score of 16.5 and two hats, making it the highest scoring restaurant of the year at that time.



“With the chef talent involved, I knew it would be good,” says Boys, “but I wasn’t expecting such a cohesive tasting menu of finely tuned dishes. It’s a long way from avocado toast and slow-cooked lamb shoulder.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up While Three Blue Ducks has been important in the evolution of NSW’s dining scene – it helped redefine breakfast cafe food in Sydney and made paddock-to-plate dining a more accessible, everyday concept – it’s never been up for a major Good Food Guide award. The Three Blue Ducks story began in 2010 at the now-closed Bronte cafe, and has grown across the state, including an elaborate farm venture in Byron Bay and now the restaurant in Bowral. Part of its success was applying cheffing techniques to casual and cafe food – a concept that is much more common these days – led by two former fine-dining Tetsuya’s chefs, Mark LaBrooy (who is no longer involved) and Darren Robertson. The Three Blue Ducks at Burradoo is in a restored 1823 heritage farmhouse. Jennifer Soo



Along with Regional Restaurant of the Year and New Restaurant of the Year, presented by Aurum Poultry Co., tonight’s ceremony will also feature the announcement of 15 other awards, including T2 Tea Restaurant of the Year, Oceania Cruises Chef of the Year, T2 Tea Cafe of the Year and Oceania Cruises Service Excellence. The coveted Good Food Guide hats will also be announced. “Since Quay and Oncore closed this is the first time since the 1980s that the Guide has started the reviewing season with only two three-hatted restaurants,” says David Matthews, co-editor of the Guide. “Tonight we get to see whether any other contenders have made the leap.” The Good Food hat rating system – from one to the pinnacle of three – was created by the Good Food Guide more than 40 years ago to give readers a sense of what to expect in terms of food, service, experience and value for money. It’s been the cornerstone of Good Food’s rating system since. The main goal of this system, and the reviews in general, isn’t to tell readers whether reviewers like a restaurant. It’s to paint a picture of the experience, so readers can decide whether they might like it, and to explain how it sits within Australia’s dining landscape. Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide editors Callan Boys and David Matthews. Sitthixay Ditthavong



This year’s Guide, presented by Oceania Cruises and T2 Tea, features more than 500 independent reviews of restaurants, bars, pubs, clubs and cafes in regional NSW, Canberra and Sydney across various price points, cuisines, styles and suburbs, making it the largest Guide published to date. A new signature list will be launched this year: the 100 Essential Restaurants. These are the places that define dining out in NSW and the ACT right now. Diversity of cuisine, menu, geography and price point were considered when curating the list, which includes some hatted venues. The 100 Essential Restaurants list responds to the changing needs of Australian diners – recommending everything from fine-dining restaurants to food-court favourites – and also reflects how our food scene is evolving. The free 56-page Good Food Guide magazine liftout. Dion Georgopoulos This collection will be published in a free 56-page liftout in tomorrow’s Herald, and the list will be available in the Good Food app and on the web.



Since launching in 2024, the app is considered the home of the Good Food Guide and is where readers can search the full A-Z list of reviews using map and filtering functionality. The app has more than 3000 reviews and recommendations. All reviews go live on the app tonight after the conclusion of the ceremony, at about 8pm. The event will also be live blogged from 3pm, so you can follow the action. The winners of the 42nd Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide Awards will be announced on Monday, October 26, presented by Oceania Cruises and T2 Tea. The awards ceremony will be live-blogged via the Herald from 3pm; the Guide reviews will be available on the Good Food app from 8pm. Pick up a free 56-page Good Food Guide liftout in the Herald on Tuesday, October 27. The Good Food app is free for premium subscribers of the Sydney Morning Herald and also available as a standalone subscription. You can download the Good Food app here.

World.title: The best (and worst) cheeses for your gut health
World.content:
Tips & adviceGut health The best (and worst) cheeses for your gut health From cheddar to camembert, some of our favourite varieties of cheese harbour a surprising secret to better digestion. Damon Syson October 26, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We are a nation of cheese lovers, but it may come as a surprise to discover that this household staple is also a secret superfood. A recent study has revealed that the microbes in different cheeses could also offer a surprising boost for gut health. Scientists from the University of Reading tracked the microbial and biochemical changes that took place as three cheeses matured. Their findings suggest that some of the bacteria responsible for developing each cheese’s unique flavour profile may also be beneficial, “potentially producing compounds linked to reduced inflammation, cholesterol regulation and appetite control”. Not all cheeses are created equal, gut health-wise. Getty Images “The theory is that cheese acts as a kind of carrier and protector for [good] bacteria,” says Stephanie Moore, a clinical nutritionist, health coach and author of Eat Your Brain Happy. “Certain families of microbes found in cheeses – the Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus families in particular – are likely to be having a positive influence as they pass through the digestive system.” The process of making cheese invariably begins with microbes being added to milk. Depending on the type of cheese the cheesemaker wants to produce, they inoculate the milk with different moulds, yeasts and bacteria. After that, the environment the cheese is stored in for ageing, what it’s wrapped in and anything else that’s been added to the milk will determine the course of the fermentation, encouraging different microbial families to bloom. It’s a complex process, with many variables, which is why there are so many different varieties of cheese.



But which varieties are best for your gut? The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Cheddar cheese is good for your gut. iStock The best cheeses for gut health Cheddar Cheddar is the most consumed cheese in Australia and it’s excellent for gut health.



A mature cheddar will have gone through around six months of maturation through the work of helpful bacteria. “Generally speaking, the longer it is matured, the more intense and complex the flavour,” says Moore. “This tends to directly correlate with the diversity of microbes and other compounds that have developed naturally through the process.” A very mild cheddar may not have as much complexity of flavour or variety of microbes, but that doesn’t make it bad for you. “Even standard supermarket cheddar has to have gone through the milk-to-cheese maturation process,” says Moore. Parmesan “has helpful microbes”. Fudio Parmesan Parmesan has to be matured for a minimum of 12 months, with some being aged for up to two years, making it one of the longest-fermented cheeses. “That doesn’t automatically correlate with more helpful microbes, but it does tend to,” says Moore.



There’s also evidence that hard cheeses’ dense structure and high fat content help protect bacteria from the stomach’s harsh, acidic environment, meaning a lot of the good bacteria can actually reach the gut. A landmark study published in Nature Communications by researchers at the University of Parma found that the microbial communities (such as the gut-friendly Bifidobacterium strains) present in Parmigiano Reggiano could survive digestion and be detected in the human gut. Gut-friendly? You better brie-lieve it. Getty Images Brie and camembert Soft cheeses like brie and camembert are relatively young compared to cheddar and parmesan, as they’re usually aged for up to two months. However, they’re still fermented cheeses, so can contain gut-friendly microbes. The white mould Penicillium candidum, which forms the characteristic rind on brie and camembert, produces a substance called chitin that’s unique to this type of cheese.



“Chitin contains a prebiotic fibre that feeds beneficial gut bacteria,” Moore explains. A small 2022 study found that 4.5g of chitin per day improved gut diversity over three weeks, though it is worth noting that the amount of chitin found in cheese is significantly less than the amount in the study. Highly processed cheese slices have little health benefit. Getty Images The worst Burger cheese slices Moore cites burger cheese slices and cheese strings as the worst examples. “These highly processed products [contain no beneficial microbes],” she says. “There’s hardly any actual dairy in them, apart from maybe a bit of milk powder. With real cheese, once you’ve opened it, it changes over time. It gets mouldier or changes consistency. Whereas these ultra-processed cheeses can sit in your fridge for ages and barely change in appearance.”



Anything in a tube or a triangle “So-called ‘squeezy cheese’ is an ultra-processed food [UPF] containing artificial colourings and additives,” says Moore. UPFs have been found to have a detrimental effect on gut health, with a 2025 study concluding that these foods decrease the amount of good bacteria in the gut, damage the gut lining and contribute to inflammation. Soft cheese triangles like Laughing Cow are also classified as a “processed cheese spread”. Babybel, on the other hand, is not a UPF. “Babybel is fine,” says Moore. “It’s a traditional Edam-style cheese; it’s just very mild, which is why kids like it.” Babybel’s are not a UPF. iStock In the middle



Boursin Boursin is made with pasteurised cow’s milk and cream, but is unaged – it’s more like a fromage frais than a cheese. It’s relatively high in calories and saturated fat but low in protein compared with hard cheeses. “Boursin has gone through the [maturation] process, but not for very long,” says Moore. “It has then had cultures added to it, along with garlic and chopped herbs or basil and chives, which is what provides its flavour. It’s by no means microbiologically complex, but nor is it ultra-processed.” Blue cheese a good source of a compound called spermidine. Blue cheeses



The blue veins in Stilton, Roquefort and Gorgonzola are grown using a mould called Penicillium roqueforti, but that doesn’t make it a probiotic. However, blue cheese can be a good source of a compound called spermidine, which, says Moore, “is having a moment as a longevity molecule. Spermidine performs several actions that support gut health. And cheeses like Roquefort contain far more of it than non-blue cheeses.” Mozzarella and ricotta Ricotta and mozzarella are “young” cheeses. They haven’t been matured, so they won’t have a strong flavour or bacterial complexity. “Ricotta is made from the whey left over after cheesemaking and then heated,” Moore explains, “so nothing very microbial survives. Mozzarella goes through a fermentation process, but it’s then heated to make it stretchable, so not many of the live microbes remain. Mozzarella di Bufala Campana PDO, on the other hand, specifies it has to be fermented using a very specific starter culture, which creates a much richer microbial ecosystem before the curd is stretched.”



Feta Feta contains a particularly high amount of salt, with up to 3g per 100g (in contrast, mature cheddar usually contains less than 2g). A 2024 review of studies found that a diet high in salt can have a negative impact on our gut bacteria. “Feta is kept in brine, which is what makes it salty, though you can wash it before eating to get some of the salt off,” says Moore. Choose ‘cultured’ cottage cheese for better gut health. iStock Cottage cheese



Because cottage cheese is a young cheese, like ricotta or mozzarella, it doesn’t develop the more intense flavour and microbial complexity of mature cheeses. Standard supermarket versions are often heated during production, which can destroy beneficial bacteria. By contrast, “cultured” cottage cheese is inoculated with live bacterial cultures, which contribute to microbial diversity. Look for varieties with wording such as “contains live and active cultures” on the label. “A decent cottage cheese, meaning a cultured one that’s traditionally made, is a good option for gut health,” says Moore. “It’s tasty, microbially rich and a great source of protein.” The Telegraph, London Related Article The healthy, humble cheese that dietitians, shoppers and TikTokers can’t get enough of Related Article A dietitian ranks seven popular supermarket yoghurts (and reveals her top picks)

BusinessCompaniesCasinos Judgment day looms for Star casino as court decides size of fine Colin Kruger October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Federal Court is scheduled to hand down its decision this week on how big a penalty Star Entertainment should pay for repeated breaches of anti-money laundering laws that led to the suspension of its casino licences in NSW and Queensland. Star has acknowledged in its most recent annual report the existential threat the fine may pose for its business. “AUSTRAC submitted that a penalty of $400 million would be appropriate while The Star submitted that a penalty of greater than $100 million, payable in the 12 months following the hearing, would be challenging based on available liquidity options, including accessing equity markets. The Star is awaiting the court’s judgment,” it told investors in August. Star Entertainment chief executive Bruce Mathieson jnr has the job of rehabilitating the casino operator so it can regain its licence to operate the business. Monique Westermann Justice Cameron Moore is due to hand down his judgment on Wednesday morning, a day after shareholders gather for the casino operator’s annual meeting in Sydney.



It will be shareholders’ first, and possibly last, chance to meet new chairman Soo Kim, and chief executive Bruce Mathieson Jnr, who led the $300 million rescue package that saved Star from financial collapse last year. If the fine is too hefty, the company could end up in administration. The rescue handed control of the casino business to Kim’s US casino operator Bally’s and the Mathieson family pub empire also emerged with a significant stake after contributing $100 million to the deal. Star’s troubles started in 2021, when an investigation by The Age, The Sydney Morning Herald and 60 Minutes alleged Star had enabled suspected money laundering, organised crime, large-scale fraud and foreign interference in its Australian casinos for years, even though its board had been warned its anti-money-laundering controls were failing. Further inquiries led to the loss of its casino licences, a legal battle with the corporate regulator, as well as legal action by financial crime regulator AUSTRAC over the money-laundering breaches. Gambling revenue has fallen, and the casino group’s regulatory costs have mounted following the run of scandals.



Star got into more hot water this year following an investigation by this publication and the Australian Financial Review that raised questions about Star’s commitment to reforms to help it regain its casino licence, as its top executives try to make the casino operator financially viable under new regulatory restraints in NSW and Queensland. A leaked recording of Star Entertainment Group’s most senior executives has captured its Sydney casino boss and Mathieson Jnr complaining of the risk and compliance measures forced on to the group. Star Entertainment chairman Soo Kim. Dominic Lorrimer “We get these fines, which I think are just disproportionate to what is happening, and … all we’re doing is existing to pay a fine,” Mathieson Jnr said. “We keep on restricting ourselves tighter and tighter. We’re coming to a pretty critical time with obviously licences and all that sort of stuff, but it should be quite obvious to everyone that unless we can breathe … every time we get up to breathe, we cop another hit.”



Mathieson Jnr was conciliatory to the regulators in his letter to fellow shareholders via the annual report in August. Related Article Casinos Star’s Sydney casino licence to stay suspended “I would like to acknowledge and thank our regulators and other key stakeholders for their ongoing engagement, guidance and collaboration throughout this period of significant transformation. Their commitment and constructive involvement have been important in supporting our ongoing remediation and progress towards returning The Star to suitability.” He later told staff the new management team is “working to change” the problems inherited from previous management. Last month NSW Independent Casino Commission chief Philip Crawford extended the suspension of Star’s licence, saying questions remained over the casino’s progress in improving its governance, leadership and culture.



“There is no doubt that The Star has come a long way in addressing the matters which led to the suspension of its casino licence in 2022,” Crawford said. “However, recent allegations regarding governance, leadership and culture at the casino are serious and are being treated as such by both the manager and the NICC. World.title: ‘I’m the boss, not an employee’: The Sydney strip club owner fighting his ban from Kings Cross
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Papadopoulos had provided the tribunal with supporting statements and affidavits from his wife, Liana Papadopoulos, his mother Cleopatra Papadopoulos and his son, Dimitrios Papadopoulos, as well as a letter from his accountant, Michael Angelopoulos.

The order prevents him from entering “any high-risk venue in the Kings Cross and Sydney CBD entertainment precincts”.

Last week, the NSW Civil and Administrative Appeals Tribunal knocked back an application from the Cyprus-born 53-year-old to review a decision of the Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority to slap him with a Long-Term Banning Order.

It took two alleged violent assaults on women working at his club, one of which involved alleged choking, another where he allegedly slapped his penis in the face of one of the women, as well as a separate alleged assault on a man who visited the club, before Papadopoulos was finally prohibited by authorities.

But Papadopoulos’ colourful legal history proved no impediment to his subsequently owning and operating two clubs, Sydney Elements and Showgirls, on the same Kings Cross stretch notorious for its history of sleaze, crime and brutality.

In 2005, his sentence served, he was the subject of bankruptcy proceedings.

On March 15, Papadopoulos was arrested and charged with seven offences which allegedly had taken place in and around the club, including the serious indictable charge of “intentionally choke a person without consent” involving a female employee of the club whom the married man appears to have been involved with .

It was Sydney Elements, which bills itself as “Sydney’s Premier Stripclub and Nightclub”, and where “VIP packages” start at $1000, where all the trouble started.

As Papadopoulos told the tribunal, through his barrister Greg James KC, a former judge, the ban prejudices his business interests and represents a restriction of his “fundamental rights”.

Such a ban presents a problem for a man who owns two Kings Cross strip clubs. His wife told this masthead he is a good man, husband and father who is innocent.

But none of it made a difference. Dr Tahlia Gordon, the Senior Tribunal member who heard the case, said she was satisfied “that if Mr Papadopoulos attended Sydney Elements or Showgirls, there is a sufficient risk that he could engage in trouble-making behaviour and cause a problem”.

It also raises questions about the safety of strip club workers in a red-light district that has been somewhat cleaned up over the past decade.

The tribunal’s decision, handed down last week, contains extraordinary detail about the apparent operation of the club and the alleged violence at least two of its employees had been subjected to.

In filing his application to reverse the ban, Papadopoulos said “the order has an immediate and substantial impact on my livelihood”.

Still, the accused nightclub owner told police they should drop the ban application. He was entitled to the presumption of innocence. He was “of good character with no prior convictions for matters of violence”, and his bail conditions did not prohibit him from going to Sydney Elements.

It is understood Papadopoulos will defend all the charges against him.

Things got even worse for Papadopoulos on March 28, when he was charged with “assault occasioning actual bodily harm” in relation to an incident at Sydney Elements on March 10.

Six days later, NSW Police informed Papadopoulos they would be applying to the Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority for the ban order on him.

Papadopoulos then allegedly grabbed Victim 1 under her armpits and pulled her away from the bar.

Cut to 2am on January 9 this year, when Papadopoulos and Victim 1 were behind the main bar at Sydney Elements. They argued, and he allegedly placed his left hand on her head, grabbed a handful of her hair, and yanked her from the chair, snapping her head back with the force of the pull.

Embarrassed, Victim 1 wanted to leave the apartment, but Papadopoulos told her if she left, he would kill her.

According to police, “Victim 1 was confused as she did not remember what had happened, and the accused stated, ‘It was probably because I put my penis in your face’.”

A short time later, police say, Victim 1 was with Papadopoulos at his nearby Potts Point residence, when he told her that “multiple staff members had been traumatised by what happened earlier at Sydney Elements”.

It was 3am and Victim 1 was “highly intoxicated and lying on the ground” when, according to police, the accused kneeled next to her, pulled his penis from his pants and “used his penis to slap the side of Victim 1’s face”.

According to police facts, on September 29, 2025, the accused and “Victim 1”, a female employee of the club, were in a private room at Sydney Elements with about 10 other staff members.

He stopped, only to go through her phone to find evidence of her cheating on him. She later took a photograph of her bruised neck.

At about 2am on March 9, Victim 1 was again at the accused’s Potts Point home, lying next to him in bed, when he straddled her and placed his hands around her neck, restricting her breathing.

Yet more alleged violence was to come.

Victim 1 tried to leave, but he grabbed her and pinned her arms behind her back, while pushing her into an office. When Victim 2 tried to intervene, Papadopoulos placed his hand around her throat and moved her away. This alleged assault was also captured on CCTV.

A short time later, another assault is alleged to have occurred when Papadopoulos dragged Victim 1 and another employee, Victim 2, to the basement of the club.

The whole thing was captured on CCTV but the accused later told police the footage was “AI-generated and a conspiracy”.

Things came to a head on March 11, at about 9.30 pm, when Victim 1 and Papadopoulos began arguing while together at Sydney Elements.

She told him she was going to quit on the spot, which allegedly made Papadopoulos angry, and he allegedly pushed her face with force, then grabbed her by the neck and pinned her against a wall, holding her there for about a minute.

He took her phone and locked it in a safe, police allege.

Later that night, he was charged with three offences including common assault, and stalk or intimidate with intent to cause fear of physical or mental harm (domestic violence). Then on March 15, he was charged with another seven offences including the “intentionally choke a person without consent” rap.

A fortnight later, Papadopoulos copped yet another charge, for the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

This charge related to an incident that occurred about 3pm on March 10, when Papadopoulos allegedly beat up a man unknown to him, dubbed Victim 3, who came into Sydney Elements.

According to police, Papadopoulos grabbed the man, whose “body language appeared passive”, shoved him into a wall, dragged and threw him onto the ground, punched and stomped on his torso, and then “kicked Victim 3 directly in the face with such force, causing Victim 3 to fall back on the ground, immediately unconscious and motionless”.

The man suffered concussion, bleeding from a large cut to his lip, bruising to his neck and soreness over his body.

Some of the charges will be heard in November. The remainder will be heard in March next year. Papadopoulos is expected to plead not guilty.

When contacted this week, Papadopoulos’ wife Liana Papadopoulos said: “I know he is innocent and he is fighting for his rights.

“I am not saying that because he’s my partner, I’m saying the truth.

“He is a very good man, good husband and good father.”

Papadopoulos did not respond to attempts to contact him.

These charges are not the 53-year-old’s first tango with the law. In 1998, Papadopoulos passed $1500 to a local cop, when he was operating a different nightclub on the Kings Cross strip.

Back then, Papadopoulos was a 25-year-old with “strong family ties and real prospects of rehabilitation”, or so said his lawyer in a submission to the NSW Court of Appeal in 2000.

Papadopoulos wanted his jail time cut; after all, his sentencing judge had said he “apparently ran a place of entertainment which was otherwise within the law”. His appeal was denied.

Once his time was served, Papadopoulos’ name popped up in the Federal Court list in 2005, as the respondent in bankruptcy proceedings brought by lawyer Victor Berger, who was struck off in 2018 for overcharging an elderly woman by $137,543.

The bankruptcy application against him was granted in September that year.

‘I’m the boss, not an employee’

The goals of the Liquor Act are to regulate the sale of liquor “in a way that is consistent with the expectations, needs and aspirations of the community”, and to “facilitate the balanced development, in the public interest, of the liquor industry”.

The legislation is supposed to minimise harm associated with the misuse and abuse of liquor and ensure that the sale, supply and consumption of liquor contributes to the amenity of community life, as opposed to detracting from it.

Under the act, a Long-Term Banning Order can be imposed if a person has been charged with, or found guilty of a serious, violent indictable offence, and is also the licensee or manager of the premises, or is either working on the premises as an employee, or in a volunteer capacity.

Papadopoulos did not dispute he had been charged with serious indictable offences, namely, two counts of intentionally choke a person without consent, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and stalk or intimidate intending to cause fear of physical or mental harm.

But through his barrister Greg James KC, Papadopoulos submitted that it would be “unjust” to impose an LTBO on someone who may ultimately be found not guilty, and that if the tribunal could not be satisfied the evidence supported the charges, it should not uphold the ban.

But the most creative argument put by Papadopoulos’ barrister was that the ban should not apply because his client was not employed by Sydney Elements.

He was the boss.

James told the tribunal that “at the time of the alleged serious indictable offence, Mr Papadopoulos was at Sydney Elements as the sole director, secretary and shareholder of MLP Investments (NSW) Pty Ltd and Element MP Pty Ltd, the owner of the premises”.

Papadopoulos’s company interests have owned the Potts Point venue since 2013, when it last traded for $4.55 million.

The tribunal heard he has since invested $17 million in Sydney Elements.

It has clearly been a lucrative business. Papadopoulos also owns a Sutherland Shire property with a swimming pool that fronts a private-title beach. A Sylvania property is also registered to his name, and Papadopoulos’ second company, MGM Ventures, owns an inner-west property that is the registered home of his mother.

But the “mere fact” that he was owner and director of Sydney Elements didn’t mean Papadopoulos was an employee, working there or performing services of any kind.

His barrister argued that his client had “overall responsibility for the day-to-day operations of Sydney Elements”, which included tasks like managing staff and overseeing staff rosters.

He works full-time and “needs to be on call to deal with issues at the venues, as and when they arise”.

Furthermore, he did not have a responsible service of alcohol certificate, and as such, was not qualified to serve alcohol. He doesn’t receive a wage.

The iconic Coke sign in Kings Cross. Flavio Brancaleone

Papadopoulos’ “fundamental rights”

The respondents, the NSW Police and the Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority, counter-argued that Papadopoulos was, for the purposes of the act, a volunteer.

Further, they told the tribunal “that it would be an unusual lacuna in the Liquor Act if someone in the position of Mr Papadopoulos, who on his own evidence asserts day-to-day control over a high-risk venue, was found to be outside of reach of [the act] because he was not the licensee or manager, was not a volunteer, or did not have a written contract of employment”.

The tribunal rejected Papadopoulos’ narrative. Dr Gordon found that “Mr Papadopoulos plays an essential role in managing two high-risk venues in the Kings Cross precinct”.

If he was not technically a worker at the venue, then he was a volunteer.

Papadopoulos argued that his absence from Sydney Elements “has caused significant prejudice” to the operation of the business, and was “untenable because of the issues arising at the premises”, such as “staff conflicts and stock controls”.

The ban would also harm his plans to develop the venue into a five-storey hotel.

Most importantly, the ban restricted his “fundamental rights”.

He was so desperate to have it lifted that he even proposed a compromise: that he could be at Sydney Elements only between 11am and 11pm.

The tribunal rejected it all, and upheld the ban. Dr Gordon said that it “sends a clear message” to “troublemakers”.

A former manager of the now defunct but once popular nightspot Sapphire Lounge, who did not want to be named, said Papadopoulos was “the worst fucking operator in the Cross”.

The former club manager said the LTBO would be pretty useless, seeing as Papadopoulos’ other club, Showgirls, is across the road.

“So he can just stand there, and walk past and do what he wants.”

There is some consolation for Papadopoulos: the ban applies for only 12 months.

And the clock started ticking down on July 8 this year, when it was issued.

As of July 7 next year, depending on the outcome of his criminal proceedings, Papadopoulos will be at liberty to go wherever he likes on the King Cross strip, including into his own clubs.

World.title: ASIC won’t sue Super Retail board over scandal that led to CEO’s sacking, says company
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessCompaniesRetail ASIC won’t sue Super Retail board over scandal that led to CEO’s sacking, says company Colin Kruger October 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Rebel Sport owner Super Retail Group says the corporate regulator does not plan to take any further action over the alleged illicit executive relationship that will see its former chief executive, Anthony Heraghty, face court this week. But the group behind well-known brands also including Supercheap Auto, MacPac and BCF, says it will face further legal bills funding his defence against the legal action by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. Former Super Retail group CEO Anthony Heraghty. Dominic Lorrimer “Following the conclusion of its investigation, ASIC has confirmed that it is not taking enforcement action against Super Retail Group, its related entities, or any current or former director, officer, employee, agent or representative of Super Retail Group, other than Mr Heraghty,” a spokesman said. ASIC declined to comment.



Super Retail sacked Heraghty in September last year and stripped him of multimillion-dollar bonuses after he admitted providing misleading information to fellow board members about his alleged relationship with HR boss Jane Kelly. Jane Kelly. “In light of this new information, the board has concluded Mr Heraghty’s prior disclosures were not satisfactory,” the company told the ASX in the statement announcing his sacking last year. ASIC instigated an investigation into Super Retail after Heraghty’s sacking and sued him last month for allegedly breaching his directors’ duties and providing misleading information to the board and financial market about his alleged relationship with Kelly. Super Retail had already spent more than $40 million in a bitter legal battle with its two former top lawyers, who claimed they were bullied and harassed over a matter centred on Heraghty’s alleged relationship.



The confirmation is timely for Super Retail’s current board, which faces shareholders on Thursday morning. ASIC’s case against Heraghty goes before the Federal Court as the meeting commences. The case is expected to raise fresh questions at the AGM about Heraghty, the board’s response, and just how much it will have to pay to defend the former CEO in this legal battle with ASIC. The retailer will have to fund his legal defence on the basis that he was a director of the group at the time the alleged conduct is said to have occurred. “As you would expect of a listed entity, Mr Heraghty is the beneficiary of a deed of indemnity, insurance and access,” the Super Retail spokesman said. ASIC chair Sarah Court says the case is not about personal relationships but “whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders”. AAP The potential issue for Heraghty is that this indemnity drops if he is found in contravention of the law, and Super Retail can force him to repay these legal expenses.



“Under this deed, Mr Heraghty will be required to repay any costs within 90 days if it is found and determined that he was not entitled to be indemnified,” the spokesman said. In its legal action, ASIC alleges Heraghty – who was recently hired by appliance group Winnings for an expected billion-dollar float on the ASX – failed to disclose and manage conflicts of interest arising from the alleged undisclosed relationship. Related Article Retail Corporate cop makes explosive claims about former Super Retail boss’ ‘intimate’ relationship ASIC alleges Heraghty continued to supervise Kelly and took part in decisions affecting her employment, remuneration, incentives, rewards and redundancy package. He also allegedly participated in board and committee discussions of complaints and anticipated legal proceedings concerning the alleged relationship.



“This case is not about private relationships, but whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders,” ASIC chair Sarah Court said. Heraghty faces a potential ban from managing companies if found in contravention of the law, and fines for breaches of the Corporations Act that can attract a penalty of up to $1.56 million per breach. Heraghty was approached for comment via his new employer, Winnings. He will have the opportunity to file a defence to ASIC’s allegations in due course. World.title: Enrolments closed, advance voting begins for 2026 Election
World.content:
Enrolments have closed and voting in the general election begins today, with party leaders among those casting their ballot on day one.

Candidates were calling for last-minute enrolments on Sunday, while the Electoral Commission acknowledged the Government's changes preventing enrolment right up until voting day would impact numbers.

As of Friday - with two days remaining to enrol - 92.4 percent of those eligible had done so. In the 2023 election 94.7 percent of eligible voters enrolled.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the Government was to blame if the 2023 enrolment figure was not reached.

"If we do not have at least enrolment equivalent to what we had at the last election, that will be an indictment on this Government, who have deliberately tried to disenfranchise people, particularly younger New Zealanders, who are less likely to vote for them," he said.

The Greens' co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the Government knew that stopping people from enrolling to vote in the two weeks leading up to election day would disproportionately affect young people, renters, Māori, Pasifika, and migrant communities.

"These are structural barriers and it doesn't have to be this way. No politician and no government should ever make it harder for anybody to engage in our democracy."

However, National leader Christopher Luxon and ACT leader David Seymour disagreed, saying enrolling was simple.

"You've seen the Electoral Commission bombard everybody with advertising. I think they've had almost a doubling of advertising around voter turnout and voter enrolment. It's pretty simple and easy to do," Luxon said.

Seymour added it was people's duty to enrol.

"If you take all the benefits of a free and democratic society, but you're not prepared to perform a task simpler than ordering a pizza on Uber Eats to be part of that society, I think that is dropkick behaviour," he said.

Seymour said low enrolment rates would be an indictment on people who choose not to enrol, not the Government, which had simply set a basic expectation.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407351970112

ACT and Labour respond to National's 100-day plan

National on Sunday released its 100-day plan, setting out the first actions it would take if re-elected.

As a prospective coalition partner, Seymour said he would not get into pre-negotiations and detail what ACT would and would not agree to.

"There are some things that will go ahead, others that won't. Just like the last three years," he said.

"What's clear is that we can work constructively together, and having the ACT Party there to curb some of the National Party's worst instincts, while also promoting positive, practical solutions to New Zealanders' problems, is a good thing."

Meanwhile, Hipkins dismissed the plan as a reheat of previous announcements.

Talk of boosting bipartisanship during leaders' debates culminated in a handshake between Hipkins and Luxon at one point, with the pair agreeing to sit down together within the first 100 days of the next term and hash out what big things they could work together on.

RNZ asked Hipkins whether there was any part of National's 100-day plan he could get on board with.

He said National had shown no interest in collaborating on things that matter.

"They've shunned every overture from the Opposition in the last three years to work constructively together on big issues. I think that's unlikely to change if they continue to be the Government."

Calvin Samuel/RNZ

Hipkins doubts Opportunity's Future Generations Commissioner

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong on Sunday announced her party would establish a Future Generations Commissioner to hold governments to account for the long-term impacts of their policies if elected.

Wong said it would stop short-term thinking and guide development of long-term national goals.

Hipkins said he would be open to having a conversation about it, but any commission must be more than "just talk".

He was sceptical of those sorts of organisations - pointing to the Productivity Commission and Families Commission - saying they came up with good ideas, but those could not go anywhere without political support.

"We have a history of setting up sort of think tanks, advocacy groups that don't really affect positive, meaningful change.
